passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 249–250
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

Not much is known about the past of St. Moses the Black before his repentance. He was most probably one of the Barbarian tribes. His life was so evil that it was said that there was no sin he did not commit. He was born between the years of 330 and 340 AD. It seems that he was a slave of a head of a tribe that worshipped the sun, but because of his extreme evil nature, his master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become the head of an evil gang.

Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ:

Even though an extreme evil-doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking from it to proclaim itself to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened to meet with St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells) coming out of his cell and heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: “What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “I heard that you are a good servant of God. Therefore, I escaped and came to you to let God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins and my great evils.”

St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he has been. Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to contemplate.

For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a loud voice, he confessed all his evil crimes again, with such contrition of heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 252–253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Ordained as a Priest

Ordained as a Priest:

Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: “Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said to him: “There you became all-white Moses.” He responded by saying with humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.”

His Virtues:

He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, but it happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.

Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticism, he was granted by God to perform miracles and signs.

A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from going. When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the wilderness.

Moses stood in the church and confessed publicly about all his sins and evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became allwhite. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would leave it, all evil will come back to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your feet.”

His Strife:

St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macarius to find for him a secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept counseling him to stand fast until the devil would get tired of him. He gave him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it.” Father. Abba Isidore took him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 251–252
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Strife

There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly angels, about whom the saint said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and returned to his cell.

Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks at night, take their water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to move, until some brethren happened to come to the well, and they carried him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he regained his ability to move.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and carried them to the church. When the thieves realized that he was Moses, who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.

Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. Abba Isidore told him that, to keep him from thinking that by his ascetic efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual repentance, God would fight on our behalf.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Virtues

When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a week. During that week, some guests came to visit Fr. Moses. He prepared food for them to eat. On seeing smoke rising from his cell, the brethren said to one another: “Look, Moses has broken his fast and is preparing food for himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they said to him: “Father Moses! You have disregarded the commandment of men, but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”

His Martyrdom:

Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” He told them: “There, they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred monks. Then, he hastened to come down and ran forward to receive his crown of martyrdom.

So, Abba Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, when he was seventy-five years old (or eighty-five). He earned three crowns: the 1st for love and intense asceticism, the 2nd for monasticism and priesthood, and the 3rd for martyrdom. He was counted the first martyr in the Scetis, and he had so many great teachings. His body was kept along with that of his spiritual guide Abba Isidore in one tube at the Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 254–255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6)” • Then, the brother asked: “If a man beat his servant for something wrong he did, what should the servant say?” The saint answered: “If he was a good servant, he would possibly say: ‘Have mercy on me, for I made a mistake.’ Thus, he would blame himself and draw the mercy of his master.” • In general, a man should never condemn his neighbor. When in the Old, the hand of God came heavy on the firstborn of the Egyptians, there was no house without a dead son in it. For us, it meant that we should concentrate on our sins and not worry about those of our neighbors, for it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor.

To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad about his neighbor, because it would make you fall in condemnation. Do not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This would bring you peace.

[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria- Diocese of Los Angeles] [Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of OrthodoxWiki]

[Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of Wikipedia]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, p. 258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands

If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take the monk to the nearest location of the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.

Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not having a steady residence, teaching, preaching, and converting multitudes to Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in the year 372 AD.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

[Baring-Gould: February 7]

Notes: [2] These tribes were known by the name ‘Saracens’… It is worth mentioning that the name ‘Saracens’ was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, pp. 255–256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.

Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to spend the night at her place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.

[The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, pp. 257–258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — The Tribes of Saracens

The Tribes of Saracens:

The Arabian tribes populating the area of Rhinoclura in-between the eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes joined forces together and formed one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.

Choosing Moses as a Bishop:

Those Christian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be their bishop. Then, when Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those united tribes.

Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands:

On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then, St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Confessor, p. 257
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE CONFESSOR

This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, at the start of the heresy of Novatian. The rest of the confessors were: Fr. Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the system and wrote another message to Cyprian.

After spending about a year in prison (eleven months and few days), St. Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views as unorthodox.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948]

[Baring-Gould: November 25]

Notes: [1] ‘Novatian’ was a Roman bishop and theologian of the 3rd century who took a strict position on readmission of apostates during the persecutions at the time…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, p. 255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went deep in the wilderness and lived for thirty-five years in a spot having olive and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended the wild beasts.

His Multiple Falls and Repentances:

Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the devil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, pp. 240–241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — The Bitterness of Anguish

St. Moises (Moses) was one of the prominent fathers and saints of the church in the 8th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.

St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Scetis, where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox faith. He used to spend most of his time in worship, that it was said that he did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

The Bitterness of Anguish:

During his bishopric, the Umayyad rulers of Egypt subjected the Copts to extremely severe persecutions, and great anguish dwelt upon the church. The bishops returned to their monasteries to concentrate on prayers and fasts, imploring God to lift that anguish. However, St. Moises remained among his people to encourage them and to keep them holding fast to their faith against the snatching wolves. St. Moises also got the grace to perform miracles and signs, healing sicknesses, as well as the grace of prophecy.

Due to these intolerable persecutions at the time, the number of Copts who converted to Islam reached 24,000 persons. When some archons came to seek from St. Moises to pray to the Lord to lift the anguish from His people, he told them: “My children, be assured that the governor who is persecuting you will perish within this month,” and this was what did happen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 253–254
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

Of his Sayings:

• To a brother in the Scetis who sought from him a word of encouragement, he said: “Go and sit in your cell, it will teach you everything.” • The man who flees from the world is like ripe grapes, but he who dwells among the distractions of men is like sour grapes. • If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I promise you that the Barbarians would never come here, but if we do not, this place will soon become desolate. • According to Fr. Poemen, Fr. Moses was once asked: “How can a man become like dead to his neighbor?” The older saint said to him: “Unless a man keeps in his heart that he has been three days in the grave, he will not be strong enough to do that.” • It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbor, and he should not condemn him in anything. • It is good for a man to die to every work which is evil before he departs from the body, so as not to offend anyone. • Unless a man feels in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not listen to him. A brother asked him about the meaning of that, and the saint said: “Whoever focuses on his sins, would never see those of his neighbor.” • Unless your prayers conform to your behavior, your struggle would not be of any benefit. When the saint was asked to explain, he said: “We should apply what we pray about, for when man forsakes his own will, he reconciles with God and God will listen to his prayers.” • A brother asked him: “What would help the man in his every endeavor?” He answered him: “God is the One who helps, for it is so written: "God is our refuge and strength. A very present help in trouble" (Psalm 46:1).” • When the brother added: “What then is the benefit of fasting or spending sleepless nights, father?” The saint answered: “These practices make the soul meek and humble, for it is written: "Look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins" (Psalm 25:18). So, once the soul reaps the fruits of these practices, God would have compassion on her.” • Then, the brother asked: “What will man do with every temptation he encounters or every evil thought coming to him?” The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?"

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Libyan, p. 256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE LIBYAN, ST.

This saint was from Libya. He was so humble and compassionate all the time that God granted him the grace to perform the miracles of healing the sick. He once said: “When I was young, I lived in a monastery. There, it happened that eight monks dug a well, and seventy others built a wall around it, in the hope that they would get water from it. They dug it down to the depth of about twenty yards, but no water was found. They were very much grieved and intended to fill it up with dirt. However, by noontime, when Abba Pieour came over suddenly to the location of the well and was informed about what they were doing, he rebuked them saying: ‘Why did you despair, O you of little faith?’ Then, he went down to the bottom of the well, and he prayed there. Afterward, he pushed an iron rod in the well bottom three times, saying: ‘O God of the saints, I pray, do not waste the effort of these men, but send them plenty of water.’ In a short while, the water erupted from the well and wetted everyone around.

After praying a thanksgiving prayer, Abba Pieour intended to go in his way. They tried to make him have a meal with them, but he said: ‘I have accomplished what I came here to do, I did not come here to eat.’”

This was a good lesson for the brethren about faith and the trust in God.

[The Paradise of the Saints, p. 69]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Guirgis El-Mozaĥem, pp. 213–214
passages.text:
Saint: GUIRGIS EL-MOZAĤEM (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

The setting of the Fatimid State in Egypt (909-1171 AD), had unique importance, as the Fatimid turned Egypt from a colony into an independent state, and the Caliph El-Muåzz Li-Din Allah (953-975 AD) was a role model in dealing with all Egyptians with justice, without discrimination between a Christian and a Muslim. Still, under the Caliph El-Aziz Bi-Allah (975-996 AD), a wave of anger prevailed on the Muslim mobs, when they saw how some of the Copts reached the position of a minister and gained the favor and trust of the Caliph.

The most serious of those incidents was what happened in the region of Talkha in the governorate of Daqahlyia, near the end of the 10th century AD, because of a person named El-Mozaĥem. El-Mozaĥem was the son of a Christian widow called Mariam and a Muslim father by the name of Gomoåa el-Ăatawy, who married his wife by force against the will of her parents who were from a village called Daroteen in the province of Talkha. El-Mozaĥem was the third son among six brothers and one sister. He spent his first twelve years on his father's religion, but noticing how his mother used to go to church every Sunday, he felt a great urge to follow her to see what was going on in the church. On her return from the church, he used to ask her to give him a piece of the Corban she usually would bring back with her, which he greatly savored. He continued to follow his mother every Sunday, and eventually, he decided to become a Christian. On the occasion of the feast of the Virgin St. Mary, he headed to Abba Zacharias, the bishop of Damietta, and asked him to baptize him. However, the church priests were afraid of the consequences. So, he asked them a favor, not to drain the Holy Water from the font of baptism, and after the departure of the entire congregation from the church, he took off his clothes and plunged in the water three times in the name of the Holy Trinity. Afterward, he felt as being a Christian, and he was just eighteen years of age at the time. Later on, he got married to a girl named Siola. She was the daughter of hegomen Abanob of the church of Busat el-Nasara in the province of Talkha.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — Imprisoned along with the Pope

Imprisoned along with the Pope:

The last of the Umayyad caliphs Marwan ibn Muĥammad (Marwan II: 744-750 AD), arrested the 46th Pope of Alexandria, St. Khael I (743-767 AD). Bishop Moises stayed in the company of the pope, and he longed to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When the soldiers brought them to the tent of Marwan, they forced St. Moises on his knees, raised his feet, and beat him with bronze clubs on his sides and neck. His tormentors were seeking from him a bribe to set him free. The saint did not utter a single word, for he did not understand their Arabic language. When Marwan gave the order to cut the head of Pope Khael I, and the swordsman led him to the place of execution, St. Moises ran after him, despite the attempts of the swordsman to keep him away. An angry soldier intended to kill him if it was not for some officials who did not let him do it. Then, he was cast in prison along with Pope Khael I, and their feet were placed in chains, among many others. However, St. Moises prophesied that they would eventually come out safe from that prison, which was realized when Marwan was defeated by the Abbasids dynasty.

His Prophesy concerning the Umayyad Caliphate:

During the revolt of the Coptic Bashmurians (Coptic rebels) due to the intolerable Umayyad persecution, St. Moises disciple asked him a question concerning when that calamity would come to an end, the saint prophesied: “God will not forsake His church to the end, but He will save her, and this caliphate (of Umayyad) will vanish and be replaced by some other.” This prophecy was realized in 750 AD when the Umayyad dynasty was replaced by the Abbasids.

records.question: Who was St. Mary the Egyptian?
records.answer:
St. Mary the Egyptian was a woman who lived in the 4th and 5th centuries AD. She was originally from Alexandria, Egypt. From the age of 12, she was defiled by lust and evil thoughts and lived a life of carnal pleasures for 17 years after the death of her parents, without financial need but to fulfill her desires. She traveled to Jerusalem to attend the feast of the Holy Cross, where she was mysteriously prevented from entering the Church of the Resurrection due to her unworthiness. In deep shame, she prayed to the Virgin Mary for intercession and pledged to abandon her sinful life.

Following this, she crossed the Jordan River and lived in the wilderness near the place where the Lord Christ fasted for 40 days. There, she spent 45 years in harsh asceticism, battling severe hunger, thirst, and carnal temptations, sustained by God. She was aided by the intercession of the Virgin Mary and lived a life of repentance and prayer. She was encountered by Fr. Zosimus, a priest who brought her Holy Communion in her final years. She died around the year 421 AD, and her life became a great motivator for spiritual striving. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on the 16th of Baramouda every year [1][2][3][4][9][14].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, pp. 146–147
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — His Encounter with Mary the Egyptian

St. Mary, the Egyptian lived in the 4th and 5th centuries AD, and her biography was told by a priest called Zosimus, who lived in one of the monasteries in Palestine for 53 years. When the evil thoughts of loftiness started to creep into his mind, God sent him one of the monks who led him to a monastery close to the Jordan River, where he was told that he should spend the rest of his life. The monks of that monastery were elderly hermits who practiced harsh asceticism in all their lives. The monastery was close to the wilderness where the Lord Christ spent His 40-days fasting. It was the habit of those monks there to spend these 40 days in the desert outside the monastery to return only on the day of Palm Sunday. These monks used to have the Holy Communion before they would go on the first Sunday of the Great Lent. Then they would proceed to the wilderness. Fr. Zosimus followed the rest of the monastery’s hermits in their wilderness outing.

His Encounter with Mary the Egyptian:

It happened one year, on his way back to the monastery just before the end of Lent, Fr. Zosimus saw from afar a ghost, whom he first thought to be a demon and made the sign of the Cross on him. Then, he realized that it was a human being. The elderly Zosimus hastened behind him, and when the ghost kept running away, he cried out to him to stop running. The spirit stopped and dived into a pit in the sand, calling Zosimus by his name and saying to him, “I am a woman. If you want to help a sinner, please leave for me your robe to cover my nakedness.” Amazed at how she called him by his name, he left his robe for her. She covered herself with it and asked him, being a priest, to bless her. Equally amazed at her knowledge that he was a priest, he asked her to bless him too and to pray for him. Then, he asked her in the Name of the Lord Christ, to tell him about her identity, why she came to this place, how she survived living in such a desolate and horrible wilderness, how long did she dwell there, and how did she manage to endure all that?

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, pp. 147–148
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — The Saint Tells Her Story

The Saint Tells Her Story:

She started her confession and asked him not to be shocked by her horrible sins, and requested from him to keep praying for her while listening to her. Then she began to tell him her story: “I am an Egyptian woman from Alexandria. Since I was 12 years of age, my mind started to get defiled with lust and evil thoughts, through the impact of the evil which prevailed at that time. What kept me from committing the actual sin, then, was my fear and respect for my father. Yet, once both my father and my mother died, I found myself free to do whatever I wanted. So, I got down to the abyss of the defiled physical sins and delivered myself to the carnal pleasures all through the following 17 years. That was not out of any financial needs, but it was to fulfill my evil desires.

Then, one day in the summer, I saw a gathering of Egyptians and Libyans in the sea-port, on their way to sail to Jerusalem to attend the feast of the Holy Cross. So, I planned to join them, although I did not have the money for the fare. However, I paid for my trip by fulfilling my pleasures with the other travelers.” In deep shame, she looked up at Fr. ‘Zosimus’ and said: “Do you see Father, how shrewd and guilty I was. Woe to my disgrace. The goal of my travel to that Holy City, above all, was to lead the souls to perdition.

Once we reached Jerusalem, I committed many other evil things in the Holy City. When the feast of the Holy Cross came, the multitudes set forth to the Church of the Resurrection. And when it was my turn to enter into the Church amid the dense crowd, it happened that my feet were, as though, nailed to the ground. I could not move an inch. A hidden power kept me from entering into the church despite my repeated trials to do so.

Then, I realized that I was the only person who was denied the entry into the church among that entire great crowd who were able to get in and out without any hindrance. Right away, I retreated to a quiet corner near the gate, and I perceived that what was keeping me from entering into the church was my unworthiness due to my unspeakable corruptions. So, I exploded in a bitter fit of crying. After a little while, I looked up, and I saw the portrait of the Virgin St. Mary right above my head. And in big shame, I cried out: ‘O Holy Virgin! I perceive the extent of my filth and unworthiness to enter into the house of God. With my dirty soul, I do not even dare to look up at your real portrait. Oh, my shame, and my lowliness before you.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, pp. 148–149
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — The Saint Tells Her Story

With my dirty soul, I do not even dare to look up at your real portrait. Oh, my shame, and my lowliness before you.’

I asked out of my whole heart the intercession of the Virgin Mary on my behalf; I asked her to allow me to enter the church to honor the Holy Cross. I pledged not to resume my evil life any longer and sought her guidance in helping me to bid farewell to the world and its whole pleasures. Feeling then, that my request was well-received, I set forth to take my place among the incoming multitudes and found out that I could enter into the church without hindrance. Extremely terrified, I worshipped down to the ground, shed dense tears at the Holy Cross, and kept praying, not aware of the passing of time, until mid-noon, seeking God’s help, with the intercession of the Virgin St. Mary, to guide me in what I was supposed to do. Here, I heard a voice saying to me: ‘Cross over the Jordan; for there you will find a place for your Salvation.’ I spent that night near the church, and in the morning, I went in my way. Then, I met a man who gave me three silver coins, saying, ‘Take what God has given you.’ I purchased three loaves of bread and asked the baker about the way to the Jordan River. Crossing through the city gate, I felt completely transformed. Then, I reached a church by the name of St. John the Baptist near the River. There, I kept crying, washed my face with the water of the holy River, entered the church, confessed my sins, and got the Holy Sacraments. Then, I crossed the River, and, seeking the intercession of the Virgin St. Mary, I continued walking in the barren desert until I came to this location we are on, where I spent the last 45 years sustained by God.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, p. 150
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — Her Departure

Her Departure:

In the following year, and in the appointed time, the priest set forth to the designated place, where he found the saint worshipping to the ground, with her face directed toward the East, and her hands motionless. Perceiving that she was already dead, he worshipped beside her, cried, and prayed on her the funeral prayers. Up to this moment, he realized that he did not even come to know her name; but when he got close to her, he found a written message saying, “Father Zosimus! Bury here the body of the miserable Mary and leave to the dust this sinful body. Pray on my behalf.”

Fr. Zosimus realized that she died the year before after she had the Holy Sacraments he brought for her. It is believed that she reposed in the year 421 AD. Returning to his monastery, Fr. Zosimus kept saying to himself: “Indeed, the tax-collectors, the sinners and the adulterers will precede us to the Kingdom of Heaven.” St. ‘Mary’s life was a big motivator for so many to expand their spiritual strive. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on the 16th of Baramouda every year.

[Fragrant Bouquets from the Biographies of the Righteous and Saints, pp. 249-253]

[The Vita of St. Mary of Egypt written by St. Sophronius, the patriarch of Jerusalem (634–638 AD)]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Virgin Theotokos., p. 156
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE VIRGIN THEOTOKOS.

While they were going in their way, some Jews came and tried to prevent them from burying her. When one of them stretched his hands to hold the coffin, his arms separated from his body and remained hanging until he believed and showed remorse on his evil deed. By the supplications of the saintly disciples, his arms were attached back to his body.

It happened that Thomas the Apostle was not present at the time the Virgin St. Mary reposed. However, in his way back to Jerusalem, he saw her shrouded body being carried by the angels to be taken up to heaven; and he was advised by one of the angels to hasten and kiss her pure body, which he did. When he arrived to join the disciples, and they told him about her departure, he said to them, “I shall not believe unless I see her body, for you already know how I doubted the resurrection of the Lord Christ.” They took him to her tomb and were shocked and surprised to see it empty. However, Thomas, the Apostle, told them how he saw her pure body with the angels carrying it up to heaven. The Holy Spirit told them that God did not intend for her pure body to remain on earth, and the Lord Christ promised his pure disciples to let them see her in the flesh again, and they waited for this true promise until the 16th of the month of Mesra when it was fulfilled. She lived on earth 60 years: she spent 12 years in the Temple, 30 years in the house of the righteous Joseph the Carpenter, and 14 years in the house of St. John the Evangelist, according to the commandment of the Lord, who said to her: “Woman! Behold your son,” and to John: “Behold! Your mother” (John 19:26-27). The first church, which was built in the name of the Virgin St. Mary, was in the city of Philippi, in Greece. That happened after the preaching of St. Paul and St. Barnabas to the Gentiles in that city, and when many of them believed, they built that church.

The Virgin St. Mary provided twice special blessings to the Land of Egypt. The first time when she fled to Egypt with the infant Jesus and St. Joseph the Carpenter, running away from king Herod who intended to kill the infant. the second time when she appeared in spiritual ways, inside and outside the domes of the church consecrated in her name in the area of El- Zeitoun, in the suburbs of Cairo on the 2nd of April 1968 (24 Baramhat 1684 AM). Her appearances continued for many consecutive nights.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, p. 157
passages.text:
Saint: MARY (The martyr)

This saint was born in Atrib. Later on, she got married to a good man called Theodore and gave birth to a son, whom they called Sergius. When her son went to the governor Kyriacos and confessed his Christianity, the governor tortured him, brought the statue of an idol, and ordered him to worship it. The young man, instead, kicked the statue and it fell down shattering into pieces. Before such a scene, the governor Kyriacos instantly believed in Christianity, saying, “A god, who cannot save himself, how could he save others?” The minister Ohius then came forward and took over torturing Serguis with fire and other means. When Serguis’ mother and sister arrived at the torturing spot, they kept weeping for seeing him in that manner. However, that minister ended up having Serguis’ head cut off by the sword.

His mother, Mary, his father, and his sister then came forward and confessed the name of the Lord Christ, and had their heads cut off by the sword too. They all received the crowns of martyrdom on the 13th of Amshir.

[Female Martyrs of Christianity, p. 91]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Israelite, pp. 150–151
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE ISRAELITE (The martyr)

During the early life of St. Mary, the Israelite, she did not know the Lord Christ, and she led a sinful life. When she wanted to repent and to return to the righteous life, the Lord sent to her a saintly man who preached her and revealed to her the way of salvation through believing in the Lord Christ. He told her that the soul would have to give an answer for all her deeds on the Day of Resurrection. After death and departure from this world, everyone will be rewarded according to his deeds. The man explained to her the fearful punishments for the evildoers. She asked him: "What are the proofs to what you have said to me since the ‘Torah’ that God gave to ‘Moses the Prophet’

and also my Fathers did not mention that? So, confirm to me the truth of what you just have said with Biblical and logical proofs."

After he explained and confirmed to her all these concepts, she became convinced in her heart and mind. Then, she asked him: "If I repent for my evil deeds, would God accept me?" He replied: "If you believed that Christ had come to the world for the Salvation of the human race, and if you walked in the way of repentance, God would accept you.” So, Mary believed and repented. When the governor of the region knew about her, he brought her before him. Then, when she insisted on her Christianity, he ordered her beheaded by the sword, and she received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 7 Baramhat]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Armenian, p. 146
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE ARMENIAN (The martyr) — A Brave Captive gets martyred

A Brave Captive gets martyred:

This St. Mary was a captive of a Muslim man, one of the soldiers of the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt Al-Zahir Rukn al-Din Baibars (1260-1277 AD). Her master tried to persuade her to deny her faith in the Lord Christ. But, she refused to go along and proclaimed that she was a true Christian. The man viciously tortured her in his house while she held fast to her faith. When the man got tired of tormenting her without any results, he finally reported her to the Sultan using falsehood, saying, “I have a Muslim maidservant who claims to be a Christian.” The Sultan brought her before him and asked her to declare her Islam, which she refrained to do and persisted on confessing her Christian faith. The Sultan ordered his men to burn her alive. They dug a large pit at the gate of Zoweila in Cairo, where a great multitude came to watch. Then, they brought Mary to the edge of the fiery pit to scare her up and force her to change her mind. However, the saint bravely shouted: “It is great for me, O Sultan, to deliver my soul into the hands of my Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ.” Then, she quickly jumped into fire, where she received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 27 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, pp. 149–150
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — Fr. Zosimus Blesses Her

Fr. Zosimus Blesses Her:

At the end of her talk, she bowed before Fr. Zosimus, the priest to bless her, and he did. Then, she implored him not to tell anyone about her life, asked him to come to visit her in the following year on the Covenant Thursday, bringing with him the Holy Communion. She promised to be waiting for him at the Riverbank.

Getting the Holy Communion:

In the following year, when the monks went out during the Great Lent, as they used to do every year, Fr. Zosimus was ill with high fever. However, after the Holy Liturgy on the Covenant Thursday, he carried the glorified Body and Blood of the Lord Christ and took with him as well some beans and dates, then went to see the saint and waited for her to come at the bank of the river as she promised. After a long wait, he saw her on the other side of the river coming toward him. She made the sign of the Cross on the water, and then she crossed the river walking on the water. Seeing that miracle, the priest Zosimus attempted to bow before her. She cried out loudly, “O Father priest, what are you doing? Did you forget that you are carrying the Holy Sacraments?” She then approached, worshipped with reverence, took the Holy Sacraments, then raised her hands toward heaven, crying out: “Lord, let your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen Your Salvation.” (Luke 2:29-30) She asked him to come to her in the following year, in the same place, to pray for her. She made the sign of the Cross on the river, crossed it back walking on the water, and disappeared from his sight.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1084 “What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?”, pp. 236–237
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1084. What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?

In addition to the monthly commemoration of the Virgin Mary on the 21st of every Coptic month, we celebrate the following feasts:

a. The annunciation of her birth (7th Mesore / 13th August). On this feast we celebrate the conception of St. Mary, the living ark of the covenant, the dwelling of the Most High, and the second heaven.

b. Her birthday (1st Pashons / 9th May). Copts usually commemorate the day a saint passed from this world; their martyrdom or departure to paradise — but they insist on honoring St. Mary on her the day of her birth as a joyful day.

c. Her entry into the temple (3rd Kiahk / 12th December). We learn from the tradition of the Church that St. Mary’s life was consecrated to God in fulfillment of her mother’s vow, for she had vowed to consecrate her firstborn — whether a son or a daughter — to serve the Lord all the days of his or her life.

d. Her departure (21st Tobe / 29th January).

e. The revealing of the assumption of her body (16th Mesore / 22nd August). This feast is preceded by the fifteen-day fast of St. Mary.

f. The consecration of the first church in her name at Philippi (21st Paone / 28th June). This feast also coincides with the commemoration of the Virgin’s miracle of melting iron in the city of Bartus.

g. The apparition of the Virgin Mary above her church in Zeitoun (24th Paremhotep / 2nd April). This apparition is considered unique among the whole history of Marian apparitions. It began on 2nd April 1968 and was repeated on most days for hours at a time and for many months. These apparitions appeared above the domes of the Church of St. Mary and were seen by several hundred thousand people, of all ages and positions, Christians and Muslims. Every night, the people would gather around the church, pray, and praise God, waiting to see the dazzling spectacle of St. Mary standing above one of the domes. She was seen kneeling before the cross, or at other times, carrying the baby Jesus. These apparitions were accompanied by the apparition of birds in the form of doves. Among the fruits of these apparitions were the repentance of many and the occurrence of countless miracles.

Notes: [624] Jerome Palmer, Our Lady Returns to Egypt (Culligan Publications, 1969): p. 1.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Virgin Theotokos., pp. 155–156
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE VIRGIN THEOTOKOS.

This saintly virgin was born in the city of Nazareth, where her parents lived. Her father Joachim was carrying sorrowful heart because he was barren. Her mother Ĥenna was very grieved too, and she vowed to God with a contrite heart, saying, “If you give me a fruit, I shall give her back to Your Holy Temple.” When the fullness of time arrived according to the Divine Plan, the angel of the Lord came down and announced the good news to the elder Joachim, who, in turn, told his wife Ĥenna about what he saw and heard. They both rejoiced and gave thanks to God. Then, Ĥenna conceived from Joachim and gave birth to a saintly girl, and they called her Mary.

When Mary reached three years of age, her mother brought her forth to the Temple. There, she spent 12 years, during which she was fed by the hands of angels. When her parents passed away, the temple priests decided to betroth her to a good man to keep her and take care of her because it was not proper to keep her in the Temple after reaching that age. Therefore, the priests gathered 12 pious men of the tribe of Judah to choose from among them one that they would give Mary to. The priests brought these men’s canes inside the Temple, and it so happened that a dove came and stood on the cane which belonged to Joseph the Carpenter. By that sign, they knew that the Lord selected Joseph, who was a righteous man, to take care of the young Mary. She remained with him until the Archangel Gabriel came down to bring her the good news that the Son of God would be incarnated within her.

After the ascension of the Lord Christ to heaven, the Virgin St. Mary was always praying in the holy sepulture, anticipating the happy day in which she would be loosened from the bonds of the flesh. Then, she was told by the Holy Spirit that she would soon depart from this mortal world. When it was the designated time, the disciples and the virgins of Mount Olive came to her. While the Virgin St. Mary was lying on her bed, the Lord Christ Himself came to her with thousands of angels around Him, comforted her, and told her about the perpetual happiness she was going to enjoy. Rejoiced, she stretched her hand and blessed the disciples and the virgins, and delivered her pure soul in the hands of her Son and God, who took her up to the high dwelling places. As to her pure body, they shrouded it and carried it to the Gethsemane. While they were going in their way, some Jews came and tried to prevent them from burying her. When one of them stretched his hands to hold the coffin, his arms separated from his body and remained hanging until he believed and showed remorse on his evil deed.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Virgin Theotokos., pp. 156–157
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE VIRGIN THEOTOKOS.

Her appearances continued for many consecutive nights.

The Church celebrates the Birthday of St. Mary on the 1st of Bashons, her Entrance into the Temple on the 3rd of Kiahk, her Departure on the 21st of Toba, the Ascension of her body to Heaven on the 16th of Mesra, Building the first Church in her name on the 21st of Paona, Consecrating the church in her name in the ‘Muĥarraq’ monastery, which the Lord Christ blessed by his presence along with His Apostles, on the 6th of Hator and her Apparition in the church of El-Zeitoun on the 24th of Baramhat.

[Synaxarion: 6 Hator, 3 Kiahk, 21 Toba, 24 Baramhat, 1 Bashons, 21 Paona, and 16 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mariaam, the Righteous, pp. 93–94
passages.text:
Saint: MARIAAM, THE RIGHTEOUS, ST.

St. Mariaam, this Ethiopian man was born to a mother called Rommanet El-Dahab, who was the daughter of the Ethiopian king David. His father was Fag, the king of Ethiopia. Horrible persecution by Islamic invaders took place against the church of Ethiopia. At that time, the Muslims caught him and castrated him to make a eunuch out of him. However, the saint counted that as a profit for the sake of his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Then, they sent him to the Arab king, who was from a Turkish origin. On the road, they tortured him and hanged him once upside down on a camel; then, they left him naked in the intense heat of the sun while thirsty. However, after the death of the Arab king, he was released and returned to Ethiopia. There, he built several churches, cared for the poor and the needy, and celebrated all the feasts of the saints. When his departure drew near, he set his slaves and maidservants free. In the Ethiopian Synaxarion, it was recorded that this saint reposed on the 21st of the Coptic month of Baba.

Notes: [1] In its Arabic version…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary, the Egyptian, p. 149
passages.text:
Saint: MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. — The Devil Battles with Her

The Devil Battles with Her:

Then, Fr. Zosimus, the priest, asked her about her life in the wilderness. The saint told him about the battles she fought along those years, saying, “I spent the first 17 years suffering from severe hunger and thirst. However, that was nothing compared to what I went through in fighting the vicious battles against the evil carnal desires as if I was fighting actual beasts. All the horrible sins and the iniquities I have committed have played back into my mind. Several times, the thousands of carnal memories and impure thoughts which came to attack me brought so much pain to my heart and went through my veins like live coal, which caused me to cast myself on the ground supplicating out of my whole heart for them to be lifted away from me. I often remained in such a position for several days and nights. Then, a Divine light, like a circle of fire, surrounded me, through which the tempter could not pass through anymore. The Holy Virgin was a great help to me in my life of repentance. All along the way, she kept holding my hand, guiding me through and praying on my behalf. When I ran out of bread, I started to feed upon some herbs and plant roots, which I found in the ground. As for my clothes, they were utterly worn out with time, that I suffered the burning sun and trembled from the desert cold that I was often on the brink of losing my consciousness. Since I crossed the Jordan, you are the first human face I saw. However, the Merciful God has instructed me in the knowledge of the Holy Bible and the psalms.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary Magdalene, pp. 145–146
passages.text:
Saint: MARY MAGDALENE, ST.

The Lord Christ healed St. Mary Magdalene (from ‘Magdala’) by driving seven unclean spirits out of her. She was one of the women who served the Lord in Galilee (Luke 8:1-2). She also was present when He was crucified and went to His tomb along with two others, to find the grave empty. According to the Gospel of St. Mark, she was the first to see the Lord Christ after His resurrection (Mark 16:9), and St. John added that the Lord entrusted her to carry a message to His brethren (John 20:11-18).

Among the women who were mentioned in the Gospel, there was “The Sinful Woman” (Luke 7:37-50), whose name was not mentioned, Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha (Luke 10:38-42) and Mary Magdalene. According to the Eastern Tradition, they were considered to be three different persons, whereas according to the Western Tradition, the three of them are considered to be one person (the sinful woman, Mary, the sister of Martha, and Mary Magdalene). However, St. Ambrose (374-397 AD) was on the opinion that this issue should be left unanswered. In any case, the Western Tradition views St. Mary Magdalene as a fantastic role model for the repentant person. Since 1969, the Eastern tradition has been taken into consideration in the New Western Roman calendar. St. Mary Magdalene is celebrated by the Western Church on the 22nd of July.

[The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, p. 230]

Notes: [1] Proposed by the Roman Pope ‘Gregory the Great’ (590-604 AD).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mammaty, the Muăallem, p. 44
passages.text:
Saint: MAMMATY, THE MUĂALLEM

This muåallem's name was Abu el-Maliĥ, known as Mammaty. He lived in the 11th century AD during the Fatimid caliphate of Al-Mustansir bi-Allah (1036-1094 AD), and the vizierate of Badr el-Din al-Jamali the prince of the army (1073-1094 AD). He was known for his wealth, comfortable living, and his charity activities. The reason behind being so-called Mammaty was that he used to distribute what he had on the needy during one of the harsh famines in Egypt; and it happened that when the hungry Muslim children would see him on the streets, they would follow him begging him and crying out: “Mammaty! Mammaty!” Also, he used to have compassion for them and grant them grain and food to satisfy their hunger.

Mammaty was the grandfather of Asåad ibn Mohazab ibn Zakaria, who converted to Islam during the rule of Shirkuh, in the days of the Fatimid caliph Al-Ăadid li-Din Allah (1160-1171 AD).

[The History of the Coptic Church, p. 455]

Notes: [1] ‘Mammaty’ in Arabic could mean: “I am dead hungry…”

details.fact: St. Mary the Egyptian lived in the 4th and 5th centuries.
details.quote: St. Mary the Egyptian was a woman who lived in the 4th and 5th centuries AD.

details.fact: Her story was told by Zosimus, a priest-monk.
details.quote: She was encountered by Fr. Zosimus, a priest who brought her Holy Communion in her final years.

details.fact: Zosimus encountered her while returning from the wilderness before the end of Lent.

records.question: Who was St. Demiana and how was she martyred?
records.answer:
St. Demiana was born near the end of the 3rd century AD to two pious Christian parents; her father Marcus was a governor in the Nile delta region. She was baptized at one year old in El-Mayma monastery. Growing up, she was known for her piety, beauty, richness, and virtues. When a prince proposed to marry her, she refused, expressing her desire to live a virgin life devoted to God. At age 18, she declared her decision to live as a virgin, which her father supported by building her a separate palace where she lived with 40 other virgins who also vowed virginity. Together, they practiced an ascetic life of fasting, prayer, and praise, turning the palace into a place of continuous worship [1][2].

During the persecution under Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), her father Marcus initially renounced his faith and burned incense before idols. St. Demiana rebuked him firmly and tearfully, urging him to return to the true faith. Her words moved him to repentance, and he publicly confessed his Christian faith before the emperor, for which he was beheaded [2][3].

After her father's martyrdom, the emperor sent soldiers to arrest St. Demiana and the 40 virgins. She encouraged the virgins to remain steadfast, and none fled. They were subjected to severe tortures, including being placed in the Hinbazeen (a machine with two wheels with sharp blades that shred flesh), combed with iron combs, having gypsum and vinegar rubbed into their wounds, having their skulls broken, and their bodies skinned. Despite this, St. Demiana was miraculously healed twice by the Archangel Michael. A white dove also appeared to heal her wounds during torture. Throughout, she glorified the Lord and counted herself unworthy to partake in the Lord's sufferings. Finally, the leader ordered that her head and the heads of the 40 virgins be cut off, and they all received the crowns of martyrdom. Before her execution, she cried out: “I confess the Lord Jesus Christ; on His name I die, and by it, I shall forever live.” She was martyred on the 13th of Toba [4][5].

Her body rests in the church built by Queen Helena near Bilqas in the Nile Delta, consecrated by Pope Alexander I. Several churches in Egypt bear her name [4].
