passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, pp. 555–556
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Her Upbringing

Her Upbringing:

St. ‘Demiana’ was born to two pious Christian parents near the end of the 3rd century AD. Her father ‘Marcus’ was a governor on ‘El-Burullus,’ ‘Zaåfaran,’ and the ‘Saysaban valley’ (northeast of Gharbiah governorate) in the Nile delta. When St. ‘Demiana’ reached the first year of age, she was baptized in ‘El-Mayma’ monastery, south of the city of ‘Zaåfaran;’ and her father for three days held a massive banquet for the poor and the needy. After a little while, her mother reposed.

A Prince Propose to Marry the Saint:

Growing up, the saint was known for her piety, beauty, richness, and virtues. Then, when her father told her that a prince proposed to marry her, she answered him: “Why do you want me to get married, while I want to live with you? Why do you want me to leave you?”

Amazed at her response, her father postponed talking about the issue of marriage for a while. Then, her father noticed how his daughter adored reading the Holy Bible, and how she used to resort to her private room to pour a flow of tears of love before God her Savior. She had a secure attachment to the church, and the frequency of her prayers and fasting was so high. She had so many of her girl-friends spending time with her practicing an ascetic way of life in prayers and continuous praise to God.

On reaching the age of 18 years, she proclaimed to her father her decision to live as a virgin, which was welcomed by him. He also, to fulfill her wish, built for her a separate palace of her own in the region of ‘Zaåfaran,’ to worship God along with 40 other girls who vowed virginity as well.

St. ‘Demiana’ rejoiced and appreciated her father’s actions, which surpassed the mere emotional love, to offer his only daughter as a lovesacrifice to God. The saint, together with her friends, lived a marvelous ascetic life of fasting combined with prayers and praise, turning the palace into heaven, in which the sound of exaltation was perpetually heard.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, pp. 556–557
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — A Prince Propose to Marry the Saint

St. ‘Demiana’ rejoiced and appreciated her father’s actions, which surpassed the mere emotional love, to offer his only daughter as a lovesacrifice to God. The saint, together with her friends, lived a marvelous ascetic life of fasting combined with prayers and praise, turning the palace into heaven, in which the sound of exaltation was perpetually heard.

The Fall of Her Father;

During the wave of persecution, stirred up by emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284- 305 AD), Demiana’s father ‘Marcus’ was scared and became feeble and burned incense before the idols. On hearing about it, ‘Demiana’ came out of her seclusion, after seeking from her friends to keep praying for the sake of her father to return from his vanity.

When she met with her father, she bravely and firmly said to him: “I wish I heard the news of your death, rather than to hear that you have forsaken the true God. If you persist on your vanity, I shall denounce you as my father here and before the throne of the Divine Judge, and you would have no portion in the eternal inheritance, kept by God for those who love Him and keep His covenant.” She bitterly rebuked him on his denial of His Christ under whatever circumstances. She sought from him not to fear death, but to fear the destruction of the soul and body together. She begged him not to appease the emperor at the expense of his faith and eternity. Along with her firmness and complete frankness, her tears of love unceasingly flowed while she was telling him: “If you persist in denying the True God; You would not be any longer my father and I would not be your daughter.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, p. 557
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Her Father Returned to His Faith

Her Father Returned to His Faith:

His daughter’s words and tears inflamed ‘Marcus’ heart that he cried out with bitterness and remorse for his shameful deed. In true repentance and with the spirit of humility and renewed hope, he said to her: “Blessed is the moment I saw you, my daughter, for you brought me up from the deep pit in which I have fallen. My life is renewed in preparation for encountering my Great Lord, who, I am sure, will receive my soul.”

Then, with the spirit of thanksgiving to God who woke his heart up, he proclaimed: “O my God, I give You thanks for You have taken away the darkness of infidelity from my heart; ‘The snare is broken, and we have escaped’ (Ps. 124:7)”. He then instantly set forth to Antioch, to proclaim his Christian faith before Emperor Diocletian and show his regret for having burnt incense before the idols.

The emperor was amazed by the new attitude of that governor, who was always known for his obedience, and on seeing how he proclaimed his faith with such strength, the emperor gently rebuked ‘Marcus’ and did not hasten to punish him. He was hoping to convince him to re-deny his living faith. But, as ‘Marcus’ persisted on his stand, the angry emperor ordered his head to be cut off. This happened on the 6th of Abib, on the feast of the saintly apostles.

The news spread in the whole land, and the heart of his daughter St. ‘Demiana’ became jubilant; for the sake of her father who was saved from the eternal destruction, to partake of the glories of his Christ.

The emperor felt sorrow to lose ‘Marcus,’ whom he appreciated and cherished. Then, he heard that his daughter was behind the restoration of her father to his Christian faith. So, he sent a regiment of his soldiers with their tools of torture to take revenge from her and the virgins who lived with her. On seeing the soldiers surrounding her palace, and how they set the instruments of torture to terrify them; St. ‘Demiana’ assembled the virgins, and she proclaimed with the spirit of conquest that the emperor has the intention to scare them; and it was the time to receive the crowns of martyrdom for whoever wanted to take advantage of the occasion. Then, she asked them, whoever among them intended to enjoy it, let her stay, but whoever has fears, let her flee through the back door. However, none of the 40 virgins had a fear of death, but with great joy, all proclaimed that they hold fast to their Christ, and would never flee.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, p. 558
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Fellowship of Passion with Christ

Whenever that leader tortured her, the Lord was glorified in her. Finally, the leader ordered cutting her head off, together with all the heads of the other virgins with her, and all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

Before the sword struck the saint’s neck, the saint cried out: “I confess the Lord Jesus Christ; on His name I die, and by it, I shall forever live.”

She was martyred on the 13th of Toba. Her body is still there in the church built by Queen ‘Helena,’ the mother of Emperor ‘Constantine the Great’ (306- 337 AD), located close to the town of ‘Bilqas’ in the north of the Nile Delta. That church was consecrated by pope ‘Alexander I’ (312-328 AD) on the 12th of Bashons. Annexed to that church is the convent of St. ‘Demiana.’

Several churches were built all over Egypt in the name of this great martyr.

[El-Mahaba Bookstore: The Biography of St. Demiana]

Notes: [1] The ‘Henbazin’ is a machine made of two wheels with sharp blades, a person is pressed between the wheels, then on turning them in opposite directions, the person’s flesh is torn out into shreds.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, pp. 557–558
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Fellowship of Passion with Christ

Fellowship of Passion with Christ:

The leader of the regiment met with the saint, told her that the emperor promised to give her great wealth and to make her a noble princess if she worshiped his gods. She answered him: “Are you not ashamed to call those idols gods when there is no god except the Lord of heaven and earth? I am prepared to die for His name’s sake, along with all those who are with me.”

Provoked to anger, the leader ordered four soldiers to place the saint into the ‘Hinbazeen’ chamber and to start her torture. The other virgins bitterly cried out when they saw their matron being pressed and her body being slashed. Then barely alive, the saint was thrown into prison. There, the Archangel ‘Michael’ came down at midnight and healed all her wounds.

In the morning, the soldiers came to check up on her, expecting to declare her death to their leader, but to their amazement, they saw her free of any wounds. Provoked to anger, the leader assumed that ‘Demiana’ was a sorcerer, and he declared that all effort would be made to disable her sorcery.

On seeing the saint was restored to full health, the multitudes cried out: “We believe in the God of ‘Demiana.’” So, the soldiers’ chief ordered killing them all, and considering that the saint was responsible for leading so many ‘astray,’ he put in his heart to double her tortures. He ordered combing her body with sharp iron combs, then rubbed into her wounds gypsum soaked with vinegar, but she kept being exultant, counting herself unworthy to partake of the passions of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Then, she was cast again in jail. On the next day, the leader himself went to check on her expecting to see a corpse, but he almost collapsed when he saw her entirely healed by the Archangel ‘Michael’ who revisited her. He furiously tortured her in so many different ways: breaking her skull and skinning her body. A white dove came down from heaven, hovered above her, and healed her from all her wounds.

Whenever that leader tortured her, the Lord was glorified in her. Finally, the leader ordered cutting her head off, together with all the heads of the other virgins with her, and all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dominica, the Virgin, p. 637
passages.text:
Saint: DOMINICA, THE VIRGIN, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was living at the time of emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), and she was accused of breaking the idols down. The emperor ordered to cast her to the wild hungry beasts. However, the beasts did not harm her. So, they cut her head off around the year 303, and she received the crown of martyrdom.

[Butler: July 6]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasia, pp. 175–176
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIA, ST. (The martyr)

This Saint was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD) around the year 250 AD, and celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 1st of Baba...

She was the daughter of Christian parents in Rome; they raised her in fear of God. Her heart was full of the Love of God, longing for the angelic life of virginity since her childhood. She joined a convent in Rome to practice the monastic life with firmness, eating food once every two days, and in the Great Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays.

When the mother-superior went to attend a feast in the city, she took with her the virgin Anastasia. In the town, they happened to see soldiers torturing some Christians. So, the virgin Anastasia stopped to rebuke them on their oppression and the hardness of their hearts. However, the soldiers arrested her and brought her forth to the governor. Before the governor, she confessed the Lord Christ. He tortured her severely, crucified her and ignited fire underneath her. And as she persisted in her faith, he ordered to cut her head off by the sword, for which she became exultant, prayed, and delivered her head to the swordsman to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Encratis, p. 22
passages.text:
Saint: ENCRATIS (The martyr)

She was martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) around the year 304 AD on the 16th of April, by Dacian the Governor. The Spanish Christian poet Prudentius used to boast that his city Saragossa delivered to paradise a significant number of martyrs, more than any other city in Spain. In a poem, he narrated the events of the martyrdom of St. Obthatius along with seventy others who testified to the Lord Jesus Christ in one day. When he mentioned those martyrs by name, he included a girl by the name of Encratia whom he called ‘The Girl on Fire’ and ‘The Girl with the Exalted Spirit,’ because she endured extraordinary wounds in her body. They broke her bones, pulled out her nails, cut off her breasts, opened up her belly, and dragged her intestine and liver out. Finally, her head was cut off to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius, pp. 577–578
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

The emperor was amazed and embarrassed; how a man like ‘Nestor’ could prevail over his vast wrestler, and he inquired about the situation and was informed by his men that ‘Demetrius’ prayed for him and made the sign of the Cross over his face.

In anger, the emperor ordered to strike ‘Nestor’ until he would consent to burn incense before his gods and to worship them. When he refused, the emperor ordered to stab him by spears to tear his body off until his death. So, they did that in front of ‘Demetrius’ to terrify him and lead him to deny his faith in the Lord Christ. However, he told them: “Do whatever you like, for I shall never worship or burn incense, except before my Lord Jesus Christ the True God.” So, the soldiers stabbed him with spears until he delivered his pure spirit in the hands of the Lord.

Some believers took his holy body, and they kept it hidden in a marble coffin until the end of persecution. Then, a great church was built in his name in ‘Thessalonica,’ where his relics were hidden. In the saint’s name, many miracles were performed, and fragrant myrrh oil flowed from his tomb, which healed whoever has used it with faith. Since the 7th century, a large quantity of the miraculous myrrh oil flowed on the walls and columns of that Church; and it was plenty enough for all people present to wipe it off and transfer it into their vessels.

[The Synaxarion: 29 Baba] [Orthodox Church in America Web Site: Lives of the Saints: Demetrius the Myrrh-Gusher of Thessalonica]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bibiana, the Virgin, pp. 352–353
passages.text:
Saint: BIBIANA (VIVIANA), THE VIRGIN, ST. (The martyr)

A church was built in Rome under the name of St. ‘Bibiana’ (Viviana), in the 5th century AD.

It was said that she was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Julian the Apostate’ (360-363 AD). She was the daughter of ‘Flavian’ (Flavianus), who was the governor of Rome. He was known for his zeal about the Christian faith with his wife ‘Dafrosa,’ and on that account, he was fired from his position, was branded on his forehead with hot iron, and was exiled to a place called ‘Aquapendente’ (the water of the bull), where he died in exile.

The Western Church celebrates his memorial on December 22. As to his wife, she was put under house arrest, together with her two daughters ‘Bibiana’ and ‘Demetria.’ Finally, the head of St. ‘Dafrosa’ was cut off. Her memorial is celebrated by the Western Church on the 4th of January.

The two girls ‘Bibiana’ and ‘Demetria’ stayed in their house, but they were in great need after all their possessions were taken away from them. They practiced prayers and fasting following a harsh ascetic way for five months. However, the new governor ‘Abronianus’ kept threatening them every day of torture if they would not deny their Christ.

Finally, he brought them for trial before the court of justice. During that trial, St. ‘Demetria’ fainted and collapsed, and then delivered her pure soul to the Lord. Then, the governor brought her sister ‘Bibiana’ to an evil corrupted woman by the name of ‘Rufina,’ to lure her to sin and to seduce her to deny her faith with empty devious promises. St. ‘Bibiana’ totally rejected all the advances of that evil ‘Rufina,’ and in spite of being beaten viciously by ‘Rufina;’ sometimes using whips and other times by iron nails which tore off her flesh, the virgin ‘Bibiana’ endured the torture with great perseverance.

Eventually, ‘Rufina’ had to relay to the governor her failure in her mission.

The governor ordered that St. ‘Bibiana’ be tied up to a post, then to be lashed with a lead-coated whip until her flesh was torn apart entirely, and she delivered her pure soul in the hands of God. Later, her body was cast unto a heap of trash, yet no animals nor birds of prey approached her remains. After two days, a pious priest called ‘John’ carried her body and buried her beside her mother and sister.

[Butler, Alban. Lives of the Saints, Volume XII, 1866]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Didymus, p. 588
passages.text:
Saint: DIDYMUS (The martyr)

A young Christian man who volunteered to rescue St. ‘Theodora’ from a house of harlotry; where she was forced to stay in, because of her holding fast to the Christian faith; during the persecution of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD). His biography is given under the title “Theodora and Didymus,” the martyrs.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sophia and the Fifty Virgins, p. 180
passages.text:
Saint: SOPHIA AND THE FIFTY VIRGINS (The martyrs)

In one of the convents close to the city of Edessa (El-Roha) in Iraq, fifty virgins were living with their pious mother-superior Sophia. All of them earnestly worshipped God with continuous prayers and fasting. The pagan Emperor Julian (360-363 AD), on his way to fight with his army the Persian king Shapur II (309-379 AD), they passed by this convent. The evil emperor ordered his men to kill all the nuns and their mother-superior and cut them into pieces, and then to rob all that in their convent. So, they all received the crowns of martyrdom. This took place on the 10th of Hator.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dionysia, p. 593
passages.text:
Saint: DIONYSIA, ST. (The martyr)

In the days of persecution stirred up by Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD), in the year 250 AD, in the city of ‘Troas’ in Asia Minor; three Christians were presented to the governor, their oldest was a man called ‘Nicomachus,’ who at the beginning confessed his faith, and refused to sacrifice to the god, but when they started torturing him, and the pain was too much for him, he cried out, “It is a mistake. I never was a Christian; I shall sacrifice to the gods.” They brought him down from the tool of torture; but the moment he put the flesh of the sacrifice on his lips, he fell dead, as a denier.

A 16 years old girl called ‘Dionysia,’ observing this scene, cried out. “Poor miserable man, for the sake of a few moments of pain, you earned for yourself indescribable eternal pains.” Then, she was brought before the governor who inquired from her if she was a Christian. She answered him: “Yes, I am; that is why I am sad for that miserable man who could not endure a few moments more to gain eternal comfort.” The governor sought from her to do likewise, or else she would be tortured and burnt alive.

The next day, ‘Andrew’ and ‘Paul,’ the companions of ‘Nicomachus,’ were brought before the judge, who decided to deliver them to the mob to stone them to death. Their feet were tied together and were dragged outside the city to be stoned there. Meanwhile, ‘Dionysia’ was led to receive her final verdict, when she met the crowd that was dragging ‘Andrew’ and ‘Paul’ to their death. On seeing them passing by, she managed to get away from her guard and cast herself on the two of them, crying: “Let me die with you upon the earth, that I may live with you forever in heaven,” but the governor denied her request and ordered cutting her head off by the sword.

[Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 164] [A. J. Mason: The Historic Martyrs of the Primitive Church, 1905, pp. 137-9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Marciana, the Virgin, p. 61
passages.text:
Saint: MARCIANA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This lady St. Marciana was an inhabitant of Rusuccur (Rosso) in southwestern Mauritania, and during the persecution of Emperor Diocletian (284- 305 AD), she despised the glory of the world for the sake of acquiring the heavenly grace. So, she proclaimed her rejection of the pagan gods in front of the rulers. She was severely beaten and was insulted by being offered to the Roman soldiers to defile her, but God rescued her and miraculously kept her virginity, by a Roman soldier who came to protect her and proclaimed his faith too in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Finally, she was martyred by being torn into pieces by the horns of a wild ox and a leopard in the execution arena at Caesarea in Mauritania; about 100 miles away from the nowadays city of Algiers. Her martyrdom took place in the year 303 AD.

[Butler: January 9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damian, p. 551
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIAN, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was martyred in Antioch. He endured vicious tortures until he delivered his soul into the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 23 Mesra]

records.answer:
Saint Verena was a virgin from the town of Garagous in the district of Qus in the governorate of Qena. She was a nurse and a relative of St. Victor (Boctor), one of St. Maurice’s associates, and joined the military in the Theban Legion, which was sent to Switzerland. When St. Maurice, St. Victor, and the other members of the Theban Legion were martyred by order of Emperor Maximian (286-305), Verena traveled to Agaunum to have the blessing of their bodies and to look for the relics of St. Victor.

Afterwards, she lived as a hermit in a place called Solothurn in Switzerland, dwelling in a cave from which she would go to nearby villages to offer acts of mercy and kindness to the villagers and the poor. She fasted and prayed continuously and was credited with several miracles. Verena was also a spiritual counselor for young girls and cared for their physical health due to her nursing expertise.

It is said that she spent the rest of her life in a cave near present-day Zurich in Germany. Her piety greatly influenced the local people, who built a church over her grave, engraving her portrait carrying a pitch and a comb. This church was destroyed in the 9th century during the German tribes' invasion, and later a Benedictine monastery was established on the site. St. Verena remains honored and appreciated throughout Switzerland [1].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Verena, p. 320
passages.text:
Saint: VERENA, ST.

St. Verena was a virgin of the town of Garagous in the district of Qus in the governorate of Qena. And, as a nurse and a relative of St. Victor (Boctor), one of St. Maurice’s associates, she also joined the military in the Theban Legion, which was sent to Switzerland.

Verena was still in Milan when the word was received that St. Maurice, St. Victor, and the other members of the Theban Legion, who had proceeded north, were all martyred by order of Emperor Maximian (286-305). Verena traveled to Agaunum, where they were killed to have the blessing of the bodies of those martyrs and to look for the relics of St. Victor, her relative.

Afterwards, she led the life of a hermit in a place called Solothurn (in Switzerland), she dwelt in a cave from which she used to go to the villages around to offer acts of mercy and kindness to the villagers and the poor. As a hermit, Verena fasted and prayed continuously. Several miracles were attributed to her intercession. Verena was a spiritual counselor for young girls, and due to her expertise as a nurse, she used to look after their physical health.

It was said that she had spent the rest of her life in a cave near present-day Zurich in Germany. Her piety had such a great influence on the people in the area, that when she reposed in peace, the people in that region built a church over her grave, on which they engraved her portrait carrying a pitch and a comb. That church was destroyed along with the whole village when the German tribes invaded the region in the 9th century. Later on, a monastery for the Benedicts was established on that site. St. Verena is still the object of honor and appreciation all over Switzerland.

[The Story of the Coptic Church; Book 1, p. 140]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Veronica, p. 321
passages.text:
Saint: VERONICA, ST.

The name Veronica means ‘the True Icon.’ According to the Church Tradition, St. Veronica was the one who wiped with her veil the blood from the face of the Lord Jesus Christ, motivated by her love for Him, and moved with sympathy for His pains when he fell under the weight of the Cross. On returning home, she found that the image of his face miraculously imprinted upon that veil she used, with the passion clearly shown on it. According to the Western tradition, Veronica went to Rome, where she healed Emperor Tiberius (14-37) by the power of that veil she carried. Before she reposed, she left it to the Roman Pope St. Clement I (88-99).

According to the Tradition in France, Veronica was the wife of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:2-10), set forth together with her husband, the ex-tax-collector, who sold all his possessions, to preach the Lord Christ. When they reached France, they spread Christianity in its southern region.

And there are many other unconfirmed views about the identity of Veronica. One of them says that she was Martha, the sister of Lazarus; another one says that she was the daughter of the Canaanite woman, and a third one says that she was the woman with the flow of blood.

In the early 15th century, the exact location of Veronica’s house was found; and it became assigned as one of the Way of Crucifixion Stations in Jerusalem. And this veil (handkerchief) is still there in the cathedral of St. Peter in Rome; as a proof of the authenticity of this story.

[Butler: July 12]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Burrier of Martyrs, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE BURRIER OF MARTYRS

This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 miles from Rome. In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius, the priest, Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes.

The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September.

[Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 Vol.; London 1877-1887]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Febronia, the Virgin, p. 113
passages.text:
Saint: FEBRONIA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) — Being Persecuted

The young man, being himself the son of a Christian mother and having compassion on Febronia, started questioning her hesitantly and with respect. Selenus was disappointed by the way his nephew treated the saint and promised her if she would forsake her religion, he would marry her to Lysimachus, and she would enjoy freedom and richness.

The saint answered him, saying that she has a treasure in heaven, and wealth not made by man and that she was already betrothed to the non-mortal Groom. The governor was provoked to anger to hear her answer. He ordered to tie her between four pillars and to scourge her. His men broke 17 of her teeth and cut her breasts off, ignoring the screams of protest from the multitudes of people who were in court. When they found out that she was still alive, they cast her before a wild ox that tore her up by its sharp horns. She was martyred in the year 304 AD. By ordering from Lysimachus, St. Febronia's relics were gathered and buried in a grand funeral procession. Her martyrdom was the cause that many pagans converted to Christianity and sought to be baptized, including Lysimachus himself, who became a monk in the days of Emperor Constantine the Great (306-337 AD).

[Baring-Gould: June 25]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 668–669
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

Many nuns were given the gift of true leadership and spiritual discernment, like St. Sarah of whom it was said that she lived for sixty years on the banks of a river, but never lifted her eyes to look at it. Many of her sayings were preserved in the sayings of the desert fathers and mothers.

St. Hilaria: In the fourth century, the daughter of Emperor Zeno fled to Scetis where she led a life of asceticism in the attire of a male monk. When her sister, Theopiste, was possessed by an evil spirit, the elders of the wilderness sent her to St. Hilaria to pray for her, and did not know that St. Hilaria was a woman. She prayed all night for her and embraced her. Theopiste was healed, and she told the emperor about the monk, “Hilarion,” who healed her and was embracing her, so her father was disturbed. He called for her to come to the palace, where she revealed to him that she was his daughter after he had promised not to prevent her from going back to her cave.

St. Syncletica: Some historians regard her to be the equal of St. Anthony, the star of the wilderness; for as St. Anthony was the father of all monks, St. Syncletica was a mother to that group of virgins which transformed the fertile valley of Egypt into a dwelling place for the grace of God. She was born to noble parents who settled in Alexandria to be close to the School of Alexandria. They had two sons and two daughters, so they wanted to educate them in all sciences, which were only offered in the School of Alexandria. This family was shocked at the death of Syncletica’s youngest brother in his childhood, while the older one departed on the night of his wedding. These two shocks caused Syncletica to ponder and contemplate the pleasures of the world and see them as nothing but a deceptive mirage. Syncletica persevered in her fasting, prayer, asceticism, and worship in her parents’ house till they departed to heaven. Then, she distributed her money on the poor and took her sister to their family’s tomb, where they lived for a few years. During this period, she redoubled her fasts, prayers, and ascetic practices. A substantial number of young women went to visit her. Some went simply to see her and take her blessing, while others came seeking solutions to their problems. It was natural for some of them to be influenced by her example and desire to stay with her and participate in the life of asceticism and contemplation.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Restituta, the Virgin, pp. 13–14
passages.text:
Saint: RESTITUTA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This lady St. Restituta was a Roman virgin of noble origin, and was martyred in the year 271 AD in the town of Sora in Italy. She became the patron saint of that city where she was buried. It was said that the Lord Christ appeared to her and instructed her to go to Sora, and an angel led her to that town. There, she stayed in the house of a widow, and when the saint healed her son from leprosy, the mother and her son, along with 39 others, were converted all to Christianity. When the region’s governor Agathius heard about her activity, he arrested her and cast her into prison. And, when she refused to sacrifice to the idols, she was scourged and sent back to prison. There, she was left seven days without food or drink while tied with heavy chains. When an angel appeared to her, the iron chains melted like wax, and she was healed of her wounds, and no longer felt any hunger or thirst. On seeing that, a number of her guards proclaimed their faith in Christ and received the crowns of martyrdom. Finally, St. Restituta was martyred together with Cyril, the priest, and others, who believed through her, by cutting off their heads and then throwing their bodies in the river Liri. Later on, their bodies were retrieved and buried with honor.

[Baring-Gould: May 27]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, pp. 117–118
passages.text:
Saint: SEVERUS, PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH, ST. — His Burial

And, according to Fr. John, nobody knew whether the body got shorter or the grave got a little bigger?! Only God who allowed for this miracle to happen knows, for He honors those who honor Him, even after they repose.

Then, the writer of this biography addressed Domadius, the man of God, saying: “By what I wrote, I am plucking a rose from a garden or a beautiful bunch of grapes from a vine and presenting it to you and the readers.”

His Feasts:

On the 2nd of Baba, the day he came to Egypt. On the 14th of Amshir, the day he reposed. On the 10th of Kiahk, the day his body was moved to El-Zugag monastery.

[Deacon Yousif Habib: Lectures about the Church History, Alexandria, 1974] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Severus of Antioch, by Linda Knezevich; pp. 2123-5]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Valeriana, p. 317
passages.text:
Saint: VALERIANA (The martyr)

St. Valeriana was martyred, together with Victoria and the bishop Fidentius. They possibly were among the 20 martyrs, in whose names a church in Hippo (in north Africa) was built. St. Augustine commended those martyrs.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 1100]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Magna, the Virgin, pp. 32–33
passages.text:
Saint: MAGNA, THE VIRGIN, ST. — A Life of Virginity

St. Magna was born in the city of Ancyra in Turkey. She had her heart flared up with the Divine love, that she was spending most of her nights praying and praising God. Her father was arrested when she was young. Then, a young man asked to marry her, and her mother wanted to give her in marriage, but Magna tried to proclaim her desire for a life of virginity and that she dedicated her life to her Heavenly Groom. However, her mother did not approve and forced her to get married.

A Life of Virginity:

After the wedding, Magna prayed to God to grant her the wisdom and to help her keep her virginity. She kept giving excuses to her husband to keep him away. Then, God allowed for him to get seriously ill and eventually to pass away.

A Life of Monasticism:

Magna distributed all that she inherited from her husband on the poor and the needy and then joined a convent in Ancyra which included about 2,000 nuns. Magna believed in the necessity of the continuous handwork that she chose to clean the lavatories with great joy, besides practicing prayers, fasting, calm sessions of reading the Holy Bible, and eating only one meal in the evening. She was the object of amazement and love of the other nuns, that when she was inflicted with severe illness, the nuns came to her cell, where, with great difficulty, she managed to ask them to continue their unceasing strife to get to enjoy the heavenly crown. She then put her arms on her chest in the form of a Cross and delivered her pure soul in the hands of her Creator and Savior.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, p. 669
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

Some went simply to see her and take her blessing, while others came seeking solutions to their problems. It was natural for some of them to be influenced by her example and desire to stay with her and participate in the life of asceticism and contemplation.

She left her family’s tomb and took her colleagues to live with her in a building outside the city, where she devoted her life to serve them, becoming a role model and a living example to what she called for in her teachings. For this reason, her colleagues loved her, were loyal to her, and happily obeyed her. Year after year, the number of young women who became her disciples increased; some of them would spend some time with her and then return to their homes, bearing the grace that they received from St. Syncletica’s example back to their families.

When this saint was eighty years old, she was in very good health, but became suddenly ill. Sores covered her body from head to toe, to the point where she lost the ability to speak. The pain of the sores was intensified by a severe fever. The saint’s patience was comparable to that of Job, for she endured all that befell her with thanksgiving and long-suffering. Three days before her departure, she saw a multitude of angels with a group of virgins, who approached her saying, “We came to call you, so come with us.” As soon as she heard these words, she became a new person and was engulfed in bright light. She lived after that for three full days during which the nuns were enlightened with a heavenly light that was reflected on them from their ill abbess, then she departed to the Church of the firstborn.

St. Athanasius the Apostolic wanted to make her greatness more widely known, so he began to write her biography; but he departed before finishing it, so one of her disciples completed it after his departure. He wrote the biography of St. Anthony describing him as the father of monks and wrote the biography of St. Syncletica describing her as the mother of nuns and virgins.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Febronia, the Virgin, pp. 112–113
passages.text:
Saint: FEBRONIA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) — In the Convent of Nisibis

In the Convent of Nisibis:

St. Febronia was the niece of St. Bryene, the mother-superior of a convent in Nisibis on the border between Syria and Asia Minor; Bryene had the responsibility of raising her niece physically and spiritually.

Bryene was firm in raising her niece and trained her to eat only once every two days and to lie on a thin wooden board. St. Febronia did not care for the world outside the convent but focused on her spiritual life and on her growth in virtues to become worthy of her heavenly Groom.

Febronia loved the Holy Bible, that she kept on reading it day and night, and interpreted it to the other nuns once every week, with the attendance of many women from the nearby city. During those sessions, Bryene asked her niece to hide her face with a veil to keep the women in attendance from being distracted by her beauty and to keep her from being attached to any of them.

Being Persecuted:

All of a sudden, the period of peace in the convent came to an end when Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) started persecuting the Christians. In Nisibis, the imperial orders were followed with extreme ferocity by the Governor Selenus. All the clergy, the bishop, and all the nuns fled the area except for Bryene, Febronia (who was recovering from a severe illness), and Thomais, her colleague (a nun), who later on wrote the saint’s biography. When the soldiers of the governor arrived at the convent, they took only St. Febronia along with them and did not care for the other two old nuns. The next day, they brought Febronia before Governor Selenus, who sought from his nephew Lysimachus to interrogate her. The young man, being himself the son of a Christian mother and having compassion on Febronia, started questioning her hesitantly and with respect. Selenus was disappointed by the way his nephew treated the saint and promised her if she would forsake her religion, he would marry her to Lysimachus, and she would enjoy freedom and richness.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Aphronia, pp. 204–205
passages.text:
Saint: APHRONIA (The martyr) — Her Monastic Life

Her Monastic Life:

St. Aphronia lived in Mesopotamia, ‘Almissah.' When her heart kindled with the love of God and was longing to dedicate all her energies to worship, she joined a convent. In that convent, her aunt ‘Auriana’ was the mothersuperior, so she became one of her disciples. She was very keen on the study of the Holy Bible and on practicing the monastic life with enflamed zeal.

Her Martyrdom:

When Diocletian stirred up persecution against the Christians, the 50 virgins in the convent, out of fear forsook the convent and went into hiding. Only ‘Oriana,' the mother-superior, Aphronia, and another nun remained there.

When the soldiers came, they took hold of the old mother-superior and oppressed her. The 20 years old Aphronia, sought from them to leave the older woman alone and take her instead. So they did, they tied her with ropes and brought her over to the governor, while the mother-superior followed. There, the governor asked her to worship the idols and gave her many promises, all of which she rejected.

As the tender treatment of the governor did not work, he resorted to violence and threats. He ordered, striking her with a rod, while the mother kept praying to God to grant her strength and endurance. Intending to humiliate her, the governor ordered his men to tear her clothes off. Here, the mother ‘Auriana’ could not bear seeing them expose her body, screamed: “May the Lord split you open, O vicious beast, for humiliating this fatherless young girl."

The governor was provoked to anger by the words of that old woman, and he ordered to press ‘Aphronia’ in the Hinbazeen and to tear her body by sharp iron claws, while she kept praying to the Lord to support her in her strife.

As the saint persisted on confessing the Lord Christ, the governor ordered to cut her tongue and to crush her teeth, but the Lord kept healing her. And finally, they cut her head off by the sword, and she received the crown of martyrdom around the year 305 AD...

The Coptic Church celebrates her martyrdom on the first day of Abib.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Potamiæna, pp. 483–484
passages.text:
Saint: POTAMIÆNA (The martyr)

This virtuous virgin martyr Potamiæna has also been mentioned under the biography of St. Basilides, the soldier who was assigned to guard her. He was the one who did her the favor of not making her take off her clothes during her martyrdom, for which she prayed to God on his behalf. He eventually followed her steps and gained the crown of martyrdom by proclaiming his faith in the Lord Christ. Her story was told by the historian Eusebius (265- 340 AD). Also, it was told by St. Palladius (363-430 AD). Palladius quoted the story from St. Isidore of Alexandria (318-403 AD), who quoted it from St. Abba Anthony the Great (251-356 AD).

St. Potamiæna was born by poor Christian parents in the 2nd century AD. Her mother Marcella, cared for her education, so she encouraged her to listen to Origen (184-254 AD) in his interpretation of the Holy Bible at the first School of Alexandria. She worked in fear of God as a maidservant at the home of a rich man. However, Satan, filling the heart of that man with unclean thoughts toward her, kept on provoking her to commit evil with him, but she held firm to her purity and chastity. Failing to seduce her, her master informed the governor of Alexandria Claudius Subatianus Aquila (205-210 AD), about her and accused her of being Christian. That evil rich man gave the governor a considerable sum of money to torture her until she would submit and consent to do evil with him. St. Potamiæna endured much suffering and was finally put in a pot filled with boiling oil, to deliver her soul in the hands of her Heavenly Groom.

[H. Musurillo: Acts of Christian Martyrs, Oxford 1972, Ch. 9]

Notes: [1] ‘Eusebius’ in his book: “Church History, Bk VI, Ch. 5”...

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasia, pp. 175–176
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIA, ST. (The martyr)

This Saint was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD) around the year 250 AD, and celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 1st of Baba...

She was the daughter of Christian parents in Rome; they raised her in fear of God. Her heart was full of the Love of God, longing for the angelic life of virginity since her childhood. She joined a convent in Rome to practice the monastic life with firmness, eating food once every two days, and in the Great Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays.

When the mother-superior went to attend a feast in the city, she took with her the virgin Anastasia. In the town, they happened to see soldiers torturing some Christians. So, the virgin Anastasia stopped to rebuke them on their oppression and the hardness of their hearts. However, the soldiers arrested her and brought her forth to the governor. Before the governor, she confessed the Lord Christ. He tortured her severely, crucified her and ignited fire underneath her. And as she persisted in her faith, he ordered to cut her head off by the sword, for which she became exultant, prayed, and delivered her head to the swordsman to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Euthalia, p. 87
passages.text:
Saint: EUTHALIA (The martyr)

St. Euthalia was a virgin who was martyred in Leontini in Sicily, around the year 257 AD. She is said to have been killed by her brother Sermilianus when he discovered that she became a Christian.

The Roman Pope, ‘Paul V’ (1605-1621 AD) added her name to the Roman Calendar, to be celebrated by the Church of the West on the 27th of August.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Euthalia (1), Vol II; p. 394]

records.question: Tell me about St. Rebecca and her five children.
records.answer:
St. Rebecca was a widow living in Kemola, in the district of Qus, Upper Egypt, with her five children: Agathon, Peter, John, Amon, and Amouna. She devoted herself to raising her children in the Lord’s ways, filling their hearts with love for God [1]. 

They received a night vision from Archangel Michael, who announced that they would receive the crowns of martyrdom near Alexandria and that their bodies would be moved to Naqraha in El-Behairah [1]. Filled with joy and anticipation, they prepared for martyrdom, praying for mercy on the Church and strength to hold fast to the faith. When Emperor Diocletian ordered the destruction of churches and persecution of Christians, St. Rebecca encouraged her children to remain steadfast and not fear death, seeing it as the most precious gift one can give courageously [2]. An angel appeared to comfort them and assure them of their impending crowns of martyrdom [2].

They appeared before Dionysius, governor of Qus, who demanded they burn incense to idols. They refused, confessing their Christian faith, and endured severe torture with courage and joy. Their steadfastness led many witnesses to convert and be martyred as well. They were imprisoned with many others, including bishops and priests [2].

Because Agathon was well-known and beloved, the governor sent them to Armenius, governor of Alexandria, who tortured them further by pulling out their teeth and imprisoning them. Archangel Michael appeared again, healing and encouraging them. Despite the tortures, they remained unharmed, which amazed the guards and led to more conversions. Armenius ordered their execution by hanging them upside down, boiling them in oil (which spilled and killed some soldiers), and finally beheading them. Their bodies were cast into the sea [3].

A rich Christian man was instructed in a vision to retrieve and care for their bodies, which were later moved to several churches and are currently kept in a church named after them in Sonbat, Zefta province. Their martyrdom is commemorated on the 7th of Tout [3].

Each child is recognized as a martyr: Agathon (the oldest son), Amon, and Amouna are specifically mentioned as children of St. Rebecca [4][5][6].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Rebecca and her Five Children, p. 10
passages.text:
Saint: REBECCA AND HER FIVE CHILDREN (The martyrs) — Archangel Michael Appearing to Them

Archangel Michael Appearing to Them:

The story of St. Rebecca (Refqa) and her children shows how much a Christian family would be willing to do to enjoy the Heavenly Crowns. Nothing did occupy the heart of this widow besides the thought of enjoying the Divine bosoms along with her five children, no matter how much that would cost them. Hence, this family did not lose their happiness amid their sufferings. On the contrary, their labors turned into a source of collective joy for the whole family and a living testimony before the people to learn from their experience. In the meantime, as the hearts of the members of that family were raised to heaven, God sent His angel several times to support them and bring happiness to their suffering hearts. For the holy life is a source of joy to the striving believers, as well as to the Heavenly Hosts.

This woman was widowed, as a mother of five children: Agathon, Peter, John, Amon, and Amouna. They were living in Kemola of the district of Qus in Upper Egypt. Their mother cared very much in raising her children in the Lord’s ways, and their feelings were kindled with the exalted love of God.

In a night vision, Archangel Michael proclaimed to them that they would be receiving the crowns of martyrdom near Alexandria; and their bodies would be moved to Naqraha in the governorate of El-Behairah (near Damanhur).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Rebecca and her Five Children, p. 11
passages.text:
Saint: REBECCA AND HER FIVE CHILDREN (The martyrs) — Preparing for Martyrdom

Preparing for Martyrdom:

Having enjoyed seeing the Archangel Michael, the mother and her children were filled with joy and anticipated the time they would receive the crowns of martyrdom, for which they were prepared their whole life.

When Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) ordered destroying the churches, burning the Holy Bible and torturing the Christians until they deny faith; St. Rebecca urged her children to hold fast to their faith; and reminded them of the saying of the Lord: “In the world, you will have tribulation” (John 16:33); and “Do not fear death.” And, she told them that the most precious gift a person could give is his own life, if he gives it without hesitation or remorse, but with courage and joy. They kept supplicating to God to have mercy on His Church and to hold His people fast in the faith.

While praying, when an angel of the Lord appeared to them, proclaimed that they would receive the crowns of martyrdom in the name of Christ, comforted and gave them the good news: “God be with you, and will give you strength until you consummate your strife; so do not fear death, but testify to the Lord.” Then, they were filled with a fantastic, joyful peace.

When it was time, they distributed their possessions on the needy, then set forth to appear before Dionysius, the governor of Qus, who asked them to burn incense before the idols. They all cried out, saying: “We are Christians, and only worship the Lord of heaven and earth, in whose hands are all men.” Attempting to no avail to seduce them by many gifts, the governor threatened to kill them if they persisted on confessing the name of Christ, to which they proclaimed their longing to die, to encounter their beloved Christ face to face. So, the governor tortured them severely, starting with their mother, who endured with perseverance and kept encouraging her children. They, too, did endure torture with courage and joy, that many of those present proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ and were martyred. Then, the governor ordered to put the saint and her children in prison, which was already packed with a multitude of people, together with bishops and priests.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Rebecca and her Five Children, pp. 11–12
passages.text:
Saint: REBECCA AND HER FIVE CHILDREN (The martyrs) — Before Armenius, the Governor of Alexandria

Before Armenius, the Governor of Alexandria:

As the older son, Agathon was popular in the town and so beloved by his fellow citizens, and because of him and his mother and brothers, many were martyred; some counseled the governor to send them to Armenius, the governor of Alexandria, where no one there knew them. Because Armenius, at that time, was at Shubra, they were sent to him there; he tortured them by taking their teeth off, then cast them in prison, where the Archangel Michael appeared to them again, healed and encouraged them. In the morning, when the guards and the people were amazed to see them with no sign of wounds on their bodies, they cried out, proclaiming their faith in the Lord Christ; and the governor ordered slaying them all.

When the governor placed St. Rebecca and her children on iron beds and ignited fire underneath them, God sent rain to extinguish the fire, and more people proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ, and they were martyred. However, all that did not move the heart of the governor, but he ordered to stab the bodies of these saints and to soak their wounds with vinegar. The Archangel Michael appeared to them for the third time, healed them, and told them: “Your strife is almost over; the crowns of life are already prepared for you.”

Finally, the governor ordered to hang them upside down, then to put them into a pot filled with boiling oil, which spilled over the soldiers and killed them. They were ultimately martyred by having their heads cut off by the sword, and then their bodies were cast into the sea.

Caring for Their Pure Bodies:

In a night vision, a rich Christian man was told to be the keeper of these pure bodies. So, he paid some money to the soldiers, took the bodies, and kept them until persecution came to an end. When devastation dwelt upon the city of Naqraha, the believers moved the bodies of these saints to the St. Mina Church in the town of Debi; and was eventually moved again to the town of Sonbat (named after its Roman governor Sanabit) in the province of Zefta; where they are still there in a church built in their name. Their martyrdom was on the 7th of Tout.

[Martyrdom in Christianity; p. 173]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodota of Nicea and her Children, pp. 273–274
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOTA OF NICEA AND HER CHILDREN (The Martyrs)

This lady saint was a beautiful widow whom governor Leucadius loved and wished to marry. But, rejecting his proposal because he is a pagan; and that she put in her heart to dedicate her life to raise her three sons. However, Leucadius reported her to Nicetas, the governor of the province of Bithynia, accusing her and her sons of being Christians. This happened in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305). The governor called them and started to talk tenderly to them for the sake of their honorable origin. Then, at the interrogation, when the judge began to threaten St. Theodota with torture, her eldest son Evodus said that Christians do not fear tortures, but rather fear being forsaken by God. So, they cruelly beat the boy before the eyes of his mother, so that his blood began to flow. St. Theodota prayed that the Lord would strengthen her son in his sufferings and rejoiced in that he was being given a martyr’s death for the sake of the Truth. The governor tried to provoke the mother to have mercy on the youth of her children, but as all of them despised his threats, they were burned together alive. The memory of the holy martyrs Theodota, the child Evodus and her other two small sons is celebrated on July 29.

[Orthodox Church in America, The Lives of the Saints: July 29]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Felicitas and her Seven Sons, pp. 116–117
passages.text:
Saint: FELICITAS AND HER SEVEN SONS (The martyrs)

The governor raised their case to the emperor, who ordered killing them in different ways: the eldest son Januarius was scourged to death, Felix and Philip were beaten with clubs until they died, Sylvanus was thrown down a cliff, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were beheaded. Finally, they cut off their mother’s head by the sword.

St. Augustine’ and Pope of Rome Gregory (590-604 AD) commended that martyr mother and her seven sons, in the celebration of their martyrdom during the 2nd century AD. In his homily, Pope Gregory described what St. Felicitas has gone through. He said about her: “having seven children, she was as much afraid of leaving them behind her on earth, as other mothers are of surviving theirs. She was more than a martyr, for seeing her seven dear children martyred before her own eyes, she was, in some sort, a martyr in each one of them. She was the eighth in the order of time, but was from the first to the last in pain, and began her martyrdom in the eldest, and she only finished it in her death. She received a crown not only for herself but likewise for all her children. Seeing them in torments, she remained constant, feeling their pains by nature as their mother, but rejoicing for them in her heart by hope.”

[Butler: July 10]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Repentant, p. 245
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE REPENTANT, ST. — Her Repose

If you obey my advice and counsel, God will be with you and keep you from the evil one and from all the enemies.”

The Abbot of the monastery stood outside the cell listening until the end. He realized that this monk was wrongly accused. Then, he knocked on the door to enter and receive the blessing of the monk before his departure to find out that he has already delivered his soul. Having heard from the Abbot of the monastery all that he saw and heard, all the monks came to the body of their brother Theodore to proclaim their remorse for what they have done. When they started the ritual for burying him, they realized that he was a woman. And, the news spread all over Alexandria, and multitudes came over to seek her blessing. When her husband heard about what happened and perceiving that she was Theodora, his wife, he bitterly wept, remembering how he has previously seen her and did not recognize her while leading her camel. He then implored the Abbot of the monastery to accept him as a monk, to spend the rest of his days worshipping in her cell. As to the little kid, he remained in the monastery, grew up in grace, to be loved by everyone, and ended up eventually becoming the Abbot of the monastery.

[Chéneau: Les Saints d’Egypte, Bk 2, pp. 324-9] [The Archimandrite Michael Assaf: The Book of the Synaxarion – 11 Eilol]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Felicitas and her Seven Sons, p. 116
passages.text:
Saint: FELICITAS AND HER SEVEN SONS (The martyrs)

St. Felicitas (Felicity) has been a Christian widow of a noble origin. After the death of her husband, she lived serving God, dedicated her life to prayer and works of mercy; so that her life and that of her family came to be a role model, which had a significant impression on so many pagans, that most of them converted to Christianity. The pagan priests complained about her to Emperor Antonius Pius (138-161 AD), accusing her of turning many people away from worshipping their eternal gods, and claimed that those gods would undoubtedly get mad and harm the city, if not the whole empire. The mad emperor ordered Publius, the governor of Rome, to arrest Felicitas and her seven sons and to bring them before him.

St. Felicitas stood before the emperor, who vigorously attempted to apply pressure on her, to make her sacrifice to the gods so that he would not have to use violence against her and her sons. But she answered him: “Do not think that you could make me fear your threats, or to seduce my heart by your nice talk; for the Spirit of God inside me will surely strengthen me and will hold me fast to have victory over your threats.” The emperor said to her: “How miserable you are! If you wish to die, why would you destroy your children along with you?” The saint answered him: “My children will live forever if they are faithful to the True God, but would perish forever if they sacrifice to your idols.”

On the next day, the governor brought Felicitas and her seven sons before him, and said to her, “Have mercy on your children, O Felicitas, for they are in the peak of their youth.” The mother answered him: “Your compassion is deceitful, and your words are evil.” Then, she addressed her children, saying, “My children! Look up at heaven, where Jesus Christ and His saints are waiting for you. Be faithful in His love. Fight with courage for the sake of your lives.”

Governor Publius ordered his men to strike her on her mouth, saying to her: “How dare you provoke them to disobey the emperor?” He then brought her children one after the other, attempting to seduce them by promises and by threats, to worship the idols, and as they all refused, he ordered to cast them in prison. The governor raised their case to the emperor, who ordered killing them in different ways: the eldest son Januarius was scourged to death, Felix and Philip were beaten with clubs until they died, Sylvanus was thrown down a cliff, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were beheaded. Finally, they cut off their mother’s head by the sword.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Reparata, the Virgin, p. 13
passages.text:
Saint: REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine. When she was 12 years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249- 251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her head off, she walked with them singing praise. Finally, when she was beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she was honored by several dioceses.

[Butler: October 8]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 668–669
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

Many nuns were given the gift of true leadership and spiritual discernment, like St. Sarah of whom it was said that she lived for sixty years on the banks of a river, but never lifted her eyes to look at it. Many of her sayings were preserved in the sayings of the desert fathers and mothers.

St. Hilaria: In the fourth century, the daughter of Emperor Zeno fled to Scetis where she led a life of asceticism in the attire of a male monk. When her sister, Theopiste, was possessed by an evil spirit, the elders of the wilderness sent her to St. Hilaria to pray for her, and did not know that St. Hilaria was a woman. She prayed all night for her and embraced her. Theopiste was healed, and she told the emperor about the monk, “Hilarion,” who healed her and was embracing her, so her father was disturbed. He called for her to come to the palace, where she revealed to him that she was his daughter after he had promised not to prevent her from going back to her cave.

St. Syncletica: Some historians regard her to be the equal of St. Anthony, the star of the wilderness; for as St. Anthony was the father of all monks, St. Syncletica was a mother to that group of virgins which transformed the fertile valley of Egypt into a dwelling place for the grace of God. She was born to noble parents who settled in Alexandria to be close to the School of Alexandria. They had two sons and two daughters, so they wanted to educate them in all sciences, which were only offered in the School of Alexandria. This family was shocked at the death of Syncletica’s youngest brother in his childhood, while the older one departed on the night of his wedding. These two shocks caused Syncletica to ponder and contemplate the pleasures of the world and see them as nothing but a deceptive mirage. Syncletica persevered in her fasting, prayer, asceticism, and worship in her parents’ house till they departed to heaven. Then, she distributed her money on the poor and took her sister to their family’s tomb, where they lived for a few years. During this period, she redoubled her fasts, prayers, and ascetic practices. A substantial number of young women went to visit her. Some went simply to see her and take her blessing, while others came seeking solutions to their problems. It was natural for some of them to be influenced by her example and desire to stay with her and participate in the life of asceticism and contemplation.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theopesti, pp. 282–283
passages.text:
Saint: THEOPESTI, ST. — Her Monastic Life

He said to the bishop: “At midnight my mother called me, bid me farewell, and told me: “My son, whatever the bishop tells you, do it, and never disobey him; for I shall repose tonight and go to the Lord Christ.” She prayed for me and reposed in peace.

Knocking on the door of her room and getting no response, the bishop entered to find her already reposed, clothed by the holy monastic Eskeem, which he put on her in his night vision, along with his head cover. Then, he cried, praised, and glorified God for providing such high honors to His saints.

The bishop shrouded her the way the nuns are wrapped, and the priests carried her body to the church and prayed on her soul with great reverence. A crippled pagan man, hearing about her story, sought from his family to take him to where her body was laid. By touching her body with great faith, he was healed and started to walk and glorify God. The pagan man then, along with his entire household, was baptized on the hands of the bishop. All those inflicted by maladies came to the Church and, by touching her body with faith, they were all healed. The Church celebrates her repose on the 20th of Tout.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theopesti, p. 282
passages.text:
Saint: THEOPESTI, ST. — Her Monastic Life

St. Theopesti was married to a man from whom she had one son. Her husband passed away while she was still young, and she longed to dedicate her life to the worship of the Lord. She vowed herself to the monastic life and started practicing prayers and fasting with continuous metanoias day and night.

She encountered St. Abba ‘Macarius,’ bishop of Nikios (Abshati), now ‘Zawyet-Razin’, in the Egyptian governorate of ‘El-Menoufyia’... When she told the bishop about her vow, and him seeing how young she was, he sought from her not to rush the matter, but to test herself first for one year, before she would decide to become a nun and put on the monastic Eskeem. With obedience full of faith, she returned to her house; closed herself in a room where she carefully practiced the monastic life; without being negligent of her caring for her only son, who was 12 years old at the time. She spiritually cared for him through being a good role model, and he, in turn, cared for her needs. In his mother, the young boy saw the image of the Lord Christ, and in her life, he smelled His sweet fragrance.

Her Monastic Life:

A whole year passed, and the bishop already forgot all about what he promised St. Theopesti with; until he saw her in a night vision. She was in splendid attire, saying to him: “Father, how did you forget me until now while I am going to depart tonight?” The bishop then saw himself in the vision, standing and praying on the saint the prayers of consecrating the nuns, and to cover her head, he took off his head cove and put it on her head; then, he put on her the holy Eskeem. Then, she asked the bishop to accept from her a silver cross, which was in her hand. The next morning, when the bishop woke up, he found the silver cross in his hand. Accompanied by his disciple, the bishop headed to where she lived to see her little son meeting them with a flow of tears. He said to the bishop: “At midnight my mother called me, bid me farewell, and told me: “My son, whatever the bishop tells you, do it, and never disobey him; for I shall repose tonight and go to the Lord Christ.” She prayed for me and reposed in peace.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Agape, p. 98
passages.text:
Saint: AGAPE (The martyr)

The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of the martyrdom of the three saintly virgin sisters: Agape, Irene, and Chionia on the 8th of Baramouda. Those virgins, pious, and lovers of the Lord Christ were bound together by their bold, strong love to the Lord. They used to go often to visit a convent in Thessalonica their town, and they practiced with joy the pious ascetic life, imitating the nuns.

When Diocletian and Maximilian stirred up their persecution, those virgins escaped to the mountain, carrying with them some of the books from the convent and hid in a cave, where they continued their ascetic life.

An older woman used to visit them once every week to provide them with their needs, sell their handiwork, and to give what is left to the poor on their behalf. When an evil man saw her going that often to the mountain, he thought that she was hiding some precious items there. Therefore, one time he followed her from afar until he saw her entering that cave. He waited until she went away, and he entered the cave to find the brides of Jesus Christ praying. The evil man tied them up and brought them over to the governor.

Asking them about their faith, they confessed that they were Christians, worshippers of Jesus Christ. The governor scoffed them and provoked them to eat of what was sacrificed to the idols, which they refused. The governor then publicly burned the convent’s books he found with those sisters. Then, the emperor met with them; and the following exchange took place in his presence:

Agape: “Holy emperor! Though it is your business to care for the State and the army, yet it is not your business to talk against the Living God, without whom you cannot do anything."

Here, the governor addressed ‘Chionia’: “Talk some sense into your sister; she is foolish!” Chionia answered: “My sister is in perfect understanding. And she is perfectly correct in denying the evil sacrifices."

Addressing ‘Irene,’ the youngest sister, he said to her. “Be wiser than your two sisters." Moreover, she answered that even if what her sisters said was madness, she would accept that.

records.question: Who was St. Bishoy?
records.answer:
St. Bishoy was a Coptic Orthodox saint born around the year 320 AD in the village of Shansa, in the governorate of El-Menufyia [1]. He was one of six brothers, raised by their mother after their father passed away when they were young [1]. At the age of twenty, in 340 AD, he went to the wilderness of Scetis (Shiheet) to become a disciple of Abba Bemwah, who was a disciple of St. Macarius [1]. He lived a life of seclusion, worshipping in his cell for three years without leaving it, growing in virtue and love for God [1].

After Abba Bemwah's death, St. Bishoy and Abba John the Short prayed for guidance; an angel instructed that Abba John remain while St. Bishoy should leave and live in a cave about two miles away [2]. St. Bishoy practiced intense asceticism: he tied a rope to his hair to keep himself awake during prayers, fasted the whole week eating only on Saturdays, and memorized most of the Holy Bible, especially the Book of Jeremiah, which he loved deeply [2]. He also valued manual labor as part of spiritual life and rejected worldly wealth, instructing a rich man to give gold to the poor instead of monks [2].

St. Bishoy had a close fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ, often seeing Him and speaking with Him in visions. Jesus appeared to him multiple times, encouraging him and promising to be with him always [3]. Once, St. Bishoy carried an old man who was actually the Lord Jesus Christ in disguise; Jesus told him that because of this, his body would never see decay [12]. St. Bishoy's body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration [12].

In 407 AD, due to Berber attacks on Scetis, St. Bishoy fled to Ansena in Upper Egypt, where he formed a close friendship with St. Paul of Tamouh. They asked the Lord not to be separated in death, and their bodies were later buried together [6][7]. St. Bishoy reposed on the 8th of Abib in 417 AD at the age of 97 and was buried near Ansena; his body was eventually moved back to the Monastery of Abba Bishoy in the Natron Valley [7].

St. Bishoy is remembered for his simple life founded on love and fellowship with Jesus Christ, his intense asceticism, prayer, fasting, love of Scripture, and spiritual writings that benefited many monks and laypeople [1][2][8].
