passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — In Scetis (Shiheet)

Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it and reign with power and dominion!

St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El- Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them up. One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: ‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life.’” She answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9).

In Scetis (Shiheet):

Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple of Abba ‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 358–359
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Life in Seclusion

Life in Seclusion:

When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the guidance of God. An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the Short’ should remain alone in that location. In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left the place forsaking his friend, and dug for himself a cave near the southern rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

His Strife:

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it. Then, he used to tie the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his heart; that it was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’

He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. He believed in the saying: “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.” (2 Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus;

Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on a friendship level. He used to see Him, to talk with Him, and to enjoy His Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persistent in his great ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and behold, I shall always be with you!”

Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored at all!”

A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: “Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My commandments; I shall save him from all temptations!” He then blessed him and ascended.

Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted him and blessed him. The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with water in a basin, then the Lord ascended. St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water and left a portion for his disciple. The saint sought from him more than once to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul of Tamouh, pp. 380–381
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL OF TAMOUH, ST. ABBA

The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of this saint on the 7th of Baba, and seeks his prayers in the commemoration of the saints in the Liturgy, along with St. Ezekiel his disciple.

After the devastation of the wilderness of the Scetis around the year, 408 AD; St. Abba Bishoi fled the area and went to mount Anesna in Upper Egypt. There, he met with Abba Paul the Hermit and they both had an amazing spiritual friendship, that an angel appeared to St. Paul, saying: “Your body will be with that of Abba Bishoi.” (The two bodies are still together in one tube in the Monastery of Abba Bishoi up to this very day). It was said that later on when the bishop of Anesna decided to move the body of Abba Bishoi; his boat did not move until a hermit named Jeremiah told them about the promise of the Lord to Abba Paul, so they brought the body of Abba Paul to the boat and they moved them together to the Monastery of Abba Shenouda in Akhmim. Later on, the bodies of these two saints were moved again together in the days of the 52nd Pope Yusab I in the 9th century (831- 849 AD) to the Monastery of Abba Bishoi in the Scetis. The bodies of the two saints were kept in one tube; and this is a testimony of the spiritual friendship full of love that bound the two saints together; that even death could not separate them. This is not on the level of this mortal world but the level of the Eternal glory of both the body and the soul.

Abba Paul was known for his great love of worship, particularly for the perpetual prayers, as well as his serious asceticism, that his disciple Ezekiel told about him that he faced death six times because of his harsh asceticism.

He lived in solitude as a hermit, in perpetual strife, that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him saying: “Enough labor, My beloved Paul”. St. Abba Paul answered Him: “O my Master, let me exhaust my body for the sake of Your Name; as You have done for the sake of mankind. Even though You are God, You delivered Yourself for our sake, we who are unworthy.”

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt; p. 223-4]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 361–362
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Forsaking Scetis

Forsaking Scetis:

In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John the Short’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “Do you fear death, O man of God?” He answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell because of me!”

St. ‘John the Short’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba ‘Anthony’ where he reposed. Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain. There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose, and God granted them their wish.

St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. ‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints' bodies and buried them together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El- Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

They are now in the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy’ in the Natron Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 356–357
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

The story of this saint reveals the fantastic plan of God for the salvation of every soul; how He uses every tool to draw them to Him, and how He sets them on the highest level if they receive His call and respond to it.

This saint, also (called ‘Peter’), was born in the village of ‘Epsona,’ a suburb of ‘Akhmim.’ In his youth, he walked in an evil path; but God did not leave him there but allowed for him to fall ill, and in a night vision, He revealed to him the place of the eternal sufferings which he was heading to. He bitterly wept, and raised his eyes to heaven and cried out: “My Lord and my God! If

you heal me of this illness; I shall repent, return to You and worship You

with all my heart.” ‘Bishai’ (Peter) was healed, and he did not forget his promise to the Lord, but he was inflamed in his heart with an intense longing to experience the monastic life. He forsook the sheep he was shepherding, and set forth to the monastery where he met with St. ‘Bigol,’ the uncle of St. ‘Shenouda’ (who was to become the Archimandrite in Mount Adriba).

His Monastic Life:

God used the illness to bring that young man out of the covetousness of the body, which would destroy the soul. Once he tasted the real spiritual life, his heart got filled with so much joy to set forth firmly and be willing to do so many labors enduring daily so many harsh sufferings with a joyful heart.

He lived with St. ‘Bigol’ in a fantastic friendship, partaking together in monasticism and worship without ever getting bored, watching the nights, and opposing the temptations of the devil.

God granted him an exalted capability beyond the limits of human endurance; he used to fast, in a way that defied imagination, for a whole month not tasting anything, and by a fantastic Divine allowance, he would stand the entire night praying. God, in His love, granted him to have the deeds of other people revealed before his eyes, which he used to support them on the life of true repentance. Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Badaba, p. 287
passages.text:
Saint: BADABA, ABBA (The martyr) — Their Monastic Life

This saint was born in the city of ‘Armant’ in the governorate of ‘Qena,’ to a pious family; his father was called ‘Mina.’ The name ‘Badaba’ is derived from the Hieroglyphic word ‘Batby’: meaning (the principal/the essential) and from the Coptic word ‘Bataby’: meaning (related to the head).

A strong friendship developed between this saint and his cousin ‘Andrew,’ who was two years older. Since their childhood, both carried the same love for the heavenly Kingdom; they encountered one another on the level of the spirit, despised the pleasures of the world, concentrated on the study of the Holy Scriptures and religious books, used to fast two consecutive days with no food or drink, in addition to praying day and night.

Their Monastic Life:

They set forth together to the Eastern mountain at ‘Qasr el-Sayyad’ in the district of 'Nagh Hamadi.' There, they became disciples of St. abba ‘Isaac’ and dwelt in a cell where they performed their spiritual practices. They took upon themselves to copy down the religious manuscripts for their spiritual benefit and to sell them for little money to cover their living expenses and to give what was left to the poor.

As the sweet fragrance of Christ spread from them, their cell became a center of spiritual radiation. Abba ‘Tadros,’ the bishop of the area, came to them and ordained St. ‘Badaba’ as a priest and Andrew as a deacon. They used to perform the holy Liturgy once every forty days in a neighboring church.

It so happened that abba ‘Tadros’ once entered into that church, and he saw the face of St. ‘Badaba’ shining with an amazing splendor and a crown as though of gold on his head. So, he longed to have him and deacon ‘Andrew’ to stay with him in the diocese. However, St. ‘Badaba’ excused himself and returned to his cell, whereas ‘Andrew’ consented to do so. And, when St. ‘Badaba’ perceived that everyone was chasing him, he fled away from his cell, which the bishop dedicated as a church, later on.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef Ĥabib, the Deacon, pp. 364–365
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF ĤABIB, THE DEACON

After the Holy Liturgy and the rites of ordination, he went back to his work. He submitted his resignation on the same day in order to dedicate all his time and effort to a better activity.

When Fr. Bishoy came back from the Syrian Monastery in the Natrun Valley after the 40 days the new priest has to spend after his ordination; he found Yousef Ĥabib had dedicated himself to serve, day and night, in that new church of St. George in the district of Sporting in Alexandra. He took upon himself, without being asked by anyone, to support Fr. Bishoy at the beginning of his ministry in a new church that had no deacons, cantor, or ministers. Yousef Ĥabib was a first-class ecclesiastical man who elaborately knew by heart all the Church hymns and sang them with the spirit of prayer in a very touching voice. With that beginning, Yousef Ĥabib became the teacher of the Church’s young men and boys and let them absorb the spirit of the Fathers. He raised them on the love of the church and her hymns. Then, when the church came to have a cantor, her beautiful choir of deacons and her affairs started to settle down. Yousef Ĥabib withdrew himself in humility and self-denial and shifted his whole effort towards a new field to revive our ecclesiastical heritage.

Yousef Ĥabib, for a long time, has been fond of the biographies of the Saints, in particular of those whose fragrant life stories had not been published before. He started to travel to the desert monasteries to search in their libraries treasures about what was hidden, and he brought to light tens of biographies and rare stories. He also used to research in the libraries of the Coptic Museum and the library of the Patriarchate, etc. He even purchased a permanent train travel permit to go back and forth to Cairo twice a week for that purpose. He used to translate, research in the biographies of the Saints and their sayings, then returned home to publish them in small booklets, to the benefit of ministry, and for the improvement of the souls.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai of Antioch, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI OF ANTIOCH, ST. (The martyr)

‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was ordained as a priest because of his piety. His brother and his mother went to Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to take care of their bodies. Then, he felt the longing to partake in their crowns. So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies.

The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: ‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren greatly rejoiced, and all of them set forth toward the mountain. The saint, because of his old age, was at the rear. There, he encountered an older man overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passingby monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he did carry him and walked without feeling any labor. However, the older man started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself. He then looked at Him and said: “The heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the earth; how can a sinner like me carry You?” To this, the Lord Jesus Christ smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration up to this very day. Once the brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yusab El-Abaĥ, the Bishop, pp. 373–374
passages.text:
Saint: YUSAB EL-ABAĤ, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

When Abba Yusab became advanced in age, carrying on his shoulders the troubles of 91 years in serving the Church he loved, he took refuge in the hospitality of pope Butros VII (El-Gawli). However, he was longing to set forth to heaven in the monastery of Abba Anthony, so he moved there and delivered his soul in the hands of the Lord on the 24th of January 1826; within a few days of his arrival to the monastery. He was cared for and buried by the monks of the monastery. After several years of his burial, his body was found intact. So, they took it out and put it in a special burial place in the church of the monastery. The Coptic Church honored that revered bishop and righteous theologian by including him in the Synaxarion in the day he reposed.

Of his Words:

• If we break our fast while the Church is fasting; we would be removing ourselves, and would become a stumbling block to others and a reason behind the fall of the weak. • Do not fast on bread and salt, while you are devouring the flesh of the others by condemnation and abomination. And, do not proclaim that you fast clean fasting while getting dirty through all those iniquities.

[Amir Nasr: St. Abba Josab (El-Abah), Bishop of Girga and Akhmim, Cairo 1985]

[The Coptic Encyclopedia: Yusab, by Khalil Samir, S.J.; pp. 2360-62]

Notes: [1] Such as the custom of celebrating martyrs by large banquets, for which musicians, singers and poets were hired, out of vainglory; and to which the poor were not invited… [2] Book title in Arabic is: "سالح المؤمنين”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Badaba, p. 288
passages.text:
Saint: BADABA, ABBA (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

In the era of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), while ‘Ariana,’ governor of ‘Ansena’ was visiting Upper Egypt to torture the Christians, the bishop came to know that the governor arrived at ‘Esna,’ and was killing all its inhabitants. The bishop gathered all his congregation, urged them to hold fast to their faith, to receive the suffering with joy, blessed them, and bid them farewell. He then went, together with his cousin ‘Andrew,’ and St. ‘Christotholo’ to Esna, and there, they confessed the Lord Christ, and suffered many tortures. The Lord Christ appeared to St. ‘Badaba’ and said to him: “Have comfort, O My beloved ‘Badaba’; I am with you.” Then, He ascended to heaven, surrounded by a multitude of angels.

The three of them received the crowns of martyrdom on the 29th of Abib. At the time, St. ‘Badaba’ was 68 years old, of which he spent 15 years in his father’s house, 49 years in the monastic life, and three and a half years as a bishop on ‘Qift.’

Recently, the bishop of ‘Qift,’ the reverent abba ‘Theophilus,’ wrote the biography of St. ‘Badaba’ the martyr. And, it was published by the clerical ‘Rushdi Wasef Behman’ through the Anba Rowes Press in 1984.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yusab El-Abaĥ, the Bishop, pp. 371–372
passages.text:
Saint: YUSAB EL-ABAĤ, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

St. Yusab el-Abaĥ set forth to the monastery of Abba Anthony, where Fr. Ibrahim St. Anthony, the Abbot of the monastery welcomed him and gave him his blessings. Then, the Abbot sought from the elder Fathers to test him for a while. After that, they joyfully admitted him. Yousef lived among them with the gladness of heart. Earning their love and trust, they prayed over him, clothed him with the monastic attire by the name of Yousef St. Anthony.

He started to study the old manuscripts which were kept in the monastery library, and he searched through the wealth of Church literature and theology until he acquired a good deal of the religious culture and the general knowledge. And, in addition to his spiritual strife in prayers, fasting, and asceticism, he used to serve the elderly fathers with love; until they recommended him for the grace of the priesthood. He was ordained as a priest, then as a hegumenus. He ministered the holy altar and the Holy Sacraments with humility and a contrite heart; that he was filled with the Divine Grace and became well-known.

His Relationship with the Popes of Alexandria:

Abba Yusab was a contemporary of 5 of the popes of Alexandria: 1- He was born during the reign of the 105th Pope Yoannes XVII (1727-1745). 2- He became a monk during the reign of the 106th Pope Marcos VII (1745- 1769). 3- He was ordained as a bishop by the 107th Pope Yoannes XVIII (1769-1796). 4- He participated in the election and the ordination of the 108th Pope Marcos VIII (1796-1809). He also was the head of the bishops who prayed over his body after he departed, and gave a eulogy in which he enumerated that pope’s virtues. 5- He took part in the election and the ordination of the 109th Pope Butros VII (El-Gawli: 1809-1852).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abahor, the Monk, p. 29
passages.text:
Saint: ABAHOR, THE MONK, ST.

This father from ‘Abraht’ in the area of the ‘Ashmonein,’ was an elect monk who surpassed many saints in his worship. Loving solitude and living alone in the wilderness, he was envied by the devil who appeared to him and said: “In the wilderness, you can overcome me because you are there alone, but I challenge you if you are brave, go to Alexandria." He instantly set forth to Alexandria, where he stayed sometimes serving the prisoners.

It so happened that some horses were galloping in midtown, and one of them knocked down a little kid who instantly died. As St. Abahor was standing at the place where that incident took place, the devil provoked some people around to shout aloud, claiming that it was the old monk who killed him. When many started to revile and to scoff him, St. Abahor calmly took the kid to his bosom, prayed in his heart to the Lord Christ, and then made the sign of the cross on him. The kid came back to life, and he gave him to his parents. Those around him glorified God and started to make it up to the old monk, who, fearing from the vainglory, he fled to the wilderness, where he dwelt for days in a monastery.

When it was time for him to depart from this world, he saw a group of saints calling him to join them, for which he greatly rejoiced, became joyful, called his spiritual disciples to inform them that he will soon depart to the Lord Christ, and provided them with his last commandment. Hearing that, they much grieved that they will be orphans after his departure. He felt sick for a little while, and then he delivered his soul in the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 2 Kiahk]

records.question: Who was St. Anthony, the Father of the Monks?
records.answer:
St. Anthony, the Father of the Monks, was born around the year 251 AD in the village of Komn Al-Aros (Qiman El-Arous), Egypt, to wealthy parents [1][10]. After his father's death, he was deeply moved by the mortality of the world and sought eternity. At the age of eighteen, he heard the Gospel reading of Matthew 19:21, "If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me," which he took as a personal call to dedicate his life to God. He sold his inheritance, gave the proceeds to the poor, and placed his sister in a convent [1][10].

He initially lived near the Nile, practicing strict asceticism and prayer, and later moved to the inner wilderness around 285 AD, dwelling in a cave on Mount Al-Kalzam near the Red Sea to live a life of seclusion and spiritual struggle against demons [1]. Around 305 AD, he began to guide disciples who sought his spiritual training, thus founding the monastic movement and the order of seclusion [2].

St. Anthony was not a member of the clergy but a civic founder of monasticism, focusing on seclusion without interfering with the Church hierarchy. Despite his love for solitude, he remained connected to the Church, supporting Pope Athanasius the Apostolic and the martyrs, and opposing Arianism [2][10][11]. He was known for his cheerfulness and inner joy despite his ascetic life and lived to the age of 105 [2].

Though illiterate, St. Anthony overcame Greek philosophers by the purity of his heart and was comforted by God through his mind rather than books [2][3]. He is remembered for teachings such as the importance of loving one's neighbor and the spiritual authority gained through obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures [3].

He is considered the founder of Christian monasticism worldwide and is celebrated on the 22nd of Toba in the Coptic Church [1][3]. He died in 352 AD after a life that inspired many disciples and monastic leaders [10][11].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthonius, and Other Saints with That Name, pp. 195–196
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONIUS, and Other Saints with that Name (The martyrs) — ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr

Often confusion takes place between the martyrs who carried the name ‘Anthony,' among whom are:

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr:

He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop assigned him to build a Church, the pagans were stirred up against him and killed him.

ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr:

St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to ‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his Christ, he ordered him chained and sent him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built. Abba Anthony’s idea was that if a monk wished to visit those living there, he could start walking after he finished eating at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone.

His Personality and the Role of Nitria;

Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away from the crowd and refrained from performing any miracles, claiming that he was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba Amon.

St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM

Besides his discipleship to Alexander, there were two other great influences in his life:

1- From his seventh year to the fifteenth he lived during a period of severe persecution (303 - 311 CE). He knew many among the Alexandrian martyrs and confessors from whom he learned the Orthodox faith and a loving intimacy with the Holy Scriptures. He did not accompany them to the arena of persecution but his heart was aflame with divine love, facing every struggle for the sake of Christ.

2- After he heard about St. Anthony the hermit, he hurried to the wilderness and lived with him for about three years, practicing the ascetic and righteous life and the deep fellowship with God. Providence arranged this close relationship with Anthony so that during his exiles and flight he never felt lonely. Instead he considered it a good opportunity for him to have a bit of solitude and seclusion, praying for his people and writing to them. He was obliged to become the historian of St. Anthony .

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of St. Anthony Mountain, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN

On the 26th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidrak St. Anthony and his Companions, p. 147
passages.text:
Saint: SIDRAK ST. ANTHONY AND HIS COMPANIONS (The martyrs)

A monk from the monastery of St. Anthony by the name of Sidrak, left his monastery with a colleague by the name of Fadl-Allah and accompanied them their close friend Daoud el-Banna. They all came down together from the mountain of St. Anthony to receive the crowns of martyrdom Those saints were martyred during the rule of the Circassian Mamluks (1382-1517) .

They were following the lead of St. Anthony, the Father of all Monks, who came down to Alexandria in the days of Emperor Maximian (286-305 AD) saying: “Let me go to where the fire of sufferings is. If the Divine care allowed for my martyrdom, I would be ready; and if not, I shall at the least stand by those persecuted among the children of St. Mark the Evangelist...”

[The Patriotism and History of the Coptic Church, p. 250]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisoes, the Great, pp. 168–169
passages.text:
Saint: SISOES, THE GREAT, ST. — Abba Anthony his Role Model

After the repose of Abba Anthony the Great, St. Sisoes (Shishoi/Shishai) was one of the most shining pillars of faith among the Fathers of the wilderness. Therefore, this saint is referred to as St. “Sisoes the Great.” Shishoi means: The Son of the High One. He was an Egyptian by birth, and when he reached 20 years of age, he forsook the world and sought refuge in the wilderness of Scetis in the year 340 AD, and became a disciple to St. Macarius. In the year 356 AD, longing for a life of more tranquility, he crossed the Nile to the Mountain of St. Anthony right after his departure, to have the blessings of the life and virtues of St. Anthony as light and helper in his new life. He set forth to a life of seclusion until the year 426 AD when he reached the age of 106 years, and because of old age, he returned to the wilderness of Scetis, and reposed after a little while when he reached 110 years of age. About him, Abba Poemen (Bemen) said: “He exalted beyond every limit, and surpassed all the achievements of the other saintly Fathers.”

Abba Anthony his Role Model:

St. Sisoes was acting as if Abba Anthony the Great was watching him and listening to his instructions to his disciples. He strove to imitate that great teacher in all his life: in his asceticism, in his spiritual practices, in his commitment to silence and his longing for prayers. Therefore, his fame spread, and so many people came to him requesting to be his disciples. At this point, he had to forsake his love for silence and seclusion, to fulfill a higher goal, namely loving care of his disciples. Abba Sisoes’s brother came to visit him in the cave of Abba Anthony, where he was staying. The saint amiably said to his brother: “In this cave, a lion used to live; now it is inhabited by a fox.”

St. Sisoes always was complaining that he did not reach the statue of St. Anthony. Once, a monk asked him: “Father! Have you not reached the level of St. Anthony?” He answered: “If I had only one of the virtues of that monk, I would have become a torch of Divine Love.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 667–668
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia): He was born in upper Egypt around the year 290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the year 290 A. D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he established many monasteries in Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles.

St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart. He led an ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness to become his disciples.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pelosianus, p. 396
passages.text:
Saint: PELOSIANUS, ST.

This saint was a friend of Abba Anthony the Great (251-356 AD). He took part in burying Abba Anthony along with his fellow monk Isaac. It seems that St. Jerome (342-420 AD), who told us about him, has met him somewhere.

[Jerome: Vita Hilarionis, 30; 31]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef, Father [a Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great], p. 367
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF, FATHER [A Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great]

This Father Yousef was one of the prominent elders of the wilderness in the 4th century. All we know about him is that he happened to go to visit St. Anthony the Great in the company of two fellow elder hermits. St. Anthony tried to put them to the test, so he asked them about specific topics in the Holy Bible. The first and second hermits gave some answers. To them, St. Anthony said that their responses were not satisfactory. However, when Fr. Yousef said humbly: “I truly say, O Father, I do not know. I am utterly helpless in that concern.” Over his response, St. Anthony said: “Fr. Yousef alone found the right answer, by saying: ‘I do not know.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, p. 160
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

He was the founder of the monastic movement in ‘Nitria’ (Bernoug). Here, we need to distinguish between three monastic zones within the Natron Valley (Wadi El-Natrun) which often get mixed up:

1- The ’Nitria’ (Bernoug) zone, which received the first spark of the monastic movement through Abba Amon. 2- The ‘Celia’ (the Cells) zone, which is about 10 miles south of the ‘Nitria’ zone. 3- The ‘Scetis’ (Askeet) zone, which is located to the south of the former two zones.

His Monastic Life:

Saint Amon the great was born around the year 275 AD near the region of Marriott. He was raised as an orphan, and when he reached 22 years of age, his uncle forced him to get married despite his refusal. When he got married, he and his bride agreed on living virgins. Eighteen years later, the saint set forth to the desert of ‘Nitria’ (the city of Nitria or Bernoug is 14 kilometers Southwestern of the city of Damanhur). He was the first monk to reach that area, and he built for himself a cell there, in which he lived for 22 years. During that time, he used twice a year to visit his wife, who was living with many pious virgins. The location of the ‘Nitria’ zone was convenient to be the cradle of the commencement of that monastic movement. That area was close to the countryside and to the desert at the same time. In the beginning, the monks, who followed St. Amon, worked to earn their living by cropping the wheat, and it was easy for them also to acquire the linen to weave, instead of the palm leaves. The area also provided them with the ‘Natron’, which they could extract from the lake and sell to the villages around them. However, the region was always infested by mosquitos because of its swamps.

A congregation of hermits started to gather around the saint. They all lived in a life midway between the system of seclusion and that of the cenobite. Abba Amon was the first head of such a monastic congregation in Nitria, and many of his disciples became great fathers. Abba Amon used to visit Abba Anthony to seek his blessing and guidance. And when Abba Anthony came to visit him, he asked his advice concerning some pious monks, who tried to live a solitary life and build for themselves cells far away from the congregation. After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built.

records.question: Who was Pope Cyril I of Alexandria?
records.answer:
Pope Cyril I of Alexandria, also known as "Cyril the Great" and "Cyril the Pillar of Faith," was the 24th Pope of Alexandria. He is notably linked to the second great Christological controversy, leading the Second Ecumenical Council in Ephesus in 431 AD, which condemned Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople. Cyril is considered one of the outstanding Fathers and theologians of the Church, with the patristic understanding of the Incarnation largely attributed to him [1][16].

Born between 375 and 380 AD, Cyril was raised in a pious and wealthy family originally from Memphis (Arcadia). After the death of his grandparents, an Ethiopian nursemaid who loved Christianity cared for his uncle Theophilus and his mother. This nursemaid converted to Christianity after a miraculous event at a pagan temple and was baptized along with the children. Cyril received extensive classical and theological education in Alexandria, including instruction from his uncle, Pope Theophilus. He was knowledgeable in religious books, the Holy Bible, and the sayings and biographies of the Church Fathers. He also had a talent for memorizing Church hymns and singing them with a steady voice [1][6][16].

Cyril was sent to the Theological School of Alexandria to study philosophical sciences to defend Christianity against heretics. He also spent five years in the Nitrian Desert at the Abu-Maqar Monastery under Abba Serapion, learning ascetic and ecclesiastical knowledge. After his studies, he was ordained a deacon and then a priest by his uncle, gaining admiration for his sermons and biblical interpretations. He accompanied his uncle to important Church councils, including the Council of the Oak in 403 AD [6].

He became Patriarch of Alexandria in 412 AD, succeeding his uncle Theophilus. His ordination was unanimous and took place shortly after his uncle's death. Early in his papacy, he annulled the excommunication of St. John Chrysostom, honoring him and including his name in the Commemoration of the Saints in the Divine Liturgy of St. Mark [13].

Pope Cyril I defended the Orthodox Faith against various challenges, including the writings of Julian the Apostate, the Novatian heresy, and violent revolts by the Jews against Christians in Alexandria. He was falsely accused of involvement in the death of the philosopher Hypatia. His most critical challenge was opposing the heresy of Nestorius, who claimed that Jesus Christ had two persons and two natures. Cyril refuted this and upheld the unity of Christ's person [10].

Thus, Pope Cyril I was a learned, devout, and courageous leader who played a crucial role in defining Christological doctrine and defending the faith during his tenure from 412 to 444 AD [1][6][10][13][16].
