Saint: MEDIUS (The martyr)

His martyrdom is celebrated with the deaconess Dionisa(Denisa) by the Church on the 13th of Baramouda.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasia, pp. 175–176
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIA, ST. (The martyr)

This Saint was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD) around the year 250 AD, and celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 1st of Baba...

She was the daughter of Christian parents in Rome; they raised her in fear of God. Her heart was full of the Love of God, longing for the angelic life of virginity since her childhood. She joined a convent in Rome to practice the monastic life with firmness, eating food once every two days, and in the Great Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays.

When the mother-superior went to attend a feast in the city, she took with her the virgin Anastasia. In the town, they happened to see soldiers torturing some Christians. So, the virgin Anastasia stopped to rebuke them on their oppression and the hardness of their hearts. However, the soldiers arrested her and brought her forth to the governor. Before the governor, she confessed the Lord Christ. He tortured her severely, crucified her and ignited fire underneath her. And as she persisted in her faith, he ordered to cut her head off by the sword, for which she became exultant, prayed, and delivered her head to the swordsman to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Menodora, Metrodora & Nymphodora, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: MENODORA, METRODORA & NYMPHODORA (The martyrs)

They were three orphan sisters who lived a life of seclusion, with works of mercy and love, in Bithynia. In the days of the persecution against the Christians stirred up by Emperors Diocletian and Maximian (284-305 AD), they were arrested and brought before Fronto, the governor of the province. Fronto was attracted to their beauty and simplicity and suggested to defend them and release them if they agree to worship his gods. The virgin saints rejected his request, preferring death instead. Failing to make them change their minds, the governor ordered to beat their eldest sister Menodora so violently to death to bring fear to her other two sisters. Yet, even the scene of her torn off corpse, which they left to rot in the intense heat of the sun, did not terrify them. Then Metrodora said to the governor: “Being three branches of the same blessed tree, we shall never bring shame to our good roots by fulfilling your request.” So, she was tortured by fire after being violently beaten; then, she was beheaded. Nymphodora, the youngest, was also martyred as a result of her severe beating by her tormentors. They all were martyred in the year 304 AD.

[Butler: September 10]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius, pp. 577–578
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

The emperor was amazed and embarrassed; how a man like ‘Nestor’ could prevail over his vast wrestler, and he inquired about the situation and was informed by his men that ‘Demetrius’ prayed for him and made the sign of the Cross over his face.

In anger, the emperor ordered to strike ‘Nestor’ until he would consent to burn incense before his gods and to worship them. When he refused, the emperor ordered to stab him by spears to tear his body off until his death. So, they did that in front of ‘Demetrius’ to terrify him and lead him to deny his faith in the Lord Christ. However, he told them: “Do whatever you like, for I shall never worship or burn incense, except before my Lord Jesus Christ the True God.” So, the soldiers stabbed him with spears until he delivered his pure spirit in the hands of the Lord.

Some believers took his holy body, and they kept it hidden in a marble coffin until the end of persecution. Then, a great church was built in his name in ‘Thessalonica,’ where his relics were hidden. In the saint’s name, many miracles were performed, and fragrant myrrh oil flowed from his tomb, which healed whoever has used it with faith. Since the 7th century, a large quantity of the miraculous myrrh oil flowed on the walls and columns of that Church; and it was plenty enough for all people present to wipe it off and transfer it into their vessels.

[The Synaxarion: 29 Baba] [Orthodox Church in America Web Site: Lives of the Saints: Demetrius the Myrrh-Gusher of Thessalonica]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sophia and the Fifty Virgins, p. 180
passages.text:
Saint: SOPHIA AND THE FIFTY VIRGINS (The martyrs)

In one of the convents close to the city of Edessa (El-Roha) in Iraq, fifty virgins were living with their pious mother-superior Sophia. All of them earnestly worshipped God with continuous prayers and fasting. The pagan Emperor Julian (360-363 AD), on his way to fight with his army the Persian king Shapur II (309-379 AD), they passed by this convent. The evil emperor ordered his men to kill all the nuns and their mother-superior and cut them into pieces, and then to rob all that in their convent. So, they all received the crowns of martyrdom. This took place on the 10th of Hator.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Burrier of Martyrs, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE BURRIER OF MARTYRS

This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 miles from Rome. In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius, the priest, Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes.

The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September.

[Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 Vol.; London 1877-1887]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damian, p. 551
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIAN, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was martyred in Antioch. He endured vicious tortures until he delivered his soul into the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 23 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Reparata, the Virgin, p. 13
passages.text:
Saint: REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine. When she was 12 years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249- 251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her head off, she walked with them singing praise. Finally, when she was beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she was honored by several dioceses.

[Butler: October 8]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mania, p. 47
passages.text:
Saint: MANIA, ST.

So many saintly virgins used to live in Ancyra in Turkey. They lived in convents following a strict blessed ascetic life. Their numbers reached about 2,000 virgins. One of them, her name was Mania, was quite well known. She was forced by her mother to get married. However, she kept on excusing herself from any physical relationship with her husband, by claiming illness. After a little while, her husband died, and she dedicated her whole life to Christ.

She lived such a holy life in the fear of God that the other virgins used to seek her blessing. They felt ashamed of their sins whenever they see her around. She was always compassionate toward the poor and the strangers, and she worshipped the Lord from her whole heart until she reposed in peace.

[The Paradise of Saints, p. 44]

records.question: How did he die?
records.answer: St. Moses the Black died as a martyr when Barbarians attacked the monastery where he lived. Although he knew about the attack beforehand by the Spirit and sought to escape, he chose to stay with seven brethren who refused to flee. The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. One of the seven who escaped saw seven crowns descending from heaven on the martyred monks. St. Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, at the age of seventy-five or eighty-five. He earned three crowns: for love and intense asceticism, for monasticism and priesthood, and for martyrdom. He was counted as the first martyr in the Scetis [3].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 249–250
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

Not much is known about the past of St. Moses the Black before his repentance. He was most probably one of the Barbarian tribes. His life was so evil that it was said that there was no sin he did not commit. He was born between the years of 330 and 340 AD. It seems that he was a slave of a head of a tribe that worshipped the sun, but because of his extreme evil nature, his master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become the head of an evil gang.

Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ:

Even though an extreme evil-doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking from it to proclaim itself to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened to meet with St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells) coming out of his cell and heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: “What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “I heard that you are a good servant of God. Therefore, I escaped and came to you to let God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins and my great evils.”

St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he has been. Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to contemplate.

For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a loud voice, he confessed all his evil crimes again, with such contrition of heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 252–253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Ordained as a Priest

Ordained as a Priest:

Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: “Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said to him: “There you became all-white Moses.” He responded by saying with humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.”

His Virtues:

He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, but it happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.

Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticism, he was granted by God to perform miracles and signs.

A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from going. When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Virtues

When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a week. During that week, some guests came to visit Fr. Moses. He prepared food for them to eat. On seeing smoke rising from his cell, the brethren said to one another: “Look, Moses has broken his fast and is preparing food for himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they said to him: “Father Moses! You have disregarded the commandment of men, but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”

His Martyrdom:

Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” He told them: “There, they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred monks. Then, he hastened to come down and ran forward to receive his crown of martyrdom.

So, Abba Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, when he was seventy-five years old (or eighty-five). He earned three crowns: the 1st for love and intense asceticism, the 2nd for monasticism and priesthood, and the 3rd for martyrdom. He was counted the first martyr in the Scetis, and he had so many great teachings. His body was kept along with that of his spiritual guide Abba Isidore in one tube at the Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the wilderness.

Moses stood in the church and confessed publicly about all his sins and evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became allwhite. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would leave it, all evil will come back to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your feet.”

His Strife:

St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macarius to find for him a secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept counseling him to stand fast until the devil would get tired of him. He gave him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it.” Father. Abba Isidore took him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 254–255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6)” • Then, the brother asked: “If a man beat his servant for something wrong he did, what should the servant say?” The saint answered: “If he was a good servant, he would possibly say: ‘Have mercy on me, for I made a mistake.’ Thus, he would blame himself and draw the mercy of his master.” • In general, a man should never condemn his neighbor. When in the Old, the hand of God came heavy on the firstborn of the Egyptians, there was no house without a dead son in it. For us, it meant that we should concentrate on our sins and not worry about those of our neighbors, for it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor.

To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad about his neighbor, because it would make you fall in condemnation. Do not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This would bring you peace.

[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria- Diocese of Los Angeles] [Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of OrthodoxWiki]

[Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of Wikipedia]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 251–252
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Strife

There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly angels, about whom the saint said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and returned to his cell.

Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks at night, take their water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to move, until some brethren happened to come to the well, and they carried him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he regained his ability to move.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and carried them to the church. When the thieves realized that he was Moses, who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.

Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. Abba Isidore told him that, to keep him from thinking that by his ascetic efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual repentance, God would fight on our behalf.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, p. 258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands

If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take the monk to the nearest location of the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.

Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not having a steady residence, teaching, preaching, and converting multitudes to Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in the year 372 AD.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

[Baring-Gould: February 7]

Notes: [2] These tribes were known by the name ‘Saracens’… It is worth mentioning that the name ‘Saracens’ was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, pp. 255–256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.

Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to spend the night at her place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.

[The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, pp. 240–241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — The Bitterness of Anguish

St. Moises (Moses) was one of the prominent fathers and saints of the church in the 8th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.

St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Scetis, where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox faith. He used to spend most of his time in worship, that it was said that he did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

The Bitterness of Anguish:

During his bishopric, the Umayyad rulers of Egypt subjected the Copts to extremely severe persecutions, and great anguish dwelt upon the church. The bishops returned to their monasteries to concentrate on prayers and fasts, imploring God to lift that anguish. However, St. Moises remained among his people to encourage them and to keep them holding fast to their faith against the snatching wolves. St. Moises also got the grace to perform miracles and signs, healing sicknesses, as well as the grace of prophecy.

Due to these intolerable persecutions at the time, the number of Copts who converted to Islam reached 24,000 persons. When some archons came to seek from St. Moises to pray to the Lord to lift the anguish from His people, he told them: “My children, be assured that the governor who is persecuting you will perish within this month,” and this was what did happen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Confessor, p. 257
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE CONFESSOR

This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, at the start of the heresy of Novatian. The rest of the confessors were: Fr. Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the system and wrote another message to Cyprian.

After spending about a year in prison (eleven months and few days), St. Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views as unorthodox.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948]

[Baring-Gould: November 25]

Notes: [1] ‘Novatian’ was a Roman bishop and theologian of the 3rd century who took a strict position on readmission of apostates during the persecutions at the time…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — Imprisoned along with the Pope

Imprisoned along with the Pope:

The last of the Umayyad caliphs Marwan ibn Muĥammad (Marwan II: 744-750 AD), arrested the 46th Pope of Alexandria, St. Khael I (743-767 AD). Bishop Moises stayed in the company of the pope, and he longed to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When the soldiers brought them to the tent of Marwan, they forced St. Moises on his knees, raised his feet, and beat him with bronze clubs on his sides and neck. His tormentors were seeking from him a bribe to set him free. The saint did not utter a single word, for he did not understand their Arabic language. When Marwan gave the order to cut the head of Pope Khael I, and the swordsman led him to the place of execution, St. Moises ran after him, despite the attempts of the swordsman to keep him away. An angry soldier intended to kill him if it was not for some officials who did not let him do it. Then, he was cast in prison along with Pope Khael I, and their feet were placed in chains, among many others. However, St. Moises prophesied that they would eventually come out safe from that prison, which was realized when Marwan was defeated by the Abbasids dynasty.

His Prophesy concerning the Umayyad Caliphate:

During the revolt of the Coptic Bashmurians (Coptic rebels) due to the intolerable Umayyad persecution, St. Moises disciple asked him a question concerning when that calamity would come to an end, the saint prophesied: “God will not forsake His church to the end, but He will save her, and this caliphate (of Umayyad) will vanish and be replaced by some other.” This prophecy was realized in 750 AD when the Umayyad dynasty was replaced by the Abbasids.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

Abba Moises continued to accompany Pope Khael I, faithful to him and to the church all along during the bitter tribulations. Then, when he completed his strife and was in a right old age, he had a short illness and knew the time of his departure. So, he called his congregation, blessed them, commanded them, and asked them to pray for him. They all wept and asked him to remember them before Christ. He stretched out his hand, prayed, bid them farewell, and departed in peace.

The Church of Saint Mina in Marriott:

Bishop Moises was with pope Khael I when the Chalcedonians (Melkites Byzantine Christians) tried to take possession of the great church of St. Mina in Marriott to take away its marble pillars and adornments. They bribed the caliph Marwan II and asked him to issue an order to Ăbdel Malek ibn Mousa, the governor of Egypt, to give them the possession of St. Mina's church in Marriott. When the decree was delivered to Ăbdel Malek, he held a council under a judge by the name of Ăyssa to decide who had the possession of that church, and he asked the two parties to defend their rights before him. Here, Pope Khael I asked the most prominent of his bishops and archons, including St. Moises, to attend the governor's council. Still, as the Chalcedonians bribed the judge, he took the stand against the Orthodox Copts and refrained from listening to their defense. Some archons suggested paying a bribe to the judge to take their side, but St. Moises rejected such a counsel, saying that it would not befit for the pope or the bishops to pay bribes to anyone, and he prophesied that God would never forsake them. Then, when judge Ăyssa was about to write his verdict in favor of the Chalcedonians, he was fired from his position and was replaced by another judge called Abu el-Ĥuseiny, who happened to be just and honest. The new judge issued his verdict in favor of the Copts, and the Copts kept St. Mina church in their possession.

The church celebrates him on the 11th of Mesra.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 57]

[The Synaxariun: 11 Mesra] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Kha’il I, by Subhi Y. Labib, pp. 1410-2]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, p. 255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went deep in the wilderness and lived for thirty-five years in a spot having olive and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended the wild beasts.

His Multiple Falls and Repentances:

Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the devil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, pp. 257–258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — The Tribes of Saracens

The Tribes of Saracens:

The Arabian tribes populating the area of Rhinoclura in-between the eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes joined forces together and formed one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.

Choosing Moses as a Bishop:

Those Christian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be their bishop. Then, when Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those united tribes.

Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands:

On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then, St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises and his Sister Sarah,, pp. 239–240
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES AND HIS SISTER SARAH, (The martyrs) — Their Martyrdom

These two saints were born to wealthy Christian parents. When their parents passed away, St. Moises (Moses) intended to become a monk after giving his sister Sarah in marriage and handing their whole wealth to her. However, when he discussed the idea with his sister, she responded to him by saying: “If you get married first, then I would follow suit.” He told her: “I have committed so many sins, which I intend to atone for by leading a monastic life, for I cannot get married and care for my salvation at the same time.” She answered him: “How would you cast me in the snares of this world, and care only for your salvation?” Then, he answered her: “Whatever you choose will be yours.” She responded: “All that you would do, I shall also do, for we are of one father and one mother.” Then, they distributed all their wealth to the poor and the needy. St. Moises brought his sister Sarah into a house of virgins, and he joined a monastery near Alexandria, and for the following ten years, they did not see one another.

Their Martyrdom:

Then, when Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) incited persecution against the Christians, in the days of the 14th Pope St. Dionysius the Great (246-264 AD), so many believers were martyred. At that time, St. Moises sent to his sister to bid her farewell, and let her know of his decision to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. She hastened to her mother-superior, sought to be released, got the blessings of her sisters, and joined her brother on his way to Alexandria. There, they both confessed together the Lord Jesus Christ, and after being tortured by many tools, they had their heads cut off by the sword, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 253–254
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

Of his Sayings:

• To a brother in the Scetis who sought from him a word of encouragement, he said: “Go and sit in your cell, it will teach you everything.” • The man who flees from the world is like ripe grapes, but he who dwells among the distractions of men is like sour grapes. • If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I promise you that the Barbarians would never come here, but if we do not, this place will soon become desolate. • According to Fr. Poemen, Fr. Moses was once asked: “How can a man become like dead to his neighbor?” The older saint said to him: “Unless a man keeps in his heart that he has been three days in the grave, he will not be strong enough to do that.” • It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbor, and he should not condemn him in anything. • It is good for a man to die to every work which is evil before he departs from the body, so as not to offend anyone. • Unless a man feels in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not listen to him. A brother asked him about the meaning of that, and the saint said: “Whoever focuses on his sins, would never see those of his neighbor.” • Unless your prayers conform to your behavior, your struggle would not be of any benefit. When the saint was asked to explain, he said: “We should apply what we pray about, for when man forsakes his own will, he reconciles with God and God will listen to his prayers.” • A brother asked him: “What would help the man in his every endeavor?” He answered him: “God is the One who helps, for it is so written: "God is our refuge and strength. A very present help in trouble" (Psalm 46:1).” • When the brother added: “What then is the benefit of fasting or spending sleepless nights, father?” The saint answered: “These practices make the soul meek and humble, for it is written: "Look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins" (Psalm 25:18). So, once the soul reaps the fruits of these practices, God would have compassion on her.” • Then, the brother asked: “What will man do with every temptation he encounters or every evil thought coming to him?” The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?"

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q965 “How can someone with family commitments implement the practice of this pilgrim?”, pp. 100–101
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 965. How can someone with family commitments implement the practice of this pilgrim?

The prayer practices described by this pilgrim have been practiced both by monastics and married people for many generations. Each person practices this prayer according to his own circumstances and abilities. From this pilgrim, we learn a number of things:

a. Faith in the power of the name of Jesus and of calling upon Him.

b. Awareness that prayer is the mother of virtues and good deeds.

c. Concern for nurturing conversation with the Lord Christ, whether in communal or personal worship, as part of any work, or while eating, drinking, sleeping, etc.

d. To ask for the grace of God to work in our lives, bestowing patience in our striving with a spirit of humility.

e. In our spiritual exercises, we should be chiefly concerned with focusing our attention on interior prayer if we wish our lives to be fruitful.

f. The confession of our weaknesses and sins, and our need for the mercy of God.

g. That we need times of silence in order to hear to the voice of God.

h. The focusing of our attention on attaining salvation and forgiveness of sins.

i. Even though the Jesus Prayer is extremely simple with few words, St. John Chrysostom reminds us of the awe with which the seraphim utter this name, as they glorify Him and worship Him; so, let us not practice this prayer carelessly.

j. The need to appreciate the power of the name of our Lord Jesus.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q960 “What is the “Jesus Prayer”?”, p. 93
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 960. What is the “Jesus Prayer”?

The goal of sacred worship — and of prayer in particular — is closeness to God through constant dialogue with Him. Hence, both scripture and holy tradition provide a varied approach to prayer through which the believer is able to attain to constant prayer without ceasing. The believer begins with prayer in every work he undertakes; even before he sleeps. He participates in liturgies, prays the psalms, and his own personal prayers. To preserve his thought from distraction, he offers up prayers that cannot be counted with words or sentences, remembering always the presence of God in his life, so that he lives in a state of constant communication with Him; prayers that he can recite or repeat at any time, even when he is performing any kind of work. Being confident in the power of the name of Jesus, the believer repeats it often. This is what we call the Jesus Prayer.

The Desert Fathers often recited this prayer or other short prayers, which represent a cry to the Lord. St. Augustine used to repeat this prayer: “Make haste, O God, to deliver me. Make haste to help me, O Lord” (Ps. 70:1); and he encouraged the faithful to repeat it on every occasion: at home; at work; while eating or drinking; while awake or asleep; in grief or joy; when spiritually zealous or lukewarm in worship — for this prayer is particularly helpful. St. Augustine used to call this short prayer, “the arrow prayer,” for it shoots an arrow into the heart of the devil and prevents him from distracting our thoughts so long as we pray it. St. John of the Ladder (Climacus) urges us to employ this short prayer saying, “Let your prayer be completely simple. For both the publican and the prodigal son were reconciled to God by a single phrase.”

Notes: [293] St. John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent, trans., Colm Luibheid and Norman Russell (Paulist Press, 1982) 28.5: p. 251.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q976 “What practical steps can one take to practice the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 105–106
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 976. What practical steps can one take to practice the Jesus Prayer?

First: Concentrate all your thoughts on our Lord Jesus Himself. Remember the name of Jesus slowly, gently, and calmly.

Second: Let the recitation of the name be from the soul’s inner depths, without loudness or violence, even internally. When Elijah was commanded to stand before the Lord and prepare to encounter Him, he was told, “‘Stand on the mountain’ … and behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind tore into the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces, but the Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire, And after the fire a small voice. When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out and stood in the entrance of the cave. Suddenly a voice came to him and said, ‘What are you doing here Elijah?’” (1 Kings 19:1–13).

Third: Recite your prayer in serenity and simplicity, or more specifically, with gentleness. As a bird that flies up to the height it intends and then gently glides, flapping its wings only from time to time to maintain its altitude, so the soul, if it flies up to glide upon the thought of Christ Jesus and is sated by remembering Him, can cease to repeat the holy name and instead rest in other thoughts; namely, thinking about Jesus. It is natural for moments of lukewarmness to intrude upon this practice. But if at any time you begin your recitation once more, you find the name of Jesus upon your lips spontaneously, and returning to your thoughts continually, silently, and internally. Thus, you will experience the verse: “I sleep but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). However, this prayer cannot be prayed inattentively: “Because of the fragrance of your ointment, the virgins love you. Draw me away; the daughters of Jerusalem will run after you” (Song 1:3–4).

Fourth: We should be drawn toward the name of Jesus by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that calling on the name of Jesus becomes in our lives one of the fruits of the Holy Spirit Himself.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q966 “What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?”, pp. 102–103
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?

Thirst after Jesus; then he will satisfy you with his love. Shut your eyes to the precious things of the world; then you will be deemed worthy of a peace given by God to reign in your heart.”

St. Gregory the Theologian says that all Christians should repeat the name of the Lord in their prayer, more times than the number of their breaths: “Not only should we pray the name of Jesus Christ without ceasing, but we must also practice it and teach it others, to every person on the face of the earth, for it is fitting and beneficial for all.”

St John Cassian says, “It is not some kind of imagination, conversation, or mere words — it is like a spark that flies off that burning coal which is the movement of the heart, and from the activity of the inextinguishable Spirit who raises the mind above every materialistic thing which can be seen or touched; and thus he pours out his prayers with groanings and sorrows which cannot be uttered.”

St. John Chrysostom says, “I implore you, brethren, never to neglect the rule of this prayer. Whenever you eat, drink, travel, or do anything, cry without ceasing: ‘Lord, Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy upon me!’” He also says, “Do not estrange your heart from God, but abide in Him and guard your heart always by remembering the Lord Jesus Christ, until the name of the Lord becomes rooted in the heart and it ceases to think of anything else. May Christ be glorified in you.”

Abba Agathon says, “There is no labor greater than praying to God. For every time a man wants to pray, his enemies the demons try to prevent him; for they know that nothing obstructs them so much as prayer to God. In everything else that a man undertakes, if he perseveres he will attain rest. But in order to pray a man must struggle to his last breath.”

St. Athanasius says, “Christ did not command us to fill our prayers with ten thousand phrases and to come before Him merely to recite them … We do not come to teach Him, but to wrestle with Him; that we may cling to Him with the persistent cry: ‘Lord Jesus Christ Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner!’ He is living and active, working day after day for the salvation of all.”

Fourth: We should be drawn toward the name of Jesus by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that calling on the name of Jesus becomes in our lives one of the fruits of the Holy Spirit Himself.

Fifth: We should be careful not to despise other forms of prayer.

Sixth: We must forget ourselves and put our egos to death while the name of the Holy God comes alive in our spirits: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Seventh: Repetition of the Jesus Prayer should not lessen our participation in the divine liturgy or in other Church rites such as the Midnight Praises.

Eighth: The best kind of prayer is that which is prayed when we are moved by the Holy Spirit.

Ninth: The goal of the Jesus Prayer is to praise Him, crying out with Thomas the apostle: “My Lord and God!” (John 20:28). We should be concerned most of all with the Lord of glory, Jesus, being present in our lives.

Tenth: Calling on the name of Jesus grants us salvation in every kind of need in our lives.

Eleventh: Through the name of Jesus, we receive more than we ask: “Whatever you ask the father in my name, He will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in My name. Ask and you will receive” (John 16:23–24). He is both the one who grants the gift and the gift itself, satisfying all our needs. “He became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 972. What did St. Macarius the Great say about the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

“Always remember the holy name, our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the pearl which the wise merchant purchased (Matt. 13:45–46) by selling all the desires of his heart, brought into the inner rooms of his house, and found it sweeter than honey in his mouth. He who keeps this jewel in his heart shall be granted a great reward in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q408 “What is “the Jesus Prayer”?”, p. 303
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › Titles and Names of the Savior that Witness to the Works of His Love — 408. What is “the Jesus Prayer”?

Let us conclude this survey of the names and titles of Christ by mentioning the effectiveness of the “Jesus Prayer” in our lives. When the believer experiences the power of the name of Jesus, he cries out with blind Bartimaeus, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47, Luke 18:38). This prayer is found in the biography of Abba Philemon (6th to 7th century). It is also found in the letters of Saints Barsanuphius and John of Gaza (beginning of the 6th century), Dorotheus of Gaza, and St. John Climacus. The Church employs it as a spiritual practice for her children, with the addition of part of the prayer of the tax collector who beat his chest saying, “God be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

St. Anthony the Great says, “Do not cease from reciting the name of the Lord Jesus, but hold onto to His name with your mind, repeat it with your tongue, and say in your heart: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me; My Lord Jesus Christ help me.’ Also say: ‘I praise You, my Lord Jesus Christ.’”

It was also known to St. Macarius the Great and St. Evagrius.

St. Macarius the Great says, “Be attentive to the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with a remorseful heart and let it pour forth from your lips. Let the name reflect back upon you. Do not bury it in your thoughts only for display, but be alert whenever you cry it out, saying, “O my Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me!” Then, in serenity you shall see His divinity resting in you; He will bring to naught the darkness of pain that is in you; and He shall purify your inner man to be like the purity of Adam dwelling in paradise. This is the blessed name that St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, p. 99
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

Now do you understand what prayer without ceasing is?’

‘Yes indeed, Father, and in God’s name teach me how to gain the habit of it,’ I cried, filled with joy.

‘Read this book,’ he said. ‘It is called The Philokalia, and it contains the full and detailed science of constant and interior prayer, set forth by twenty-five holy Fathers. The book is marked by a lofty wisdom and is so profitable to use that it is considered the foremost and best manual of the contemplative spiritual life’ …

He opened the book, found the instruction by St. Symeon the New Theologian, and read: ‘Sit down alone and in silence. Lower your head, shut your eyes, breathe out gently and imagine yourself looking into your own heart. Carry your mind, i.e., your thoughts, from your head to your heart. As you breathe out, say, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.” Say it moving your lips gently, or simply say it in your mind. Try to put all other thoughts aside. Be calm, be patient, and repeat the process frequently.’”

The old man asked the pilgrim to return to him so he could monitor his progress, and for honest confession, for it is silly to attempt such spiritual works without a guide to mentor us. The pilgrim felt a powerful desire to experience interior and continual prayer. The pilgrim learned that there was a village near the monastery, so he went and sought accommodation there, in order to remain near the old man. He found work tending the garden of a peasant for the summer, and was provided with a small, isolated hut in which to live.

For a week he followed the instructions of the old man, but he was soon beset by feelings of laziness and boredom and sleepiness. Certain thoughts assailed him, so he began to read the words of the Fathers and force himself to recite the Jesus Prayer. He confessed all this to the old man, who then asked him to repeat the prayer three thousand times a day, while standing or sitting, lying down or walking. The pilgrim received this instruction with joy and returned to his hut. It was difficult for the first two days, but after that it became an easy matter, so that whenever he ceased, he felt an urge to continue again.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q966 “What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?”, pp. 101–102
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?

The Lord Christ granted His name to His disciples, not only so they could perform wonders, heal the sick, and cast out demons — He assured them of the power of His name when He said, “Whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you” (John 16:23). Thus, by His name we approach the Father and enjoy His eternal glories. Indeed, the seventy apostles came to understand the power of the name of Jesus, as is evident from their words upon their return from their mission: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name!” (Luke 10:17). Isaiah the prophet, in his song of thanksgiving, expressed the power of the name of God, saying, “The desire of our soul is for Your name, and for the remembrance of You. With my soul I have desired You in the night. Yes, by my spirit within me I will seek you early” (Isa. 26:8–9).

St. John Climacus (of the ladder) says, “Flog your enemies with the name of Jesus, for there is no stronger weapon in heaven or earth.”

St. Cyril the Great says, “He among those who do not yet believe in God and who despises the name of God confesses the power of the Most Holy One when the rays of the truth shine upon him.”

St. Barsanuphius and St. John say, “The remembrance of God’s name utterly destroys all that is evil and wicked.”

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “If any disbelieve the power of the Crucified, let him ask the devils.”

St. Ephrem the Syrian says,

“Jesus, glorious name, Secret bridge which leads across from death to life, to you I have come and stopped, at yod your letter I am held. Be a bridge for my speech, that it may cross to the truth. Make your love a bridge for your servant: by you let me cross to your Father. Let me cross and say ‘Blessed be he who made his might gentle through his Child.’”

St. Isaac the Syrian speaks of the practice of the Jesus Prayer, saying, “It is not becoming that great things should fall into our hands easily: lest the gift of God should be thought to be cheap because of its being acquired without difficulty. All that is acquired with labour, is guarded with caution. Thirst after Jesus; then he will satisfy you with his love. Shut your eyes to the precious things of the world; then you will be deemed worthy of a peace given by God to reign in your heart.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q970 “How did St. Augustine practice continual prayer through the name of Jesus?”, p. 104
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 970. How did St. Augustine practice continual prayer through the name of Jesus?

Having experienced the power of the name of Jesus in his repentance from sin, St. Augustine proclaimed, saying, “No one can pray in the name of the Savior if he is praying for something other than salvation.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 99–100
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

The pilgrim received this instruction with joy and returned to his hut. It was difficult for the first two days, but after that it became an easy matter, so that whenever he ceased, he felt an urge to continue again.

He returned to the old man, who told him to stay calm and to increase the number of recitations with the grace of God. He returned to his hut and continued to recite the prayer for a whole week without much trouble. And he learned how to keep his mind from distraction. The old man then said to him: “Now I give you permission to say your Prayer as often as you wish and as often as you can. Try to devote every moment you are awake to the Prayer, call on the Name of Jesus Christ without counting the number of times, and submit yourself humbly to the will of God, looking to Him for help. I am sure He will not forsake you, and that He will lead you into the right path.”

The pilgrim goes on to say, “After no great lapse of time I had the feeling that the Prayer had, so to speak, by its own action passed from my lips to my heart. That is to say, it seemed as though my heart in its ordinary beating began to say the words of the Prayer within each beat. Thus for example, one, ‘Lord,’ two, ‘Jesus,’ three, ‘Christ,’ and so on. I gave up saying the Prayer with my lips, I simply listened carefully to what my heart was saying. It seemed as though my eyes looked right down into it; and I dwelt upon the words of my departed mentor when he was telling me about this joy. Then I felt something like a pain in my heart, and in my thoughts so great a love for Jesus Christ that I pictured myself, if only I could see Him, throwing myself at His feet and not letting them go from my embrace, kissing them tenderly, and thanking Him with tears for having of His love and grace allowed me to find so great a consolation in His Name, me, His unworthy and sinful creature! … ”

“Again I started off on my wanderings. But now I did not walk along as before, filled with care. The calling upon the Name of Jesus Christ gladdened my way. Everybody was kind to me, it was as though everyone loved me.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q408 “What is “the Jesus Prayer”?”, pp. 303–304
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › Titles and Names of the Savior that Witness to the Works of His Love — 408. What is “the Jesus Prayer”?

This is the blessed name that St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).”

Abba Evagrius says, “Tormented by the thoughts and passions of the body, I went to find the Abbot Macarius. I said to him: ‘My father, give me a word that I may live by it.’ Then Macarius said to me: ‘Attach the rope of the anchor to the rock and, by God’s grace, the ship will cross the diabolic waves of the deceptive sea and the tempest of the darkness of this vain world.’ I said to him: ‘What is the ship, what is the rope, what is the rock?’ The Abbot Macarius said to me: ‘The boat is your heart: guard it. The rope is your spirit: attach it to our Lord Jesus Christ who is the rock that has power over all the diabolic waves and surges that the saints are contending with; for is it not easy to say with each breath: Our Lord Jesus, the Christ, have mercy on me; I bless You, my Lord Jesus, help me? And as the fish struggling against the current can be caught unawares, we also, if we patiently persist in faithfully reciting the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, He will snare the devil by his nose (“one pierces his nose with a snare” Job 40:24) because of what he has done to us, and we who are weak shall know that help comes to us from the Lord Jesus Christ.”

And Abba Jacob says, “I once went to Abba Isidore and I found him writing, so I sat by him and noticed that from time to time he raised his eyes to heaven and his lips would move without me hearing any sound; so I said to him, ‘What are you doing, Abba?’ He said to me, ‘Do you not do the same?’ I said to him, ‘No, Abba.’ He then told me, ‘If you do not do that, Abba Jacob, then you have not yet become a monk, not even for a single day.’ And this is what he used to say: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, help me. My Lord Jesus Christ have mercy on me. I praise You, My Lord Jesus Christ.’”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 98–99
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

As they walked together to the monastery, he chatted with the old man about the topic of prayer without ceasing. The old man told him the following:

a. This question needs spiritual understanding and not academic teaching.

b. Some employ worldly wisdom inappropriately to explain divine matters. Some think that preparatory good works are necessary before prayer. On the contrary, prayer is the mother of virtues and good works.

c. The apostle testifies that prayer has the priority over good works when he says, “I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made” (1 Tim. 2:1). Without prayer, no good work can be performed; and without prayer, we cannot know how to encounter God and enter into dialogue with Him.

As they spoke, they came up to the monastery and the end of their conversation, so the pilgrim hastened to ask the wise old man:

“‘Be so kind, Reverend Father, as to show me what prayer without ceasing means and how it is learnt. I see you know all about these things.’

He took my request kindly and asked me into his cell. ‘Come in,’ said he; ‘I will give you a volume of the holy Fathers from which with God’s help you can learn about prayer clearly and in detail.’ We went into his cell and he began to speak as follows. ‘The continuous interior Prayer of Jesus is a constant uninterrupted calling upon the divine Name of Jesus with the lips, in the spirit, in the heart; while forming a mental picture of His constant presence, and imploring His grace, during every occupation, at all times, in all places, even during sleep. The appeal is couched in these terms, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.” One who accustoms himself to this appeal experiences as a result so deep a consolation and so great a need to offer the prayer always, that he can no longer live without it, and it will continue to voice itself within him of its own accord. Now do you understand what prayer without ceasing is?’

‘Yes indeed, Father, and in God’s name teach me how to gain the habit of it,’ I cried, filled with joy.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q975 “How can we persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, p. 105
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 975. How can we persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

To persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer is to persevere in seeking to encounter the Lord Jesus and to surrender our hearts to Him, that His kingdom may abide within them. The scholar Origen says, “Let us search for Him with abundant labor that we may find that for which we search in abundance … He is within us.”

records.question: Why was he called 'Bishoy the Jeremian'?
records.answer: St. Bishoy was called "Bishoy the Jeremian" because he had a special love for the Book of Jeremiah. It was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of the Book, which deeply influenced his spiritual life [6].
