passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — In Scetis (Shiheet)

Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it and reign with power and dominion!

St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El- Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them up. One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: ‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life.’” She answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9).

In Scetis (Shiheet):

Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple of Abba ‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 360–361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian

An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian:

By a Divine arrangement, Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian’ came once to meet with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. ‘Bishoy’ talked in the Coptic tongue; the later sought from God to give them both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monastic experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’

After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. ‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother started to run to catch him. St. ‘Bishoy’ called him and said he would never be able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’

Emperor Constantine visited Him:

St. ‘John the Short’ once went to visit his friend St. ‘Bishoy,’ and while he was still outside his cell, he heard him talking to someone inside. Knocking on the door and entering, he found no one with the saint. Asking him with whom he was talking, he answered: “Emperor Constantine came to visit me and told me: ‘I wish I have abandoned my kingdom and became a monk; for I did not imagine how the monks enjoy such an honor and great glory. I see how those who depart were carried by the wings of eagles; and how they were received with great honor in heaven.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 361–362
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Forsaking Scetis

Forsaking Scetis:

In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John the Short’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “Do you fear death, O man of God?” He answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell because of me!”

St. ‘John the Short’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba ‘Anthony’ where he reposed. Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain. There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose, and God granted them their wish.

St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. ‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints' bodies and buried them together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El- Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

They are now in the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy’ in the Natron Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren greatly rejoiced, and all of them set forth toward the mountain. The saint, because of his old age, was at the rear. There, he encountered an older man overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passingby monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he did carry him and walked without feeling any labor. However, the older man started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself. He then looked at Him and said: “The heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the earth; how can a sinner like me carry You?” To this, the Lord Jesus Christ smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration up to this very day. Once the brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai of Antioch, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI OF ANTIOCH, ST. (The martyr)

‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was ordained as a priest because of his piety. His brother and his mother went to Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to take care of their bodies. Then, he felt the longing to partake in their crowns. So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies.

The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: ‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 358–359
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Life in Seclusion

Life in Seclusion:

When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the guidance of God. An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the Short’ should remain alone in that location. In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left the place forsaking his friend, and dug for himself a cave near the southern rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

His Strife:

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it. Then, he used to tie the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his heart; that it was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’

He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. He believed in the saying: “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.” (2 Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus;

Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on a friendship level. He used to see Him, to talk with Him, and to enjoy His Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persistent in his great ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and behold, I shall always be with you!”

Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored at all!”

A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: “Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My commandments; I shall save him from all temptations!” He then blessed him and ascended.

Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted him and blessed him. The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with water in a basin, then the Lord ascended. St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water and left a portion for his disciple. The saint sought from him more than once to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Love for the Salvation of All Souls

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls:

Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted to Judaism and lived with her. When he happened to encounter some monks, he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something?” They answered in the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?! Nobody can overcome the tricks of Satan in women, except that one whom God is with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God saved him, and he came back and repented.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai Anoub, p. 355
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI ANOUB, ST. (The martyr)

He was a soldier in the days of ‘Cyprian,’ the governor of ‘Atrib’ (now Banha). When Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) stirred up persecution on the Christians, this soldier came forward and proclaimed his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He was arrested, and the governor tortured him, but when he did not forsake his faith, or deny his Christ, his head was cut off in ‘Matarieh’ in the region of ‘Ăin-Shams;’ a suburb of Cairo, on the 19th of Paona.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Jeremiah, the Monk of Menoufia, p. 357
passages.text:
Saint: JEREMIAH, THE MONK OF MENOUFIA

The Roman Emperor Anastasius I (491-518), was exiled to Egypt before he sat on the throne. There, he resided in the province of Menouf, where he had so many friends. One of the nobles counseled him to visit a saintly monk living in the neighborhood by the name of Jeremiah, to get his blessing. He went in the company of some friends. When they asked the monk to bless them, he gave every one of them a special blessing, except for Anastasius. Anastasius was very sad and told his friends that the man refrained from blessing me because he was aware of my sins. When they could not cheer him up, they went and told the monk about it. So, Jeremiah called Anastasius over to him and told him in the presence of three of his friends: “When I saw God's hand raised above your head, I felt no need of further blessing after that of God's.” Then, he advised him, saying: “God who will appoint you an emperor, seeks from you to keep away from bad behavior; and in particular not to approve of the decree of the council of Chalcedon.” The prophecy of the saintly has fulfilled in the year 491, and Emperor Anastasius had a significant relationship with the Egyptian Church, and his days were full of peace. Yet, some of the followers of the papal throne of Rome who were uncomfortable with the situation, provoked a man by the name of Webtalianus to proclaim the zeal over the Chalcedonian decree; and he gathered so many people around him and tried to take over the throne from Emperor Anastasius. However, he failed and was defeated.

[Fr. Manasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church; 1983; pp. 276-277]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Jerome, p. 359
passages.text:
Saint: JEROME (HIERONYMUS), ST. — In Antioch

In Antioch:

St. Jerome's relatives were all stirred up against him because he encouraged his sister to hold on to virginity and asceticism. So, he lefte Italy and went to the East through Greece. He settled down in Antioch in the year 374. There, he was welcomed and given hospitality by St. Evagrius, whom he loved so much and by whom he was strongly influenced and became attached to the Eastern world and its monastic life. He also was acquainted with Apollinaris, the bishop of Laodicea, whom he later opposed when he deviated from the Orthodox Faith.

Beside his ascetic life, St. Jerome dedicated his time to study the Holy Bible. He lived a solitary life in the wilderness of Chalcis, southeast of Antioch, for four years, where he learned the Hebrew language, at the same time, he suffered severe physical troubles, as was evident from what he wrote candidly to his spiritual daughter Eustochium. “Although the sun was so fiercely hot to terrify even the native monks here, I counted myself as though living amid the luxuries of the busy Rome. In this exile or prison, which I chose for myself to avoid hell, although I lived in the company of scorpions and beasts, yet I counted myself as though dwelling among the exotic Roman dancers. My face was so pale from the intense fasting, yet my soul became strong in its strife against evil desires. My cold body, which became entirely dried up and looking as if it was dead before its time, was still persistent in carrying evil desires. Therefore, I cast myself spiritually at the feet of the Lord Jesus, washing them with my tears and training my body on fasting the whole week. I was not ashamed to reveal the temptations which dwelt upon me, and I did not cease striking my chest day and night until I regain the peace.” When St. Jerome returned from the wilderness to Antioch in the year 377, his talents started to show up. So, bishop Paulinus applied some pressure on him to force him to accept the priesthood. However, he received the ordination under the condition that it would not be bound to a specific church. That was to dedicate himself to the word of God wherever God would call him to go.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef Ĥabib, the Deacon, pp. 364–365
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF ĤABIB, THE DEACON

After the Holy Liturgy and the rites of ordination, he went back to his work. He submitted his resignation on the same day in order to dedicate all his time and effort to a better activity.

When Fr. Bishoy came back from the Syrian Monastery in the Natrun Valley after the 40 days the new priest has to spend after his ordination; he found Yousef Ĥabib had dedicated himself to serve, day and night, in that new church of St. George in the district of Sporting in Alexandra. He took upon himself, without being asked by anyone, to support Fr. Bishoy at the beginning of his ministry in a new church that had no deacons, cantor, or ministers. Yousef Ĥabib was a first-class ecclesiastical man who elaborately knew by heart all the Church hymns and sang them with the spirit of prayer in a very touching voice. With that beginning, Yousef Ĥabib became the teacher of the Church’s young men and boys and let them absorb the spirit of the Fathers. He raised them on the love of the church and her hymns. Then, when the church came to have a cantor, her beautiful choir of deacons and her affairs started to settle down. Yousef Ĥabib withdrew himself in humility and self-denial and shifted his whole effort towards a new field to revive our ecclesiastical heritage.

Yousef Ĥabib, for a long time, has been fond of the biographies of the Saints, in particular of those whose fragrant life stories had not been published before. He started to travel to the desert monasteries to search in their libraries treasures about what was hidden, and he brought to light tens of biographies and rare stories. He also used to research in the libraries of the Coptic Museum and the library of the Patriarchate, etc. He even purchased a permanent train travel permit to go back and forth to Cairo twice a week for that purpose. He used to translate, research in the biographies of the Saints and their sayings, then returned home to publish them in small booklets, to the benefit of ministry, and for the improvement of the souls.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidhom Bishai, p. 144
passages.text:
Saint: SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr)

On the 17th of Baramhat in the year 1561 AM (25 March 1844), the Coptic Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Sidhom Bishai.

Sidhom Bishai was a trader of wood in the city of Alexandria. He used to go twice every year to Damietta to purchase lumber, which was imported through its harbor. Being an archdeacon who loved the old churches, Sidhom Bishai on hearing that the wooden roof of St. George el-Muzaĥem Church in the town of Basat in the district of Sherbin had collapsed; he took on himself the responsibility of repairing the damage done and provided a full ship load of wood for that purpose. At the same time, during his visits to Damietta, he used to attend the Holy Liturgies in St. George Church. One time, it happened that a non-Christian stroked shoulder against him on his way to the church aiming to block him from going to the Church. But, seeing how muåallem Sidhom Bishai paid little attention to that evil man, he was provoked to anger and paid some street boys to insult him. Then, it happened that the Mofti of the town was passing by; and these boys falsely accused Sidhom Bishai of insulting Islam, its “Prophet” and the “Quran.” Those false accusations, finding the expected fertile soil in the Moftis ears; he chose two of equally evil people around as witnesses. Through these people, they rigged the case against muåallem Sidhom Bishai. He was then 40 years of age, well known for meekness, kind-hearted and loving for all, not at all expected to utter what they falsely claimed that he has done.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius of Jerusalem, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS OF JERUSALEM — Monk, Priest, and Theologist

Monk, Priest, and Theologist:

Fr. Hesychius (Hezecius/Esytius/Isysius/Isacius) of Jerusalem is known to have been born in Jerusalem in the 2nd half of the 4th century AD and lived through the 1st half of the 5th century. He was thought to have been a disciple of St. Gregory, the Nazianzus (329-390 AD). He was a monk and probably a presbyter in the church of Jerusalem; and, he was considered by his contemporaries as a great theologian. Fr. Hesychius devoted himself to a solitary life, plunged into the wilderness, where he, with a bee-like enthusiasm, gathered the flowers of virtue from the Fathers there.

He was ordained as a priest by the patriarch of Jerusalem against his will. According to Theophanes, the Confessor (760-818 AD). in the year 412 AD, Fr. Hesychius got great fame as a priest and a preacher of the church of Jerusalem and was commended by St. Cyril of Sythopolis (525-559 AD) as being the teacher of the church, and a theologian of great fame. It was also said that he accompanied Juvenal, the patriarch of Jerusalem, to consecrate the church of the monastery of Euthymius around the year 428 AD. He reposed in the middle of the 5th century around 438 AD.

He was fond of meditating in the Holy Bible. From these interpretations, and got broad knowledge about the Divinities. Fr. Hesychius followed the approach of Origen, in using the symbolic interpretation for every verse in the Holy Bible, and he refused the literal interpretation. He also was an opponent of philosophy, since the heretics used it to corrupt the teachings of the Church. He gave so many sermons and recorded the Ecclesiastical History around the year 428 AD. All this work has been lost, including an attack on Nestor, in which he posed so many tough questions with their right answers. Fr. Hesychius defended the faith against the Arians, the Apollinarians, and the teachings of the Antiochians. In his debates concerning the Nature of the Lord Christ, he depended upon the statements made by St. Cyril of Alexandria (412- 444 AD) and adopted the theological views of Alexandria concerning the Nature of Christ though he did not utilize the exact theological expressions used by Alexandria.

records.question: Why did Christ tell us to pray it in the plural?
records.answer:
Christ told us to pray the Lord's Prayer in the plural because God bids us to love our neighbor, so we pray for fellow believers as well as non-believers, aligning our will with God's will that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Even in private prayer, a believer should pray in the name of the entire Church, as a member of it.

St. John Chrysostom explains that Christ teaches us to make our prayer common, praying on behalf of our brethren, saying "our Father" instead of "my Father," thus offering supplications for the body in common and focusing on the neighbor's good.

St. Augustine emphasizes that by calling God "our Father," we recognize belonging to a great family where all believers, regardless of social status, are brethren under one Father in heaven.

St. Cyprian adds that the prayer is public and common, not individual, as we pray not for ourselves alone but for the whole people, since we are one. He points to the example of the three children in the fiery furnace praying together with one heart, showing the unity God desires in prayer.

Furthermore, the apostles and disciples prayed together with one accord after the Lord's ascension, demonstrating communal prayer as a model to follow [1][2].

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q932 “Why did the Lord Christ bid us to pray the Lord’s Prayer in the plural?”, pp. 57–58
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 932. Why did the Lord Christ bid us to pray the Lord’s Prayer in the plural?

God bids us to love our neighbor, so we pray for fellow believers the same way we pray for non-believers. In so doing, our will is in harmony with the will of God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4). Even in his private room, the believer ought to pray in the name of the entire Church, because he is a member of the Church.

St. John Chrysostom says, “He teaches, moreover, to make our prayer common, on behalf of our brethren also. For He says not, ‘my Father, which art in Heaven,’ but, ‘our Father,’ offering up his supplications for the body in common, and nowhere looking to his own, but everywhere to his neighbor’s good.”

St. Augustine says, “You have begun to belong to a great family [by being baptized]. Under this Father, the lord and the slave are brethren; under this Father the general and the common soldier are brethren; under this Father the rich man and the poor are brethren. All Christian believers have various fathers on earth, some noble, some obscure; but they all call upon one Father which is in heaven … Therefore do they understand that they are brethren, seeing they have one Father. Now let not the lord disdain to have his slave for a brother, seeing the Lord Christ has vouchsafed to have him for a brother.”

In a similar vein St. Cyprian says in his commentary on the Lord’s Prayer: “Before all things, the Teacher of peace and the Master of unity would not have a prayer to be made singly and individually, as for one who prays to pray for himself alone. For we say not ‘My Father, which art in heaven,’ nor ‘Give me this day my daily bread;’ nor does each one ask that only his debt should be forgiven him; nor does he request for himself alone that he may not be led into temptation, and delivered from evil. Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but the whole people, because we the whole people are one. The God of peace and the Teacher of concord, who taught unity, willed that one should thus pray for all, even as He bore us all in one. This law of prayer the three children observed when they were shut up in the fiery furnace, speaking together in prayer, and being of one heart in the agreement of the spirit; and this the faith of the sacred Scripture assures us, and in telling us how such as these prayed, gives an example which we ought to follow in our prayers, so that we may be such as they were: ‘Then these three,’ it says, ‘as if from one mouth sang a hymn, and blessed the Lord’ (Hymn of the Three Young Men, Dan.3:51 LXX).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q932 “Why did the Lord Christ bid us to pray the Lord’s Prayer in the plural?”, p. 58
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 932. Why did the Lord Christ bid us to pray the Lord’s Prayer in the plural?

They spoke as if from one mouth, although Christ had not yet taught them how to pray … Thus, also we find that the apostles, with the disciples, prayed after the Lord’s ascension: ‘They all,’ says the Scripture, ‘continued with one accord in prayer, with the women, and Mary who was the mother of Jesus and with His brethren’ (Acts 1:14).”

Notes: [165] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew Homily 19.6 (NPNF I/10:131) amended. [166] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 9.2 (NPNF I/6:288) amended. [167] St. Cyprian of Carthage, Treatise 4: On the Lord’s Prayer 8 (ANF 5:449).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q911 “Why are we taught not to repeat words in vain when we pray (Matt. 6:7)?”, p. 35
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 911. Why are we taught not to repeat words in vain when we pray (Matt. 6:7)?

St. Augustine says, “Our Lord first of all cut off ‘much speaking,’ that you might not bring a multitude of words unto God, as though by your many words you would teach Him. Therefore when you pray you have need of piety, not of wordiness. ‘For your Father knows what is needful for you, before you ask Him’ [Matt. 6:8]. But lest perhaps any should say here, ‘If He knows what is needful for us, why should we use so much as a few words? Why should we pray at all?’ He knows Himself; let Him then give what He knows to be needful for us. Yes, but it is His will that you should pray, that He may give to your longings, that His gifts may not be lightly esteemed; seeing He has Himself formed this longing desire in us. The words therefore which our Lord Jesus Christ has taught us in His prayer, are the rule and standard of our desires. You may not ask for anything but what is written there.”

Notes: [94] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 6.4 (NPNF I/6:275) amended.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q914 “Why did the Lord Christ pray?”, p. 36
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 914. Why did the Lord Christ pray?

St. Cyril the Great says, “for what, forsooth, does He [Christ] pray, if He is full, and needs nothing that is the Father’s? To this we reply, that He permits Himself, in accordance with the manner of the dispensation in the flesh, to perform human actions whenever He wills, and as the season requires, without being liable to blame for so doing. For if He ate and drank, and is found partaking of sleep, what is there absurd, if also having humbled Himself to our measure, and fulfilled human righteousness, He not unfitly offered up prayer?”

“All that Christ did was for our edification, and for the benefit of those who believe in Him; and by proposing to us His own conduct as a sort of pattern of the spiritual mode of life, He would make us true worshippers. Let us see, therefore, in the pattern and example provided for us by Christ’s acts, the manner in which we ought to make our supplications unto God. We must pray secretly and in concealment, and with no one seeing us: … ‘But you, when you pray, go into your inner room’ (Matt. 6:6). For we ought to pray, not seeking after glory, but ‘lifting up holy hands’ (1 Tim. 2:8), while the soul, as it were, mounts aloft to the contemplation of God, withdrawing from all tumult, and quitting worldly anxiety. And this we must do not with fickleness, nor with a listless feebleness; but, on the contrary, with earnestness and zeal, and a patience worthy of admiration: for you have heard that Jesus did not merely pray, but that He also passed the night in this duty … Though divinely begotten as the Word by God the Father, yet He humbled Himself unto emptying, even to becoming our brother, by being made like unto us, and similar in all things to the inhabitants of the earth, sin only excepted. For having become like unto us from His exceeding gentleness and love to mankind, He disdains not human things: but sets before us His conduct as a type of goodness unto the end, that we may be earnest in following His footsteps.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q914 “Why did the Lord Christ pray?”, pp. 36–37
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 914. Why did the Lord Christ pray?

For having become like unto us from His exceeding gentleness and love to mankind, He disdains not human things: but sets before us His conduct as a type of goodness unto the end, that we may be earnest in following His footsteps.”

St. Cyprian says, “If He who was without sin prayed, how much more ought sinners to pray? And if He prayed continually, watching through the whole night with uninterrupted petitions, how much more ought we to watch nightly in constantly repeated prayer! The Lord prayed and asked not for Himself — for why should He who was guiltless pray on His own behalf?— but for our sins, as He Himself declared, when He said to Peter: ‘Behold, I Satan has desired that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail’ (Luke 22:31–32).”

“But if for us and for our sins He both laboured and watched and prayed, how much more ought we to be instant in prayers; and to pray and to entreat the Lord Himself, and then through Him, to make satisfaction to God the Father! We have an advocate and an intercessor for our sins, Jesus Christ the Lord and our God, if only we repent of our sins past, and confess and acknowledge our sins, whereby we now offend the Lord, and for the time to come engage to walk in His ways, and to fear His commandments.”

Notes: [97] St. Cyril of Alexandria, A Commentary upon the Gospel According to St. Luke: Part I, trans. R. Payne Smith (Oxford University Press, 1859) 70: pp. 322 amended. [98] St. Cyril of Alexandria, A Commentary upon the Gospel According to St. Luke: Part I, trans. R. Payne Smith (Oxford University Press, 1859) 23: pp. 94, 96 amended. [99] St. Cyprian of Carthage, Treatise 4: On the Lord’s Prayer 29–30 (ANF 5:455) amended. [100] St. Cyprian of Carthage, The Epistles of Cyprian 7.6 (ANF 5:286).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q931 “Why is the Lord’s Prayer important?”, p. 57
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 931. Why is the Lord’s Prayer important?

St. Augustine says, “The Son Himself, as you heard when the Gospel was read, taught His disciples and His faithful ones this Prayer. Good hope have we of obtaining our cause, when such an Advocate has dictated our suit. The Assessor of the Father, as you have confessed, who sits on the right hand of the Father; He is our Advocate who is to be our Judge. For from thence will He come to judge the living and the dead. Learn then, this Prayer also which you will have to repeat.”

St. Cyprian says, “Let us, therefore, beloved brethren, pray as God our Teacher has taught us. It is a loving and friendly prayer to beseech God with His word, to come up to His ears in the prayer of Christ. Let the Father acknowledge the words of His Son when we make our prayer, and let Him also who dwells within in our breast Himself dwell in our voice. And since we have Him as an Advocate with the Father for our sins, let us, when as sinners we petition on behalf of our sins, put forward the words of our Advocate. For since He says, that whatsoever we shall ask of the Father in His name, He will give us (John 16:23), how much more effectually do we obtain what we ask in Christ’s name, if we ask for it in His prayer! (cf. John 14:6)”

Notes: [163] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 8.1 (NPNF I/6:284) amended. [164] St. Cyprian of Carthage, Treatise 4: On the Lord’s Prayer 3 (ANF 5:448).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q942 “Why do we conclude the Lord’s Prayer by glorifying God with the words, “For Thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory forever and ever”?”, p. 73
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 942. Why do we conclude the Lord’s Prayer by glorifying God with the words, “For Thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory forever and ever”?

St. John Chrysostom says, “manifold as your weakness may be, you may of right be confident, having such a One to reign over you, Who is able fully to accomplish all, and that with ease, even by you … He not only frees you from the dangers that are approaching you, but can make you also glorious and illustrious.”

“This He [God] desires you duly to perform, rather than the shutting of the doors, even to shut the doors of the mind.”

“For because He Himself is invisible, He would have your prayer be so likewise.”

Notes: [237] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 19.10 (NPNF I/10:134) amended. [238] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 19.3 (NPNF I/10:129). [239] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 19.4 (NPNF I/10:130).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q947 “What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?”, p. 79
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Prayer of the Mind and Contemplation — 947. What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?

St. Clement of Alexandria says, “Prayer is, then, to speak more boldly, converse with God. Though whispering, consequently, and not opening the lips, we speak in silence, yet we cry inwardly. For God hears continually all the inward converse.”

St. Aphrahat says, “Again our Savior taught the prayer and said, ‘You should pray secretly to the Hidden One; He sees everything’ (Matt. 6:6). For he said, ‘Enter the inner chamber and pray secretly to your Father, and the Father who sees in secret will reward you’ (Matt. 6:6). But why, my beloved, did our Savior teach and say, ‘Pray to your Father in secret with the door closed?’ I will explain this to you as much as I have understood. For he said, ‘Pray to your Father in secret with the door closed.’ What is the door that he said to close? If not your mouth, which is (the door to) the temple in which Christ dwells as the Apostle said, ‘You are the temple of the Lord’ (1 Cor. 3:16), for him to enter into your inner man, to this house, cleanse it from everything that is unclean, while the door, that is your mouth, is to be closed. If that was not so, how would you understand this matter? For if it happens to you that you were in a land, and there is no house and door, would you not pray in secret? Or if it happens to you again that you were on the top of a mountain, would you not pray?

“And our Savior showed this that God knows the will of the heart and of the thought, just as our Lord said, ‘Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him’ (Matt. 6:8). It is written in the prophet Isaiah, ‘Before they who were chosen by me call, I will hear them, and before they make the cry I will answer them’ (Isa. 65:24). Isaiah said again about the wicked, ‘Even though you multiply prayer I will not listen’ (Isa. 1:15). He said again, ‘They may cry in my ears with a loud voice, but I shall not hear them’ (Ezek. 8:18). But he said this about deceitful prayer, which is not accepted. For you must hear with excellence all the words, then you will understand their power.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q966 “What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?”, pp. 102–103
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?

Thirst after Jesus; then he will satisfy you with his love. Shut your eyes to the precious things of the world; then you will be deemed worthy of a peace given by God to reign in your heart.”

St. Gregory the Theologian says that all Christians should repeat the name of the Lord in their prayer, more times than the number of their breaths: “Not only should we pray the name of Jesus Christ without ceasing, but we must also practice it and teach it others, to every person on the face of the earth, for it is fitting and beneficial for all.”

St John Cassian says, “It is not some kind of imagination, conversation, or mere words — it is like a spark that flies off that burning coal which is the movement of the heart, and from the activity of the inextinguishable Spirit who raises the mind above every materialistic thing which can be seen or touched; and thus he pours out his prayers with groanings and sorrows which cannot be uttered.”

St. John Chrysostom says, “I implore you, brethren, never to neglect the rule of this prayer. Whenever you eat, drink, travel, or do anything, cry without ceasing: ‘Lord, Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy upon me!’” He also says, “Do not estrange your heart from God, but abide in Him and guard your heart always by remembering the Lord Jesus Christ, until the name of the Lord becomes rooted in the heart and it ceases to think of anything else. May Christ be glorified in you.”

Abba Agathon says, “There is no labor greater than praying to God. For every time a man wants to pray, his enemies the demons try to prevent him; for they know that nothing obstructs them so much as prayer to God. In everything else that a man undertakes, if he perseveres he will attain rest. But in order to pray a man must struggle to his last breath.”

St. Athanasius says, “Christ did not command us to fill our prayers with ten thousand phrases and to come before Him merely to recite them … We do not come to teach Him, but to wrestle with Him; that we may cling to Him with the persistent cry: ‘Lord Jesus Christ Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner!’ He is living and active, working day after day for the salvation of all.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q939 “What does He mean by “bread” when He says, “Give us this day our daily (or essential, or tomorrow’s) bread” (Matt. 6:11)?”, p. 69
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 939. What does He mean by “bread” when He says, “Give us this day our daily (or essential, or tomorrow’s) bread” (Matt. 6:11)?

The word “daily” has been understood in two ways. In his commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, Origen explains that the word we usually translated as “daily,” epiouios, is derived from ousia, which means “essence” or “essential”; while others believe that it is derived from epienai, which means “of the coming day.” Similarly, James Strong, in his “Greek Dictionary of the New Testament,” explains that the word is derived either from epiousa, epi, or eimi, meaning “for subsistence,” “needful,” “daily,” or “tomorrow’s.”

St. Jerome says, “The Hebrew Gospel according to Matthew reads: ‘Give us this day tomorrow’s bread,’ in other words, the Bread that You will give us in Your kingdom, give us this day.”

Notes: [212] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 7.7 (NPNF I/6:282) amended. [213] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 8.5 (NPNF I/6:285). [214] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 6.10 (NPNF I/6:277). [215] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 7.7 (NPNF I/6:282) amended. [216] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 9.6 (NPNF I/6:289) amended. [217] St. Cyprian of Carthage, Treatise 4: On the Lord’s Prayer 18 (ANF 5:452). [218] Tertullian, On Prayer 6 (ANF 3:683). [219] Origen, On Prayer 27.2 (ACW 19:93). [220] Origen, On Prayer 27.6 (ACW 19:96). [221] Origen, On Prayer 27.8 (ACW 19:97–98). [222] Origen, On Prayer 27.13 (ACW 19:102). passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q940 “Why does God not forgive us our trespasses unless we also forgive our brethren their trespasses?”, pp. 69–70
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 940. Why does God not forgive us our trespasses unless we also forgive our brethren their trespasses?

In practice, we witness our own wickedness in that we do not generally pardon others for the things they do against us; and in that we are strangers to the goodness of God. We ought to approach prayer in a spirit of love, without any malice or hatred towards anyone, regardless of his stance against us or against the Church. Our forgiveness towards him in our hearts is manifest to God Himself. Thus do we fulfil the apostolic command: “If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom.12:18).

Abba Isaac says, “Whoever then does not from his heart forgive his brother who has offended him, by this prayer calls down upon himself not forgiveness but condemnation.”

St. Augustine says, “‘forgive us our debts’ … For debtors are we, not in money, but sins. You are saying perchance at this moment, and you too. We answer, Yes, we too. What, you Holy Bishops, are you debtors? Yes, we are debtors too. What you! My Lord. Be it far from you, do not yourself this wrong. I do myself no wrong, but I say the truth; we are debtors: ‘If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (1 John 1:8). We have been baptized, and yet are we debtors. Not that anything then remained, which was not remitted to us in Baptism, but because in our lives we are contracting ever what needs daily forgiveness.”

“What man is there that lives so, that this prayer is not necessary for him? He may puff himself up, justify himself he cannot. It were well for him to imitate the Publican, and not swell as the Pharisee, ‘who went up into the temple’ (Luke 18:10–11), and boasted of his deserts, and covered up his wounds. Whereas he who said, ‘Lord, be merciful to me a sinner’ (Luke 18:13), knew wherefore he went up. Consider, my brethren, this prayer the Lord Jesus taught His disciples to offer, those great first Apostles of His, the leaders of our flock. If the leaders of the flock then pray for the remission of their sins, what ought the lambs to do?”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q933 “Why do we address God thus: “Our Father who art in Heaven”?”, p. 60
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 933. Why do we address God thus: “Our Father who art in Heaven”?

Nor is even our mother the Church passed by, if, that is, in the Father and the Son is recognized the mother, from whom arises the name both of Father and Son. In one general term, then, or word, we both honor God, together with His own, and are mindful of the precept, and set a mark on such as have forgotten their Father.”

Notes: [168] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 7.2 (NPNF I/6:280–281) amended. [169] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 8.2 (NPNF I/6:284) amended. passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q944 “Why are the supplications in the Lord’s Prayer ordered this way?”, p. 74
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 944. Why are the supplications in the Lord’s Prayer ordered this way?

St. Augustine sees a clear distinction between those supplications that concern the future eternal life for which we hope and those whose fulfilment begins from now but continue in eternity — namely, “Hallowed be Thy name, Thy Kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in Heaven” — and those supplications that only concern our present life —“Give us this day our daily bread, forgive us our trespasses, lead us not into temptation, deliver us from the evil one.” In eternity, we will not need daily bread and will not ask for forgiveness since we will sin no more. There will be no tempter to fight against us, and thus we will not pray for deliverance from the evil one.

Notes: [245] St. Augustine of Hippo, Our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount 2.10.36–37 (NPNF I/6:45–46).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q905 “Are communal prayers necessary?”, p. 32
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 905. Are communal prayers necessary?

The believer feels that he is in communion with his brothers and sisters in prayer even in his private room, and thus he prays for all and asks for their prayers on his behalf. St. Basil wrote to one of the widows, “be mindful of God and have the fear of Him in your heart, and invite all to a union with you in your prayers. For great is the assistance of those who are able to move God.”

St. Ambrose says, “For if according to the Lord’s saying, that that which two shall have agreed upon on earth concerning anything which they shall ask, shall be done for them, as He says, by My Father, Who is in heaven, for: ‘Where two or three are gathered together in My Name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matt. 18:19) … how much less, where the full congregation is gathered in the Name of the Lord. Where the demand of all is unanimous, ought we to doubt that the Lord Jesus is there as the Author of that desire, and the Hearer of the petition.”

“Believe, then, that the Lord Jesus is present at the invocation of the priest, Who said: ‘For where two or three are, there I am also’ (Matt. 18:20). How much where the Church is, and where His Mysteries are, does He vouchsafe to impart His presence!”

Notes: [85] St. Basil of Caesarea, Letters 1–185 174 (FOTC 13:337). [86] St. Ambrose of Milan, Letters 63.3 (NPNF II/10:457). [87] St. Ambrose of Milan, On the Mysteries 5.27 (NPNF II/10:320).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q936 “Is He not the King of Kings? So why do we pray, “Thy kingdom come”?”, pp. 63–64
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Model Prayer — 936. Is He not the King of Kings? So why do we pray, “Thy kingdom come”?

But he who has already renounced the world, is moreover greater than its honours and its kingdom. And therefore he who dedicates himself to God and Christ, desires not earthly, but heavenly kingdoms. But there is need of continual prayer and supplication, that we fall not away from the heavenly kingdom, as the Jews, to whom this promise had first been given, fell away; even as the Lord sets forth and proves: ‘Many,’ says He, ‘shall come from the east and from the west, and shall recline with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth’ (Matt. 8:11). He shows that the Jews were previously children of the kingdom, so long as they continued also to be children of God; but after the name of Father ceased to be recognised among them, the kingdom also ceased; and therefore we Christians, who in our prayer begin to call God our Father, pray also that God’s kingdom may come to us.”

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “A pure soul can say with boldness, Thy kingdom come; for he who has heard Paul saying, ‘Let not, therefore, sin reign in your mortal body’ (Rom. 6:12), and has cleansed himself indeed, and thought, and word, will say to God, Thy kingdom come.”

St. Gregory of Nyssa says, “We again ask the Lord to save us from corruption and that death may be taken away or as it was said: ‘Your kingdom come,’ namely, that the Holy Spirit may dwell in us and purify us.”

Tertullian says, “Our wish is that our reign be hastened, not our servitude protracted [in this world].”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q900 “Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?”, pp. 23–24
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 900. Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?

St. Basil the Great says, “It may be that He delays answering a prayer so that your zeal and your desire to approach Him may be multiplied, and that you may appreciate the gift of God and guard it carefully when you have received it. That which a person receives with great effort, he strives to protect, lest in losing it his labor will have been in vain.”

St. Augustine says, “He, who was not willing to give [the unjust judge in Luke 18:2], gave what was asked, because the other did not faint in asking. How much more then shall that Good One give who exhorts us to ask, who is displeased if we ask not? But when at times He gives somewhat slowly, it is that He is showing us the value of His good things; not that He refuses them. Things which have been long desired, are obtained with the greater pleasure, whereas those which are given quickly, are held cheap.”

“Some things, indeed, we wish because we are in Christ, and other things we desire because still in this world … Abiding, therefore, ourselves in Him, when His words abide in us we shall ask what we will, and it shall be done unto us. For if we ask, and the doing follows not, what we ask is not connected with our abiding in Him, nor with His words which abide in us, but with that craving and infirmity of the flesh which are not in Him, and have not His words abiding in them. For to His words, at all events, belongs that prayer which He taught, and in which we say, Our Father, who art in heaven (Matt. 6:9). Let us only not fall away from the words and meaning of this prayer in our petitions, and whatever we ask, it shall be done unto us … But when His words abide only in the memory, and have no place in the life, the branch is not to be accounted as in the vine, because it draws not its life from the root.”

Abba Isaac, the disciple of St. Anthony, says, “We sometimes ask for things opposed to our salvation and that we are most providentially refused our requests by Him who sees what is good for us with greater right and truth than we can. And it is clear that this also happened to the teacher of the Gentiles when he prayed that the messenger of Satan who had been for his good allowed by the Lord’s will to buffet him, might be removed, saying: ‘For which I besought the Lord thrice that he might depart from me. And He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness’ (2 Cor. 12:8– 9).”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian, pp. 219–220
passages.text:
Saint: TAKLA HAYMANOT, THE ETHIOPIAN, ST. — His Childhood

His Childhood:

In the biography of St. Takla Haymanot, many events were mentioned about God’s work within him during his childhood. Among these was that: after his parents sold all that his mother Sarah brought from the palace of the king from splendid attire, gold, silver, and pearls and distributed their price on the poor, the land went through a severe famine, and so many people were suffering. The mother was crying bitterly longing to give something more to the poor. The suckling baby, seeing her tears, pointed his little hand toward a small cup of flour and touched it. The flour started to flow heavily from that cup. His mother hastened to bring all that she had in her kitchen for the suckling to touch with his hand to let her have plenty to give to the poor. The little child was baptized, and called by the name ‘Fish Hazion,’ (meaning: the Joy of Zion), to be raised in a life of piety and worship with a spirit of asceticism, along with humility and love for everyone.

His Ordination:

Having reached 20 years of age, the metropolitan of Ethiopia Abba ‘Girguis II’ ordained him as a deacon in the days of the 75th Pope, St. Cyril III of Alexandria (1235-1243). During the ordination, the metropolitan kissed him, declared that he would be beloved by God and that the angel of the Lord would always accompany him with a sword of fire in his hand. St. Takla Haymanot lived a life of purity and chastity; and when his parents urged him to get married, he refrained, proclaiming his desire to live a celibate life. However, when they forced him to do so, he lived with his wife like brother and sister until she reposed in the Lord. Then, the metropolitan of Ethiopia ordained him as a priest. His mother reposed on the 22nd of Mesra, and his father followed her after only four days.

This young priest lived in his parent’s house for another seven years. Then, it happened one day when he went out to hunt animals, that the Archangel Michael appeared to him and told him that such action is not befitting for a priest, but he should instead dedicate his life to prayers, to the study of the Holy Bible and teaching. He told him also that God has granted him the gift of healing of the sick and performing miracles, and that his name from now on would not be Fish Hazion, but Takla Haymanot. It was also said that the Lord Jesus Christ put His hand on him and blessed him after calling him to the preaching work and promised to be with him and support him. The saint then distributed all his parents’ wealth on the poor, bid farewell to the inhabitants of his city, and set forth to preach.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian, pp. 218–219
passages.text:
Saint: TAKLA HAYMANOT, THE ETHIOPIAN, ST.

St. Takla Haymanot occupies a prominent standing in the Ethiopian Church as being one of the pillars of the Ethiopian monastic life. He lived during the years 1215-1313 and was the cause of salvation to so many. His father, the priest Tsega Zeab (=Gift of Faith), was married to a charming and rich girl by the name of Egzie Haraya (=Choice of God) or Sarah in Hebrew. They both lived a life of piety, loving the poor and the needy. Not having any children, Sarah sought from her husband to distribute all their possessions on the poor and to release all their slaves and maidservants. After asking her not to have them act in a rush on that matter, her husband, the priest, found her still persistent in her position. So, he rejoiced in her counsel and did according to her heart’s desire. The slaves and the maidservants were intensely grieved, for they used to feel as members of the household, and some of them sought to remain with them in the house as brothers and sisters, which they did.

When the pagan Matolomy became the king of Ethiopia, he started to persecute the Christians. He sent his soldiers everywhere around to apply their acts of violence against the Christians. One of the soldiers reached the house of the priest and planned to kill him with his spear. But, the priest managed to flee from his home and dived into a lake. The soldier stood by on the shore, waiting for him to come out of the water to kill him. After spending a long time waiting, the soldier assumed that the priest had already drowned. However, it happened that when the priest dived in the lake, he found the Archangel Michael covering him as though in a tent. Later on, when he came out of the water, he found that his wife was taken as a captive and the church was devastated. He then cried bitterly.

It happened that when the soldiers realized how beautiful the wife Sarah was, they brought her up to their king as a precious gift. He ordered them to keep her in one of his houses and adorn her with gold, silver, expensive jewelry, and magnificent attire. On the other hand, she abstained from the superb food, and her tears never ceased to flow. By night, when all went to sleep, she took off the precious attire and put on her simple garment, prayed to God seeking salvation from that evil situation. And, she asked the intercession of the Archangel Michael, whose feasts she used to celebrate every month, by giving many gifts to the poor. Then, God sent his archangel to comfort her and to give her the good news that she would be granted a child who would be a cause of blessing to so many.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian, pp. 220–221
passages.text:
Saint: TAKLA HAYMANOT, THE ETHIOPIAN, ST. — His Preaching and Monastic Ministry

His Preaching and Monastic Ministry:

St. Takla Haymanot set forth to the region of Katata, where its inhabitants worshipped the idols, the trees, and the sun. There, the people were stirred up against him, mainly that they heard the voice of the devil from the tree, their idol, seeking from them to send him away. As for him, he stood afar, faced the East, raised his hands, and prayed, asking God to destroy that tree. So, the tree was uprooted and moved toward the saint, and then the devil confessed publicly that he was leading the people to vanity. On his hands, God performed so many miracles, which caused many to believe and be baptized in the water of the River. The region’s prince was saddened by uprooting that tree because it was producing a high income for him. And, when he came to inspect it, he found out that the saint ordered to use its wood to build a church. However, the prince fell ill, and the saint healed him in the name of the Holy Trinity. This miracle made him, his wife Acrocina and his three sons, get baptized, and the children's names were replaced with Christian ones. Together with them, many other people were also baptized. His ascetic life merged with his preaching work, so he was a true hermit who spent most of the forty days fasting period in the wilderness in a robust ascetic way, to come back to his brethren and children to care for them with stronger love.

The people got so attached to him, but in obedience to the Lord’s commandment, he had to move from one city to another in Ethiopia, to preach the Gospel, and to oppose the idol worship and the works of sorcery. So, he faced significant troubles and opposition; but God supported him with the miracles and the healings He performed through him.

Besides his preaching work, he lived as a Father to so many monks. In the monastery which the saint founded in the Amhara region, he practiced the monastic life with the spirit of worship and watching the nights, in addition to serving the others and ministering to the poor. The monks of the area considered him as an angel and not as a normal human being. The monastery turned into a center of preaching. It was said that the Abbot of that monastery died, and he was bitterly mourned by all. Here, St. Takla Haymanot came to where the corpse was and prayed to God, who raised the monastery’s Abbot from the dead. The nephew of the risen man was a priest, and he came rushing to cry at the feet of the saint seeking his forgiveness. He confessed to him that he used to envy his uncle on what God has granted him of gifts, and how badly he was aspiring to occupy his place as the Abbot of the monastery after his death.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian, p. 221
passages.text:
Saint: TAKLA HAYMANOT, THE ETHIOPIAN, ST. — His Preaching and Monastic Ministry

The nephew of the risen man was a priest, and he came rushing to cry at the feet of the saint seeking his forgiveness. He confessed to him that he used to envy his uncle on what God has granted him of gifts, and how badly he was aspiring to occupy his place as the Abbot of the monastery after his death. And, asked the saint to pray on his behalf, and commended him for his holy life and his love even for those envious people.

When the saint felt that temporal glory would chase him after raising that monastery’s Abbot from the dead, he cried out to the Lord to take him away from that place. The Archangel Michael advised him to go to the monastery of St. Istifanos (Steven), headed by ‘Iyasus Mo’a’ (=Jesus overcomes). He forsook the region of Amhara, until he reached the river, where the angel walked along with him on the water to reach that monastery.

St. Takla Haymanot dedicated his time to worship and making metanoias with incredible perseverance that the Lord allowed him to see the heavenly Jerusalem and the thrones of glory prepared for those who strive. There, he heard a voice calling his name, telling him that he would be counted among the 24 priests and was given a golden censor to raise incense with them, and to praise the Lord along with them. From that monastery, he moved to the monastery of Abuna Aregawi on the high mountain of Debre Damo. There, he met with Abbot Yoĥannes (John), the Abbot of the monastery and the spiritual mentor of Iyasus Moʹa. Abbot Yoĥannes clothed St. Takla Haymanot with the monastic Great Eskeem, and he remained there for 12 years practicing the ascetic life. Then, after bidding the Abbot of the monastery and the brethren farewell, they tied him to a rope to bring him down from the monastery on the top of the mountain to the valley below. However, during that process, the rope was torn, and everybody assumed that the saint would fall to his death. But, behold! They watched how amazing wings emerged out of the saint’s back to let him fly and get down safely. That is why he is often portrayed like a Cherub with six wings. Then, the saint kept moving from one monastery to another; and the power of God kept working with him and within him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian, pp. 221–222
passages.text:
Saint: TAKLA HAYMANOT, THE ETHIOPIAN, ST. — His Preaching and Monastic Ministry

That is why he is often portrayed like a Cherub with six wings. Then, the saint kept moving from one monastery to another; and the power of God kept working with him and within him.

It was also said that he went to Jerusalem, where he met with the 78th Pope of Alexandria, St. Gabriel III (1268-1271); he got the blessing of the Holy Tomb and the blessed sites, then headed to the wilderness of Scetis in Egypt. There, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and asked him to go back to Ethiopia. There, he lived and had so many disciples sharing his monastic life. And, when he consummated his strife, the Lord Christ appeared to him, to tell him that he was about to depart. Then, he was inflicted with the plague and reposed in the Lord around the year 1313 AD.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yamata, p. 348
passages.text:
Saint: YAMATA, ST.

According to some historians like August Dillmann (1823-1894), who in the year 1880, said that this saint is also called Matthew. This is probably why, there was confusion with another saint by the name Abba Matthew, who appeared in Howzen, and he went to Ethiopia many years before the nine saints who came from Upper Egypt. They also claimed that he established a monastery in Gomalta.The Ethiopian Church celebrates him on the 28th of Baba.

[The Paramus Monastery: The Ethiopian Monasticism; 1999; p. 104]
