The Christian School started as a Catechetical School where candidates were admitted to learn the Christian faith and some Biblical studies to qualify for baptism. Admittance was open to all people regardless of culture, age or background.

By the second century, its substantial influence on church life can be seen from the following:

1- It satisfied the thirst of the Alexandrian Christians for religious knowledge, encouraged higher studies and created research work in a variety of fields.

2- It incubated numerous spiritual and well-known church leaders throughout the years. Many of them merited to succeed St. Mark.

3- Through its missionary zeal, it won many souls to Christianity from Egypt and abroad.

4- In true ecumenical spirit it attracted students from other nations, many of whom became leaders and bishops in their own churches.

5- It established a common awareness of the importance of education as a basic element in religious structure.

6- It offered the world's first systematic theological study curriculum.

7- It used philosophy as a weapon against pagan philosophers, thus beating them at their own game. [11]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q873 “What is the relationship between asceticism and the ecclesiastical life?”, p. 665
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 873. What is the relationship between asceticism and the ecclesiastical life?

I have spoken often of asceticism in the Coptic Church, its theological understanding, its life of worship, and its behavioral implications. It will be sufficient, then, to add the following few points:

1. The influence of the ascetic life on the Coptic worship is clear. There are many hymns that bring joy to the soul; the Church fasts more than half of the year; her liturgies are centered around waiting for the coming of Christ with an eschatological mindset.

2. The Coptic Church is known for her numerous martyrs, to the extent that some scholars regard the fact that the Coptic Church still exists till our present day as a divine miracle. Entire cities were martyred, and the martyrs faced their persecutors with joy, waiting for their crown of martyrdom.

3. Ascetic and spiritual thought influenced Alexandrian theology, which bears a salvific mindset, so that her theology was centered around salvation (Soteriology). Theology is not about some philosophical ideas for research, as much as it is tasting God’s salvific work in the believer’s life.

4. The ascetic life does not mean being in enmity with the flesh, but rather viewing the flesh as being sacred and a helper for the soul.

5. The ascetic life paved the road to start the ascetic movements in all their forms (solitude, coenobitism, and semi-eremitism). These movements aimed for a life of unity with God, in one form or another. This is why the believers understood solitude not as isolation from people, but as solitude with God. Even if a monk lives in the wilderness alone, his heart is never isolated from the rest of humanity, but he rather bears them with love in his heart, as he prays for them and suffers with their sufferings, longing for the salvation of everyone.

6. Many Egyptian fathers resisted exaggeration in asceticism, especially if done without discernment or wisdom.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q791 “Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?”, p. 599
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 791. Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?

a. The Liturgy of St. Basil the Great. The Coptic Liturgy differs from the Byzantine Liturgy of the same name. This Liturgy is the one that is most often used.

b. The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian. Often used on special occasions and feasts. Prayers of this Liturgy address the hypostasis of the Son. It is not unique in doing so because there are other liturgies with the same style, such as other Egyptian liturgies, three Ethiopian liturgies, the Syrian Liturgy of Saints Addai and Mari, and the Syrian Liturgy of St. Jacob.

c. The Liturgy of St. Cyril (St. Mark the Evangelist). St. Cyril of Alexandria compiled it and edited the older Liturgy of St. Mark; so it came to be named after him. Its use is less widespread than the previous two.

Sellers states: "The teaching of Athanasius and later representatives of the School of Alexandria come before us as a striking example of the dependence of Christological on soteriological thoughts. Consequently, if we are to appreciate their doctrine of the Person of Jesus Christ, we must first briefly consider their doctrine of His Work as Savior [1] ."

Before discussing the Christian dogmas of the Coptic Orthodox Church and the Alexandrian Fathers, I would like to observe that Alexandria, the great cosmopolitan city , was the most suitable place for the gospel of Christ to be adopted and for its divine truth to be declared in theological teaching and terms.

In the first century, when St. Mark the Evangelist visited Alexandria, there were three communities : the Egyptian, the Jewish, and the Greek; each had its own culture.

It is well known that the ancient Egyptians were religiously minded by nature and upbringing since early times [2] . The famous historian Herodotus stated that (the Egyptians are religious to excess, far beyond any other race of men). Their spiritual curiosity led to the revelation of many fundamental ideas of faith and prepared their minds to accept the Christian dogmas without a great deal of difficulty. The "oneness of Godhead" was not novel to the Egyptian mind, for their philosophers believed in One Supreme Being. The best example was king Ikhnaton (1383- 1365 B.C.), who believed in One God and struggled to preach this idea throughout Egypt. At the same time, every central town recognized some triad, not too different from the "Holy Trinity." Also, they believed in the world to return and in the resurrection etc. [3]

The Jews had their schools not only in Alexandria but in many other countries. Judaism, the cradle in which Christianity was nurtured [4] , flourished in Alexandria. It had produced the Septuagint version of the Old Testament, where Jewish theology was integrated with Hellenist philosophy. Perhaps the most notable exponent of this philosophy was the Alexandrian Jew Philo (c 30 B.C. - c 45 A.D.), who was drawn to the Greek philosophers but maintained that all their best ideas had been anticipated in the Jewish scripture. Two aspects of his thought are of particular interest in studying Christian doctrine [5] :

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q877 “What is the Coptic monastic movement today?”, p. 671
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 877. What is the Coptic monastic movement today?

One of the most notable characteristics of the Coptic Orthodox Church today is the constant increase in the number of those wanting to join the monastic life, leading to the restoration of many of the deserted monasteries. Monasteries for men are spread in the wilderness, whereas convents are located within the towns and cities.

Pope Cyril VI reconstructed the monastery of St. Mina, close to Alexandria. Likewise, Pope Shenouda III renovated the monastery of St. Pishoy in the Wadi Natrun, where he established a patriarchate because of his great love for monasticism, and he regularly spent approximately half of each week there.

Moreover, many of the youth who immigrated to the United States, Canada, and Australia joined monasteries after succeeding in their careers.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril VI, the 116th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 534–535
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL VI, The 116th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — How the State saw the Immigrants in the Days of Gamal Ăbdel Nasser

How the State saw the Immigrants in the Days of Gamal Ăbdel Nasser:

‘Gamal Ăbdel Nasser’ was about to close the door shut on the Egyptians, concerning immigrating to North America, Canada, and Australia; and the government considered any immigrant – most of whom were Christians – as traitors; and consequently they had no hope of coming to visit their beloved country – Egypt.

The immigrants used to fear to go to any Egyptian embassy or consulate, nor to encounter any of those in charge and did their best to hide their addresses, to avoid any chance to bring harm to themselves or their relatives in Egypt.

The Church, at that time, was between two millstones; being a national church, it had to submit with its whole heart to the temporal authority, and to carry all love and loyalty to Egypt; at the same time, she is the mother who would never disregard nor forget her children, wherever they are.

Hatred Miraculously turned into Close Friendship:

By a noble miraculous act, that hatred turned into a close friendship between the president and the pope that they started to exchange visits. The State even contributed to making up for the deficit in the finances of the patriarchate. The president himself partook in the celebration of laying the cornerstone of the new magnificent cathedral in the region of Abba ‘Roweis.’

Caring for the Outer World:

During his time, pope ‘Cyril VI’ established many churches to care for the Copts in Europe and elsewhere. A metropolitan was ordained for the throne in Jerusalem, to preserve the possessions of the Coptic Church there.

In Africa, he organized the church of Ethiopia, spiritually and administratively. He ordained Abba ‘Basilius’ as a patriarch (Catholicos) on it, who was ordained in Egypt in June 1959 in the presence of Emperor ‘Haile Selassie’ of Ethiopia, who presented the pope with the long Sash of Solomon. The pope visited Ethiopia in October 1960, where he was welcomed indescribably.

For the first time in modern history, we come to hear of Ecumenical Councils. Pope ‘Cyril VI’ headed the Council of the non-Chalcedonian Churches, held in ‘Addis Ababa,’ Ethiopia in January 1965. In conjunction with the patriarch of Antioch, the patriarch of Armenia, and the Catholicos of the Syrian Church in India, they all agreed on individual decisions leading to the deepening of their understanding of their mutual theological Orthodox concepts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gabriel II, the 70th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 147–148
passages.text:
Saint: GABRIEL II, The 70th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Shepherding Activities

There was a complete reversal of the formal policies of Coptic persecution that had existed during the harsh reign of Caliph Al-Ĥakim bi-Amr Allah (996-1021 AD). Some authorities began to fear that Islamized Copts might be tempted to abjure their new faith and return across-the-board to their Coptic Christian beliefs. This, indeed, may have been one of the factors that precipitated the rebellion of Ĥasan, Al-Ĥafizs son, against his father, which led to the temporary deposition of the Caliph and the application of restrictive measures on the Copts. It was during this interlude that Ĥasan arrested and incarcerated Pope Gabriel II. The pope was released after a compulsory payment of 1,000 dinars that had been raised by the Coptic archons and wealthy merchants.

His Relationship with the Ethiopian Church:

The Church of Ethiopia was headed by a metropolitan, aided by seven Coptic bishops. When the metropolitan requested from the king of Ethiopia, an increase in the number of bishops, for fear that it might be a plan to ordain an independent patriarch for Ethiopia, the pope refused the request, which provoked them there to ordain Ethiopian bishops without referring to the pope or the Coptic metropolitan in Ethiopia. Pope Gabriel II sat fourteen years on the Seat and then reposed in peace on the 10th of Baramouda in the year 1145 AD.

[Kamel Saleh Nakhla: Pope St. Gabriel II, known as Ibn Turayk] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Gabriel II ibn Turayk, by Subhi Y. Labib, p. 1127-9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril IV, the 110th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 523–524
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL IV, The 110th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Patriotism and Visit to Ethiopia

It was also claimed that he intended to unite with the English Episcopal Church, despite the continuous attempts of England to create animosity between the khedive and the pope; and between the Ethiopian king and the pope; but both attempts failed, by the divine grace and the wisdom of this pope.

The British leaders did their best, as well, to plant the doubt in ‘Saåiid Pasha’ concerning the intention of the pope; and convinced the khedive not to try to resolve the controversy with Ethiopia, before bringing the Egyptian army toward the border between Egypt-Sudan and Ethiopia. They also asked him to go, by himself to ‘Khartoum,’ Sudan. At the same time, they claimed to the king of Ethiopia, that the pope’s visit to him was to distract his attention, to make it easier for ‘Saåiid Pasha’ to attack him and take over Ethiopia. The angry Ethiopian king thought of killing the pope, except for the intervention of the queen and the officers of the court who counseled him to investigate the matter more carefully.

The pope wrote to the khedive to tell him that his mission was about to succeed, until the army movement to the border; and sought from him to give the orders for retreat. When the Ethiopian king realized the true intentions of the pope, he apologized to him, signed a treaty, and delivered it to the pope who sought his permission to return home. The Ethiopian king provided the pope with so many gifts for him and for ‘Saåiid Pasha,’ and allowed him to return to Cairo on the 7th of Amshir 1574 AM (1858 AD), after an absence of about a year and a half; and sent along with him the king’s personal priest and an Ethiopian minister who carried with him the signed treaty.

However, because of the grand celebrations of the Copts for the safe return of their pope and the lifting of the Cross up in processions along the streets, the khedive was offended. The evil people and the British found their chance to attack the pope, and they stirred up the khedive against him, that he refused to receive him, despite that the pope tried several times to see him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius II, the 111th Pope of Alexandria, p. 576
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS II, The 111th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Pope’s Care for the Coptic Schools

The Pope’s Care for the Coptic Schools:

Among the most important achievements of this pope was the completion of the construction of the great St. Mark Cathedral in the province of ‘El- Azbakieh’ in Cairo; and ensuring the development and progress of the Coptic schools.

When the Ottoman sultan ‘Ăbdul-Ăziz’ (1861-1876) came to visit Egypt earlier in the year 1863, khedive ‘Saåiid Pasha,’ invited the scholars, the ministers, and the religious leaders to meet him. It was the custom in that era that whoever was called on to greet the sultan, was to kiss his hand or the hem of his robe. When it was the turn for the Coptic Pope ‘Demetrius II,’ he kissed the chest of the sultan instead. The sultan was disturbed, and so did the audience, who considered it as an improper daring from the pope. However, when the pope was asked about the meaning of that unusual kissing, unprecedented by anyone else, the pope answered: “By doing this, I kiss the hand of the King of kings and the Sultan of the Sultans; for it came in the Holy Bible: ‘The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord’ (Prov. 21:1)”. This was translated for sultan ‘Ăbdul-Ăziz’ into the Turkish language by Fr. ‘Salama,’ the secretary of the pope. On hearing the translation, the sultan smiled with pleasure and donated 1,000 acres of the government farmland to the Coptic schools.

Later on, khedive ‘Ismaåiil Pasha’ increased that gift by an additional 500 acres in the province of ‘Sharqieh.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril IV, the 110th Pope of Alexandria, p. 523
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL IV, The 110th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Administrative Office for the Patriarchate

Administrative Office for the Patriarchate:

As far as the organization of the church was concerned, it was the first time we hear about establishing records and archives for the church possessions and endowments and adequately organizing them. As well as caring for the affairs of the priests and their families, and recording the incomes and budgets of the churches. The pope established an office for running the affairs of the patriarchate and set for it an elaborate system to define the responsibilities and limits for the endowment managers to follow accordingly. He divided the workers in that office into two departments: one to supervise the endowments of the church, oversee the endowment manager's actions, review their income and expense accounts. The second department to manage the religious and legal events, headed by a priest under the metropolitan of Cairo. Both departments were under the direct supervision of the pope himself.

His Patriotism and Visit to Ethiopia:

Regarding his patriotism, pope ‘Cyril IV’ was a good friend of the grand sheikh of ‘Al-Azhar,’ and its other leaders. He held with them scientific and theological debates in an atmosphere of love, tolerance, and amiability.

We should also remember that in the days of that great pope, starting from the beginning of the year 1856, the khedive allowed the Copts to be drafted in the army and to apply for the military service like their Muslim brothers. This took place right after he annulled the tax previously placed on the non-Muslims in the year 1855.

As a patriot, he traveled to Ethiopia at the end of Mesra 1572 AM (1856 AD) to resolve a problem concerning the border between Egypt-Sudan and Ethiopia. Khedive Saåiid Pasha sent him, accompanied by two Turkmen from the government, and during that long trip, the pope learned the Turkish tongue.

Although the pope was apprehensive of the attitude of the Ethiopian king ‘Theodorus,’ yet the king welcomed him kindly, and his visit to Ethiopia had a tremendous friendly outcome that replaced the animosity between the two countries. Some British politicians, perceiving his attempts to oppose their influence in Ethiopia, and for fear of him seeking a union of the Orthodox churches, accused him of planning to bring Ethiopia under the protection of Russia. It was also claimed that he intended to unite with the English Episcopal Church, despite the continuous attempts of England to create animosity between the khedive and the pope; and between the Ethiopian king and the pope; but both attempts failed, by the divine grace and the wisdom of this pope.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodosius II, the 79th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 272–273
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOSIUS II, The 79th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Troubles

After the departure of the 78th pope Joannes VII on the 21st of April 1293, the throne of St. ‘Mark’ stayed vacant for about 15 months. Then, the bishops assembled together, without informing the archons, and they chose the monk Theodosius of the monastery of Abu-Fanah in El-Minya governorate, to become the new pope. He was originally called Ăbd el-Messiĥ ibn Abi Makkin, and was known by the name Ibn Rubil of the city of Beni-Khasim. He was ordained as a pope by the name of Theodosius II in the year 1294 AD.

His Troubles:

The new pope sat on the papal throne in a period of tranquility and peace, after all the tribulations his predecessor encountered. Unfortunately, however, being a lover of money, somehow, he practiced the Simonism. That behavior caused the congregation to be highly offended, particularly that his own ordination was made without their consent. Even though many of his bishops tried to advise him to stop that practice, yet he did not listen, that some of them stopped mentioning his name in the liturgical prayers for some time. In his days, Jegbiason, the king of Ethiopia, sent a message to sultan Muĥammed ibn Qalawun, to inform him how he was treating the Muslims in his country with great love. And, he asked him to treat the Copts likewise, to maintain a relationship of love and cooperation between their countries. Also, in his days, Daoud, the king of Nubia, invaded Upper Egypt; then, when the pope intervened, he withdrew his armies.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Marcus II, the 49th Pope of Alexandria, p. 69
passages.text:
Saint: MARCUS II, The 49th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Friendship with the Governor

Friendship with the Governor:

After he was ordained, the new pope visited the governor of Egypt, Labib el-Dawla. Once the governor got to know the pope, a close friendship grew between the two of them. Then, when the governor told the pope that he could seek whatever he would want; the pope asked him to allow for building the churches required to serve the people and to allow repairing what needed to be repaired, and his request was instantly granted.

A Message of Fellowship to his Brother the Patriarch of Antioch:

The new pope also sent a message of fellowship to his brother, the patriarch of Antioch, who replied by a similar message, expressing his happiness for the unity of the Orthodox Faith.

The Decisions of the Chalcedonian Council:

Only a few number of people among the Copts approved the decisions of the Chalcedonian council. The new pope prayed day and night with tears for the sake of their return to the upright faith. God, responding to his prayers and tears, moved the heart of their leader, who was called Abraham, as well as the heart of his father George to true repentance. Pope Marcus welcomed them back into the Orthodox faith with all their followers, and he gave them the Holy Sacrament and ordained George and his son Abraham as bishops on their congregations.

Corrupt Politics and Sufferings:

In the time of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786-809 AD), his reign from Baghdad was marked by scientific, cultural and religious prosperity, but once he died, there was a fierce fight between his sons: Al-Ma’mun and Al- Amin for the caliphate, and a significant part of this fight was on the portion of Egypt. Also, Egypt suffered from accommodating about 15,000 refugees expelled from the land of Andalusia (Spain), after they attempted a revolt against the independent Umayyad caliphate there, but were defeated and exiled to Egypt. When they arrived, these exiled trouble-makers created chaos, burned the houses of worship, and disturbed the peaceful residents of Egypt. To comfort and strengthen his people, the pope kept wandering among them in Alexandria, until the exiled Andalusian made life very difficult for him. The pope finally had to forsake Alexandria and moved from one city to another. This kept going for about five years to avoid falling into their hands. Finally, prince Ăbd al-Ăziz the governor of the eastern provinces managed to bring peace to the land.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 128–129
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Ordained as a Pope

His sixth and final trip took place in November 2002. He conducted an extended “Silver Jubilee” tour for about seven months in 1996, which took him to Europe, Canada, the USA, and Australia. In April 2008, he made a second historical trip to Ethiopia following the resolution of the strain in the relationship between the two Churches caused by the communist coup in Ethiopia decades earlier.

Falling out with President Sadat:

Ten years into his papacy, in 1981, Pope Shenouda III had famously fallen out with President Anwar el-Sadat (1970-1981) of Egypt. The relationship between the two men deteriorated for several reasons:

• Since coming to power, President Sadat had started encouraging the growth of Islamism in the country as a means to fight communist groups and solidifying his power. During the term of office of Sadat's predecessor, Gamal Ăbdel Nasser, Islamic groups such as the “Muslim Brotherhood” had been suppressed.

• Sadat had also pushed forward a constitutional amendment that would have allowed him to stand for re-election as president more than twice. To make the constitutional amendment more appealing to the populace, Sadat bundled it with another constitutional amendment declaring “Islamic Shariåa Law” as the primary source of legislation, an action viewed as a step towards a more radically Islamic Egypt.

• Under Sadat, the government released a census in 1977 that understated the number of Christians living in Egypt, even contradicting earlier released censuses.

• The years from 1972 to 1981 saw an increase of violence against the Christians of Egypt, culminating in a massacre of Christians in a poor district of Cairo in 1981.

• Pope Shenouda was of the opinion that President Sadat's peace treaty with Israel was ill-timed and should have been part of broader comprehensive peace in the Middle East.

Pope Shenouda also saw president Sadat as becoming increasingly dictatorial following his acclaim in the international arena for the peace accord with Israel. In September 1981, Sadat rescinded the presidential decree of 1971, recognizing Pope Shenouda as the “Pope of Alexandria.” And, Pope Shenouda was banished to a desert monastery in the Natron Valley. However, the Copts continued to view Pope Shenouda as their pope, and he continued to conduct his duties from his desert monastery: in reality, the Sadat's decision was ineffective. Sadat was assassinated a month later, on the 6th of October 1981, by the Islamic extremists. In January 1985, Pope Shenouda III was fully reinstated by Sadat's successor, President Hosni Mubarak (1981-2011)…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 129–130
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Israel

Israel:

Pope Shenouda III did have some arguments with then-president Anwar el- Sadat over both the Camp David Accords and the president's inadequate response to the growing Islamism. His stance toward Israel was summarized by his words: “From the Arabic national point, we should not abandon our Palestinian brothers and our Arabic brothers by normalizing our relations with the Jews. From the Church's point of view, Copts who go to Jerusalem betray their Church in the case of "Al-Sultan Monastery" that Israel refused to give back to the Copts.”

Suicide Bombers:

In the light of September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the U.S.A.; Pope Shenouda III said about the suicide bombing used as a fighting tactic; for the people who support or feel good about these acts, they are at fault because of multiple reasons:

First, ignoring a tragedy of killing an innocent group of people. Second, not thinking about the wrong impression they would cause by showing their satisfaction with these murderous acts. Third, they are considered accomplices in these crimes. Fourth, they are committing a wrongful act not approved by religion.

Church Growth:

The papacy of Pope Shenouda III saw an expansion of the Coptic Orthodox Church in North America. While there were only 4 Coptic Orthodox churches in all of North America in 1971, today there are more than 200. Pope Shenouda established the first diocese in the lands of immigration for the Coptic Orthodox patriarchate in 1991, the diocese of Birmingham, and he consecrated and enthroned a General bishop for the United Kingdom at the time, bishop Missael to oversee the diocese.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cosmas II, the 54th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 473–474
passages.text:
Saint: COSMAS II, The 54th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Troubles of the Church during his Papacy

Matters became worse when the caliph issued a decree to dismiss all the Copts from the government administration and to replace them with Muslims or Islamized Christians. As a result, many of the Christians, to save themselves from humiliation and utter poverty, apostatized to Islam.

However, not long after the replacement of Copts by Muslims in the administration, the finances of the country began to suffer apparent reduction. Even wealthy Muslims, such as ‘Ibn Said aI-Asfahani,’ were victimized by Muslim officials. The poll tax (Jizyah), which had been 2 dinars, has become as high as 15 dinars. Living in the country grew almost intolerable, and many Copts preferred to deny their faith to save their skins, while Pope ‘Cosmas II’ felt helpless and looked upon the despicable situation in tears. A new official, ‘Al-Ĥarith ibn Miskin,’ proved to be even worse than his predecessor, and the persecution of the Copts continued.

At that time, Byzantine raiders attacked and plundered the city of ‘Damietta,’ and the governor employed Coptic slave labor to strengthen the walls of that city as well as other vulnerable cities; such as ‘Alexandria,’ ‘Rosetta,’ ‘Burullus’ and other coastal towns. Eventually, the authorities became aware of the need to restore the Copts to the administration to recover Egypt’s depleted economy. Also, the Copts were employed in shipbuilding and handling the fleet and in the manipulation of seafaring crafts. These were badly needed by the Muslims in defense of their coastal fortifications, as well as for launching counterraids on Byzantine shores and islands.

His Departure:

It appears that, near the end of the reign of caliph ‘al-Mutawakkil,’ the worst pressures on the Copts in Egypt were partially lifted. This might explain the return of relative prosperity to the country during the closing days of the patriarchate of the Pope ‘Cosmas II.’ In such a peaceful atmosphere, Pope ‘Cosmas II’ departed from this world and joined his ancestors, after sitting on the St. Mark throne for seven years and seven months. His departure was on the 21st of the Coptic month of ‘Hator’ (858 AD).

[Fr. Menasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church, pp. 356]

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Book 2, p. 435] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Cosmas II, by Subhi Y. Labib, p. 636-7]

Notes: [1] History of the Patriarchs, Vol. 2, pt. 1, p. 7.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril VI, the 116th Pope of Alexandria, p. 534
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL VI, The 116th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Ordained as the Pope of Alexandria (1959-1971)

Ordained as the Pope of Alexandria (1959-1971):

As the newly elected pope, according to the Church rite, was accompanied by the bishops from his monastery of the ‘Paramus’ to the patriarchate, on Sunday the 10th of May 1959.

Since his ordination, his door in the papal residence in ‘El-Azbakieh,’ Cairo, stayed open day and night before all. He chose disciples from the young men and had a diverse ministry.

On the Spiritual Aspect, he kept holding a holy liturgy daily with such spirituality and love that flared up the hearts of the people, drawing all to the love of God, the Church, and one another.

On the Construction Aspect, he started by reconstructing his beloved monastery of Mar Mina, which became a ruin in the 10th century. There, prayers, hymns, and monastic life resumed in that part of Marriott. He reconstructed, as well, the monasteries of ‘Scetis’ and those in Upper Egypt. He also laid the cornerstone of a new Cathedral and a ‘Clerical College’ in the region of Abba ‘Roweis’ in ‘Ăbbasiah’ Cairo, besides many other churches and convents.

On the Cultural Aspect, besides encouraging the Sunday schools, and ordaining two bishops; one for education, and another for scientific research, he set a particular building for the new printing machine, presented to him by the church in Austria.

On the Patriotic Aspect, the new pope chose to start his ministry in Egypt, by what the popes along the past generations used to do; he paid a visit to the head of the Republic ‘Gamal Ăbdel Nasser’ on the 15th of October of the same year.

There was an initial period during which ‘Gamal Ăbdel Nasser’ used to aim his hatred actively towards the Copts. At the time, the relationship between the pope and the president was taut. The pope’s only refuge was to cry out to the Lord and to seek the intercession of St. Mark, the preacher of Egypt.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John XVII, the 105th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 406–407
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN XVII, The 105th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Effect of the Catholic Intrusions

(Matthew 24:13). This great pope succeeded, to a great extent, and by the grace of the Holy Spirit, in keeping Coptic heritage, we received from our fathers. Among the essential manuscripts, this pope left to his church is the Psalms of the Agpeya, the Ten Commandments; the Seven Holy Sacraments; and the Evangelic advice.

The Roman papal deputy in Egypt sent a message to his Catholic congregation (all of whom were in Upper Egypt), to confirm the treaty agreed upon between him and the Coptic pope in the year 1794 AD, through the help of the ambassador of Austria, in which it came:  Those married of the two sects have the freedom to choose where they prefer to pray, either in the Coptic or the Catholic churches.  From now on, mixed marriages are not allowed between Copts and Catholics.  No priest is allowed to go to the houses of the other sect to preach.  No one is to be forced to pray in a specific church, but should be free to choose.  In case of any controversy between the two churches, it should not be referred to the local authority, but the heads of both churches to resolve and to punish the aggressor. From the unregular events in the days of Pope John XVII, was the coming down of darkness and the appearance of the stars at noontime, for two hours, that the people thought that the ultimate resurrection was at hand, and the fire ignited in the church of the Virgin St. Mary in Ĥaret el-Rum, on the eve of the Sunday of Resurrection. When even though the men of the governor managed to put it out, yet it was utterly robbed by the mob under the pretense of helping to put the fire out.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril IV, the 110th Pope of Alexandria, p. 525
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL IV, The 110th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Pope Cyril IV Care for the Education of Girls, Family, and Children

He also put a condition that both the bride and the groom have to make a clear and personal proclamation of their consent and approval of getting married in front of the priest before he officiates that Sacrament. Also, he requested that both parties should be given an ample chance to study one another before they get married.

Due to the invasion of foreign missionaries to Egypt, the pope used to meet weekly with his people and the priests to keep them alert with his profound belief that the real reforms should start with the priest and would end up with the child, also it could work the other way around.

The Unity of the Churches:

The pope’s heart desire was to unite the Orthodox churches all together, so he did his best to get united with the Greek Church, which the Russian Church was part of. At the same time, he cared for his Church to keep her doctrines and traditions intact.

Having very good relationships with the non-Orthodox Churches, relationships founded on love and mutual trust with their heads, the pope was accused of seeking the protection of the foreign countries, which stirred up the rulers against him.

His relationship with the English Episcopal Church was perfect, and that Church had all intentions to help the Coptic Church to reconstruct the church and school buildings that have been destroyed by the ‘Darawish.’

Other Works:

During his days, abba ‘Basilius,’ the Coptic Metropolitan of Jerusalem managed to get a court decision establishing the right of the Copts to hold the possession of the ‘Sultan’s Monastery’ in Jerusalem with a decree from the Ottoman sultan ‘Ăbdul Majid I’ (1839-1861).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexandros II, the 43rd Pope, pp. 133–134
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDROS II, THE 43rd POPE — His Troubles

When they did, they managed to deliver the funds to the governor. During the rule of that governor, he banned the use of the Coptic language in the departments of the government and the schools and punished everyone who challenged his order.

After ‘Ăbdallah,' ‘Qurra ibn-Sharik’ became the governor of Egypt (709- 715 AD) And, the same tragic situation continued, and the pope had to go to visit Upper Egypt to collect more money for the governor. In Upper Egypt, the Christians greatly rejoiced to receive their pope, because no pope ever came to visit them since the 38th pope St. ‘Benjamin I’ (623-662 AD). The taxes were much raised, in particular on the Copts, who had to sell the silver vessels of the altar to pay the taxes, and they had to replace them with wooden or glass vessels. The Moslems, as well, were furious against that governor.

Once, it happened that some evil men went to the governor, claiming that the Pope had his people forging the coins. So, the governor sent his men to insult the Pope and beat the people around him to the point of near-death. Then, as the claim proved to be false, they departed from the patriarchate.

Besides those external troubles, the Pope experienced difficulties stirred up from within, by the priests of the churches in Alexandria. Since the days of Emperor Constantine, these churches used to get financial help from the patriarchate, however, because of the higher taxes imposed by the governor, the Pope could no longer continue to send aid to these churches. When the priests and the elders protested against him, the Pope had to tell them how even the vessels of the Holy communion came to be glass instead of silver because of the anguish that dwelt upon the Church. Refusing to accept his argument, the Pope had to rebuke them and drive them out. However, when they left, they turned very hostile towards the Pope.

Besides those troubles, the whole country experienced a great famine and an epidemic disease, and many people died from hunger and illness. The Pope and the bishops had to wander in the land to support their people because of what they were going through.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Christodoulus, the 66th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 431–432
passages.text:
Saint: CHRISTODOULUS, The 66th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Pope was Re-arrested

The Pope was Re-arrested:

Another persecution was stirred up when some Copts attempted to reopen the closed churches. An enormous tax was imposed on the Copts of Alexandria in exchange for giving them the keys to one of their churches to be opened for worship.

The pope was again arrested and 9,000 Dinars were robbed from his residence’s safe. Then, they released him through the intervention of some Coptic officers of influence in the government.

The Monasteries were Attacked:

While the pope was visiting the monasteries of the ‘Natron Valley,’ the followers of ‘Nasir el-Dawla,’ the head of the ‘Turks,’ attacked the monasteries. They slew many monks, captured, and tortured the pope. Eventually, he was saved by one of his Coptic children, called ‘Abu el-Tayyib,’ the chief clerk of ‘Nasir el-Dawla,’ after he had to pay 3,000 Dinars as a redemption.

Stopping the Provisions:

As the conditions of the Copts considerably declined, the pope ordained a metropolitan by the name ‘Victor’ (Boctor) on Nubia; and that metropolitan asked ‘Guirgis’ the king of Nubia to send provisions to help the Copts in Egypt, but the soldiers of ‘Nasir el-Dawla’ stopped the delegates of the king of Nubia at the border of Egypt and committed them to return to their king with the provisions.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Peter VII, the 109th Pope of Alexandria, p. 420
passages.text:
Saint: PETER VII, the 109th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Wisdom in Action

His Wisdom in Action:

When the Copts in the village of his birth El-Gawly, faced extremely rough troubles, the wise pope called the prominent Copts in the village and requested from them to present 200 Feddans (Acres) of their best land, as a gift to Sherif Pasha. Then, by motivation from the pope, Sherif Pasha appointed muåallem Bishai Malyoshi from Assiut as the responsible person for that piece of land. The pasha also assigned to him 36 Feddans of it to live on and so there were no more troubles for the inhabitants of that village.

His Deep Patriotism:

As Moĥammed Ăli Pasha was making significant progress in his campaigns and invasions, the Russian empire was worried that this might interfere with their plans for the East and the Ottoman empire. So, the Russian Tsar sent one of his princes to meet with the Pope of Alexandria, the head of the largest Christian Church in the East, to urge him to seek the protection of Russia.

The prince, being used to the great magnificence of the Russian churches and the superb attires of their bishops, expected in Alexandria to enter into a great palace, to meet the court of the pope and to behave with a certain protocol. However, he was shocked to find himself standing before someone wearing a simple old woolen garment and around him were scattered some old chairs. He did not believe his eyes when the man told him he is the patriarch of the Copts. Before such simplicity, the Russian prince bowed down, kissed his hands, and sought his blessings. Asking him about the secret of this simple life, the pope answered him that it is befitting of the bishop to follow the lead of our Lord Jesus Christ who became poor for the sake of the sinners and asking him about the condition of the Coptic Church, he answered that the church was well as long as God was taking care of her.

When the prince indicated that he was concerned about what the Coptic Church was suffering from the rulers and offered Russian protection, the pope simply asked him: “Does your king live forever?” The prince answered: “No, my lord Father, but he dies like anyone else.” Then, the pope said to him: “You, therefore, live under the care of a mortal king. However, we live under the care of an immortal king: God”. Here, the prince found nothing to say, except to bow again before the pope seeking his blessing.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Great, p. 95
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE GREAT, ST.

A hermit in Mount Nitria, whose name is mentioned along with SS. Macarius, Pamponius, Heraclius and other saints. They became famous and drew many around them, in the days of Emperor Constantius II (337-361 AD), and kept the Upright faith, set by the Fathers of the Nicene Council.

St. Serapion the Great was a contemporary of St. Anthony the Great, and he was visited by St. Paula, the Elder in 386 AD, by Melania, the Elder in 387 AD, and by Palladius in 390 AD...

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 614]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Abbot, p. 94
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE ABBOT, ST.

This St. Serapion was a priest and one of the most famous Fathers. He was mentioned in the book: On Illustrious Men written by St. Jerome, as follows:

“We saw him in the region of Arsinoe (Fayyum), an elder father in charge of many monasteries that embraced about 10,000 monks, and he cared for all their needs. Those who harvested the fields used to bring to him 12 bushels of wheat, to give to those in need in the area. He used to distribute these needs by his own hands, and to send to those in Alexandria their portions as well.

The Fathers of the wilderness used to do that regularly, always taking care of the poor in Alexandria. But, because of being occupied with the life of spiritual strife, they used to just fill boats with food and clothes and send them every year to the capital; on account of that, the poor around them in the desert were not that many.

We also saw in the region of Babylon (Old Cairo) and Memphis (El- Badrashin) so many great Fathers, who were adorned with good deeds, blessed and well accepted by God.” The name of St. Serapion was also mentioned in the biography of the Libyan recluse Marcus Atheniensis, who cared to bury his body.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 613]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, p. 90
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, BISHOP OF THMUIS, ST. — His Defense of the Orthodox Faith

This St. Serapion was given the title Scholastic, due to his mastering of both the spiritual and temporal knowledge. For some time, he was the dean of the Theological (Catechetical) School of Alexandria, however, because of his love to the ascetic life, he became a hermit in the desert and a friend of St. Anthony the Great (251-356 AD). St. Serapion had to forsake his seclusion, to sit on the bishopric throne of Thmuis (Temy) in Upper Egypt, near Diospolis (Luxor).

His Defense of the Orthodox Faith:

St. Serapion attended the Council of Serdica in the year 343, where he joined the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373) in defending the Upright faith. According to St. Jerome, he was also exiled by Emperor Constantius II (337-361 AD). He partook of opposing the Macedonian and the Arian heresies and authored an excellent book against the Manicheans heresy.

Some of His Writings:

St. Serapion authored many books, most of which were lost, but his most famous work was Euchologion, discovered and published at the end of the 19th century.

According to the historian Socrates, St. Serapion often repeated the statements that summarized the exaltation of Christianity, saying:

“The mind is purified by spiritual knowledge (i.e., by holy meditation and prayers), the spiritual passions of the soul are purified by the charity, and the irregular appetites are purified by abstinence and penance.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serabamon, Bishop of Nicius, pp. 86–87
passages.text:
Saint: SERABAMON, BISHOP OF NICIUS (The martyr) — His Christianity and Monastic Life

His Christianity and Monastic Life:

This St. Serabamon was the bishop of Nicius. It happened that he was born in Jerusalem to a Jewish father by the name of Ibrahim, who was the son of Levi, the son of Joseph. This Joseph happened to be the brother of Simeon, the uncle of the archdeacon Steven the first martyr. They all were from the tribe of Judah. St. Serabamon was given the name of Simeon after his great grandfather’s brother. When Simeon’s father died, he wanted to convert from Judaism to become a Christian. An angel of the Lord appeared to him, told him to go to Abba John (Yohanna), the bishop of Jerusalem, who taught him the principals of Christianity and the Incarnation of Jesus Christ; but did not dare to baptize him in Jerusalem for fear of the Jews.

The Virgin St. Mary appeared to Simeon and told him to go to the city of Alexandria in Egypt to see the 16th Pope of Alexandria St. Theonas (282-301). Accompanied by an angel in a human form, he reached Alexandria and went to the Pope St. Theonas. The pope was informed about him in advance through an angel, who told him how great that man would become. The pope welcomed him, instructed him, and baptized him under the name of Serabamon, which means “Who was Born in the faith of his Fathers,” according to the 19th pope St. Alexandros I (312-328 AD), the author of his biography.

In Alexandria, Serabamon kept studying the Holy Bible and contemplating in the Passions of the Lord Christ for His love of humankind. He was supported by Pope Theonas and his disciple deacon Peter (Botros), who dearly appreciated Serabamon because of his great eagerness towards studying and worship. Deacon, Peter noticed how his face shined with joy and gladness when he was pursuing that. Once, Peter was astonished when he found Serabamon explaining clearly to him what he did not understand, as if a prophet or one of the Evangelists has interpreted them to him. When the deacon Peter hastened to tell the pope about the wisdom of Serabamon and the depth of his spiritual knowledge and his amazing ability to interpret the Holy Scripture, the pope remembered what the angel said about the saint, and he told the deacon about that.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, pp. 91–92
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, BISHOP OF THMUIS, ST. — His Exile and Departure

His Exile and Departure:

On the 18th of May 353 AD, Pope Athanasius sent a delegation of five bishops and three priests, headed by bishop Serapion, to Emperor Constantius II after his conquests and reigning over both the East and the West. The papal delegation was carrying to the emperor a document signed by 80 bishops from Egypt in support of Pope Athanasius and refuting the evil reports presented by the Arians against him. However, the emperor's response was to send St. Serapion to exile, for the sake of his Upright faith; and hence was called the Confessor. This saint was chosen based on his ability to defend the Upright faith, and his firm stands in encountering the emperor and opposing the Arian pressure. It was said that St. Serapion reposed in his exile around the year 370 AD, even though the exact date is not certain.

Letters of St. Athanasius to Him:

St. Athanasius the Apostolic sent him five dogmatic letters: 1- A letter sent in 339 AD, while in exile, concerning the death of Arius, in which St. Athanasius denied that Arius changed his views or that he reconciled with the Church before he died. 2- Four very important letters about the Holy Spirit, which the pope wrote in response to a request from St. Serapion, who was complaining that the teaching against the Holy Spirit, considering Him as a created being, albeit higher than the angels, was very quickly spreading. Those letters are counted as the first methodical theological research about the Holy Spirit.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Egyptian Martyr, pp. 94–95
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE EGYPTIAN MARTYR — A Desire for Martyrdom

A Desire for Martyrdom:

This St. Serapion was a wealthy inhabitant of Binosah (Babousah) in Lower Egypt, with a strong love of giving alms. At the time of persecution, he heard that Armanius governor of Alexandria arrived in the area to torture the Christians. Serapion came to encounter him, along with a friend called Theodorus and a third, a shepherd of cattle, named Thomas. And, when they confessed the Lord Christ before him, the governor cast them in prison.

On hearing about it, his fellow citizens came carrying arms to kill the governor and to set him free. However, when the saint told them that it was his desire to be martyred in the name of Christ, they went their way.

His Torture:

The governor took him along on a boat to Alexandria, where he tortured him with the Henbazin; cast him in a pit of fire, and put him in a pot filled with molten tar. In all of this, God kept healing him. And when they finally crucified the saint and continued beating him with a rod, an angel of the Lord came down and released him.

The governor then handed the task of torturing him to a prince called Orion, who took him by boat to his town. They landed the boat someplace by night; to be surprised in the morning to realize that they landed at the home town of the saint. Amazed, Orion heard a voice saying to him: “This is his home town.” After violently torturing him, they cut his holy head by the sword. He received the crown of martyrdom, and Orion took off his shirt, wrapped it around the saint's body, and delivered it to his family.

.[The Synaxarion: 27 Toba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, pp. 92–93
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, BISHOP OF THMUIS, ST. — St. Serapion Writings

St. Serapion Writings:

1- Against the followers of Mani: a work that revealed the eloquence of St. Serapion in both the theological and philosophical fields. He only criticized the main points in the views of the followers of Mani, in particular their Dualism view, (concerning the god of light and the god of darkness); their objection about the Old Testament and some parts of the New Testament. He also proved the contradiction and lack of logic within their views. 2- His Letters: A comforting letter he wrote to bishop Evgokius who was ill; a letter to the monks in Alexandria, in which he used the expression “Homosius Trias,” meaning (The Trinity equal in Essence); and a condolence letter to some disciples of Abba Anthony after he reposed in the year 356 AD. 3- Other works which, according to some scholars, were his, like A Sermon on Virginity; A Letter to the Confessors; and some fragments of Interpretations of the Book of Genesis, referred to by St. Jerome. 4- The Divine Liturgy by St. Serapion This version represents the Ecclesiastical Liturgy in Egypt in the 4th century (Probably referring to an earlier period). This Liturgy carried a reflection of the views of the School of Alexandria in the 3rd century concerning the Divinity of the Logos ‘The Word,’ after adding to it what suited the 4th century in response to the Arian heresy. So many prayers that came in this Liturgy are the same as those included in the Liturgy of St. Mark, concerning the Anaphora (The Ecclesiastical system) of the Ethiopian Church.

All prayers address God, being the Father of the Only Begotten-Son, and it gives Him thanks for the sake of His compassion, proclaimed through the salvation works of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Of the Divine Liturgy by St. Serapion:

• I implore You, O Lord, to send Your Holy Spirit to our minds. Grant us to understand Your inspired Holy Bible, to be able to interpret them with uprightness and worthiness. So that all believers present here would benefit from them. Grant us the spirit of light, to recognize You as the Truth. And Jesus Christ whom You sent (John 3:17). Grant us the Holy Spirit, to be able to proclaim widely, Your indescribable mysteries. • May the Lord Christ and the Holy Spirit talk within us, And May they glorify You through us.

(Butler, March 21)

Notes: [1] Fr. ‘Tadros Y. Malaty’ covered this Liturgy in his book “Christ in the Eucharist Sacrament”…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, pp. 90–91
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, BISHOP OF THMUIS, ST. — With St. Anthony the Great

With St. Anthony the Great:

According to St. Jerome, St. Serapion was a personal friend of St. Anthony the Great, and his name was mentioned twice in the book “Life of Anthony” written by the Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic. The first time, when the pope was talking to the brethren about the visions of Abba Anthony, who often used to suddenly interrupt his speech for a while before he resumes it again, and they would assume that the saint has seen a vision. St. Anthony used to tell St. Serapion about these visions. It was also said that St. Anthony while sitting on the mountain, he often saw what was going on in Egypt. The second time, when he knew that his departure was near, he requested that his clothes be distributed, giving one of sheepskin to Pope Athanasius and the one he has gotten new from bishop Serapion to be given back to him worn out, to keep.

Heading a Monastic Congregation:

According to the historian Sozomen, before St. Serapion was ordained as a bishop, he was the abbot of a monastic congregation in Upper Egypt, and that he was well known for his fantastic sanctity and eloquence. His close friend, Pope Athanasius, also mentioned in his letter to Dracontius, that he was the abbot of a significant number of monks.

His Support of Pope Athanasius:

St. Serapion supported the Pope in his strife against the Arianism. Being like his right hand, the pope used him as his deputy during his frequent absences from the throne. In the year 340 AD, the pope let him declare the date of the Passover; and it is believed that he let him write the Passover papal messages during the two years 341 and 342 AD.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serabamon, Bishop of Nicius, pp. 88–89
passages.text:
Saint: SERABAMON, BISHOP OF NICIUS (The martyr) — Performing Signs and Miracles

Performing Signs and Miracles:

His biographer Pope Alexandros I talked much about how St. Serabamon opposed Arius and Meletius. He also said about the saint: “Living in his city became like living in the monasteries of monks. The miracles and signs performed by him were not less than those performed by the Apostles Peter and Paul. He healed the sick and drove the unclean spirits out, screaming and begging him not to torture them with his prayers.”

His Care for the Poor and the Rich:

His city became like one family; the rich were urged by him to provide the poor generously with their necessities.

His Martyrdom:

After Emperor Diocletian (284-305) denied the faith, he was told how bishop Serabamon hindered idol worship by his teachings. When the emperor visited Alexandria, he called him in. Once the saint arrived at Alexandria, he was arrested and spent the night in prison, where he joined Pope Peter and some priests who saw his countenance shine like an angel. Emperor Diocletian tortured the bishop with every tool he had, and the Lord Christ kept healing him of every wound. And when the emperor saw how a multitude of people proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ because of him, he decided to give him to Ariana the governor of Ansenah to torture him and to cut his head off if he persists on his faith. Then, it happened that Ariana was in Alexandria at that time, so he took the saint with him by boat. When they reached Nicius, and the boat stopped and could not be moved, they took the saint to the northern side of the city, where they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom. Afterward, his people came and moved his body with great honor to the church.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Marcus, the Hermit, p. 91
passages.text:
Saint: MARCUS, THE HERMIT, ST.

Farewell, O my body, the object of labor and need; because of you, I suffered hunger, thirst, cold, and heat. Get adorned with splendor and glory.

Farewell, O my eyes, which watched the nights; Now! Close your eyelids. Farewell, O my bare feet, which got tired of standing long in prayers. Farewell, O my brethren the saintly hermits, who dwell in mountain caves and seclusion in the wilderness.

Farewell, O the imprisoned, and the persecuted for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

Farewell, O Church believers. Farewell, O you poor in spirit. Farewell, O earth; I pray all who live on you, would live in peace and the love of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

He then embraced St. Serapion and said to him: “Farewell, O my son and beloved brother. May the Lord Jesus Christ reward you for your labor on such a long journey. I implore you to keep everything I have on my miserable body; add nothing on it; leave it in the same condition that God created it.”

Then, St. Serapion heard a beautiful voice like music coming from heaven, saying: “Come forth, my son Marcus. Come and have rest in the places of true happiness and spiritual joy.” The elder St. Marcus cried out, saying: “Let us kneel on our knees, and raise our hands toward heaven.”

At this moment, unseen angels came into the cave, and set forth up to heaven carrying the spirit of Abba Marcus crowned with the crown of glory.

St. Serapion kept on singing all night long. Then in the morning, he dug a pit, in which he buried the body of the saint and closed the cave opening with a great number of rocks. Then, he prayed to God to help him find his way back to his cell. He went slowly down to the desert, and when night came, the two angels, whom he has seen in his dream, appeared to him again and said: “This morning you made a grave for a man, the whole world was unworthy of him. You have done a work of mercy that immensely pleased God. Now, please walk by night, when the weather is milder than by day.”

Obeying the two angels, St. Serapion followed the angels, who came to him by night and disappeared by day until he reached the place where his friend the monk John dwelt.

Notes: [1] Dr. Michael Max Eskander: The History of the Church in Pentapolis… He referred to a “Manuscrit grec de Bibliothèque de Digoin d’après Chéneau: ‘Les Saints d’Egypte’, tom. 1, p. 409.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, p. 110
passages.text:
Saint: SEVERUS, PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH, ST. — Romanius Vision

Romanius Vision:

In a night vision, the head of the monastery Romanius saw in a desert full of thorns and thistles, a beautiful woman clothed in worn-out clothes looking sad, with the tears flowing on her cheeks and chest. And he heard a man telling his partner: “Behold, here comes Severus to uproot the thistles from this land, to sanctify a vineyard for the Lord of hosts.” Then, the man addressed the sad woman saying: “Do not be afraid, O City of Antioch; for behold Severus, an upright man, will come and build upon the foundation of the holy Councils.”

His Care for the Hand-work:

Despite his illness, Severus diligently worked as much as his energy allowed him; and advised the monks to work with their hands. Because of his acute illness, the Abbot of the monastery kept on counseling him to take it a little easy on himself and to take care of his body while practicing the virtues. And, he ultimately managed to convince him.

A Vision of a Monk in the Monastery:

In a night vision, a blessed monk saw while praying, the angel of the Lord, say to him: “Look at this land, at the court of this monastery.” And he saw two men, of incredible honor and shining faces approach Severus and proclaim to him the secret of the Orthodox Faith. When the monk, asked the angel who were those wise men talking to Severus, he answered him that they were St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory the Theologian; and that they were guiding Severus to the basis of Faith, for he was going to be the guardian of the Upright Faith, and that he would shepherd a great congregation in Antioch, as well as in the whole Universe. The fame of Severus spread all over the East and the West, and many priests, monks, and laymen came to seek from him his interpretation of the Holy Bible and the dogma.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Corinthian Martyr, p. 94
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE CORINTHIAN MARTYR

This St. Serapion was originally from Corinth in Greece. He was martyred in Egypt, along with Niceporus, under the rule of Emperor Numerian (283-284 AD) in the year 284 AD.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 613]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1142 “What do we know about the seraphim?674”, pp. 277–278
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 5: The Believer and the Heavenly Hosts › The Order of the Heavenly Hosts — 1142. What do we know about the seraphim?674

They claim that they can see Him clearly without any limitation!”

And St. John Chrysostom continues: “Indeed God, even to those hosts, is imperceivable and unapproachable, yet He condescends to appear in the way described in the vision … God who is not limited by place; but by His love for us, appears sitting on a throne, surrounded by heavenly hosts.”

Again, he says, “The visions seen by the prophets are never visions of God’s very essence, for if they had seen His essence, they would not have seen Him in different forms. He is simple, without form or body and He does not sit, stand up, or walk.”

When the servant beholds the service of the angels, he is comforted by knowing that the troubles and weaknesses of the Church will certainly come to an end one day and she will praise together with the heavenly hosts eternally. Here, the Church is an icon of heaven, enjoying a taste of this heavenly service. In a certain homily in Coptic, the Church is defined as “A place of consolation, a place of meeting of angels, and a place of the cherubim and the seraphim.” It is said that St. Pachomius would see the church filled with angels.

The work of every servant or prophet in the Church is to attract every soul to the Lord, that it may become a throne where He can dwell and establish His inner kingdom, till it becomes like a heavenly seraph, burning like fire. Each seraph has six wings: with two he covers his face as a sign of the fear of God, since he cannot comprehend the fullness of divine brilliance; and with two he covers his feet as a sign of modesty; and with two he flies, soaring in the heavens. While the cherubim carry the divine throne, the seraphim flutter around the throne, crying to one another, declaring that God is “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and that His glory fills all the earth (Isa. 6:3).

Some people believe that the seraphim proclaim the holiness of God in order to draw the minds of human beings towards taking their own holiness seriously, so they may be able to draw closer to the One who is Himself Holy. The believer is called to follow the example of the prophet Isaiah, who accepted the live coal from the altar of God, brought to him by a seraph with tongs, with which he touched his lips and purged his sins (Isa. 6:6–7).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexander Akimetes, pp. 119–120
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDER AKIMETES, ST.

This saint was born in Asia Minor and was educated in Constantinople, where he received the Faith through his love of reading the Holy Bible. He then went to Syria to practice ascetic life. He practiced the experience of fellowship than that of seclusion, and after 11 years of his monastic life, he dedicated himself to preaching in Mesopotamia (Al-Missa). And, it was said that he was the one who brought ‘Rabulas’ to the Faith, who became the bishop of Edessa (Al-Roha) later on.

He established a vast monastery near the Euphrates. However, he did not stay long there, for he took a large number of its monks and went to Antioch for a while; although, his visit stirred up so many troubles. So, he finally had to leave and establish a new monastery in Constantinople. Once more, some evil people set up against him and managed to expel him from there. So, he built another monastery at ‘Gormon’ on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, where he reposed in the year 430 AD He was famed for establishing in his monasteries a large Choir, which was divided into several groups. These groups would rotate throughout the day, each new group relieving the one before it, to create uninterrupted prayer and worship twenty-four hours a day without ceasing. Hence, they were called ‘Akimetes’ or ‘Acoemetae,' meaning (The Sleepless Ones).

[Butler’s Lives of Saints, Feb. 23]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Repentant, pp. 95–96
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE REPENTANT — His Weakness before Persecution

This man was a Christian native of Alexandria, Egypt. It happened that he became weak during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) and ended up burning incense before the idols. His episode was used by the 14th Pope St. Dionysius of Alexandria (246-264 AD), as practical evidence against the heresy of the Novatians who were very adamant not to accept the repentance of those who denied faith during the persecution The pope wrote to bishop Fabius of Antioch (253-256 AD), one of this heresy followers, explaining how wrong that heresy was.

His Weakness before Persecution:

Even though Serapion lived a long blameless life, yet he eventually weakened near the end. However, he had remorse for his sin, and he fervently begged the congregation for forgiveness and to be re-admitted to the Church. Still, because of the influence of the followers of the Novatian heresy, his request was always denied. Then, it happened that Serapion fell severely ill and could not talk for three days; and once he regained consciousness, he sent his grandson to seek the priest. The priest also happened to be too ill to go to Serapion, yet he managed to send the Holy Sacraments to him. Serapion lived until he received the Holy Sacrament, and then he reposed in peace. In his defense, Pope Dionysius used this incident as a Divine proclamation and evidence against the views of the Novatians.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 612]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serabamon, the Hegomen, pp. 89–90
passages.text:
Saint: SERABAMON, THE HEGOMEN, ST. — Hegomen of the Monastery of Abu-Yeĥness

Hegomen of the Monastery of Abu-Yeĥness:

This St. Serabamon, the hermit, became the hegomen (abbot) of the monastery of Abu-Yeĥness. He was a monk in that monastery from an early age. He remained in his worship and in serving the older monks for 32 years until he was ordained as a hegomen on the monastery to supervise its affairs. Since then, he increased his devotion and asceticism. Although, he used to fast the whole day, from the day he became a monk until the day he reposed.

After 20 years in this fellowship, he closed on himself in a room in one of the churches and was not seen for almost ten years, during which he broke his fast only on Saturdays and Sundays.

A Cross of Fire:

When it was time for him to depart from this world, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a night vision. The angel handed him a Cross of fire, saying: “Take this in your hand.” He said to the angel: “How could I hold fire with my hand?” The angel answered him: “Do not be afraid, for the Lord Christ will not let it have authority on you.” Then, the saint took the Cross from the angel, who added: “Be strong; first have the communion of the Holy Sacraments... and after three days, I shall come back to take you with me.”

On telling the elders about his vision, they wept, bid him farewell, and sought from him to remember them in Heaven. He, in turn, asked from them to remember him in their prayers, and he reposed on the third day, with the elders all around him.

[The Synaxarion: 5 Baramhat]
