passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dorothy, the Virgin, p. 651
passages.text:
Saint: DOROTHY, THE VIRGIN, ST. (The martyr) — In the House of Theophilus

Then, he shouted aloud: “Blessed are You Jesus, my God, Groom of ‘Dorothy;’ and blessed are all those who believe in You, and who die for the sake of faith in You.”

When one of those present hastened to inform the governor what had happened, he did not believe until he called ‘Theophilus,’ who confessed his faith before him. Then, he was put under severe torture and was finally crowned with the crown of martyrdom.

It was said that ‘Dorothy’s body was carried to Rome, where it was kept in a church carrying her name, on the banks of the River ‘Tiber.’

It became a tradition to paint the portrait of the saint carrying roses and apples, and in the celebration of her feast, a special rite is practiced to bless the roses and apples.

[Butler: The Lives of the Saints, February 6]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Repentant, p. 245
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE REPENTANT, ST. — Her Repose

If you obey my advice and counsel, God will be with you and keep you from the evil one and from all the enemies.”

The Abbot of the monastery stood outside the cell listening until the end. He realized that this monk was wrongly accused. Then, he knocked on the door to enter and receive the blessing of the monk before his departure to find out that he has already delivered his soul. Having heard from the Abbot of the monastery all that he saw and heard, all the monks came to the body of their brother Theodore to proclaim their remorse for what they have done. When they started the ritual for burying him, they realized that he was a woman. And, the news spread all over Alexandria, and multitudes came over to seek her blessing. When her husband heard about what happened and perceiving that she was Theodora, his wife, he bitterly wept, remembering how he has previously seen her and did not recognize her while leading her camel. He then implored the Abbot of the monastery to accept him as a monk, to spend the rest of his days worshipping in her cell. As to the little kid, he remained in the monastery, grew up in grace, to be loved by everyone, and ended up eventually becoming the Abbot of the monastery.

[Chéneau: Les Saints d’Egypte, Bk 2, pp. 324-9] [The Archimandrite Michael Assaf: The Book of the Synaxarion – 11 Eilol]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Repentant, pp. 244–245
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE REPENTANT, ST. — Her Repose

Her Repose:

In a night vision, the Abbot of the monastery saw as though heaven was opened, and there was a throne on which a beautiful bride was sitting, with an angel standing next to her. When he asked about the identity of the bride, he was told that she was the monk Theodore. The monastery Abbot instantly hastened to the cell of that monk, to hear him talking to the young boy, saying:

“My son, my sun is about to set, and I am about to leave you in the hands of God, the Father of all the fatherless, with the hope that the Abbot of the monastery will not forsake you; and the monks will have compassion on you… My child! Do not search for your origin and genealogy, for the best genealogy comes from virtue. Do not seek the worldly glories, for the happy man is not the glorious man. According to the Lord Jesus: “Blessed, are you when they revile and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for my sake” (Matt. 5:11). Pray for the sake of the sinners. Help the weak, and do not be slothful on the way to perfection. Serve your neighbor as though he was your master, to be accepted by Jesus Christ, who took the form of a slave, for our sake. Keep on praying, so as not to enter into temptation. And if you are tempted, hold fast before the temptation. And when it comes to an end, do not stop praying, lest it would go back and overcome you.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Genevieve, pp. 165–166
passages.text:
Saint: GENEVIEVE, ST. — Her Asceticism

Her Asceticism:

St. Genevieve only ate on Sundays and Thursdays, only bread of barley and boiled beans, and drank only water. She clothed herself with sackcloth, slept on the bare ground without a mattress after spending several hours praying at night. Finally, she reposed in peace around the year 500 AD.

Among the miracles that happened after her departure to heaven, which reflected her intense love and compassion on people, was one that took place in the year 1129 AD, when a plague spread in France. The people carried the saint's coffin and paraded along the streets of the city, and the plague stopped at once. The church there, still celebrates the anniversary of that miracle up till now, on the 13th of January every year.

[The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, second edition, p. 145] [Jesuite Fr. Peter Fromage: Biography of the Righteous, Beirut 1877]

Notes: [1] The heresy of ‘Pelagius’ was opposed by St. ‘Augustine.’ Pelagius’ considered that man could be saved by his own human struggle; by this way Pelagius belittled the role of the Divine Grace

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Susan, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: SUSAN, ST. — Her Monastic Life

This saint was born in the region of Edessa (El-Roha) to a noble family. She was given the name Susan (Sawsan), which means the Lily flower. She was raised by her parents as a true Christian, so she used to begin her day and end it with prayers. She used to go regularly to the church to have communion in the Holy Sacraments. Her blessed life, delicate behavior, genuine humility, and her love for the poor and the needy made her the object of admiration of her parents, who prophesied for her a shining spiritual future.

Her Monastic Life:

One day, she sought her parent's permission to travel to Jerusalem to worship at the tomb of the Savior and to get the blessings of the holy sites. She also informed them that in case it was God's Will, she would intend to join a convent there, to be in the company of saintly virgins. When her family faced her request with strong opposition because of her young age, she fervently kept praying to God to grant her what her heart desired.

Susan started to search for a way to travel to Jerusalem; until she found a caravan of pilgrims, heading to the Holy Land. She asked them to let her join the procession, and they allowed her to tag along. After having the blessings of the holy places, they intended to return home. However, she requested from them to leave her there. Despite their objection to her request for leaving her behind far from her hometown; she managed to hide from them. Then, she searched around and found a convent for virgins in the region between Ashkelon and Gaza, and she set forth to it.

On encountering the convent's mother-superior, she asked to be admitted in the convent. The mother-superior agreed to let her stay with them on a temporary basis, until they would find someone from her hometown to go and inform her parents about what happened to her. From that time on, Susan started to train herself on a life of asceticism, obedience, and the works of virtues. But, the convent mothers attempted to keep that little girl from overdoing her asceticism and counseled her to progress gradually, yet with discernment. Susan continued to watch the nights standing in the corner of her room all night long, raising prayers, praises, and Psalms, and to spend her days executing what was requested from her without a murmur. She did not talk except if she was asked to, and her talk was limited to a few peaceful and straightforward words. Susan continually bowed her head and rarely looked up. Her fellow sisters had difficulty in looking at her face. She never laughed and never hurt the feelings of any of them, but came to be a good role model to everyone around her. They all wondered who that little girl was, whom they reluctantly accepted because of her young age.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Canoness, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE CANONESS

This saint Theodora was a Church woman (Canoness), to whom St. Basil the Great wrote a magnificent letter (# 173 [302]), in which he explained the strength of the rules of the Evangelical life which she adopted. And, he apologized to her that he ceased from writing more in his letter, lest it would probably fall in somebody’s hand, and he would read it.

[New Advent; Fathers of the Church; Letters of St. Basil of Caesarea: 173]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Genevieve, pp. 164–165
passages.text:
Saint: GENEVIEVE, ST. — Her Severe Illness

Her Severe Illness:

Genevieve was inflicted by a severe illness that left her in a coma that lasted for three days, and she was on the brink of death. However, God gave her a night vision to comfort her, in which she saw the saints in their glory and the wicked in their sufferings. She saw her soul had set forth as though to Mount Golgotha, to see the Lord Jesus Christ crucified. This vision became so engraved in her heart and gave her the support she needed in her strife.

Once more, she was inflicted by leprosy, and she was abandoned by everyone, but God healed her to become a guide to the virgins in Paris.

Knowing the Inner Thoughts of Others:

For her great love of the salvation of her brethren, God granted her the grace of understanding the inner thoughts of others and what was going on in their minds, and she used that to exhort them to repentance. A girl who vowed virginity fell into the sin of adultery, on meeting with the saint, who exhorted her to repent. The girl perceived that the saint had complete knowledge of the place, date, and time of her sin, and the girl felt shame and did repent sincerely.

Building a Church:

Saint Genevieve once revealed to some priests her longing to build a church in the name of St. Dionysius, the martyr. They explained to her that they couldn't do that without having the needed building materials. Yet, the next morning they, miraculously found all the building materials required in a forest nearby, which they used to build that church.

God also granted the saint the grace of casting demons out and performing miracles. This given powers made some jealous people accuse her of deception. However, St. Germanus came to her defense.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Taor, the Virgin, p. 222
passages.text:
Saint: TAOR, THE VIRGIN

Having told us about the blessed mother Talida, St. Palladius presented to us a chapter about one of the nuns who were under her care, namely Taor, the virgin. This virgin lived 30 years in the convent in a hard monastic life, not caring for have any lovely monastic attire, veils, or even footwear. She used to say: “I need nothing of all that, for I do not have to go to the market.” Every week, all the rest of the nuns used to go to the church to partake of the Communion, except that nun who would stay behind in the convent in wornout clothing and never ceased to work and strive. Besides being pure and chaste, she was filled with wisdom and prudence. She did not care for her outer adornment, but she adorned her heart for her Eternal Groom.

[W. Budge: The Paradise, 1972, Vol. 1, p. 153]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Thomaies, pp. 289–290
passages.text:
Saint: THOMAIES (The martyr)

This lady saint was a young woman of 18 years of age, whose husband was a hunter who was frequently away from home. It happened that her father-inlaw wanted to rape her, but she refused and tried to convince him that she considered him as her father and ought to treat him as such. Once again, he wanted to rape her by force, and she fought fiercely against him. He held his son’s sword and threatened to kill her, and she responded that she would rather die than to fall in such evil. So, he struck her with the sword to fall a martyr of purity and chastity. Right afterward, that evil man was inflicted with blindness; and he confessed to his son about what happened. He sought from him to deliver him to the authorities to get his punishment, somehow realizing that it was better for him to be chastised here than to lose his eternity.

When Abba Danie’, the hegomen of Scetis, heard about that, he attended her funeral and considered her as a martyr. He sought to have her body buried in a monastery near Alexandria (the 18-miles monastery). Some of the monastery’s monks protested about the burial of a murdered woman’s body among the bodies of the hermit Fathers. But, Abba Daniel was able to convince them to honor such a pure young woman by having her body buried in the tomb of the Fathers.

[Deacon Yousif Habib: Abba Daniel, p. 63]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Thecla the Virgin and her Friend Justina, p. 236
passages.text:
Saint: THECLA THE VIRGIN AND HER FRIEND JUSTINA

This St. Thecla was the daughter of St. Isidore in the 3rd century. Once, she was healed of paralysis by the prayers of St. Alpheus. Then, she dedicated her life to the Lord. She managed to arrange a refuge to St. Agathon, the bishop of Lipari, and others at the time of persecution and cared for the bodies of the martyrs. After the persecution, she played an active role with her friend Justina in preaching the Gospel among the women in the region of Sicily under the supervision of bishop Agathon. They also built two churches, handed over a pagan temple that was in her possession to be used by the Christians, and gave her own house to the bishop. The West celebrates her on the 10th of January.

[Sabine Baring-Gould: “Saints Thecla, Virgin, and Justina”; Lives of the Saints, 1897]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Quiteria, the Virgin, pp. 6–7
passages.text:
Saint: QUITERIA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

St. Quiteria enjoyed considerable fame in the south of France and north of Spain, in Aire in Gascony, where her relics are kept, and many churches were established on her name. She was the daughter of a prince of Galicia in Spain. She was baptized without her father’s knowledge and dedicated her virginity to the Lord. And, she had to flee away from her father’s house, when he tried to force her to forsake her Christianity and to get married to a pagan man. Her father sent men after her to kill her. When they found her, her head was cut off by the sword. She was martyred in the 5th century AD. Her portrait includes a dog, for she was counted as the intercessor of those mauled by rabid dogs.

[Baring-Gould: May 22]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora of Baetica, pp. 238–239
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA OF BAETICA

This saint Theodora was a lady living in the region of Hispania Baetica in Spain at the end of the 4th century. She was a widow of a man named Lucinius, who was an educated rich man with whom she lived with complete integrity; while being in contact with St. Jerome in Bethlehem. When her husband passed away in the year 399, St. Jerome wrote to her a letter in which he commended her man and his good qualities. Then, he sent her another letter in which he praised the teachings of Abigaus, the blind presbyter of Baetica.

[New Advent; Fathers of the Church; Letters of St. Jerome: 75 & 76]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Susan, pp. 199–200
passages.text:
Saint: SUSAN, ST. — Her Seclusion

Her Seclusion:

After a while, St. Susan found for herself an underground cave, suitable for her to dwell as an anchorite. The other nuns kept her company, visiting her one at a time every week. And after some persistence, she allowed them to provide her with a pot of water and some dry crumbs of bread.

Monk Samuel, the Biological Brother of St. Susan:

Her brother, who was called Samuel, was a monk in a monastery in Palestine. On hearing that his sister was worshipping God in the Marriott desert, he planned on traveling to her with some of his fellow monks, hoping to be able to join her in a nearby location. They were seeking to be in someplace away from the religious controversies and persecutions that prevailed because of the Chalcedonian Council. And, they envisioned that this new location would suit them very well.

They set forth to Marriott, where Samuel encountered his sister Susan. They comforted one another with words of grace, and he asked for her permission to allow them to dwell with his brethren monks in the nearby region. Then, they built a wall around the tower where the nuns dwelt. Afterward, they built for themselves a monastery nearby.

At that time, the mother-superior St. Susan continued to live as a recluse in her cave. She kept visiting the nuns now and then to make sure of their safety.

The monks, getting to know of her coming, they used to come as well to wait for her outside the door, to get her blessing, to ask her questions, and to listen to her teachings and her words to support them in their lives. Granted by God the gift of healing both the physical and spiritual maladies, she continued living in that place for more than 15 years, and then she reposed in peace.

[The Female Saints: Sawsan, Shirin, Paula, Poline, Helaniah & Fabiola; p. 8]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martha, p. 110
passages.text:
Saint: MARTHA, ST.

St. Martha was the sister of Lazarus and Mary of Bethany. She was preoccupied with serving the Lord Christ (Luke 10:38-42; 12:1-2). The Lord said to her: “I am the resurrection and the Life” (John 10:25). She responded by confessing faith, saying, “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are, the Son of God who is to come into the world” (John 10:27). St. Martha is considered to be the intercessor of those who care for the needy, and is celebrated by the Western Church on the 29th of July.

[The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, p. 226]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dorothea, pp. 643–644
passages.text:
Saint: DOROTHEA, ST. — Her Decision to Live in Seclusion

Her Decision to Live in Seclusion:

This saint was born into a wealthy, highly respected family from Alexandria. Dorothea was raised as a Christian, full of love, and was very highly educated. Later on, when she feared that her beauty might cause her soul to fall into arrogance or might be an obstacle with men; she decided to forsake the world and to set forth to the desert to live in seclusion with her Lord.

Before Emperor Maximian:

Before she got a chance to put her decision into action, she was surprised to be called by Emperor Maximian (286-305 AD), who have seen her once before, wanted to marry her. The emperor never thought that any girl would dare to reject his proposal, so he was amazed to hear that she had declined his request, suspecting that such a negative response would not come except through a religious motive. The emperor investigated the matter and discovered that she was a Christian.

This discovery made him more persistent in overcoming her rejection. He sent her several delegates to inform her, sometimes mildly, and other times with threats, that there had no choice. She was either to approve the proposal of the emperor or face death in the most vicious of ways. But she gave only one answer from the beginning to the end: “My body, the temple of the Holy Spirit in which God dwells, shall never be defiled by marrying an idolworshipper, even if it is the emperor himself. Go and tell your master to stop talking about vain pleasures, while shedding the blood of Christians.”

Fleeing to the Desert:

In the darkness of the night, trusting in God, her guardian, ‘Dorothea’, set forth to realize her decision. She was accompanied by some of her faithful maidservants, who joined by their own free choice, and hastened toward the desert to dwell in its tranquility under the shadow of the Almighty.

To avenge his pride, ‘Maximian’ issued a decree to arrest a significant number of the Christian virgins in Alexandria, and to bring them to trial. There, he gave them a choice between worldly evil desires or torture to death. They unanimously proclaimed: “Death in any way is our choice over life in sin.” And, all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

As for ‘Dorothea’ and her group; they dwelt long years in the desert, in sweet intimacy with their Lord. This drew a multitude of virgins to join them, and ‘Dorothea’ became like a mother to them all.

[The Faithful Synaxarion: 23 Amshir]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amois, pp. 156–157
passages.text:
Saint: AMOIS, ST.

St. Amois (Amoy/Pamweh) was born in Upper Egypt. He was the spiritual father of Abba John the Short and Abba Bishoi. He was known for his great firmness with himself and was keen not to get preoccupied with anyone or anything that would take his attention from the contemplation in the celestials. He never allowed his disciples to come close to him while walking to the church. And, if one of his disciples happened to ask him about some thought that came to his mind, he would answer him, then seek from him to leave him alone, saying: “I fear that after I utter edifying words, we would slide down into strange talk. Hence, I keep you away from me."

Even so, he was bed-ridden for several years because of illness; he never allowed himself to think about his cell nor to look at its contents; although lots of people have visited him and brought him so many gifts because of his illness. And, whenever his disciple ‘John’ entered into or came out of his cell, the saint kept his eyes shut, so as not to see him avoid having his mind distracted by anything around him, to keep it perpetually contemplating in the celestials. He once put about 50 bushels of wheat in the sun to dry. However, he noticed something he considered harmful. So, before the wheat had a chance to dry, he told his disciples: “Let us abandon this place." On seeing that they became sad, he said to them: “Have you become sad for the sake of the bread? I truly see monks who forsake their cells and their manuscripts without even closing the doors, but they leave them open". So, he cared to escape from any stumbling-block, whatever was the cost!

[Benedicta Ward: Sayings of the Desert Fathers; pp. 26-27]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cassian, John, pp. 396–397
passages.text:
Saint: CASSIAN, JOHN, ST. (Cassian, the Roman) — His Monastic Life

Therefore, St. ‘Cassian’ wrote his book: “De Institutis Coenobiorum” about the rules of the monastic fellowship mixed with absolute basics of the life of seclusion, and he dedicated it to St. ‘Castor.’

When St. ‘Cassian’ opened up the arms of love before all people of all races who longed for the love of Christ; he was joined by a multitude of disciples from all over the world. The West no longer was envying the East. Yet, his role was limited when some people started to have doubts about ‘Cassian's’ Orthodoxy, because of the attacks made by some of the followers of St. ‘Augustine’ on him, accusing him of having ‘Pelagian’ leanings.

St. ‘Benedict’ (480-547 AD), who established the highest monastic order in the West, and whose fame even surpasses that of ‘Cassian,’ yet was indebted to him; on account of that most of the laws of the ‘Benedict's’ monastic order were directly taken from those of ‘Cassian.’

Of His Writings:

 The monasteries are an extension of the early ecclesiastical life around the apostles in Jerusalem. The believers who treasure within themselves the zealously of the apostles would forsake the towns to practice the ideal apostolic life away from the corruption of the world.  It is something horrible and repulsive for us, monks, to see how the laymen labor and sustain children and wives, pay taxes, give alms to the poor and the needy, according to their abilities, and carry to the house of God their first fruits and sacrifices, while we monks, on the other hand, do not generate from our labor, even the necessities of our lives; but keep our hands inside our robes, benefit from the works of others; and do not heed the words of the apostle, “These hands have provided for my necessities, and for those who were with me.” (Acts 20:34) “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35) “We command you brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which he received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to follow us, for we were not disorderly among you; nor did we eat anyone's bread free of charge, but worked with labor and toil night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you… if anyone will not work, neither shall he eat. For we hear that there are some who walk among you in a disorderly manner, not working at all, but are busybodies.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paul, the Simple, p. 385
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST.

This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer who got married to a very beautiful girl. After living together for so many years, he started to take notice of so many rumors about his wife's evil behavior. However, whenever he inquired from her about the matter, she would pretend to be a pure woman. Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the evil act. On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples.

Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age. Before his persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in the valley to practice with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not leaving that mountain.

Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance, and obedience. Among those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching him lest he would collapse. He sought from him to remain a whole week outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, to loosen it and weave it anew. In all that he was obedient, worked with joy and extreme simplicity.

On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cassian, John, pp. 395–396
passages.text:
Saint: CASSIAN, JOHN, ST. (Cassian, the Roman) — His Monastic Life

In Rome, he formed a friendship with the deacon ‘Leo,’ who came to be the pope of Rome (the first to call for the Roman Papacy); to whom he dedicated a book on ‘The Divine Incarnation.’ In that period, he lost his very dear friend ‘Germanus,’ who departed from this world.

In the year 415 or 416 AD, ‘Cassian’ lived as a priest in ‘Marseilles,’ where he established a monastery for men, he dedicated it under the name of St. Victor (Boctor) and became its spiritual father and head. He built another one for women in the name of St. ‘Salvator.’ The monastic movement soon spread there, and thousands of monks and nuns populated the monasteries.

Indeed, ‘Cassian’ was preceded by St. ‘Honoratus’ (350-429 AD), who founded a monastery on one of the ‘Lerins’ islands (off the French Riviera) in the year 410 AD. ‘Honoratus’ order was chiefly borrowed from that of St. Pachomius, and the monastery carried the name of St. ‘Honoratus’ up to this day and enjoyed an excellent celebrity status during the 5th and 6th centuries, and it was a nursery for illustrious bishops and remarkable ecclesiastical writers.

However, through his two famous books, St. ‘Cassian’ was credited for establishing an elaborate system for the monastic life for the first time. His system carried the monastic ideas of the East, particularly Egypt. He provided the West with a monastic system they could accept, which paved the way to the ‘Benedictines Order.’

St. ‘Castor,’ the bishop of ‘Apt’ (in the southeast of France) was the one who requested from St. ‘Cassian’ to write about the rules of the monastic life. Therefore, St. ‘Cassian’ wrote his book: “De Institutis Coenobiorum” about the rules of the monastic fellowship mixed with absolute basics of the life of seclusion, and he dedicated it to St. ‘Castor.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Fr. John of Persia, p. 437
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF PERSIA, FR.

About Fr. John of Persia, it is said that, when some evil men entered into the region where he dwelt, he did not hesitate to comfort them and wash their feet. In appreciation for what he did and for their high respect for his person, in turn, they came to repent for their evil deeds.

In response to a brother who once questioned Fr. John of Persia, by saying: “Having so labored for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; I wonder if we shall ever inherit it.” The saint answered him: “I believe that I shall inherit the higher Jerusalem in heaven; for He who so promised is faithful. Why then would we ever doubt Him?”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Joannes, the Short, p. 368
passages.text:
Saint: JOANNES, THE SHORT, ST. — His Obedience

It also happened that Abba Bemwah sought from Joannes to go and bring a wild hyena, which was dwelling in a grave nearby. He told him, “If it approaches you, just put a leash on it and lead it over here.” Abba Joannes the Short went his way in the darkness of the night; saw the wild hyena, and when it approached him, he moved toward it, but it fled away from him. The saint kept chasing the hyena, saying, “My mentor sought from me to leash you and bring you to him.” Then, it stopped, and he caught it, leashed it, and brought it to the older saint. Abba Bemwah was amazed, and out of fear that Joannes might be overcome by pride, he told him: “I asked you to bring me a hyena, yet you went and brought me a dog,” and immediately, he asked him to release it.

His Humility:

He counted himself the lowliest of the lowly, yet not with the spirit of despair, but with that of hope in God, who “raises the poor out of the dust and lifts the needy out of the ash heap” (Psalm 113:7). Such humility, which was linked to the spirit of discernment, raised his heart to become closer to God and to enjoy the riches of the Divine Grace. Once, the brethren asked him: “Father! Should we read the psalms all the time?” He answered them: “Reading and prayers would not benefit the monk unless he is humble and loving the poor and needy.” Because of his humility, it was said, "Joannes, carries by his humility, the entire wilderness; the way a man takes a drop of water in his palm.” Moreover, because of his humility, he drew the hearts of all the brethren to love him and to respond to any of his requests.

Because of his humility, the elder fathers chose him to be a guide for St. Arsanius, the teacher of the sons of the kings. Once, an elder father met him on his way to the church, and that elder wanted to test him, so he said to him: “Go back to your place, O short man.” Without uttering a word, the saint returned to his cell. The elderly father and those with him followed the saint to see his reaction, but once he entered into his cell, they smelled a sweet fragrance of incense and heard someone telling him: “Keep your humility, O Joannes, to become the friend of the Son of God.” Amazed, they glorified God and brought the saint in a procession into the church with great honor.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Joseph of Anifo, Father, pp. 452–453
passages.text:
Saint: JOSEPH OF ANIFO, FATHER — Father Joseph of ‘Anifo’

Many Church Fathers carried the name Father Joseph in the biographies of the Fathers monks in the 4th and 5th centuries. It seems that there was a great confusion in recording the events and the words attributed to them. Among them were the following Fathers:  Father Joseph of ‘Anifo’ (Binfo). [Covered in this article].  Father Joseph, a contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great; about whom St.

Palladius said that he went to worship the Lord on the mountain with two veteran hermits when Joseph was an old man.  Father Joseph, a contemporary of Abba Bemen, who reposed in the middle of the 5th century. It was said that Abba Bemen refrained from speaking in the presence of Fr. Joseph, out of respect and appreciation.  Father Joseph of Thebes.  Father Joseph, who became a monk in Scetis, while he was a little boy.

Father Joseph of ‘Anifo’:

Father Joseph was ahead of his village Temios in the region of Senbellawayn, in its place nowadays is Tamai el-Amdid. He was so highly cultured that he used to talk directly to his guests in Greek without a need for a translator. Having become a monk, he resided in his cell in Anifo; a town destroyed some time ago by an earthquake, and in its place now is the town of Manzallah.

Offering Hospitality to Strangers:

Two brothers came to ask him about how to receive and provide hospitality to strangers; should they freely mix with them and talk to them? Before asking him, he said to his disciple, “Understand and endure what I am about to do today.” He put two pillows, one on each side of where he used to sit, and told them to sit down. He then left them, entered into his cell where he put on the attire of a beggar, came out, and walked among them, and then he entered again into his cell and put on his regular attire. Seeing how they were astonished at what he did, he asked them: “Did I become any different from the different attires?” When they answered in the negative, he told them: “This is how to receive the strangers; for the Holy Bible says: ‘Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar; and to God what belongs to God’ (Matthew 22:21). Whenever some brethren come to visit us, we should receive them with daring and joy, but once they leave, and we get back to our solitude, we shall need the wailing to abide in us.” On hearing this, they were astonished that he answered what they had in mind before they have asked him. They praised the Lord and went their way.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Badasuis, pp. 288–289
passages.text:
Saint: BADASUIS, ST. — With Father Paul

St. ‘Badasuis’ was raised by his parents while they were working for a pious man by the name of ‘Bagoush’ in the town of ‘Faw’ (near Qena) in Upper Egypt. That holy man had only one son ‘Yusab’ (Joseph), who was raised as a brother to ‘Badasuis’. So, those two grew up bound by a great friendship since their childhood.

During their youth, they kept on visiting the monastery of St. ‘Pachom,’ where they met and got acquainted with so many monks. Gradually, their hearts became so inflamed with love for the monastic life, that they ended up being monks.

With Father Paul:

Both of them became disciples of Fr. ‘Paul’ (about 527-563 AD), who cared for them and helped them grow in every good work.

Some of the instructions of Fr. ‘Paul’ to his disciple ‘Badasuis,’ to warn him against depending on the monastic appearance or attire and not on the inner life; were recorded as follows:

 “Let your heart not trust in the title and the form, but meditate in what St.

‘James’ the Lord’s brother said in his Catholicon epistle that ‘All such boasting is evil’ (James 4:16). For, as we have today, among the monks we see, those who are clothed with the holy monastic ‘Eskeem,’ to whom the angels testify that they have reached the blessings of what they wear. Also, blessed are those laymen (in the world) who properly consummated their lives. They are better and more advanced than those who wear the holy ‘Eskeem’ without fulfilling their requirements and statutes. Woe to them; it was better for them not to be born in this world. May the Just God be merciful on them, when they stand bare before the dreadful great throne, where each of us will be getting his wages on what he has done; good or evil.”  “Now, my brother! Go into your cell, live in seclusion with yourself; keep on praying and fasting alone. Do not let anyone know your strife, neither a layman nor a monk. For then, you will be worthy of seeing the glory of God.”

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 6: Christian Concepts and Everyday Life › The Virtue of Obedience — 1203. What is the nature of a ruler or leader?

St. Pachomius was a military man and known for the extreme strictness with which he governed his monastic communities. He founded more than ten monasteries for men in Upper Egypt, along with three convents for nuns, and the number of monks in his main monastery in Pbow was about fifteen hundred. He was the abbot superior over all these monasteries.

One day, when St. Pachomius was waiting for the arrival of a group of solitary monks with whom he was to meet, his personal disciple Theodore noticed that his clothes were very old and tattered, and unsuitable for company. Theodore was the one responsible for caring for the clothing of the monks. The disciple asked his teacher to change his robe before he met the guests, but the father paid him no heed. He repeated his request a second time, and a third, but still the father would not change his clothes. Later, when the father examined his own behavior in his cell, he wept bitterly that he had not obeyed his disciple. He went and confessed his sin before his disciples, the monks. Thus, did the founder of the communal monastic life consider falling into disobedience a great defeat. To his mind, obedience is not something practiced by one party alone. For those who live in love and the new life, it is exchanged by both parties with wisdom and discernment.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 667–668
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia): He was born in upper Egypt around the year 290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the year 290 A. D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he established many monasteries in Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles.

St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart. He led an ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness to become his disciples.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisinnius, pp. 167–168
passages.text:
Saint: SISINNIUS, ST.

He was initially a Cappadocian slave, but he gained his freedom. Then, he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ and became a disciple of St. Albidius. He dwelt with him on the mountain, confined himself in a cave for seven years, then settled in a tomb for three more years. He was granted the gift of driving the demons out. Then, when he was ordained as a priest, he led the people to holiness. He cared for the strangers, dedicated himself to voluntary poverty, and used to rebuke the mean rich people. God has granted him also with the victory over the carnal desires.

[The Paradise of Saints; p. 53]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Savin, pp. 69–70
passages.text:
Saint: SAVIN, ST. — His Monastic Life and Seclusion

This saint Savin was born in Barcelona in the 5th century. He was raised by his widowed mother, who sent him as a young man to be under the care of his uncle at the city of Poitiers in Gaul (France). Savin was influenced by his religious cousin, who was a role model by his talk filled with the spirit. When his cousin secretly forsook his home and went to become a monk in a monastery in Ligugé, his uncle and his wife sought from him to help them to convince their son to come back to them. St. Savin refused, reminding them of the words of the Lord Christ, that man should love God more than he loves his father and mother, and added that he also intended to join his cousin, to become a monk in the same monastery.

His Monastic Life and Seclusion:

Savin set forth to the monastery with the intension of living as a recluse. There, the abbot of the monastery Fr. Frominius led him to a place on the mountains, where he built for himself a cave, which he soon replaced by a pit in the ground. When Fr. Frominius saw what he did, he indicated to him that he has gone to the extreme in his asceticism, and he should be more lenient on himself. St. Savin replied that everyone should show remorse in the way which would suit his sins. And, he continued being clothed by his same clothes in winter and summer for a whole 13 years.

His Love for Farmers:

St. Savin used to preach the farmers in the vicinity, not just by words, but by the example and role model of his life. And God allowed so many miracles to be performed on his hands. Once a farmer aggressively prevented him from passing through his field to reach a water spring on the other side, so St. Savin struck a rock with his rod, and water came out of it in the Name of Christ.

When the saint knew about the time of his repose, he sent to inform the monastery. And, he was surrounded by the monks and laymen until he reposed in peace. A church was eventually built in his name, and his fame spread that a whole city was named after him: St. Savin de Tarbes.

[Butler: October 9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Frontasius, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: FRONTASIUS (The martyr)

He was martyred in the land of Gaul (France), together with Severinus, Severianus, and Silanus, his companions. They were all disciples of St. Fronto, who was ordained as a bishop on Vesunna (nowadays Perigneux) by the hand of St. Peter the Apostle personally.

When Fronto sent them to preach the gospel among the French, the ruler Squindo arrested and killed them all, during the first persecution stirred up by Emperor Nero (54-68 AD).

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. II, p. 569]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pius I, Pope of Rome, p. 399
passages.text:
Saint: PIUS I, POPE OF ROME

Saint Pius I (140-155 AD) succeeded St. Hyginus (136-140 AD) on the See of Rome. He was formerly a citizen of Aquileia in Italy and said to be the brother of Hermas author of the book The Shepherd in the 2nd century AD.

He was ordained as a bishop around the year 140 AD. He cared to oppose the heresies faced by the Roman Church in his time, by the followers of Valentinus and Marcion. The first Valentinus, originally from Egypt, and he dwelt in Rome between the years 136 and 165 AD, hoping to be ordained as a bishop. His book carried a lot of Gnostic thoughts. While the second Marcion, was considered one of the most influential Gnostics personalities.

Pope Pius I cared so much to commit the priests to practice the Holy Sacraments with great caution and elaboration. So, he issued a creed that says: “A priest who spills the chalice after the sanctification, has to remain in a condition of repentance for 40 days, and if he spills a drop of it, he has to remain in a condition of repentance for three days; along with wiping the place of a spill with towels and burning them.” He also cared to increase the number of ministers serving the Kingdom of God, so he ordained 12 bishops and 18 priests. He was said to be martyred on the 11th of June in the year 155 AD, even though some scholars in the West, believe that he reposed without having his bloodshed.

[Butler’s: Lives of Saints; July 11]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pammachius, pp. 345–346
passages.text:
Saint: PAMMACHIUS, ST.

He sought from them to return to the bosom of the church. For his good ecclesiastical work, St. Augustine, the bishop of Hippo, wrote St. Pammachius to thank him in the year 401 AD.

St. Pammachius turned his house in Coelian Hill into a church, and according to some, the church of SS. Giovany and Paulo (John and Paul) was built on its location later on.

St. Pammachius reposed in the year 410 AD, during the attack of the Gosians and the Alaric on Rome. He is celebrated by the west on the 30th of August. It was said that he was ordained as a priest, but that was doubted by so many scholars.

Notes: [1] The ‘Donatists’ were a rebellious congregation in North West Africa, and found some sympathizers in Italy, that accused the other believers with infidelity.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Pijimi, pp. 463–464
passages.text:
Saint: PIJIMI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

This saint was born in the town of Feesha, he was raised in a poor pious family and since his childhood he had the responsibility of shepherding the sheep of his father. That simple work had its strong influence on his inner life; since it gave him a chance to spend long time meditating into God and His care for His creation. He longed to dedicate his life to God.

In his 12 years of age, an angel appeared to him in the form of a boy of the same age, who pretended to have a wish to be a monk, and his talk inflamed Pijimi’s heart for the monastic life. It happened that three days later, three monks came to accompany him to the wilderness of Nitria where, after spending a few days, they set forth with him to the wilderness of Scetis (the Scetis of St. Macarius).

His Monastic Life:

St. Pijimi lived seven years, growing in virtue in the Lord, after which he put on the “Monastic Scheme” while he was very young. He so walked by the spirit of the Lord that the other monks used to seek his prayers and blessing; while he lived among them with the spirit of obedience and humility.

His Spiritual Strife:

As St. Pijimi’s fame spread, many men and women came to visit him, and he started worrying about falling into evil desires. So, he intensified his care about his inner life with more prayers, fasting, and hand-work. He loved the spiritual vigil, remembering what the Lord said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). Also, whenever he found himself surrounded by a multitude of visitors; he remembered the Day of Judgment and rebuked himself by saying: “What shall I do if God would call on me while I am among such a crowd, those who I am not worthy to belong to; for I am a sinner and slothful in God’s work?!”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pastaurus, p. 376
passages.text:
Saint: PASTAURUS (The martyr)

St. Pastaurus was martyred amid the afflictions that dwelt on the church in the days of the 82nd Pope Benjamin II (1327-1339 AD) in the 14th century.

When his mother denied her faith, he stayed with his father. Some reported him to the governor who attempted to make him deny his faith, but when he refused, he put him in jail. In jail, a white dove came to stand on his head. On telling that to the governor, he threatened to burn him alive, but he said to him: “Do to me whatever you wish, you have authority only on my body.”

They brought him to the arena to be insulted, reviled, and beaten by the mob. He endured all that with tranquility and perseverance. Finally, they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom. God allowed many wonders to be performed through his body.

[Wallis Budge: The Ethiopic Synaxariom, Cambridge 1928, p. 842]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pisora, the Bishop, p. 469
passages.text:
Saint: PISORA, THE BISHOP (The martyr)

Father Pisora was the bishop of the city of Masil (Fowa) in Lower Egypt. When Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) started to persecute the Christians, this bishop, desiring to offer himself as a sacrifice of love to God, gathered his congregation together before the altar and he told them about his heart’s desire for shedding his blood for the Lord. All the congregation wept, saying: “To whom would you leave us fatherless?” They tried to make him change his mind but in vain. He bid them farewell and set forth, along with three other bishops: Pisikhos, Fanalikhos, and Theodore to proclaim their faith before the governor. They were all intensely tortured by the governor, in particular when he knew that they were bishops. These four bishops endured the sufferings with perseverance, and the Lord Christ strengthened and supported them, according to His Divine promise: “Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). They partook of the fellowship of passion together with their Savior, to have the fellowship in His glories; according to the words of the apostle: “If children, then heirs – heirs of God, and jointheirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together” (Rom. 8:17).

Finally, they had their heads cut off and received the crowns of martyrdom.

The relics of St. Pisora were in Nashein el-Qanater (Nasheil, province of Tanta). Now, it is kept in the church of Qasr el-Shamå in Old Cairo.

[Synaxarion: 9 Tout]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Ptolemaeus, pp. 497–498
passages.text:
Saint: PTOLEMAEUS (The martyr)

During the long Church history, many people have carried the same name of Ptolemaeus; among them: • Ptolemaeus, the disciple of Valentinus in the 2nd century AD, which was mentioned by St. Irenaeus. • Ptolemaeus, the martyr: celebrated in the West on the 19th of October. He was martyred in Rome around the year 161 AD. His contemporary St. Justin, the martyr, has testified to him. It was said that a married woman was living in a sinful life, and then became aware of the Christian faith through this St. Ptolemaeus. After she repented, she started to lead a pious life. Having tasted the sweetness of the fellowship with God and enjoyed the holy life, her heart was so inflamed by zeal, that she kept asking her husband to receive the faith also. However, he kept insulting her and badly treating her that she had to leave him. So, the husband told the governor that his estranged wife was a Christian, and accordingly, she was arrested. In the court of justice, her mentor St. Ptolemaeus stood before the governor Urbicius to defend her, and on proclaiming his faith, he was condemned to death himself.

A Christian man by the name of Lucius, who was there during the trial, protested before the governor that Ptolemaeus was condemned for no crime he committed, which would be contrary to the wisdom of the emperor and the council of the elites. This man also fell under the same verdict. Then, the same situation was repeated with a third man, although his name was not mentioned.

[Justine Mart: Apology 2:2; Eusebius: Hist. Eccl., vol. IV, 17:2-13]

• Ptolemaeus, the soldier: (20 December) was mentioned by St. Dionysius, the 14th pope of Alexandria (247-264 AD) in a letter he sent Fabian the bishop of Antioch. The pope narrated what happened in Alexandria during the persecution in the era of emperor Decius (249-251 AD). Among those who were martyred were: Amon, Xeno, Ptolemaeus, Engines, and the elder Theophilus. • Ptolemaeus (Ptolemy), the Egyptian: According to St. Palladius, he dwelt in a region called Klimax beyond Scetis. That was an extremely barren region 12 miles away from the nearest source of water. As the rain was also rare, the saint used to collect the dewdrops in a sponge to be able to use it, and in that fashion, he lived for 15 years.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Patra, p. 377
passages.text:
Saint: PATRA (The martyr)

St. Patra (Matra) was martyred on the 10th day of the Coptic month Mesra, most probably in the year 250 AD, in the days of St. Dionysius the Great, the 14th pope of Alexandria (247-264 AD). When Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) issued a decree committing everyone to worship the idols and to deny the Lord Jesus Christ; St. Patra set forth to the idol temple, removed the golden hand of the idol, cut it into small pieces and distributed the pieces on the poor. Finding out what happened to his idol, the emperor in great anger arrested many people; but the saint daringly came to him on his own, proclaiming that he took the hand and gave its gold to the needy. The governor gave the order to burn him alive, but God sent His angel and saved him. Then, the governor ordered to cut off his hands and feet, and to nail him upside down on a tree. A blind man took some of the blood pouring from his body and put it on his eyes and he had his sight back. Ultimately the saint had his head cut off and received the crown of martyrdom.

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt, p. 103]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Petarpemtis, the Blessed, p. 404
passages.text:
Saint: PETARPEMTIS, THE BLESSED — His Fatherhood and Miracles

Another time, when another one of his disciples reposed in the Lord, and he was surrounded by the brethren, the father came and kissed his (body) corpse and addressed him, saying: “Do you want, my son, to depart now to God, or you would rather remain in the body..?” Instantly the dead man replied: “It is better for me to forsake my body to be with Christ.” The blessed father then said to him: “Therefore, my son, lie in peace; and supplicate for my sake to God.” All those around were astonished and said: “This is truly a man of God.” He shrouded him and kept reading the psalms all night, then buried him.

Another time, standing before the deathbed of one of his disciples, who was known for his slothfulness and laziness, the brother kept weeping to beg the father to pray for him to be given another chance instead of the years he lost in slothfulness. Firmly, yet with love, the father rebuked him, and said: “I am ready to seek from God for your sake if you promise not to add to your sins new ones.” He fervently implored the Lord, then told the brother that God gave him three more years. The brother lived those three years in fantastic strife, and once those years came to an end, the father came to see his disciple before his departure. According to St. Palladius, this saint was not a regular man, but he came to be a chosen vessel by God whose actions amazed everybody!

In the simplicity of heart and fantastic faith, God performed countless miracles through St. Petarpemtis. According to his disciples, he walked on water. When they left him in a closed shut upper room, the angels carried him to the place he wished to reach, and he told his disciples that, in a night vision, God revealed to him the Heavenly Goodness prepared for the true monks, which no one could utter or describe. All that for the sake of his amazing faith together with the simplicity of his heart and his humility filled with love for God and men.

[St. Jerome: History of the Monks; ch. 16]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hippolytus, the Roman Pope, pp. 271–272
passages.text:
Saint: HIPPOLYTUS, THE ROMAN POPE (The martyr) — Controversy with the Two Roman Popes Zephyrinus and Callixtus I

There is a big disagreement among the scholars concerning the identity of St. Hippolytus (Abulides/Poltus: 170-235 AD) and the writings attributed to him. There are two versions about this saint:  According to what came in the Roman history, he was the officer responsible for St. Laurence during his imprisonment. So impressed by the saint, Hippolytus believed and was baptized. After the martyrdom of the saint, he helped in shrouding and burying his body. Because of that, he was brought before the emperor, who rebuked him for disregarding his official status and ordered to scourge him, together with nineteen Christians who were scourged to death. Then, they tied the legs of the saint by a long rope to two of the wildest of horses, and released them to drag the saint on the ground until the saint's blood covered the roads, the trees, and the rocks. He delivered his soul in the year 235. The believers wiped out his blood by their kerchiefs and gathered his scattered flesh.  According to the second version, which seems closer to the truth, he was a priest who lived at the beginning of the 3rd century; a man of knowledge, and one of the most prominent authors of theology in the early Roman Church; most probably a disciple of St. Irenaeus (c. 120-200.

Controversy with the Two Roman Popes Zephyrinus and Callixtus I:

St. Hippolytus blamed Pope Zephyrinus (199-217), the bishop of Rome, for being too slow in exposing and opposing the heresies; and even accused him of heresy for being lazy with these heretics. Also, he fought his successor Pope Callixtus I (217-222), regarding the Person and the Nature of the Lord Christ and Forgiveness. Concerning the Person of the Lord Christ, he discerned between three stages in the Divine Word:

He is the self-reason in the mind of God; He is the uttered Word to achieve the creation; and He is the incarnate Word Jesus Christ. He said that the Word (Christ) is distinguished from the Father in such a way that Pope Callixtus I, accused him of believing in the existence of Two Gods.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sanctus, the Deacon, p. 60
passages.text:
Saint: SANCTUS, THE DEACON, ST. — His Commitment to Silence

His Commitment to Silence:

St. Sanctus was one of the famous martyrs of Lyons in Gaul (France) [with SS. Pothinus, Attalus, Blandina, and some others. He was martyred in the era of Emperor Marcus Aurelius (161-180) in the year 177. St. Sanctus was a deacon in Vienne who endured extreme suffering from severe torture. Yet, the rulers and his executioners could not get from him one single word or information about his name, home town, or nationality. His answer to all their questions was only his statement: “I am a Christian,” and nothing more.

Disfiguring Him:

Failing to extract any information from him, the angry governor ordered torturing him without mercy. After using on him all the known ways of torture, they tied hot iron plates on the most sensitive parts of his body, burned them, and yet he kept steady healthy and fresh. The body of St. Sanctus was so immensely disfigured to be recognizable as a human being. But, when they found out that he was still healthy, after assuming that he died, they resumed putting those plates on other parts of his body. On seeing how he was miraculously healed, they put him on an iron chair and ignited fire underneath him. Finally, he delivered his pure soul under torture.

[Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 151]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Apolidus, Pope of Rome, p. 208
passages.text:
Saint: APOLIDUS (Hippolytus), POPE OF ROME, ST. (The martyr)

On the 5th day of Amshir, the church celebrates the appearance of the body of St. ‘Apolidus’ (Hippolytus), the Pope of Rome. He was a virtuous and a perfect man in his generation. He was chosen to the Roman See after Father ‘Augius.' This happened in the first year of the enthronement of Abba ‘Cladianus,’ the 9th Pope of Alexandria. Pope ‘Apolidus’ was always keen on teaching his people and guarding them against the pagan influences, confirming them in the faith of the Lord Christ.

When reports of St. ‘Apolidus’ reached the infidel Emperor ‘Claudius Caesar,’ he arrested him and tortured him severely. The emperor then tied his feet with a heavy stone and cast him in the sea on the 5th day of Amshir.

On the following day, one of the faithful found the body of the saint floating on the water, and the stone was bound to his feet. The man took it to his home and shrouded the body. The news spread in the city of Rome and all the neighboring cities, and it reached Caesar, who asked for the body, but the man hid it. This father left a great wealth of teachings about the Incarnation, and several sermons about Christian teaching. He also established 38 laws.

[The Synaxarion 6 Amshir]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pontinus, the Martyr, p. 479
passages.text:
Saint: PONTINUS, THE MARTYR — His Father Proclaimed His Faith

His Father Proclaimed His Faith:

With joy, the boy set forth to tell his father what happened to him. Being prudent, the father listened to him to the end, probably not to lose him; but it so happened that the father himself, drawn by the talk of the boy, set forth with him to the pope to seek his counsel and he joined the rows of the catechumen, together with his son to get eventually baptized.

When the father reposed while his son was 20 years old, the young man distributed all his inheritance to the poor and the needy. He was loved by Emperor Philip the Arab (244-249 AD) and his son, who received Christianity on his hands.

However, during the time of Emperors Valerian and Gallienus (253-268 AD), Pontinus escaped to Cimella, near the city of Nice in France, where he was arrested by governor Claudius. The latter delivered him to wild bears in the amphitheater. However, those bears devoured the executioners but did not harm the saint. In anger, the governor ordered that the saint’s head be cut off. His relics were kept in the monastery of St. Ponte, near Nice, whereas his head was kept in Marseilles. He was martyred around the year 257 or 258.

[Baring-Gould: Lives of Saints, May 14]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pammachius, pp. 344–345
passages.text:
Saint: PAMMACHIUS, ST.

St. Pammachius was born around the year 340 AD from a noble Roman family called ‘Furii.’ He was a layman and a close friend of St. Jerome (Eronimus), since the time they were studying together. Some people thought that he became St. Jerome's assistant since St. Jerome issued many of his books under this man's name. Two examples for this were his interpretation of some of the Books of the Minor Prophets (around the year 406 AD) and his interpretation of the Book of Daniel (around the year 407 AD).

In the year 385 AD, St. Pammachius married Paulina, the second daughter of St. Paula; one of the great friends of St. Jerome.

It so seems that St. Pammachius was a religious man, for we saw him complaining to St. Siricius, the bishop of Rome (384-399 AD) denouncing a monk named Jovinian who was not following the upright faith, and he proclaimed that there was no difference between virginity and matrimony and that the reward was the same in Heaven, regardless of the way a man would live on earth. He also shared with Halphidius, the denial of the perpetual virginity of St. Mary. Jovinian was condemned earlier by both the bishop of Rome and by St. Ambrose of Milan. In addition, St. Pammachius sent some copies of the writings of that heretic to St. Jerome, which resulted in that both St. Jerome and St. Augustine decided to write detailed treatises to refute him.

However, St. Pammachius was not comfortable with the harsh reaction of St. Jerome in his response to Jovinian which was probably because on one side St. Pammachius was a very compassionate and tender man, and on the other side, he felt in St. Jerome's response a commendation for virginity and belittling for the sanctity of matrimony. St. Jerome hastened to send several letters to St. Pammachius to clarify his views. He showed him that he would never touch the sanctity of matrimony nor defile the marriage relationship, even though he also commends virginity. He gave him the following comparison: if the virginity would be as gold, the matrimony, to him, would be counted as silver. It seemed that St. Pammachius was comforted by St. Jerome's response.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, p. 368
passages.text:
Saint: PAPIAS, BISHOP OF HIERAPOLIS, ST.

This St. Papias was a bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor (around the years 80-160 AD) during the 2nd century; according to St. Irenaeus (130-202 AD). He was a disciple of St. John the Evangelist and a friend of St. Polycarp.

St. Papias was a man of high culture, of rich knowledge in the Holy Bible; who had a special interest in gathering and collecting the oral narratives concerning the life of the Lord Jesus Christ. He authored his famous work ‘Expositions of the Oracles of the Lord’ in five volumes, out of which, unfortunately, we only have few quotes in the writings of Irenaeus and Eusebius.

In this work, he gave his remarks on the Gospels of Mark and Luke; as well as he cared for the oral narratives through eye-witnesses.

He was the first to talk about the ‘One Thousand Year’ reign in a literal sense, saying that the Lord Jesus Christ will reign on the earth during that time. He assumed that he was explaining what came in the prophecies. However, this concept was rejected by the Mother Church.

[Rev. B. Schmid: Manual of Patrology; St. Louis 1903, p. 85]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pisus, the Monk, pp. 469–470
passages.text:
Saint: PISUS, THE MONK

This saint was a monk in the monastery of Abba Yeĥnes Kama in Scetis during the days of the 66th Pope Christodoulos (1046-1077 AD) in the 11th century. This monk enjoyed a great relationship with the Lord His Savior; that when a plague came upon Egypt, and 21,000 children died because of it; a delegation came in terror to seek from this monk to pray for the sake of the people of Egypt. This saint prayed all night until dawn; then came to the delegation to say: “Return in peace and say to those who sent you that our Lord Jesus Christ has compassion on us and He will take this plague away from us by His Grace.” This was the case, and the plague disappeared on their return.
