passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexander Akimetes, pp. 119–120
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDER AKIMETES, ST.

This saint was born in Asia Minor and was educated in Constantinople, where he received the Faith through his love of reading the Holy Bible. He then went to Syria to practice ascetic life. He practiced the experience of fellowship than that of seclusion, and after 11 years of his monastic life, he dedicated himself to preaching in Mesopotamia (Al-Missa). And, it was said that he was the one who brought ‘Rabulas’ to the Faith, who became the bishop of Edessa (Al-Roha) later on.

He established a vast monastery near the Euphrates. However, he did not stay long there, for he took a large number of its monks and went to Antioch for a while; although, his visit stirred up so many troubles. So, he finally had to leave and establish a new monastery in Constantinople. Once more, some evil people set up against him and managed to expel him from there. So, he built another monastery at ‘Gormon’ on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, where he reposed in the year 430 AD He was famed for establishing in his monasteries a large Choir, which was divided into several groups. These groups would rotate throughout the day, each new group relieving the one before it, to create uninterrupted prayer and worship twenty-four hours a day without ceasing. Hence, they were called ‘Akimetes’ or ‘Acoemetae,' meaning (The Sleepless Ones).

[Butler’s Lives of Saints, Feb. 23]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, p. 260
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — Father of the Monks

Father of the Monks:

However, during his wandering in that area, a high number of young men gathered around him seeking to be his disciples, since they were impressed by his imposing role model of holiness, love, and humility, which were planted in him by Abba Anthony.

So, as the monks gathering around him increased in number, St. Hilarion built monasteries for them. He became a father for all of them and kept visiting every monastery once every year to guide the monks and to hold them fast unto Faith. He became so burdened with labor, especially with the increasing crowd of those who came to seek his prayers and blessing.

The Saint Gets Attacked:

It happened one day that Hilarion was attacked by armed robbers while he was kneeling to pray. When he disregarded them and kept on praying, they asked him: “Don’t you fear us?” He answered, saying: “He who possesses nothing would fear no one!” When they added: “We could kill you!” He answered them: “I don’t fear death because I am always ready for it!” Perceiving the true faith through him, they were filled with fear and repented before him. St. Hilarion was attacked several times by the devil: once in the form of women to corrupt the purity of his mind. Other times in the way of wild beasts to terrify him. Yet, he kept being armed with prayers and making the sign of the Cross on himself and managed to live in the peace of God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexander of Cappadocia, p. 120
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDER OF CAPPADOCIA (The martyr)

Among many strangers who came to Milan in the days of Emperor Theodosius the Great (346-395 AD) were three men from Cappadocia: ‘Sisinnius,' ‘Martyrius’ and his brother ‘Alexander.' They were so appreciated by St. Ambrose to recommend them to St. ‘Vigilius,’ Bishop of ‘Trent,' to designate them for preaching mission. They were sent to preach in ‘Tyrolese Alps,' where they faced so much trouble, although they managed to gain so many souls to the Lord Christ.

When the pagans observed how those three men have converted a large number of the inhabitants to Christianity, they attacked the church and violently continued beating the three saints. The first (a deacon) reposed within few hours, the second (a reader) managed to crawl into a garden nearby and was found the next day, to be dragged by his feet on the rocky road to be severely bruised and eventually to repose.

Then, when the third (Alexander) fell into their hands, they tried to provoke him to deny his faith. They burned the bodies of his two companions in front of him. However, St. Alexander did not change his stand, so they burned him alive. The believers gathered their burnt relics and carried them to Trent. St. ‘Vigilius’ built a church on the location where they endured the sufferings. St. Ambrose, St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine mentioned these saints in their writings.

[Butler’s Lives of Saints, May 29]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius, the Monk, p. 252
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS, THE MONK, ST.

St. Hesychius was a saintly monk who lived in the 4th century AD. He was a faithful disciple of his mentor St. Hilarion, whom he accompanied in his travels from Palestine to Egypt. After St. Hilarion's reputation reached its peak in Gaza, he intended not to stay or to go back to Gaza, and he sailed secretly to the island of Sicily. For three years, Hesychius kept searching for the whereabouts of his mentor. Not finding him in the wilderness or the ports of Egypt, he searched for him in Greece. There, he heard about a saintly monk in Sicily who performed miracles. So, he set out to that island and cast himself on the ground, shedding tears on the feet of his mentor.

Wishing to enjoy a life of seclusion, the mentor and his disciple went to Dalmatia and from there to the island of Cyprus. Two years later, St. Hilarion sent Hesychius to Palestine to visit and follow up on the condition of the brethren there and to inspect their old monastery near Gaza. When he returned, he found his mentor disturbed by the frequency of the visitors, and planning to flee to another location. However, being too advanced in age, he managed to convince him to go deeper into the island to enjoy more seclusion. There, they lived until eventually St. Hilarion reposed, leaving his Holy Bible and some clothes to his disciple. After some time, Hesychius carried the relics of his mentor to Palestine, despite the objection of the inhabitants of the island. There, it was received by the multitudes of monks and people with hymns of praise. He was buried in the monastery he built-in Majuma. A few years later, Hesychius himself reposed.

[Baring-Gould: October 3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Heraclides, p. 244
passages.text:
Saint: HERACLIDES (The martyr)

St. Heraclides was one of the students of the school of Origen. He was martyred in Alexandria in the year 250 AD.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Heraclides (1), Vol II, p. 902]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 259–260
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — Hermit in the Wilderness of Sinai

Hermit in the Wilderness of Sinai:

Upon arriving back to his home town, he found out that both his parents passed away. Being the elder son of the family, he divided the inheritance into two portions: distributed one half among his brothers and the other half to the poor and the needy. He left nothing for himself. By such optional poverty, he set out to the desert of Sinai in the southwest of Majoma, near Gaza. There, Hilarion dwelt while being still a young man. He used to wear sackcloth underneath a tight garment, beside the leather Eskeem, given to him by Abba Anthony. His daily portion was about fifteen figs, which he ate after sunset. When his carnal desires stirred up in him, he would address his body, saying: “I shall see, O colt, how to keep you from kicking.” Then, he would cut off a portion of his already insufficient meal.

To earn his living, he used to work in the fields, in addition to making baskets; he did not depend on anyone to sustain him. Then, he built for himself a cell, more like a tomb than a dwelling place. Hilarion lived there for four years. That cell was still there when St. Jerome visited that area later on. Through the persistent reading of the Holy Scriptures, St. Hilarion managed to memorize them all by heart. This practice was common among the Egyptian anchorites.

Gaining the Blessing of the Holy Land:

St. Hilarion kept on moving around in the Sinai desert. Then, he set out to get the blessing of the Holy Land, which was sanctified by the Lord Jesus Christ, who lived there for a while. He also visited the monasteries there, enjoyed the encounter with the saintly monks and nuns, in whom he smelled the sweet fragrance of Christ.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hermias, p. 247
passages.text:
Saint: HERMIAS (The martyr)

St. Hermias was martyred in Apollonia in the year 284 AD, along with another martyr called Felix, during the reign of Emperor Numerian (283-284 AD). The Church of the West celebrates him on the 6th of July.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Hermias (2), Vol. II, p. 927]

Notes: [1] ‘Apollonia’ was an ancient town in the region of Thrace above Greece.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hermogenes, Bishop of Farma, p. 247
passages.text:
Saint: HERMOGENES, BISHOP OF FARMA

St. Hermogenes was the bishop of El-Farma (Rhinocorura) on the borders between Egypt and Palestine. He attended the Third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus in the year 431 AD. He was among the supporters of the 24th Pope of Alexandria, St. Cyril, the Pillar of Faith (412-444 AD). Pope Cyril sent him to Rome to solicit the support of the Roman Pope St. Celestine I (Caelestinus: 422-432 AD), but he arrived there after the departure of that pope. His successor Pope Sixtus III (Xystus: 432-440 AD), mentioned his encounter with St. Hermogenes in the letter he sent to St. Cyril. St. Isidore of Pelusium (d. 450 AD) wrote several letters to St. Hermogenes.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Hermogenes (7), Vol. III, p. 4]

Notes: [2] ‘Pelusium’ was near ‘El-Farma’, close to ‘Port-Saiid’, on the Mediterranean…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Abba Ehron, pp. 11–12
passages.text:
Saint: EHRON, ST. ABBA — His Seclusion

His Seclusion:

For ten years, he lived in the monastery growing in virtue, contemplation, and asceticism. All the monks loved him because of his piety and service to all of them. However, because the thought of seclusion was growing in his heart, he asked the Abbot of the monastery and the fathers to pray for him and bless him, and then he set forth to the wilderness to live in a cave on top of the mountain.

There, St. ‘Ehron’ lived a life of complete asceticism, possessing nothing and eating only some herbs and few fruits he would find on the trees growing next to a little spring there.

In Armenia:

Three years after his seclusion, an angel of the Lord guided him to leave and move to the ‘Mountain of Armenia,’ where he would become a disciple of a saintly anchorite named ‘Gregorius the Hermit.’ There, he remained for another period of three years, practicing the monastic life of prayer and contemplation under the guidance of his new spiritual father. In addition, God granted him the gift of healing the sick and driving the demons out.

In Jerusalem:

Then, St. ‘Gregorius’ and his disciple ‘Ehron’ set forth to Jerusalem to get the blessings of the holy places, but Abba ‘Gregorius’ reposed in the Lord on their way and was mourned by his disciple. ‘Ehron’ continued his journey and moved between towns and villages, healing the sick and driving the demons out, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. In his way, he went to the town of ‘Aamid,’ affiliated with the diocese of ‘Constantinople’ (probably nowadays the city of ‘Amon’ in old ‘Yugoslavia’). There, he was received by its bishop Abba ‘Tadros,’ who convinced him to receive the grace of the priesthood.

Then, priest ‘Ehron’ continued his journey, moving from one town to another, where some of the seekers of monastic life gathered around him. So, he established a small monastery for them, stayed four years guiding and training them, then blessed them and continued on his journey to the Holy Land.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore, Bishop of Cappadocia, p. 263
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, BISHOP OF CAPPADOCIA

This St. Theodore (Tadros), apparently was a shepherd before he was ordained as a bishop on Cappadocia. Even though he was freshly ordained and just got acquainted with St. Gregory of Nazianzus (329-390 AD), he was assigned to urge St. Gregory to shepherd the Orthodox congregation in Constantinople. St. Gregory wrote him in response [Letter# 222], to tell him about what he did. He told him also about the insults that came on him from the bishops of that region. He also apologized about what happened to him, being new in his bishopric.

[Smith and Wace, Vol. 4, p. 932]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hanus, p. 232
passages.text:
Saint: HANUS (The martyr)

He was a priest in Persia and was martyred in May 375 AD, during the reign of King Shapur II (309-379 AD). He was martyred along with a deacon, also called Hanus, and about forty others. Those others included two bishops, sixteen priests, nine deacons, six monks, and seven consecrated virgins.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol II, p. 844]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hermas, ‘the Shepherd's Author, pp. 245–246
passages.text:
Saint: HERMAS, ‘THE SHEPHERD'S AUTHOR

In the Muratorian Canon, it was mentioned that Hermas, the author of the book ‘The Shepherd,’ was the brother of the first bishop of Rome, Pius I (140- 155 AD). Origen (184-253 AD) believed that he was the same Hermas mentioned by St. Paul the Apostle (Rom. 16:14). In talking about himself, Hermas says that He was a slave, sold in Rome to a Roman lady called Rhoda. He began to love her as a sister. Then, seeing how beautiful she was, he desired to have her as his wife (Herm.Vis. 1:1). After she set him free, he became rich by working as a farmer and a merchant. He ended up marrying a talkative woman, and he became indifferent in caring for his family. His children plunged into evil (Herm.Vis. 1:3), and because of them, he became poor (Herm.Vis. 1:2, 2:3, 3:6). Sometimes, Hermas portrayed himself as being virtuous, chaste, simple, and free from all evil desires (Herm.Vis. 1:2). At other times, he portrayed himself as a liar and a hypocrite (Herm.Vis. 3). At the time of persecution, he and his wife held fast to their faith. However, their children denied their faith. Enthusiastic about repentance, Hermas authored his book “The Shepherd” to urge the sinners to repent. He pointed out that the purity of the Church was in danger, because of the spread of sin, and that the end was close at hand.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Helidorus, Bishop of Altinum, p. 237
passages.text:
Saint: HELIDORUS, BISHOP OF ALTINUM, ST.

St. Heliodorus (Alidor/Heliodourus) was a soldier. When he met with St. Jerome in Aquileia in Italy around the year 372 AD and became one of his disciples, he loved prayers and the study of the Holy Bible, spending days and nights in worship. However, he did not join a monastery nor was committed to a life in the wilderness. When St. Jerome decided to travel to the East, along with Fr. Eugrius and Fr. Enochensus. St. Helidorus joined them on their journey. They visited many cities in Syria. In Antioch, they met Apolinarius, who at that time had not started to spread his heresy. However, after Helidorus listened to Apolinarius interpretations of the Holy Bible, he managed to recognize among his words the seeds of the heresy's venoms. St. Jerome retreated to the wilderness in the region of Calchida on the borders of Syria and Arabia and was followed by Helidorus for a while. However, Helidorus, longing for his home town, returned to Delmasia, promising his friend and mentor to rejoin him later. Yet, when he stayed there by his parents for too long, St. Jerome sent him a message to remind him of the importance of the life of seclusion in the wilderness. He told him of his tears by which he bid him farewell, and asked him not to yield to the tears of his mother and the supplications of his father. Helidorus was much moved by this message.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hanolius, the Prince, p. 232
passages.text:
Saint: HANOLIUS, THE PRINCE (The martyr)

St. Hanolius was one of the nobles of the city of Perga in the district of Pamphylia in Asia Minor. His love for the Lord Jesus Christ made him declare his faith publicly everywhere. So, he was arrested by Barnabachus, the prince under Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). He confessed his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ before that prince, and he praised God by splendid hymns, then he cursed the idols. The angry prince ordered his men to crucify Hanolius on a wooden post. He kept praising the Lord, who made him worthy to be crucified in His name. Then, he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 5 Baramhat]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gelasius, the Hermit, pp. 161–162
passages.text:
Saint: GELASIUS, THE HERMIT

This saint was a contemporary of the 21st pope of Alexandria St. Peter II (373-379 AD). He was considered one of the most prominent fathers who took good care of the congregation in the absence of the pope while he was in hiding from the heretic Arians. St. Gelasius earned the title “The Warrior” because of the multitudes of services he performed for the Alexandrian congregation during the time of anguish, while he was only a deacon.

Eventually, he forsook the world and headed to the wilderness of the Scetis, where his spiritual efforts qualified him to shepherd over the monks in that holy site. He became a father to so many other hermits.

St. Gelasius spent his time in the wilderness transcribing the Holy Bible, and then he would give them to the hermits of his monastery to learn the Divine wisdom through them. His monks, in their turn, provided the congregation with every religious service they needed, which supported them in confronting all the religious persecution they were encountering.

[Iris H. El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, Item 403]

records.question: Who was St. Anthony of Padua?
records.answer:
I could not find anything about St. Anthony of Padua in the loaded sources.

The passages cover extensively St. Anthony the Great, also known as the Father of the Monks and the Founder of the Monastic Movement, who was born around 251 AD in Egypt and lived a life of asceticism and seclusion in the desert, founding the monastic order of seclusion and influencing many other monastic leaders [1][2][3][10]. They also mention other saints named Anthony, such as Anthony the Syrian the martyr and Antonius Al-Bebawy the martyr, but none relate to St. Anthony of Padua [4].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthonius, and Other Saints with That Name, pp. 195–196
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONIUS, and Other Saints with that Name (The martyrs) — ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr

Often confusion takes place between the martyrs who carried the name ‘Anthony,' among whom are:

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr:

He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop assigned him to build a Church, the pagans were stirred up against him and killed him.

ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr:

St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to ‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his Christ, he ordered him chained and sent him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built. Abba Anthony’s idea was that if a monk wished to visit those living there, he could start walking after he finished eating at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone.

His Personality and the Role of Nitria;

Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away from the crowd and refrained from performing any miracles, claiming that he was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba Amon.

St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM

Besides his discipleship to Alexander, there were two other great influences in his life:

1- From his seventh year to the fifteenth he lived during a period of severe persecution (303 - 311 CE). He knew many among the Alexandrian martyrs and confessors from whom he learned the Orthodox faith and a loving intimacy with the Holy Scriptures. He did not accompany them to the arena of persecution but his heart was aflame with divine love, facing every struggle for the sake of Christ.

2- After he heard about St. Anthony the hermit, he hurried to the wilderness and lived with him for about three years, practicing the ascetic and righteous life and the deep fellowship with God. Providence arranged this close relationship with Anthony so that during his exiles and flight he never felt lonely. Instead he considered it a good opportunity for him to have a bit of solitude and seclusion, praying for his people and writing to them. He was obliged to become the historian of St. Anthony .

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of St. Anthony Mountain, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN

On the 26th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidrak St. Anthony and his Companions, p. 147
passages.text:
Saint: SIDRAK ST. ANTHONY AND HIS COMPANIONS (The martyrs)

A monk from the monastery of St. Anthony by the name of Sidrak, left his monastery with a colleague by the name of Fadl-Allah and accompanied them their close friend Daoud el-Banna. They all came down together from the mountain of St. Anthony to receive the crowns of martyrdom Those saints were martyred during the rule of the Circassian Mamluks (1382-1517) .

They were following the lead of St. Anthony, the Father of all Monks, who came down to Alexandria in the days of Emperor Maximian (286-305 AD) saying: “Let me go to where the fire of sufferings is. If the Divine care allowed for my martyrdom, I would be ready; and if not, I shall at the least stand by those persecuted among the children of St. Mark the Evangelist...”

[The Patriotism and History of the Coptic Church, p. 250]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisoes, the Great, pp. 168–169
passages.text:
Saint: SISOES, THE GREAT, ST. — Abba Anthony his Role Model

After the repose of Abba Anthony the Great, St. Sisoes (Shishoi/Shishai) was one of the most shining pillars of faith among the Fathers of the wilderness. Therefore, this saint is referred to as St. “Sisoes the Great.” Shishoi means: The Son of the High One. He was an Egyptian by birth, and when he reached 20 years of age, he forsook the world and sought refuge in the wilderness of Scetis in the year 340 AD, and became a disciple to St. Macarius. In the year 356 AD, longing for a life of more tranquility, he crossed the Nile to the Mountain of St. Anthony right after his departure, to have the blessings of the life and virtues of St. Anthony as light and helper in his new life. He set forth to a life of seclusion until the year 426 AD when he reached the age of 106 years, and because of old age, he returned to the wilderness of Scetis, and reposed after a little while when he reached 110 years of age. About him, Abba Poemen (Bemen) said: “He exalted beyond every limit, and surpassed all the achievements of the other saintly Fathers.”

Abba Anthony his Role Model:

St. Sisoes was acting as if Abba Anthony the Great was watching him and listening to his instructions to his disciples. He strove to imitate that great teacher in all his life: in his asceticism, in his spiritual practices, in his commitment to silence and his longing for prayers. Therefore, his fame spread, and so many people came to him requesting to be his disciples. At this point, he had to forsake his love for silence and seclusion, to fulfill a higher goal, namely loving care of his disciples. Abba Sisoes’s brother came to visit him in the cave of Abba Anthony, where he was staying. The saint amiably said to his brother: “In this cave, a lion used to live; now it is inhabited by a fox.”

St. Sisoes always was complaining that he did not reach the statue of St. Anthony. Once, a monk asked him: “Father! Have you not reached the level of St. Anthony?” He answered: “If I had only one of the virtues of that monk, I would have become a torch of Divine Love.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 667–668
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia): He was born in upper Egypt around the year 290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the year 290 A. D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he established many monasteries in Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles.

St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart. He led an ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness to become his disciples.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pelosianus, p. 396
passages.text:
Saint: PELOSIANUS, ST.

This saint was a friend of Abba Anthony the Great (251-356 AD). He took part in burying Abba Anthony along with his fellow monk Isaac. It seems that St. Jerome (342-420 AD), who told us about him, has met him somewhere.

[Jerome: Vita Hilarionis, 30; 31]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef, Father [a Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great], p. 367
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF, FATHER [A Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great]

This Father Yousef was one of the prominent elders of the wilderness in the 4th century. All we know about him is that he happened to go to visit St. Anthony the Great in the company of two fellow elder hermits. St. Anthony tried to put them to the test, so he asked them about specific topics in the Holy Bible. The first and second hermits gave some answers. To them, St. Anthony said that their responses were not satisfactory. However, when Fr. Yousef said humbly: “I truly say, O Father, I do not know. I am utterly helpless in that concern.” Over his response, St. Anthony said: “Fr. Yousef alone found the right answer, by saying: ‘I do not know.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, p. 160
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

He was the founder of the monastic movement in ‘Nitria’ (Bernoug). Here, we need to distinguish between three monastic zones within the Natron Valley (Wadi El-Natrun) which often get mixed up:

1- The ’Nitria’ (Bernoug) zone, which received the first spark of the monastic movement through Abba Amon. 2- The ‘Celia’ (the Cells) zone, which is about 10 miles south of the ‘Nitria’ zone. 3- The ‘Scetis’ (Askeet) zone, which is located to the south of the former two zones.

His Monastic Life:

Saint Amon the great was born around the year 275 AD near the region of Marriott. He was raised as an orphan, and when he reached 22 years of age, his uncle forced him to get married despite his refusal. When he got married, he and his bride agreed on living virgins. Eighteen years later, the saint set forth to the desert of ‘Nitria’ (the city of Nitria or Bernoug is 14 kilometers Southwestern of the city of Damanhur). He was the first monk to reach that area, and he built for himself a cell there, in which he lived for 22 years. During that time, he used twice a year to visit his wife, who was living with many pious virgins. The location of the ‘Nitria’ zone was convenient to be the cradle of the commencement of that monastic movement. That area was close to the countryside and to the desert at the same time. In the beginning, the monks, who followed St. Amon, worked to earn their living by cropping the wheat, and it was easy for them also to acquire the linen to weave, instead of the palm leaves. The area also provided them with the ‘Natron’, which they could extract from the lake and sell to the villages around them. However, the region was always infested by mosquitos because of its swamps.

A congregation of hermits started to gather around the saint. They all lived in a life midway between the system of seclusion and that of the cenobite. Abba Amon was the first head of such a monastic congregation in Nitria, and many of his disciples became great fathers. Abba Amon used to visit Abba Anthony to seek his blessing and guidance. And when Abba Anthony came to visit him, he asked his advice concerning some pious monks, who tried to live a solitary life and build for themselves cells far away from the congregation. After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Sinai, pp. 438–439
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF SINAI (Al-DARAGI), ST. — His Seclusion

His Seclusion:

At the age of twenty years, his mentor Martyrius died, and St. John wanted to practice a greater asceticism; so, he withdrew to a hermitage at the foot of the mountain, about five miles from the monastery. In this isolation, he lived for some twenty years, always studying the lives of the saints and thus becoming one of the most learned church fathers. He loved perpetual prayer that he fled away from all men. He often was elevated above the ground during his prayer. He loved the life of seclusion and contemplation, to live for forty years, to be called by the people ‘The King of the Wilderness.’

He suffered much oppression from Satan and confronted his arrows by prayer, fasting, ascetic practices, and having communion of the Holy Sacraments; in the church of the Virgin St Mary, built by Emperor Justinian I (527-565 AD), about five miles away from his cell.

About his fights against the demon of boredom, he said, “Whoever concentrates in his seclusion on fighting the demon of boredom, is often harmed; for he wastes the time of prayers and the Theoria (The mental contemplation and beholding the Divine things), to fight and confront him (27- 43). While the saint was narrating about his viewing of the angels, someone asked him about the nature of the Lord before the Incarnation and the sitting of the Son on the right hand of the Father. St. John answered that the human mind cannot perceive these mysteries (47-47).

He presented to us his practical experience with Tranquility, in his essay 27; he revealed it to be his occupation with the Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “Let the contemplation in the Person of the Lord Jesus Christ get so attached to your soul; to get to know the benefit of tranquility (27:61).”

“The majesty of a king is in his wealth and the multitude of his subjects, whereas the pride of the monk is in the tranquility of his prayer (27:87).”

“Tiny lust disturbs the eye, and a little interest scatters the tranquility.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Sinai, p. 441
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF SINAI (Al-DARAGI), ST. — His Writings

Even though the book was predestined to cover the monastic asceticism, yet it was a call addressed to all to practice the virtuous life in Christ Jesus.

This book reveals to us the strong personality of St. John. We see him present in his book an accurate evaluation for specific actions, as an experienced guide of vast knowledge and as a profoundly spiritual father. It also reveals his clear awareness of the conditions of people living amid the world, their views, their customs, and their feelings. He proved that he had indepth knowledge of the human soul, which he elaborately analyzed. He is characterized by moderation, seriousness, and firmness against sin.

[Diocese of Sinai Peninsula: ‘A Ladder to God,’ 1998] [Monastery of St. George El-Ĥarf; ‘A Ladder to God,’ Beirut 1980]

Notes: [1] Clugnet, Léon. St. John Climacus.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John Chrysostom, p. 418
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, ST. — His Writings while in the Monastery

His Writings while in the Monastery:

 When St. John Chrysostom took off to the monastery, his soul became so happy. He felt as though he was in heaven itself, a feeling which remained with him all the days of his life. One time he said: “For the pious, taking refuge in a monastery is an escape from earth to heaven.” On another occasion, he described a monk in his cell saying, “As if he dwells in another world, in heaven itself; he talks only about Celestial matters; about the bosom of Abraham, the crowns of saints and the hosts surrounding the Lord Jesus Christ.” In the joy of his heart, he wanted to draw to the monastic life some of his friends in Antioch, particularly Theodore. So, he wrote his first essay, “A Comparison between a King and a Monk” (Comparatio Regis et Monachi).  In the year 373 AD, when the wrath of Emperor Valens (364-378 AD) was stirred against the Orthodox faith, he committed their hermits and monks to enlist in the military and civil services. He counted monasticism as some foolishness and carried out a fierce campaign against it. John had to write three of his books, under the title ‘Adverssus Oppugnatores Vitae Monastiac,’ in which he debated against the enemies of the monastic life; and urged the fathers to send their children to be educated by the monks to gain spiritual knowledge and achieve the virtuous life.  When his friend Theodore was swept away by his infatuation by a beautiful woman called Hermoine, and he forsook his monastic life to marry her; John hastened and wrote him two letters: ‘An Exhortation to Theodore’ (Paraeneses ad Theodorum Lapsum), calling him to repent and to resume his monastic life. In these letters, he waged all his oratorical arts of sad sympathy, tender entreaty, bitter reproach, and terrible warning, to reclaim his friend to what he believed the surest and safest way to heaven. He said: “To sin is human, but to persist in sin is devilish; to fall is not ruinous to the soul, but to remain on the ground is.” The appeal had its desired effect; Theodore resumed his monastic life and became a bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia and one of the first biblical scholars afterward.  ‘Ad Stagirium a Daemone Vexatum’; an essay he wrote in three books addressed to a young monk named ‘Stagirius’ to encourage him to pass through such severe trial. This monk happened to plunge into such fierce ascetic practices, and then he was inflicted by attacks of epilepsy. Some people thought of him as being possessed by an unclean spirit.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Irenus, p. 305
passages.text:
Saint: IRENUS

St. John Cassian (360-435 AD), told the story of that man. It is the story of the fall of an old monk that caused great grief to the Fathers and brethren. He says that during his days, that old monk Irenus lived in the wilderness for 50 years in intense ascetic life, isolation, and seclusion. But Satan managed to strike him with the curse of pride, and let him lose the wisdom and discernment. Satan once appeared to him in the form of an angel of light, and Irenus knelt before him. The devil convinced him to cast himself in a deep well, to experience God's care practically, confirming to him that he would not be harmed because of his virtuous life. Without any discernment, Irenus foolishly cast himself into the deep well at midnight. He remained in bad shape at the bottom of the well for some time, until the brethren found him between life and death. They brought him up while they were in great grief because of his fall after being deceived by the enemy of good. He stayed alive for two days, and on the third day, he died.

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Worship and the Fear of the Lord — 1012. Who is able to cast fear away from us?

St. John of Dalyatha says, “If you are a stranger to every external disturbance, you will hear within you the Spirit uttering glorious things,” and “If your soul is Jerusalem lauding Christ, why are the sons of Babylon [the confused] wandering in its streets?”
