passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1416 “What is the dialogue that takes place between the soul and the body at the moment of their separation?”, pp. 529–530
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › The Resurrected Body — 1416. What is the dialogue that takes place between the soul and the body at the moment of their separation?

St. Ephrem the Syrian proffers us a wonderful image of the unity of the soul with the body, and their state at the moment of death when the soul departs from the body. The soul that is sanctified in the Lord feels that she is indebted to the sanctified body; and the sanctified body feels that it is indebted to the sanctified soul. Each was a helper to the other in their striving on earth through the work of divine grace in them. With the eyes we read the word of God; with the hands we offer loving services to others; with the feet we walk towards the house of God; and the person with all his body practices prayer, fasting, worship, and prostration before the Lord. Truly, these are happy moments when the body works in union with the soul, and the person in his entirety becomes like an angel of God in heaven, and the body presents no impediment to the soul’s eternal glory.

“The soul having left the body, Is in great suffering, And feels much grief; And she is distracted Hither and thither, As to her destination; For the evil spirits desire That she should go with them Into the midst of Gehenna; And the angels also, That she should journey with them To the region of light.

“In that moment, The soul lightly esteems Her beloved friends and brethren, Those whom she held dear, And her neighbours, And those with whom she was familiar.”

This is how St. Ephrem the Syrian sees the wrestling between the forces of darkness and the angels of God: the former make every effort to attract the soul to themselves, and find their pleasure in dragging it into the fires of evil and darkness. On the other hand, the angels’ happiness and joy is to find a soul that has clung to the Lord, going out to meet the One with whom it lived while it was in the world, and then entering into the place of light or the divine abode. The love of the heavenly ones for us is manifested powerfully when the soul departs from the body, as they carry the soul to the divine presence: just as they carried the soul of the beggar Lazarus (Luke 16:22). As such, the angels praise the Creator who saved humanity from death and corruption and prepared an eternal inheritance for us.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Joannes, the Short, pp. 369–370
passages.text:
Saint: JOANNES, THE SHORT, ST. — His Strife

His Strife:

St. Joannes the Short was gifted by perseverance, similar to that of the righteous Job. He endured whatever difficulties came in his way, and he welcomed with a large heart, the questions, and the challenges presented to him by the brethren, even if they were offending him.

It happened that an elder monk used to come to him to ask about certain issues. However, the saint being ancient, he kept forgetting to get back to the elder monk with the answers; and the poor elder monk kept asking him again. After this was repeated several times, the older man was embarrassed and stopped coming back to the saint, to avoid troubling him with repeating his questions. When the saint happened to meet him afterward, he inquired from him about the reason he stopped coming to him. When the elderly monk told him, the saint sought from him to bring a candle, light it, then go and bring several others and light them from the first candle. Then, he asked him: “Do you think that the first candle was harmed by doing that? Did its light diminished?” Answering him in the negative, the saint told him: “The same way, I am not harmed by your questions, nor by those coming from all the other monks of the Scetis; for your gathering together around me makes me much closer to God.” In that way, he managed to gain the elderly with his perseverance. The Heavenly Father so covered him with his care as a reward for his continuous strive to achieve perfection, and that heavenly care was revealed to one of the monks who came to his cell and found him sleeping; he saw several angels around the saint hovering their wings on him.

Once his spiritual father wanted to test him; so he told him: “I cannot dwell any more with you in the same cell; you should go away.” So, he did for several days, in which the saint kept doing metanoias with humility, saying: “Forgive me father; because I sinned.” He remained outside the door of the cell for seven days and seven nights, and on Sunday, when his spiritual father came out to go to the church, he found St. Joannes the Short lying down outside the cell and the angels placing seven crowns of light on his head. That spiritual father hastened to welcome him inside the cell with love and joy.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John Chrysostom, pp. 418–419
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, ST. — Towards Seclusion

Towards Seclusion:

St. John Chrysostom lived for four years in the monastery, practicing a life of fellowship, which he counted as the best of his whole life. The monastic writings he addressed to his friends to draw them to monasticism, or to defend the monks and monastic life, drew the eyes of people to him, to come in multitudes to his cell, and to make him lose his tranquility. His writings to Theodore and Stagirius’ revealed to the church his talent in ministry, the flaring of his heart toward the salvation of others, and his wisdom in caring for them.

He felt that he had, then, to escape from the vainglory to seclusion to practice a perfect life. According to Palladius, he did that on three stages, each time he spent eight months, in almost complete deprivation of sleep, day and night, elaborately studying the Gospel of Christ. By excessive selfmortification, at the end of those two years, John collapsed, losing all his energy and was inflicted with some paralysis. Feeling that he could not go on in such a life, he returned to the church of Antioch.

His Deaconship:

Around the year 381 AD, John returned to Antioch, where its bishop Meletius welcomed him with intense joy and ordained him as a deacon, against his will. Amid the religious and social ecclesiastical commitments, John used every chance to write and study. As he was not allowed to give sermons, being only a deacon, he occupied himself with writing in two different domains: advocate books and ascetic ones.

He wrote an advocate essay on St. ‘Babylas’ and against Julius, addressed to the Gentiles: (De S. Babylia s. contra Julianum et Gentiles), and a second one ‘Against the Jews and the Gentiles, to confirm the Divinity of the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Contra Judaeos et Gentiles quod Christian sit Deus).

During his ministry as a deacon, he wrote about the Christian life using an ascetic approach: ‘On Virginity,’ ‘On Remorse’ (De Compunctione), ‘To a Young Widow,’ ‘On the One marriage,’ ‘On the Vain Glory’ and ‘On the Raising of Children’ (De Inani Gloria et de Educandis Liberis).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Fr. John of Kilex, p. 430
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF KILEX, FR. — Of His Sayings about the Sanctification of Heart and Dwelling

Of His Sayings about the Sanctification of Heart and Dwelling:

 St. John of Kilex, the abbot of the monastery of Raithu said to the brethren:

“My children! As we have forsaken the world, let us also forsake the desires of the body as well.”  Let us follow the lead of our fathers. I wonder how they have dwelt in this place with both the anguish and the tranquility.  Let us not pollute this place, which was purified from demons by our fathers.  This place is for hermits and not for job-seekers.

Notes: [1] ‘The Monastery of Raithu’ was near the monastery of St. ‘Catherine’ in Sinai.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1412 “How can we behold God?”, p. 522
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › The Final Judgment — 1412. How can we behold God?

Now as long as we are in this state of faith, what is said of us? ‘We see now through a glass darkly; but then face to face’ (1 Cor. 13:12).”

The scholar Origen says, “Whoever has a pure heart will see God (cf. Matt. 5:8). Whoever does not, will not see what the other beholds. I think we should understand something similar of Christ, too, when he was seen in the body. Not everyone who laid eyes on him was able to see him. They saw his body, but, insofar as he was Christ, they could not see him. But his disciples saw him and beheld the greatness of his divinity.”

St. Clement of Alexandria says, “For what rational cause remains any more to the man who has gained ‘the light inaccessible’ (1 Tim. 6:16) for reverting to the good things of the world?”

And St. John Chrysostom says, “Now He here calls ‘pure,’ either those who have attained unto all virtue, and are not conscious to themselves of any evil; or those who live in temperance. For there is nothing which we need so much in order to see God, as this last virtue. Therefore Paul also said, ‘Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord’ (Heb. 12:14).”

Notes: [1265] St. Augustine of Hippo, Lectures or Tractates on the Gospel According to St. John 53.12 (NPNF I/7:295). [1266] St. Augustine of Hippo, Lectures or Tractates on the Gospel According to St. John 1.7 (NPNF I/7:9). [1267] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 3.6 (NPNF I/6:267) amended. [1268] Origen of Alexandria, Homilies in Luke 3.3–4 (FOTC 94:15). [1269] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Stromata, or Miscellanies 6.9 (ANF 2:497). [1270] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 15.6 (NPNF I/10:91) amended.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Sinai, pp. 439–440
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF SINAI (Al-DARAGI), ST. — His Visit to Alexandria

His Visit to Alexandria:

During his life of seclusion, he visited Egypt, during which he visited a monastery in the region of Alexandria. He talked about that monastery in some detail in the two essays 4 & 5, in particular, “The Horrible Confinement” house attached to it, where the sinners among the monks were sent to be chastised.

His Ministry:

Through those forty years of ministry, he used to meet with the monks and the congregation (7:54; 15:6), seeking guidance; and to visit the sick recluses (26:123). In the name of the Lord, he healed a monk called Isaac, from a constant demonical temptation. This was mentioned in his biography, recorded by the monk Daniel.

It so happened that the saint sent his disciple Moses on a mission. In the heat of noon, while the disciple was so exhausted to sleep awhile in the shadow of a vast rock, hearing the voice of his mentor waking him up; he jumped from underneath the rock, to respond to his mentor's call; and Lo! The huge rock tumbled down after he left the place. At that same moment, the saint saw a vision telling him that his disciple was in danger, and he did get up and prayed on his behalf.

Being Envied by Some Monks:

As his charisma drew so many monks and laymen to seek the guidance of St. John of Sinai and God performed so many miracles on his hands, some monks became jealous of him and accused him of being too talkative. The saint, in response, kept silent for a whole year, until his slanderers came to implore him to talk for the sake of the salvation of the souls.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Lycopolis, pp. 434–435
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF LYCOPOLIS (EL-TABAIISY), ST. — His Encounter with St. Jerome

For falsity is foreign to Christianity, and it does not matter if it is in a minor or in a major thing, and even if something good comes out of the falsity, it is foreign to us, because our Lord told us that falsity is from the evil one,” and when he had been rebuked, he became still and accepted the reproof and warning; for John admonished him with humility.

Having among us someone who was trembling for a fever, he sought from the saint to heal him. The saint said to him, “This illness is for your benefit, to heal the weakness of your faith.” He gave him oil, sought from him to anoint his body with it. The fever left him, and he walked along with us completely healed.”

To reveal to us the amazing love of that saint, his cheerfulness, and his care for the others, St. Jerome said: “The saint welcomed us, the way a father does to his children who have been away from him for a long time.

He said to us, “From where did you come, O my children? Not knowing that you have come to someone who is so miserable and poor!” When we told him that we came to him from Jerusalem for the benefit of our souls, he said, “Man should not think that he has acquired complete knowledge, but only very little of it. We should approach God in cheap ways and full faith. It is befitting for the lover of God to keep away from the earthly matters, to come close to God, and to love Him. All who would search for God by his whole heart should keep away from everything earthly. It is befitting for us to care to know God as much as is possible, for no one can get a complete knowledge of Him. He will reveal to us some of his secrets; then man would get to know what will happen before it does; glorious visions will be proclaimed to him, as they did to the saints; will do great things; and whatever he seeks from God, he will get.”

“Never despair living in such a world, for in a well designate time, we all shall depart to the place of comfort. No one should think highly about his good deeds, but always should be in perpetual repentance.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q967 “How did St. John of Dalyatha practice silent prayer without ceasing?”, p. 103
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 967. How did St. John of Dalyatha practice silent prayer without ceasing?

St. John of Dalyatha says, “Blessed is the one who forgets about worldly converse to speak with You, for all his needs are filled by You. You are his food and drink; You are his joy and his exultation. You are his garment, in your glory his nakedness is clothed (cf. 2 Cor. 5:3). You are his dwelling and his resting place, and he always goes within You to be protected. You are his sun and his day, and in your light he sees hidden mysteries. You are the father who generated him, and like a child he calls You: Father! (Rom. 8:15). You placed the Spirit of your Son in his heart (cf. Rom. 5:5; 2 Cor. 1:22).”

Notes: [312] Also known as St. John Saba or simply, The Spiritual Elder. [313] St. John of Dalyatha, The Letters of John of Dalyatha, trans., Mary T. Hansbury (Gorgias Press, 2006) 51.3–4: p. 246.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Sinai, pp. 440–441
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF SINAI (Al-DARAGI), ST. — Abbot of the Monastery of Mount Sinai

Abbot of the Monastery of Mount Sinai:

After forty years of seclusion, he was chosen to be the abbot of the Monastery of Mount Sinai. It was said by Fr. Anastasias of Sinai, that Moses the Prophet, came by himself to attend his ordination.

Even though St. John was admired by the monks before being chosen as the abbot of the monastery, he gained much more admiration afterward because of his spiritual guidance, meekness, and humility; that he reigned over their hearts.

St. John was granted by God the grace to perform signs, one of which was when the people implored him to pray to God on their behalf to give them rain to end a severe drought that came upon Palestine and God responded to his prayers.

During that period, while St. John was quite advanced in age, he was asked to write his book, namely “The Ladder of Divine Ascent.”

Back to Seclusion:

After only four years as the abbot of the monastery, he decided to get back to a life of seclusion, to prepare himself for the departure from this world. His brother George who was also, a monk in the same monastery took his place after seeking from him to pray to God on his behalf to take him soon. God did respond, and the two brothers reposed quickly, one after the other.

His Writings:

His book “The Ladder of Divine Ascent” (Scala Paradisi - in Latin) embraced thirty essays or ladder-steps. It was followed by another shorter work entitled ‘To the Pastor’ (Liber ad Pastorem - in Latin), which included valuable guidance to the leaders and spiritual fathers. It spoke about the life of the monk since his exit from the world, and his practice of the Christian virtues; like asceticism, sojourn, obedience, humility, watching, discernment, prayer, and the tranquility of the soul and the body setting forth toward the resurrection together with the Lord Jesus Christ, in faith, filled with hope, and supported by love. Even though the book was predestined to cover the monastic asceticism, yet it was a call addressed to all to practice the virtuous life in Christ Jesus.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q326 “What did sin do to me?”, p. 249
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Fall of Humanity — 326. What did sin do to me?

He also says, “For the soul in itself is neither of the nature of the Godhead, nor of the nature of the darkness of wickedness, but is a creature intellectual, beauteous, great, and wonderful, a fair likeness and image of God. It was through the transgression that the wickedness of the passions of darkness entered into it.”

Also, St. Augustine says, “As for the human being, whose nature inclines both to the nature of angels and to that of animals, God created him so. If he submits to his Creator as his true master and reverently keeps His commandments, he attains fellowship with the angels and partakes of blessed everlasting immortality, impervious to death. But if he defies the Lord his God by exercising his free will in arrogance and disobedience, he will submit to death, live as a slave to desire, and be condemned to eternal death.” He also says:

“Oh, my misery! … Darkness has prevailed over me; and although You are the Light, I veil my face from You!

“Oh, my misery! … I am afflicted by many wounds; and although You are the Comforter, the giver of peace, I flee away from You!

“Oh, my misery! … I am overwhelmed by a host of follies; and although You are the Truth, I do not seek Your counsel!

“Oh, my misery! … My ways of going astray multiply; and although You are the Way, I turn away from You!

“Oh, my misery! … With many blows, death defeats me; and although You are the Life, I stay far from You!

“Oh, my misery! … I fall into evil and banality many times; and although You are the Word through which all things were made, I separated myself from You, the One without whom I would not exist! O my King the Word; O my God the Word; O Light, the Creator; the Way, the Truth, and the Life … O You who dispel darkness, evil, straying, and death …

“O Light: without You, all would find themselves in dark night. O Way: without You, there would be nothing but going astray. O Truth: without You, there would nothing but falsehood. O Life: without You, all would be encompassed by death.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John Chrysostom, pp. 416–417
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, ST. — Fleeing from Bishopric

Fleeing from Bishopric:

John undoubtedly was at least on constant communication with one of the monastic groups, to practice their life in his own house.

Once the sweet fragrance smell of Christ strongly emerged in his heart and his household, many were drawn to him, but he was more inclined toward seclusion. When two bishopric thrones were vacant in Syria, all looked toward John and his friend Basilius to receive the shepherding task. About it, John said: “All of a sudden, there was some news which disturbed us, Basilius and myself, and filled our hearts with fear and anxiety; that we would be committed to receiving the Holy rank.”

When John met with his friend Basilius, he revealed none of his fears to him, not out of malice, but actually, for the sake of the peace of the church. They probably might have discussed the bishopric tasks and the blessing of searching for the lost sheep in honesty and faithfulness. After that encounter, Basilius considered that John has personal approval for the ordination, particularly for what he knew, more than anybody else, of his friend's acute longing for ministering the lost souls.

While Basilius proclaimed his acceptance of the ordination, expecting with joy the sure ordination of his friend John, to work together and support one another, when it was John's turn, he disappeared totally in the mountains. This action brought such a grief to the heart of Basilius, to write to rebuke him on deceiving him and what he called ‘The Betrayal of the Covenant.’

John did not want to leave his friend sorrowful, so he wrote him a great essay, to reveal the truth about his action, he did it with the spirit of frankness, clarity, humility, and love. He wrote it as a scholar. That essay, he called it: “On Priesthood” (De Sacredotio), and it was a work that nourished generations of priests and ministers.

In true spiritual eloquence, humility, yet with no shame, John revealed that the secret of his reluctance for joining a monastery was the tears of his mother. Then, he talked about the priesthood, as a Divine task, practiced by the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who works in His ministers. He proclaimed his longing and even his deep desire for ministry; and that fleeing to the mountains was not an escape from the bishopric, but rather for his feeling of unworthiness of it.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, pp. 297–298
passages.text:
Saint: IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. — Setting the System of Praise

He was born around the year 30 A.D. and was raised in Syria. Some scholars believe that he was the child whom the Lord Jesus Christ carried when He presented him as an example of humility (Matt. 18:2-4).

Seeing his kindled zeal, the apostles ordained him as a bishop on Antioch. However, there was a disagreement concerning which apostle has ordained him. According to some, Peter, the apostle, ordained Evodius as a bishop for the Christians from Jewish origin; and John, the apostle, ordained Ignatius for the Christians from Gentile origin. When bishop Evodius reposed, bishop Ignatius was put in charge of the region's Christians from both origins. Being known for his eagerness for the salvation of souls, he gained so many new Gentiles for the Lord Christ. His intense love for his people was recorded in his conversation with those who came to welcome him in Smyrna, during his trip to Rome to be martyred. He kept mentioning his congregation to them and asked them to pray for his people.

Setting the System of Praise:

While in Rome, he saw in a night vision, the angels praising and glorifying the Holy Trinity. He transferred what he heard to be used by the Church of Antioch. And from there, it was spread to all other Churches.

His Encounter with Trajan:

Hearing about his zeal on spreading Christianity, Emperor Trajan (98-117) called him and entered with him into a debate concerning the Crucified Jesus, which St. Ignatius declared that he carried in his heart. Then, the argument ended by the emperor giving an order to chain him to be sent to Rome, where he would be offered as food to the wild beasts, to please the people there.

When the bishop heard the order, he greatly exulted, knowing that the hour he was longing for has come at last. He considered that the imperial command was the best gift he has ever received. He knelt and cried out with joy: “I thank You, O Lord, for granting me the honor of the perfect love towards you; and for allowing me to be chained by iron chains like your apostle Paul.” Then, he kissed the chains, supplicating to God to keep His Church safe, after the Lord entrusted him to serve it for over forty years.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, pp. 298–299
passages.text:
Saint: IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. — To Rome

To Rome:

The saint was led guarded by ten soldiers, accompanied by two people from his Church: Philon and Agathopus. Observing how much his people loved him and how they gathered around him before his departure, the guards intentionally treated him with great despise and cruelty. In his documented account on what happened, he called them wild lions since they ignored his usual compassion toward them and what the people paid to them to treat their bishop with tenderness. They arrived at Smyrna, where he was received by St. Polycarp its bishop, besides many delegations from the Churches of Ephesus, Tralliah, and Magnesia. He used that chance to write letters to those Churches, as well as to the one in Rome; for he has heard that some believers there were trying hard to save him from martyrdom, in which he said: “I am afraid that your love for me will cause me harm. Pray that I would not be given a greater gift beyond being sacrificed to God, as long as the altar is ready. I ask you not to show me undue compassion. Allow me to be offered as food to the wild beasts; by that way, I would be granted the grace to reach God. I am the bread of God. Let me be crushed by the fangs of the beasts and let them become my grave. And let nothing be left of my body that no one has to worry about. Once the world does not see my body, I shall be truly a disciple of Christ.”

In Troas:

He was taken in a boat from Smyrna to Troas, where he wrote three more letters to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and St. Polycarp. From Troas, he sailed to Neopolis, to Philippi, then to Epirus and Tyrone. Finally, he arrived at the region of Portus, where he met with the brethren, whose joy to see him was mixed with the sadness of his close departure. He received them with love, asking them to have the courage and show him true love.

He knelt and prayed to God to put an end to the wave of persecution against His Church and to increase the love of the brethren toward each other.

Finally, the guards rushed him to the arena and released the wild beasts, which he received with a cheerful countenance. Two lions jumped on him and devoured him to leave off his body, only a few bones. The believers gathered his precious relics and sent them to Antioch. His martyrdom took place around the year 108 AD. The Church celebrates him on the 7th of Abib.

[Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty: The Two Martyrs: Ignatius and Polycarp; 1964]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theognostus, p. 278
passages.text:
Saint: THEOGNOSTUS

Theognostus (Theogust) was a priest and a theologian in Alexandria in the 3rd century AD. He was the Dean of the School of Alexandria, most probably before Fr. Peros. About him, we know very little through quotations that came in the writings of Fotius, Athanasius, and Gregory bishop of Nyssa.

His doctrinal work “Hypotyposes” came in seven books, these books were available in the time of Fotius, but they have been lost later on. In his first book, he followed the style of Origen. In the second and third books, there were some Arian tendencies. In the fifth book, he denoted bodies to the angels and demons.While in the sixth and seventh books, he dealt with the Divine Incarnation in a sound Orthodox manner. The 20th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic considered his work as one of the best testimonies against Arianism.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Fr. Theognostus, p. 278
passages.text:
Saint: THEOGNOSTUS, FR.

He was a priest from Alexandria, who was sent as a deputy of the 24th Pope Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to Constantinople, along with Fr. Sharmocinus the priest and Liontius the deacon [Cyril: Letters 37, 41]

[Smith & Wace; Vol 4, p. 990]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore Tiro, pp. 262–263
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE TIRO (The martyr)

The Byzantine Church celebrates three great saints who were officers in the army: Theodore (Tadros) (Tiro was the title of his family), Georguis and Demetrius. There is a mymar about this St. Theodore attributed to St. Gregory of Nazianzus.

This saint was a pious young officer in the Roman army. His regiment was sent to Pontus in the wintertime. And, he went to Amasea, where he refused to partake in pagan worship with his fellow officers. When he was called by the governor and the leader of his regiment to be asked about the reason for his action, he proclaimed his faith in Jesus Christ. When he was threatened of being killed, he bravely said: “Jesus Christ is my God. In case my words disturb you, cut my tongue off, and even cut every member of my body. And, may God receive them as acceptable sacrifices.” On seeing how he firmly held to his faith, he was left alone for some time, with the hope that he might reconsider and deny his Christ. When he was called again, they tried to seduce him with many promises, which he rejected. He was then violently whipped, and he endured it as a fellowship in the passion of His Christ. Then, he was cast in prison, and God sent his angels to comfort him. When he was called for the third time, he was burned alive and gained the crown of martyrdom. And, Ausiba buried his remains in Euchaita. He was martyred on the 9th of November in the year 306 AD. St. Gregory of Nyssa said about him describing his courage and the power of his intercession that he kept Pontus safe from the attacks of the Scythians who destroyed all the surrounding States. He also said about the saint: “As a soldier, he defended us; and as a martyr, he intercedes for us and seeks peace for all of us.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore, the Monk, p. 266
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, THE MONK (The martyr)

This St. Theodore was born in Alexandria and was raised in a pure Christian family atmosphere. He loved the life of serenity that he abandoned the world and lived as a monk in one of the monasteries close to Alexandria, where he practiced his prayers, fasting, and studies in the Holy Bible and the books of the Fathers. When the 20th pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373) was exiled and an intruding Arian archbishop by the name of Georgius, was installed in his place; the whole congregation was in a turmoil. It did not stop at the believers boycotting the intruder, despite the high price they had to pay, but the fathers the monks did their decisive role in that critical situation. St. Theodore, the monk left his monastery and went to Alexandria to support the people and to hold them fast to their faith. Besides, he debated the Arian clergy. When the Arian intruder archbishop, the denier of the Godhead of the Lord Christ, saw the danger of St. Theodore’s work towards his plans, he arrested him. He threatened the saint and finally ordered his men to have him tied up to the tail of a wild horse, and was set free to peel St. Theodore’s flesh off and to cover the streets of Alexandria with his blood. He eventually delivered his soul and received the crown of martyrdom on the 6th of Paona.

Even though the soul of this martyr longed to a life of solitude and a fellowship with God; yet his heart was burning for the salvation of others. He could not find comfort in his monastery, while the other souls were getting into perdition because of the deception of the Arians in the absence of their pope and their bishops. Therefore, he set forth to do his role joyfully to testify for his Christ.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, pp. 283–284
passages.text:
Saint: THEOPHILUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH, ST. — His Writings

According to Eusebius, this saint was the 6th bishop of Antioch in Syria, near the end of the 2nd century. St. ‘Theophilus’ was born to pagan parents in an area close to the Euphrates river. He was educated by the Hellenic (Greek) culture. On studying the Christian Holy Bible, he perceived that the Holy Spirit granted the prophets many prophesy about the things to come. So, he believed and obeyed God.

His Writings:

This St. Theophilus was one of the Christian apologists. However, only three books survived out of his many written works. Those books were dedicated to his pagan friend Autolycus, in which he introduced the Christian thoughts about God and His creation before the pagan world with its wrong diverse fantasies. Among his lost writings were essays against Marcion and the heresy of Hermogenes.

Of his Sayings:

+ No one can see God except those who are capable of seeing Him, when their souls’ eyes are open wide. When there is dirt on a mirror, man cannot see his face in it. Likewise, it is with the sinful. He cannot see God. + I indeed honor the emperor, yet not by worshipping him, but by praying for him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Isidore of Alexandria, p. 329
passages.text:
Saint: ISIDORE OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — His troubles

St. Theophilus attempted to recommend him as a patriarch on the throne of Constantinople, but St. Chrysostom opposed that attempt. Then, St. Theophilus sent him to Palestine with a message. There, St. Isidore sided with St. John, the bishop of Jerusalem. His position stirred up St. Jerome, who accused him of being a follower of Origen (184-254 AD). St. Jerome was totally against Origen's philosophy, while St. John of Jerusalem was supporting him.

Around the year 391 AD, there was a dispute between St. Isidore and Pope Theophilus, who accused him of giving communion to one of the followers of the Mani's heresy. The pope drove him away from Alexandria to go back to his old cell in Nitria. However, when the pope made it more difficult for him, he joined the Tall Brothers and went with them to St. John Chrysostom in Constantinople, where there were a lot of Origen's supporters. On returning from Constantinople, St. Isidore reposed in the year 403 AD, at the age of 85 years and was buried in Alexandria. The Western Church celebrates him on the 15th of January.

[Palladius: The Lausiac History, Ch. 1]

Notes: [1] This part has a lot of similarity to what happened to St. Isidore of Farma.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ephothes, pp. 24–25
passages.text:
Saint: EPHOTHES (The martyr)

The following saints: Ephothes (means "the Perfumed"), Calesti (the Splendid), and Hermoganes (the descendant of Atared), were martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) and his partner Maximianus. We do not know much about them except their names and that they were from the city of Syracusa on the island of Sicily.

[Archimandrite Michael Ăssaf: The Book of Synaxarion, Aylol 1]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodotus, Bishop of Ancyra, p. 275
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOTUS, BISHOP OF ANCYRA

Bishop Theodotus was a supporter of the Nestorian theology of the heretic Nestor. However, in the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 AD, he reversed his position and became a prominent supporter of the 24th Pope St. Cyril of Alexandria (412-444) against Nestor. This bishop was defrocked by the Nestorians at their Synod of Tarsus in the year 432 AD. Bishop Theodotus wrote so many articles, among which were: Essays against Nestor (lost); an explanation of the Nicene Creed of Faith; several essays on the feast of Nativity; and on the Purification. Also, there is a mymar which has been attributed to him, dealing with the martyrdom of St. George and his miracles...

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore, the Roman, pp. 266–267
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, THE ROMAN (The martyr)

This St. Theodore was an inhabitant of Astir, in the days of the two emperors Maximian and Diocletian (284-305). When they heard that the saint did not worship the idols, they called him and sought from him to worship their gods, which he declined. After promising to give him many honors if he denied his Christ, he rejected them and held fast to his faith. Then, they started torturing him. They whipped him, pressed him by the Henbazin, cut some of his limbs, and burned his sides with fire. In all this, he endured for his love of the Lord Christ. And, the Lord sent his angel to strengthen and comfort him. Finally, they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

The Church celebrated his feast on the 28th of Amshir.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q538 “Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”?”, p. 424
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Eminence of the Church — 538. Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”?

St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “All these things are good together, if you believe in love.” He also says that Christ is eternal life for He grants us life through His divine love, “for the drink of God is His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.”

Notes: [1092] St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Philadelphians 9 (LCL 24:293). [1093] St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Romans 7 (LCL 24:279).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodosia, p. 270
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOSIA (The martyr)

The West celebrates the two martyrs Epiphanius and Theodosia together on the 2nd of April. The story of their martyrdom has been documented by Eusebius in his account about the Martyrs of Palestine. He was affected greatly, as an eye-witness, by their sufferings around the year 318 AD. He was astonished by their bravery at their young age; for Epiphanius was 20 years old, whereas Theodosia was 18 years old. He wrote: “In Caesarea, during the fifth year of the persecution, in the feast of the resurrection of our Savior, a virgin girl by the name of Theodosia of the city of Tyre, a serious believer of less than 18 years of age, set forth to the prisoners who were charged of testifying to the Kingdom of Christ before the court of justice, to greet them and to seek from them to remember her when they stand before the Lord. She was arrested and brought before the governor, who came over her like a vicious maniac, he tortured her by cutting her breasts off down to the bones; and seeing how she kept on standing with a cheerful countenance, he ordered to throw her into the sea; then turned to the other confessors, and gave the order to send them over to work in the copper mines in Pheno (Faynan), Palestine.”

[Eusebius of Caesarea: Martyrs of Palestine 7, translated by Fr. Marcus Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Iris, p. 306
passages.text:
Saint: IRIS (The martyr)

The first martyr among Origen's students was Plutarch about whom Eusebius said, “While being taken to death, he was approached by Origen who accompanied him until the end; whom the Divine care kept him safe this time as well; even though the martyr's relatives were furious about Origen for being the cause of his death by urging him to reject the pagan religion.”

The second martyr among Origen's students was Serenus, whose testimony was louder than the fire of the furnace into which he was cast. He was followed by the third martyr Heraclides, a simple catechumen in Origen's school, and who was beheaded. The fourth was Hero, who received baptism a short time before he delivered his neck to the sword for his faith. The fifth was another Serenus, who was also beheaded after a long ordeal of tortures. Eusebius called him “an athlete of piety.” The sixth one was a woman by the name Iris (Herais), who was martyred, while still a catechumen. According to Eusebius, “she received the baptism by fire, as Origen himself says.” The seventh martyr was Basilides, who led to martyrdom, the celebrated virgin martyr Potamiæna.

[Eusebius: The Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, Ch.1-5]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athenogenes, pp. 271–272
passages.text:
Saint: ATHENOGENES, ST. (The martyr)

The Roman Church celebrates the birthday of this theologian martyr on the 18th of January; and his martyrdom on the 16th of July. And, St. ‘Gregory, the Enlightened’ fixed a feast for him in Armenia.

This saint was born in ‘Pontes,’ even though some others believe he was born in ‘Sebastia’ in Armenia. He was ordained as a bishop and was martyred around the year 305 AD, together with 10 of his disciples in the days of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD). When he was cast in the fire, he kept singing praise for the Holy Spirit: “Phos Hilaron” (Φῶς Ἱλαρόν) of his writing, as a sign of his gratitude to the Holy Spirit who granted him the gift of martyrdom. In an essay about the Holy Spirit, St. ‘Basil the Great’ (330-379 AD) referred to this praise, saying: “Whoever get to know the praise of St. ‘Athenogenes’ by which he hastened to achieve perfection by the fire, and which he left as a farewell gift to his friends, could understand the mind and thoughts of the martyrs concerning the Spirit.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Fr. Isaac, the Confessor, pp. 313–314
passages.text:
Saint: ISAAC, THE CONFESSOR, FR.

The life of that anchorite reveals the heart of a Christian, whatever his position or role is, that is inflamed with love and zeal, and is working boldly within the Church. That father loved the life of solitude and intended to live his whole life, unceasingly worshipping God, away from the confusion and preoccupations of the world. However, hearing about how the Arian Emperor Valence (364-378 AD) persecuted the Church, he could not stand sitting tighthanded. So, after continuous profound prayers, he set out to Constantinople to face the emperor. Then, he warned the emperor more than once, that very tough tribulation would dwell upon him unless he would stop persecuting the upright in faith (the Orthodox) and give them back their churches. He meant by that those churches which he took away from them by force to deliver to the Arians; but, the emperor despised him and his warnings.

When he once met the emperor coming out of the city, he got hold of the bridle of his horse and started to rebuke him. The emperor ordered his men to cast him in the nearest swamp, but the Lord saved him from it in a miraculous way. As he repeated his prophecy against him, he threw him in prison. Shortly after, the saint's prophecy was realized, and Valence was killed in the battle of Adrianople. Emperor Theodosius I (379-396 AD), who replaced Valence, released the saint and honored him.

Intending to resume his life of solitude again, his disciples insisted that he would not forsake them. So, Fr. Isaac established a monastery for them called The Dalmatian, referring to Dalmatius, one of his disciples. That monastery is considered to be the oldest monastery in Constantinople.

The saint attended the second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople; then, he reposed in good old age.

[Butler's Lives of Saints; May 30]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gregory of Nyssa, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: GREGORY OF NYSSA, ST. — His Writings

His Writings:

According to scholars, his writings were considered the most magnificent among the writings of the great Cappadocian fathers. He even surpassed those written by St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory the Nazianzus. His writings carried deep thoughts and extensive views that revealed a soul inflamed with zeal and vitality.  Doctrinal essays: He wrote four essays, refuting Amonius that was also refuting Arianism, an essay explaining the problems with Apolonarism by a request from the 23rd Pope of Alexandria, St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), an essay against Apolonarius, to show that the Body of Christ did not descend from heaven and that the Godhead did not replace the human soul, a sermon on the Holy Spirit refuting Macdonius, and several essays about the Holy Trinity, addressed to an archon named Ablabius.  Interpretational works: The most important of which was the one by which he intended to complete what was written by St. Basil on The Six Days of Creation (Hexameron), The Life of Moses, The Titles of the Psalms, fifteen sermons on the Song of Songs, On the Lord's Prayer, On the divination, and the Prophet Samuel (1 Kings 28), On the Beatitudes, and two sermons on the First Corinthian epistle.  His Ascetic works: He was called “The Father of the Inner Life.” He wrote On Virginity, On the name and work of the Christian, On Perfection, On the Life of Macrina, etc.  His Sermons: Liturgical sermons, like On the feast of the lights (the Epiphany of the Lord Jesus Christ), On the Holy Passover, and the Resurrection, On the Ascension of Christ, On the Holy Spirit in the Pentecost, On the Nativity of Christ. He also had sermons on the feasts of the martyrs and saints, like the one on St. Steven, on the feast of St. Gregory the Nazianzus, a commendation of martyr Theodore, on the forty martyrs of Sabastia, as well as lamentations in the funeral prayers, and sermons about the ideal behavior.  Letters: He also had a lot of documented letters.

[Hegemon Isaiah Michael: From Glory to Glory, 1982]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pantaenus, pp. 351–352
passages.text:
Saint: PANTAENUS, ST. — Pantaenus and Philosophy

Pantaenus and Philosophy:

Pantaenus was one of the famed Stoic philosophers, those who were ethical on the highest level; considering the greatest good is in virtue, believing in the law of nature or the law of conscience and duty. Those Stoic philosophers saw in God the energy that penetrates everything, and by which He created the natural world and kept it as such.

Pantaenus became Christian on the hands of Athenagoras (133-190 AD) the dean of the Catechetical Theological School of Alexandria, and in the year 181 AD, Pantaenus succeeded him as the dean of that School. He was credited for introducing philosophy and science into the School of Alexandria in an attempt to gain the heretics and the cultured pagans.

Even though Pantaenus was a perpetual reader of philosophy, yet he was not criticized by his church contemporaries or accused of diversion from faith. Origen (184-254 AD) testified to him saying that, in his study of philosophy, he followed the lead of his mentor Pantaenus, who managed to draw many people of culture through his knowledge of philosophy. This policy which was introduced by Pantaenus was developed further by his student Clement and re-structured by Origen.

Pantaenus as a Preacher:

The School of Alexandria was not just a religious institute that was famous worldwide, but it was a part of the church having its preaching activity besides its educational and catechetical programs. Her instructors were high-caliber spiritual church-people who dedicated their lives to study and to spread the evangelical ecclesiastical thoughts. They sanctified their lives presenting themselves as a living example in asceticism, as well as on defending the dogma and spreading the word of God; on the local and ecumenical levels. On one aspect, in the sight of the people of Alexandria, Pantaenus was not only a scholar and a teacher but the helper of many who cared for the salvation of all, so that they called him ‘Our Pantaenus’. On another aspect, when he was called by the 12th pope of Alexandria, St. Demetrius (188-230 AD) to preach in India; he responded to the call right away, leaving the School in the hands of St. Clement, for a while.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gregory the Nazianzus, p. 201
passages.text:
Saint: GREGORY THE NAZIANZUS, ST. — His Upbringing

This saint shared the title of the “Theologian” with St. John the Beloved, because of his ability to articulate the subject of the Holy Trinity with a Divine inspiration and that his spiritual life was melded to the works of the Holy Trinity. He was counted as one of the three great Cappadocian fathers: Basil the Great, Gregory, of Nyssa, and Gregory the Theologian. All three of them lived in the same era in Cappadocia in Asia Minor, and, they had their active role in opposing Arianism, after St. Athanasius the Apostolic.

His Upbringing:

He was born in the year 329 AD in the village of Arianzus, south-west of Cappadocia. His mother was St. Nonna, who converted her rich husband, the judge, to the Christian faith in the year 325 AD, and later on, her husband became a bishop on Nazianzus for forty-five years.

He lived under the care of his mother, who advised him to love the Holy Bible, the virtuous life in the Lord, and praying with piety. About himself, he tells us that, while a young man, he saw in a dream, two beautiful respectable girls wearing white attire, and standing before the throne of the Lord Jesus Christ. One of them said to him: “I am chastity,” and the other said: “I am wisdom.” Waking up, he started to have an intense longing for chastity, which perpetually increased all along with his life. He was gifted with Divine wisdom in his studies of the Divine issues and through his behavior.

He joined with his brother Caesarius the highest colleges in Caesarea of Cappadocia, where they got acquainted with St. Basil the Great. St. Gregory, in pursuing the study of the Law, he went to Caesarea of Palestine to join its school famed for teaching Eloquence in Public Speech. Then, he went with his brother to Alexandria, where St. Didymus the Blind was the dean of the School of Theology. Gregory spent a short period in Egypt, and then he sailed to Athens to increase his knowledge of philosophy. There, he met with his friend St. Basil, and they lived together in a shared spiritual life, to be said that they had one mind in two bodies.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gregory, the Wonder Maker, p. 205
passages.text:
Saint: GREGORY, THE WONDER MAKER, ST. — His Upbringing

They perceived that the truth they were seeking, they would not find in the books of philosophy or mere human thoughts, but they would gain through the light of faith and the exalted Divine proclamations to the soul. Then, the two brothers joined a group of a catechumen who was disciples to Origen and learned from his interpretations of the Holy Scriptures.

St. Gregory became a disciple to his mentor for five years. In the year 238 AD, he returned to his city: the New Caesarea, after he gave thanks to his mentor Origen in a public speech. Before a vast crowd, he commended him on his wisdom by which he led him in his studies, and the teacher wrote back to his student, calling him his honorable student, exhorting him to dedicate his gifts, and energies to the Lord, and to benefit from what he studied of philosophy in the service of faith, the way the Hebrews used the knowledge they acquired from the Egyptians in setting the Tabernacle of the Meeting.

It was said that, before going home, he stopped in Alexandria, probably to increase his knowledge in medicine and philosophy. He was characterized by pure nature and piety, even though he was not baptized yet. It happened that some evil people who tried to blemish his image, sent him a harlot while he was engaged in a debate with some pagans about philosophic issues. She publicly asked him to pay her for her services, to let those present think that he was engaged in sin with her. The saint was not disturbed but sought from someone present to give her what she requested, but once she took the money, she was possessed by an evil spirit who strongly tormented her. St. Gregory stood up, prayed over her, and drove the evil spirit out of her. Before all the audience, the woman confessed about the names of those who provoked her to distort the reputation of that pure man.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Basilides, pp. 321–322
passages.text:
Saint: BASILIDES

In the first half of the 2nd century, an essential Gnostic theologian by the name of ‘Basilides’ lived in Alexandria. That was during the days of Caesar ‘Hadrian’ (117-138 AD). ‘Basilides’ authored an interpretation of the Holy Bible in 24 volumes. He also wrote an essay titled ‘The Gospel,’ and he had many songs. However, most of his works have been lost except some quotes mentioned in the rebuttals by some saints like ‘Irenaeus,’ ‘Clement of Alexandria’ and ‘Hippolytus.’ Therefore, it is difficult to understand clearly the complete makeup of his theological views.

His gnostic tendencies appeared in the following points: 10s the Gnostics put the mind power ahead of faith, considering that man can get salvation by using his mind alone, without the proclamations of God or religion, ‘Basilides’ in his writings, proclaims that ‘faith’ is not the way by which the mind gets its freedom. The philosophy within his mind was more important to him than his faith. 11e dealt in a mental reasoning approach with the issue of ‘suffering pain’ and the existence of evil. He proclaimed that no one would suffer pain, except if he has committed evil. Concerning the martyrs, even though righteous, but what they endured was the fruit of sins they have invested in the past. Coming to speak about the passions of the Lord Jesus Christ, he entered into a problematic conflict. However, because of his extreme love for his philosophy, he stated that since ‘Jesus’ have suffered pain, he must have somehow sinned even though he proclaimed that a heavenly light came down upon Him and rose Him up to gather the elect ones and raise them to the high heavens. 12oncerning the God of the Old Testament, he considered the God of the Jews, as one of the good rulers who control the world's corners.

[J. Lebreton: The History of Primitive Church, 1946, p. 506]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athenogenes, pp. 271–272
passages.text:
Saint: ATHENOGENES, ST. (The martyr)

The Roman Church celebrates the birthday of this theologian martyr on the 18th of January; and his martyrdom on the 16th of July. And, St. ‘Gregory, the Enlightened’ fixed a feast for him in Armenia.

This saint was born in ‘Pontes,’ even though some others believe he was born in ‘Sebastia’ in Armenia. He was ordained as a bishop and was martyred around the year 305 AD, together with 10 of his disciples in the days of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD). When he was cast in the fire, he kept singing praise for the Holy Spirit: “Phos Hilaron” (Φῶς Ἱλαρόν) of his writing, as a sign of his gratitude to the Holy Spirit who granted him the gift of martyrdom. In an essay about the Holy Spirit, St. ‘Basil the Great’ (330-379 AD) referred to this praise, saying: “Whoever get to know the praise of St. ‘Athenogenes’ by which he hastened to achieve perfection by the fire, and which he left as a farewell gift to his friends, could understand the mind and thoughts of the martyrs concerning the Spirit.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athenagoras, the Philosopher, p. 271
passages.text:
Saint: ATHENAGORAS, THE PHILOSOPHER — His Writings

The dean of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; was among the prominent men of the 2nd century AD. Not much is known about his life, other than he was chosen as the head of the Catechetical Chair of the School of Alexandria, which was one of the most excellent schools in science and philosophy in the East at the time, competing against the other high school of Athens.

The pagan ‘Athenagoras’ was one of the greatest scholars, and like the other Platonic philosophers, he was fond of researching the Christian religion, aiming to expose its faults and to reveal its shortcomings. For that purpose, ‘Athenagoras’ focused on studying the Holy Bible as a critic. However, the Holy Spirit opened his eyes, and instead of presenting his findings against the Christian faith, he was overwhelmed by it and became a Christian around the year 176 AD. He received baptism, got attached to the Christians, and perceived the exaltation of the evangelic life; then, he wrote his defense of Christianity and Christians, and it was presented to Emperor Marcus Aurelius (161-180 AD) in the year 177 AD.

The characteristics of the personality of ‘Athenagoras’ have exceptional importance. He was the first philosopher whose intense zeal and diligence in studying and acquiring knowledge; qualified him to become the head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; without having to drop ‘the philosopher mantle.' He was the first known Christian to carry, besides his Faith, compassion towards philosophy.

His Writings:

He authored two essential works: “An Apology/Appeal for the Christians” (πρεσβεία) and another on “The Resurrection of the Dead.” In his writings, we could sense the philosophical mind polished by the Greek culture, coupled with his magnificent talent of expression. ‘Roberts-Donaldson’ wrote about him saying: “He quoted Greek poetry, yet his goal was so clear before his eyes, not to parade his skills or to distract his reader’s mind.”

[Proto-priest Tadros Yacoub Malaty: The Early Fathers of the School of Alexandria; 1980; pp. 33-etc]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Valentinus, the Gnostic Poet, pp. 315–316
passages.text:
Saint: VALENTINUS, THE GNOSTIC POET — His Main Gnostic Teachings

His Main Gnostic Teachings:

The Entity of his God: Like the Gnostic Basilides, he believed that God is an Absolute Being, unreachable, and could not be recognized totally. He is the First Origin or the First Depth which did not proceed from another being. After uncountable ages, He produced his wife, called the Womb or The Silence. Then, those two entities becoming the two basic Male and Female who gave birth to Christ or Logos, on whom depended the Ions (Views or half-angels). Then, through them, all things existed and melded together.

Valentinus also believed that the two – namely the Depth and the Silence – produced the Comprehension (Nous) and the Truth (Aletheia), and from the two of them, came The Word, The Life, The Humans and The Church. They also produced thirty Ions: two at a time, male and female, which represented the Christian (or the Jewish) concepts and the virtues which consummate the heavenly spiritual world (Pleroma). The last of those ions was the Wisdom (Sophia), which was longing badly to know the unrecognizable Father and fell into the darkness of despair. And Wisdom gave birth to an immature and disfigured child (laldaboath) (or probably ‘the child of Chaos’), by whom the universe was created with all its shortcomings.

So, Valentinus believed that the creation of the world was the fruit of the fall of the Wisdom, the smallest of those born by the Creator (Demiurge), known as ‘The God of the Old Testament.’

The struggle between (laldoboath) and (Sophia) was the cause of the mixing of the good with the evil; the virtues and the evil desires, in the world and within the individuals.

Jesus was sent to reform the Wisdom according to the proper understanding to take it away from its covetousness. In that way, He established the events that would realize the Salvation in the material world.

Valentinus divided humankind into three categories; as the salvation is realized by Christ who got united with the Man ‘Jesus’ (whether when he was conceived or when he was baptized), in order to grant man the knowledge which qualifies him for the salvation He is providing. That knowledge is given only to (cat.#1) the Spirituals (the Pneumatics) (1 Cor. 2:14). However, the rest of the Christians; known as (cat.#2) Natural (Psychic) (1 Cor. 2:14) would by faith and good deeds get an intermediate status in the kingdom of the Creator (Demiurge). While the rest of humankind called (cat.#3) ‘carnal or material’ (hylics), who would be preoccupied with material matters, would be delivered to the eternal damnation.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — PANTAENUS AND PHILOSOPHY (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — PANTAENUS AND PHILOSOPHY

Pantaenus was a well-known Stoic; he embraced Christianity at the hands of Athenagoras. In 181 A.D he succeeded his teacher as dean of the Theological (Catechetical) School. To him was attributed the introduction of philosophy and science into the School in order to appeal to heretics and educated pagans. Origen gives credence to this claim, saying that in studying Greek philosophy he was imitating Panteanus, who won over many educated people through his philosophical knowledge. This approach was introduced by Pantaenus, developed by his disciple St. Clement of Alexandria and then refined by Origen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Gregory, the Wonder Maker, pp. 204–205
passages.text:
Saint: GREGORY, THE WONDER MAKER, ST. — His Upbringing

His biography was documented by St. Gregory of Nyssa. He was commended by St. Basil the Great, who likened him to the Prophet Moses, because of his wonders. He said that the saint represented someone who longs very profoundly for the truth, that he did not just receive the Christian faith, but he has done that in such a convincing manner to live his life with an apostolic Evangelic spirit. So, with the holiness of his amazing life, he preached among the pagans with an elevated power.

His Upbringing:

Before his baptism, he was called Theodore. He was born in Pontus in the New Caesarea to famous and honorable pagan parents. When he was fourteen years of age, his father died. However, he completed his education, studying law, as he was a lover of knowledge and the perception of the truth.

In the year 233 AD, he traveled to the New Caesarea accompanied by his sister and her husband, a high official in Caesarea of Palestine, and his brother Athenodorus, who became a bishop later on and endured much for the sake of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. In the New Caesarea, they attended the inauguration of the school headed by Origen, and instead of going to Beirut to learn the law, Theodore and his brother stayed behind, for they have gotten so much attached to Origen and loved him, to say about him later on: “We are guided by an angel of the Lord to the right way in this life, and we are connected by love to that great man, from whom we shall certainly have benefitted. He received us warmly, even though he is Christian and had no prior knowledge of us. He showed us how happy he was for having us as if we were led to his traps to be gained to the Holy Scriptures and to be saved from the darkness of idol worship.”

On the hands of Origen, the two brothers received the Christian faith. They perceived that the truth they were seeking, they would not find in the books of philosophy or mere human thoughts, but they would gain through the light of faith and the exalted Divine proclamations to the soul. Then, the two brothers joined a group of a catechumen who was disciples to Origen and learned from his interpretations of the Holy Scriptures.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pantaenus, p. 351
passages.text:
Saint: PANTAENUS, ST.

Pantaenus was a saint and a philosopher who became the dean of the school of Alexandria around the year 181 AD. He gained great fame to be considered by the historian Eusebius (263-339 AD), the first dean of that School. About him, he said:

“At that time, the School of Alexandria was headed by a man of very exalted world fame as a scholar, named Pantaenus. There was a wellestablished custom among them to have an academy for the holy knowledge, which is still there until our present day. According to my understanding, those who run it are people of high standards; theologians with special abilities; one of whom was Pantaenus, the highest and most exalted scholar in his era.”

Searching his memory, St. Clement (150-215 AD) in his work ‘Stromata’ (Patchwork), he mentioned the blessed persons worthy of remembrance, whom he was fortunate enough to encounter and to listen to. When it came to his mentor Pantaenus, he spoke about him as the greatest and most accomplished teacher; in whose solitude he found comfort. About his encounter with him he said:

“Even though my encounter with him was just by chance, yet he was the most prominent in worthiness. In Egypt, I found him in hiding; truly like a Sicilian bee, plucking from all flowers in the gardens of the prophets and apostles, to provide the souls of his listeners with a treasure of incorruptible knowledge.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Clement of Alexandria, p. 448
passages.text:
Saint: CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — His Writings

60- Miscellanies” (Stromata); to enjoy the elevated spiritual knowledge, the ultimate goal of the Christian, through his unity with the Lord Jesus Christ, as the Groom of the soul. He had other books such as: “Who is the Rich Man who can be Saved?;” the “Collective” and “The Passover Message.”

The main feature of this saint was his view of philosophy and knowledge. The philosophy in his mind is not evil, but rather a Divine gift, which people tend to corrupt through mixing the truth with vanity. He considered the philosophers like little kids who would mature through faith. By this concept, he presented a co-existence between philosophy and religion, instead of contradiction. As regards the knowledge or the ‘Gnostics,’ according to him, it is not heresy but rather an enjoyment of the Divine proclamations through the Lord Jesus Christ – the Teacher, and through His Holy Spirit. This gift, the Christian could enjoy through the holy life in the Lord. Hence, the word ‘Gnostic’ no longer means ‘a heretic,’ but a Christian believer who walks by the Spirit of the Lord and enjoys the knowledge of God.

[Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty: The Fathers of the First School of Alexandria; pp. 53–135]

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — 8. ST. ATHANASIUS (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd)
passages.text:
GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — 8. ST. ATHANASIUS

St. Athanasius defended the Orthodox faith in the Holy Trinity against Arianism. He clarified the Church's faith that the simplicity of God does not contradict belief in the Holy Trinity, and at the same time, he depended on soteriological thought in defending the Godhead of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

He revealed the role of the Trinitarian doctrine in the life of the church, saying,

Theology is perfect in the Trinity. This is the only true piety, and this is the truth and the good. It is the faith which the Lord Himself gave, the apostles preached and the fathers kept. It is the faith on which the church is built. The trinitarian economy, the Three Hypostases are in unison the Father saves, the Son saves, the Spirit saves. This unit is not based on the knowledge of God's being, but on the knowledge of the one saving act of the Triune God [93] .

a. The Simplicity of God

St. Athanasius confirms that God is simple, not compound, nor of composite nature; He is simply One though in Three, and has one grace and unity in His energy and actions. St. Athanasius states the following:

We confess God to be one through the Triad [94] .

There is one Godhead of the Holy Trinity, and one faith in the Holy Trinity... If the Spirit were a creature, He would not be included in the Trinity; for the whole Trinity is one God. Nothing alien is mingled in the Trinity, it is indivisible and of the same nature [95] .

The Father accomplishes all things through the Word in the Holy Spirit [96] .

There is a single grace which is fulfilled from the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit [97] .

Such being the coordination and unity in the Holy Trinity, who would divide the Son from the Father, or the Spirit from the Son or the Father Himself? Who would dare to say that the Trinity was internally 'dissimilar' or 'heterogeneous'? Or to speak of the Son as 'of alien essence' from the Father, or of the Spirit as foreign to the Son? But if anyone asks how this happens, how the Son can be said to be in us when the Spirit is; or the Father, when the Son is; or how the whole Trinity is implied in the mention of one Person or is said to be in us when one Person is - if anyone asks such questions, let him first divide brightness from light, or wisdom from a wise man, or explain how such things can be.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Palamon, pp. 340–341
passages.text:
Saint: PALAMON, ST. ABBA — Palamon's Care for his Disciple's Spiritual Life

Palamon's Care for his Disciple's Spiritual Life:

St. Palamon cared a lot for all the spiritual aspects of Pachum's life. One evening he sought from him to watch along with him the whole night between prayers and handwork, and whenever they find themselves overcome by sleep, they get out of the cave to move sand from one place to another to keep awake and then return to prayers. The elder kept saying to his sleepy disciple: “Wake up Pachum, lest Satan would tempt you; for many have perished of too much sleep.” He trained him on a harsh monastic life blended with the Divine love in order to raise his heart and soul beyond the body's needs.

Once on the feast of Resurrection, the elder sought from his disciple to prepare special food, for such an exalted occasion. Pachum crushed some salt and put on it oil with a little greenery and bread. On seeing that there was too much oil on the food, the elder wept bitterly, saying: “The Lord was crucified for me, and I eat so much oil that softens the body?” Pachum apologized to the elder that the oil spilled on the meal against his will. However, the elder answered him that if it was not needed to light the lamp in the Altar, he would never have kept oil in his cave.

Palamon's Open Heart:

St. Palamon's open heart and mind, and his true love was shown clearly in his behavior toward St. Pachum when an angel came to him to establish the system of Koinonia. St. Palamon, the mentor, helped his disciple to set up his new system, although he had no experience with it, and asked that they visit each other, once every year, alternatively. He was happy with the work of his disciple, and he blessed it. A few years later, he reposed in the Lord after falling ill for a little while. The church celebrates him on the 25th of Abib.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — THE HOLY SPIRIT (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd)
passages.text:
GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — THE HOLY SPIRIT

The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal divine energy, nor just a presence of God or a divine gift, but we believe His personality is the third Hypostasis. Our Lord called Him the "other comforter" (John 14:16). The Holy Scripture introduces Him as the Creator (Job 33:4). He witnessed through the prophets, revealing the will of God and preparing mankind to accept the incarnate Son of God. He is the Life-Giver, and the source of sanctification. St. Peter considered Him God (compare Acts 5:3 and 5:4).

Christ's redeeming action is the basis of the operation of the Holy Spirit in the Church, for He grants communion with the Father in the crucified Christ. At the same time without the Holy Spirit "no man can say that Jesus is the Lord" (Cor. 12:3). Neither can the Church enjoy the presence of Christ as her Head without the Holy Spirit. Therefore, Lord said, "It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Comforter (Paraclete) will not come to you" (John 16:7). Thus, the beginning of the historical Church is to be understood pneumatologically, for she had her birth as the body of Christ in the Pentecost, and she is still nourished by the Holy Spirit who leads, guides, sanctifies, assists in worship and preaching, inspires and builds up the body of the Church.

St. Athanasius used the statement of Isaiah (63:7-14) to declare that "the Spirit of God is neither angel nor creature, but belongs to the Godhead [55] ." For St. Didymus , this statement was proof that the believers in the Old Testament had received grace from no less than "the Spirit, who is inseparable from the Father and the Son [56] ." St. Cyril of Alexandria [57] saw in the same statement proof for the identity of " ousia " (essence) between the Holy Spirit and the Father [58] .

The Alexandrian Fathers of the Church used the titles of the Holy Spirit as an argument of His divinity. Moreover, they used His works for the same aim. St. Didymus said that He who filled all creatures had to be of a different substantia than all other creatures [59] . St. Athanasius said, "If the Holy Spirit were a creature, we should have no participation in God through Him, we should be united to a creature and alien from the divine nature. If He makes men divine, His nature must undoubtedly be that of God [60] ." St. Cyril of Alexandria [61] stated that the Holy Spirit, as the One who justifies sinners and perfects the elect, does what is appropriate only to the divine and supremely exalted nature.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dionysius, the Areopagite, pp. 600–601
passages.text:
Saint: DIONYSIUS, THE AREOPAGITE, ST. (The martyr) — His Writings

His Writings:

Many scholars believe that one of the Christian Greek-language authors in the 5th/6th century attributed his writings to ‘Dionysius the Areopagite,’ to give them some credibility and apostolic value. This led some Christian, Mystic theologians, and poets in the East and the West to be influenced by those writings, such as ‘Maximus the Confessor,’ ‘Gregory the Great,’ ‘Andrew of Crete,’ and others. In the middle ages, some doubts started concerning the authenticity of those writings. However, until the 19th century, scholars have not reached a final decision in this concern.

The Elements Included in These Writings:

108he book of “The Divine Names” cared to talk about the nature and features of God, being the first origin, in whom there is nothing human, and impossible for men to perceive, except through His proclamation about Himself by His “Emanations” (through the Heavenly Hosts). 109he book of “The Heavenly Hosts” describes the nine levels of hosts that intercede between God and man. He subdivided them into three groups; each includes three ranks. 110ccording to the writer, the present world and the evil have no true existence, for evil is nothing but the absence of goodness. 111he book of “The Ecclesiastical Ranks,” which is an extension of the ‘Heavenly Emanations’ working in men on earth, through the three pastoral ranks (the Bishop, the Priest, and the Deacon). These ranks practice three Holy Sacraments: Baptism, Eucharist, and Confirmation; in the life of the three congregations: the Monks, the Laymen, and the Catechumen. The fruit of this work is also threefold: Purification from sin, Enlightenment of the soul and the body, and Secret unity with God. 112he book of “The Mystic Theology,” describes the ascension of the soul to reach an overflow of knowledge, perception, and unity with God (being Divine). The contemplation and prayer are the primary and essential ways to realize that; since they carry man outside himself to bring him forth into the vision of God in a state of overwhelming amazement. 113here are also Ten Letters by the so-called ‘Dionysius,’ which deal with the diverse aspects of this teaching. 114erhaps, the first one to use these writings was St. ‘Severus of Antioch,’ around the year 513 AD.
