passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius I, the 12th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 574–575
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS I, The 12th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA (THE VINEDRESSER) — His Piety

His Piety:

Because of his piety, he was given the spiritual ability to see through those people participating in the Holy Communion. He often asked some of them to present true repentance before being allowed to have a part in it.

Church’s Persecution:

The first years of his papacy were spent in peace; but the devil stirred up the Roman Emperor ‘Septimius Severus’ (193-211 AD) against the Egyptian Christians, declared his persecution in which a significant number of believers were martyred, among whom was ‘Leonides,’ the father of ‘Origen.’ During that time, the governor of Alexandria entered by forcing St. Mark’s Cathedral and confiscated all its treasures. He put Pope ‘Demetrius’ under arrest; then, he exiled him to ‘Osim,’ where he remained until the end of the persecution.

His Works:

93fter his return from his exile, he found out that ‘Clement,’ the dean of the School of Alexandria, had reposed, so the pope appointed ‘Origen,’ famed for his courage, zeal, and knowledge to replace him; while he was just 18 years old. 94uring his papacy, a heresy appeared and spread in the land of ‘Arabia,’ which then had a close relationship with Egypt, and their Christians were followers of the Alexandrian See. That heresy claimed that the soul dies with the death of the body. Pope ‘Demetrius’ sent ‘Origen’ to ‘Arabia’ to restore the Orthodox Faith there. ‘Origen’ succeeded in uprooting that corrupt heresy from that area, then he returned to Alexandria to resume his activity in its School.

His Repose:

He kept teaching and preaching the believers the upright faith all the days of his papacy, and when he reached a very advanced age and became very frail, he was carried on a stretcher to the church to continue serving his people. He reached 105 years of age, of which 32 years as a pope. Then, he reposed a few years before the Church persecution was resumed again with much greater ferocity by Emperor ‘Maximinus’ (235-238 AD).

He delivered his soul in the hands of God, while peace was still on the land.

[Fr. Menasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church, pp. 23-4] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Demetrius I, by Aziz S. Atiya; pp. 891-3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius II, the 111th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 576–577
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS II, The 111th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Zeal about the Orthodox Faith

His Zeal about the Orthodox Faith:

When the pope heard about the activities of the foreign missionaries in Upper Egypt, he sailed on a boat provided to him by khedive ‘Ismaåiil Pasha,’ to the cities and villages along the Nile up to the city of ‘Esnah.’ And, he managed to convince many of the believers to return to their Orthodox Church. That was how close the relationship between the government and the Church in confronting the different movements and the heresies at those great times.

His Repose:

Pope ‘Demetrius II’ reposed on the 18th of January 1870, and was buried next to Pope ‘Cyril IV’ in the tomb in the St. ‘Estephanus’ Church in ‘El- Azbakieh,’ Cairo.

Among the most prominent bishops contemporary to him were: abba ‘Yusab’ (El-Abah), Bishop of ‘Girga and Akhmim’ and Abba ‘Serapamon’ (Abu-Tarĥa), Bishop of ‘El-Menoufyya.’

[Fr. Manasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church, pp. 515-6] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Demetrius II, by Mounir Shoucri; p. 893]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius II, the 111th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 575–576
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS II, The 111th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Papacy (1862-1870)

His Papacy (1862-1870):

After the repose of the great reformer the 110th pope ‘Cyril IV’ (1853-1862), the papal throne remained vacant for about 6 months, after which the bishops and the archons unanimously decided to choose the Hegumen ‘Michael Ăbdel Sayyed,’ the Abbot of the monastery of Abba ‘Macarius’ to sit on the throne. He was ordained on the 15th of June 1862, by the name of Pope ‘Demetrius II.’

After his ordination, he went accompanied by the State men and paid a visit to khedive ‘Saåiid Pasha,’ the Ottoman ruler of Egypt and Sudan. In their first encounter, the khedive gently told him: “Do not do like what your predecessor did. Just tell me about anything you would need, and I shall do it for you.”

After the death of khedive ‘Saåiid Pasha’ in 1863, khedive ‘Ismaåiil Pasha’

took his place. In the days of ‘Ismaåiil Pasha,’ the Copts got what they never had with any other ruler, for he donated to the Coptic schools and the patriarchate so many endowments. He also gave orders to hold the final examinations of the Coptic schools after the Public schools and to hold a graduation ceremony for the Coptic schools' graduates to be attended by the princes and the elites. The Coptic schools cherished this new attitude, and khedive ‘Ismaåiil Pasha’ promoted several Copts and appointed others in major governmental positions. In the year 1869, Pope ’Demetrius II’ was invited to attend the inauguration ceremony of opening the “Suez Canal.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damianos, the 35th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 552–553
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIANOS, The 35th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Keeping the Upright Faith

However, ‘John’ is a lover of peace and tranquility, he refrained from using force to commit the Copts to forsake their doctrines, but he left it entirely up to their choosing. As Pope ‘Damianos’ kept himself away in his cell in the Natron Valley, the intruding patriarch did not enter with him into any open controversy.

In general, through all his reign, Pope ‘Damianos’ kept on teaching his people and held them fast to the Orthodox faith, and after a life abounding in fasts, prayers, and struggles against all kinds of heretical teachings and schisms for 36 years, pope ‘Damianos’ fell sick for few days and then departed to the enlightened dwelling places on the 28th of Paona in the year 605 AD.

[Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church; Vol. II, p. 163] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Damian, by E.R. Hardy; pp. 688-9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damianos, the 35th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 551–552
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIANOS, The 35th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — In the Enaton Monastery

He was a prominent scholar in civil and religious matters. At a young age, he went to the monastery of St. ‘John the Short’ and became a monk on the hand of one of the saintly Fathers in ‘Scetis.’ There, he remained to strive for 16 years, during which he was ordained as a deacon. ‘Damianos’ did absorb well the teachings of his spiritual Fathers and continued to strive day and night to get more knowledge. He became very able in words and deeds and was clothed with the Divine grace.

In the Enaton Monastery:

When the 34th pope ‘Peter IV’ (567-569 AD) sat on St. Mark’s throne, he chose ‘Damianus’ to be his secretary, and he moved him to the monastery known by the name ‘Pateron (means "the Fathers"),’ west of Alexandria. The pope wanted him to participate in carrying the burden of pastoral care, and he had to abandon the life of seclusion to be near his pope. In the ‘Patron,’ ‘Damianos’ pursued an excellent course of life, and everyone loved him.

His Papacy (569-605 AD):

Then in less than a couple of years, when pope ‘Peter IV’ reposed, the clergy and the congregation solidly decided to choose ‘Damianus’ as their new pope. However, because of the obstacles created by those in control of the government at that time, his ordination was delayed for almost three years. Then, he sat on the papal throne on the 2nd of Abib 285 AM (26 June 569 AD).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius II, the 111th Pope of Alexandria, p. 576
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS II, The 111th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Pope’s Care for the Coptic Schools

The Pope’s Care for the Coptic Schools:

Among the most important achievements of this pope was the completion of the construction of the great St. Mark Cathedral in the province of ‘El- Azbakieh’ in Cairo; and ensuring the development and progress of the Coptic schools.

When the Ottoman sultan ‘Ăbdul-Ăziz’ (1861-1876) came to visit Egypt earlier in the year 1863, khedive ‘Saåiid Pasha,’ invited the scholars, the ministers, and the religious leaders to meet him. It was the custom in that era that whoever was called on to greet the sultan, was to kiss his hand or the hem of his robe. When it was the turn for the Coptic Pope ‘Demetrius II,’ he kissed the chest of the sultan instead. The sultan was disturbed, and so did the audience, who considered it as an improper daring from the pope. However, when the pope was asked about the meaning of that unusual kissing, unprecedented by anyone else, the pope answered: “By doing this, I kiss the hand of the King of kings and the Sultan of the Sultans; for it came in the Holy Bible: ‘The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord’ (Prov. 21:1)”. This was translated for sultan ‘Ăbdul-Ăziz’ into the Turkish language by Fr. ‘Salama,’ the secretary of the pope. On hearing the translation, the sultan smiled with pleasure and donated 1,000 acres of the government farmland to the Coptic schools.

Later on, khedive ‘Ismaåiil Pasha’ increased that gift by an additional 500 acres in the province of ‘Sharqieh.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damianos, the 35th Pope of Alexandria, p. 552
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIANOS, The 35th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Keeping the Upright Faith

Keeping the Upright Faith:

In his papacy, he opposed the heretics, including the followers of ‘Meletius’ of ‘Lycopolis’ (Assuit). He wrote several messages to clarify the upright Orthodox Dogma and teachings. He expelled the followers of ‘Meletius’ from the monasteries when they attempted to corrupt the minds of the monks.

He also wrote a message responding to ‘Peter’ the Patriarch of Antioch (who succeeded Abba ‘Theophanius’), who sent him a fellowship message after his ordination. In the beginning, Pope ‘Damianus’ rejoiced to receive that message from the patriarch of Antioch, but on studying its contents, he found that it contained a serious theological error concerning the nature of the Holy Trinity. That issue implied that there was no need to believe in the Holy Trinity. With the intention not to lose his friendship or adversely affect the unity between the two churches, Pope ‘Damianos’ wrote to ‘Peter’ the patriarch of Antioch an essay, in which he explained the teaching of the Ecumenical Councils and the saintly Fathers about the nature of the Holy Trinity, but as patriarch ‘Peter’ persisted on his statements, pope ‘Damianus’ had to write him a very strongworded message, then held a council which condemned his heresy and excommunicated him. This, of course, caused controversy between the two churches, which endured for 20 years, until patriarch ‘Peter’ died.

Pope ‘Damianos’ gave special attention to writing essays and (Mymers) to defend the Orthodox faith. His writings were characterized by the eloquence and the inflamed zeal, which drew so many heretics back to the Orthodox Doctrine.

The Chalcedonian church, backed up by the Byzantine civil authorities, confiscated all the Orthodox Church buildings in Alexandria. When their patriarch who was imposed on Egypt, died in the year 569 AD, they replaced him with another called ‘John.’ ‘John’ was originally an army leader, then they ordained him in ‘Constantinople’ before getting sent to Egypt to confiscate the revenues of the Orthodox churches. However, ‘John’ is a lover of peace and tranquility, he refrained from using force to commit the Copts to forsake their doctrines, but he left it entirely up to their choosing. As Pope ‘Damianos’ kept himself away in his cell in the Natron Valley, the intruding patriarch did not enter with him into any open controversy.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasius, the 36th Pope, pp. 176–177
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIUS, THE 36th POPE — Ordained as a Patriarch

Ordained as a Patriarch:

After the repose of Pope ‘Damianus’ (576-605 AD), the clergy and the people were unified on selecting ‘Anastasius’ the priest of the Church of the Four Evangelists in Alexandria as the new pope. He was the son of an elite family in Alexandria, and he studied in the School of Alexandria, worked as a judge, and was known for his piety and his broad knowledge. He was unanimously chosen to be the patriarch on the See of Alexandria in the year 605 AD.

His Pastoral Work:

Emperor ‘Phocas’ (602-610 AD) in Constantinople, who was characterized by tyranny and violence, banned the Orthodox Popes from entering Alexandria while allowing his Chalcedonians appointees to take by force most of the churches of the great city of Alexandria, although they were ordained by a civil political authority, not a religious one. However, because of the high stature of his family, no one dared to ban Pope Anastasius from entering into the city. With the Pope’s wisdom and courage, he managed to move in and out of Alexandria, taking back some of what the Chalcedonians confiscated and reconstructed those churches destroyed by the riots stirred up by them. He built other new churches and cared to ordain a high number of priests in different locations.

Persecuting Him:

‘Eulogius,' the Chalcedonian Patriarch was so evil, that, seeing how the people gathered together around their Orthodox Patriarch, and how even the governor respected him, he sent to Emperor ‘Phocas’ – who took the throne by force – to claim that abba ‘Anastasius’ has gathered the people in the Church of St. John the Baptist, and excommunicated the Council of Chalcedon and all who follow its decree, including ‘Eulogius’ and the emperor himself. On hearing about it, the emperor ordered the governor of Alexandria to take some of the churches and their vessels by force from Pope ‘Anastasius’ and to deliver them to ‘Eulogius.' The governor came out with a regiment of soldiers, accompanied by ‘Eulogius’ and took by force the Church named after ‘Cosman & Damien,' their Mother and Brothers.' This incident stirred up the Copts, and many of the believers were martyred while they were keeping the soldiers from reaching their pope. With the situation getting worse day after day, the Pope with a sad heart, had to withdraw to the wilderness of ‘Scetis.'

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Heraclas, the 13th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 242–243
passages.text:
Saint: HERACLAS, the 13th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Facing Persecution

With the considerable increase in the number of Christians and the re-entrance of the deniers into faith, the pope felt the necessity of ordaining more bishops to help him shepherd the growing flock. So, the pope ordained 20 bishops.

On the achievements of that pope was bringing back those who denied faith in the time of persecution, in addition to drawing so many pagans to Christianity. He taught them the way to repentance and received them without the need to be re-baptized. He let them publicly proclaim repentance and seek forgiveness with sincere and fervent supplication, to return to the bosom of their glorious Church. By doing so, Pope Heraclas proved to be a merciful Father toward his children, who were weakened and fell.

The Title of Pope:

The Coptic congregation and the clergy in Egypt wanted to differentiate St. Heraclas from the rest of the bishops, so they called their patriarch by the Coptic title Pope (Baba), meaning Father. He was the first Ecclesiastical Official in the Christian World to carry such a title before it was used in Rome. Yet, according to Iris Habib Al-Masry, this title has been used since the days of the 2nd Patriarch of Alexandria St. Anianus (62-83 AD), who was ordained by St. Mark the Apostle, as was mentioned by the Arab historian Al-Maqrizy (1364-1442 AD). In one of the books entitled The Dissension, it was mentioned that the bishops of the capitals of the provinces and districts were called Metropolitans. Yet, some of the bishops had their titles since the old, such as the bishop of Antioch, who was called a Patriarch, the bishop of Alexandria who was called Pope and the Bishop of Rome who was called the bishop of the City. The word Pope is not Latin or of a Western origin, but an entirely Eastern one. And, the first to be given that title was the bishop of Alexandria whose congregation in Egypt, and particularly in Alexandria, has used it. It is to be noticed that the title Pope spread from Alexandria to Carthage before it got to Rome. This was evident from what St. Cornelius (251-253 AD) bishop of Rome wrote in one of his letters, which he sent to Cyprian Bishop of Carthage (248-258 AD): “Peace from Cornelius to Pope Cyprian.” Then the title spread to Rome in the 5th century, and in the 11th century, Gregory VII bishop of Rome held a local Council, in which he excommunicated any bishop who would call himself or others by the title Pope, confining that title to the bishop of Rome alone.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius III, the 76th Pope of Alexandria, p. 261
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS III, THE 76th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

After the repose of the 75th Pope St. ‘Cyril III’ (1235-1243 AD), the papal throne remained vacant for seven years and a half. That was because of an obligation was imposed on the Copts, during that period, to pay a fee of 3,000 Dinari to have a new Pope ordained. However, when the Copts gave a wedding gift of 500 Dinari to ‘Ezz el-Din Aybak,’ the ‘Turkman’ who became a sultan after his marriage to the queen ‘Shagaret el-Durr.’ the old fee of 3,000 Dinari was dropped.

The lot was made and Fr. ‘Paul (Boules) el-Antouny,’ known as ‘Ibn-Kalil al-Masry’ was chosen. There was also Fr. ‘Gabriel’ the monk, a relative of abba ‘Peter’ the bishop of ‘Tanbedi,’ who hoped to be chosen, supported by the prominent family of ‘El-Ăssal.’ However, he was rejected by the congregation. Abba ‘Yusab’ played an essential role in the confirmation of the ordination of Fr. ‘Paul’ the monk. Finally, everybody agreed with his ordination.

He was ordained in the church of ‘The Savior’ (Soteer), in a celebration attended by the first Coptic minister called ‘Sharaf el-Din abu-Saiid Hebat- Allah ibn Saåed el-Naizy’.

Before leaving Alexandria to the ‘Natrun’ valley, as it was the custom, the new pope consecrated several altars and ordained many priests.

He cared for reforming the spiritual condition of the clergy, annulled the ‘Simonism,’ namely, acquiring priesthood by paying money. And, he faced severe trials, when a large number of Copts were killed in ‘Damascus’ after the battle of ‘Ăin Galot’ and the defeat of the ‘Mongolians’ in the year 1259 AD. And, he reposed in the Lord in November 1261 AD. (1st day of Kiahk, 978 AM)

[Kamel S. Nakhla: A Series of the History of the Popes; V. 2; 1952, pp. 6-15]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damasus I, the Pope of Rome, p. 549
passages.text:
Saint: DAMASUS I, THE POPE OF ROME, ST. — His Opposition to the Heresies

His Opposition to the Heresies:

St. ‘Damasus’ represented a force in his opposition against the Arianism, and, enjoying the support of his close friend the 21st Pope of Alexandria, St. ‘Peter II’ (373-379 AD), they managed to accuse ‘Meletus’ bishop of Antioch, and ‘Eusebius’ of Caesarea, who were supported by St. ‘Basil the Great,’ of being Arians; and to condemn ‘Apollinarius,’ who denied that the Lord Jesus Christ had a human soul. In the year 380 AD, Emperor ‘Theodocius I’ (379- 395 AD), proclaimed that Christianity, as testified by the Roman Pope ‘Damasus I’ and the Alexandrian Pope ‘Peter II,’ was the official religion of the State.

St. ‘Damasus I’ expelled two Arian bishops from ‘Illyricum’ in the year 369 AD. However, his efforts to remove ‘Auxentius’ bishop of Milan have failed; until that bishop reposed and was replaced by St. ‘Ambrose’ in the year 374 AD. He condemned the followers of ‘Lucifer of Cagliari;’ and opposed those who denied the Divinity of the Holy Spirit.

The Bishopric of Rome:

‘Damasus’ exerted great efforts to establish the position of the diocese of Rome; and was the first to continually use the expression: ‘The Apostolic See’ for the bishopric of Rome. According to some historians, his efforts were instrumental in creating the concept of ‘The Roman Papacy,’ along with the later efforts of ‘Innocent I’ (401-417 AD) and ‘Leo I’ (440-461 AD).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Benjamin II, the 82nd Pope of Alexandria, pp. 343–344
passages.text:
Saint: BENJAMIN II, The 82nd POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

This pope was born in the town of ‘Dimiqrat,’ south of ‘Armant’ in southern Upper Egypt. He loved the life of tranquility so much that he moved to live in seclusion in the desert close to his town. However, because so many of his friends, relatives, and acquaintances used to come to visit him, he set forth to ‘Deir el-Baghl’ in mount ‘Torah’ away from any disturbance.

As his virtues couldn't hide, many of those who loved him came to visit him, seeking his advice and prayers. When abba ‘Barsum el-Ărian’ (1257-1317 AD) saw him, he prophesied that he would sit on the throne of St. ‘Mark.’ This was realized when he was chosen to succeed the reposed 81st Pope ‘John IX’ (1320-1327 AD), in the year 1327 AD. His selection and consecration found no opposition from the clergy or the laity, and he became the 82nd pope of Alexandria during the period 1327-1339 AD.

During his days, the Church passed through a tough time on the hands of the governor ‘Sharaf el-Din ibn el-Tag,’ who was a Christian converted to Islam. This evil governor desecrated the churches and monasteries and badly humiliated the monks and the nuns. The souls of the pope and bishops were embittered. Fortunately, however, that governor lasted only for one year in his position, and he was dismissed then killed by the sultan's orders. He was succeeded by another governor who was characterized by his love for both Muslims and Christians. Pope ‘Benjamin II’ took the chance to rebuild the churches and the monasteries that have been destroyed, in particular, the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy,’ which was utterly devastated.

In the 3rd year of his papacy, Pope ‘Benjamin II’ was joined by twenty bishops in the monastery of St. ‘Macarius’ to prepare the Holy ‘Myron.’

Afterward, the Church confronted a new wave of anguish, stirred up by the Mamluk sultan ‘Al-Nasir Muhammad ibn-Qalawoon’ (1310-1341 AD). However, through the intervention of the emperor of Ethiopia, a much more peaceful atmosphere started to dwell between the pope and the sultan, that condition gave more tranquility to everyone.

[The Coptic Encyclopedia: Benjamin II, by Subhi Y. Labib; p. 377-8]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius I, the 12th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 572–573
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS I, The 12th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA (THE VINEDRESSER) — Choosing Him for St. Mark’s Throne (189-231 AD)

‘Demetrius’ was raised as a farmer among the fields, and he was taking care of his father’s vines. When he reached the proper age, his parents wanted to get him married to his cousin. He did not wish to oppose them, and he submitted to their will. However, both he and his wife decided to keep their virginity. And, it was said that the shadow of the wings of the Lord’s angel covered them while they were sleeping. After his father’s death, the vines became his own.

Choosing Him for St. Mark’s Throne (189-231 AD):

When the 11th pope ‘Julian’ (178-189 AD) was about to repose, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a night vision to tell him that the person who would bring him a bunch of grapes would be the next patriarch after him. It happened the next day that ‘Demetrius,’ finding a bunch of grapes that ripped prematurely, he decided to bring it to Pope ‘Julian’ to get his blessings. Once he entered into the patriarchate, the pope took hold of his hand and said to those around him: “This is your patriarch after me,” and he narrated to the bishops and the priests the vision he saw. Then, once the Alexandrian pope departed, the clergy and the congregation solidly decided to choose ‘Demetrius’ as their shepherd, according to the counsel of their departed pope, and so, the vinedresser came to be the 12th successor of St. Mark, despite his attempts to be relieved of that great responsibility, because of his illiteracy and for being married.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theophanes, the 60th Pope of Alexandria, p. 283
passages.text:
Saint: THEOPHANES, The 60th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

After the repose of Pope Macarius I (932-952), the elder Theophanius was chosen to replace him in the year 953. His reign was a calamity over the Church, for he was most probably inflicted by a mental illness.

During the early days of his patriarchate, the Church went through severe financial problems, because of the vast taxes put upon the churches of Alexandria by the Muslim governors. In the meantime, the patriarchs at that period were expected to pay their constituents the sum of 1,000 dinars every year. When Theophanes was unable to make that payment, a dispute arose between him and his constituency, ending with his repudiation of the patriarchal garb. The pope being with a sharp nature, easily angered and unable to control his rage while seeing how the Copts of Alexandria persisted on seeking the payment; he resorted to revile and rebuked them in such a way that got out of the circle of prudence. So, the priests had to express their displeasure in him by addressing him with harsh words, which made his mental condition much worse. Some, in an attempt to calm him down, took him on a Nile sail to Babylon, but his rage so increased that it killed him. However, there was a controversy about the actual reason for his death.

[Father Manasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church, 1982; p. 456]

[The Coptic Encyclopedia; Theophanes by Subhi Labib; p. 2247]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina I, the 47th Pope of Alexandria, p. 226
passages.text:
Saint: MINA I, The 47th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — A Monk Tried to Take Over the Papacy

However, that monk Butros went too far in his arrogance with the governor, that the governor ordered his men to put him under arrest, and allowed Pope Mina I and his bishops to return to their thrones with the due honor. Pope Mina I, spent his last years interacting with his congregation and urging them to strive, as well as to renew the churches. It was a peaceful period mainly that the new governor Musa ibn Ăli (772-778 AD) followed the same pleasant path of his predecessor Ăbdel Raĥman in dealing with the Christians and the Egyptian people in general. This pope departed to the church of the firstborn, after a papacy which lasted for eight years and ten months.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk. 3, p. 385] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Mina I, by Subhi Y. Labib, p. 1631-2]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John XIII, the 94th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 396–397
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN XIII, The 94th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — A Portuguese Bishop on Ethiopia

A Portuguese Bishop on Ethiopia:

As it was difficult for the Coptic pope to send a Coptic metropolitan to his children in Ethiopia due to the hostilities between the Mamluk Sultans in Egypt and the kings of Ethiopia; king David II of Ethiopia sought from Portugal to send a Roman bishop there. A Portuguese named Poaz Parmodaz was sent, who was amazingly given the title Patriarch of Alexandria despite that was an obvious challenge to the brotherly rules and the decrees of the Ecumenical councils, the Nicene council in particular.

Arabian Tribes Attack Abba Paul and Abba Anthony Monasteries:

The era of the Mamluks was full of contradictions. At the time the Copts in Egypt lived in peace with their Muslim brethren, during the rule of Abu Saåid Qansuh al-Ghoury (1498-1500), as shown in celebrating the Nile Flood, and the feast of Nayrouz together; the flourishment of the architect, ornamentations of the buildings, agricultural engineering, and medicine, Ophthalmology in particular. Yet the devil planted tares among the wheat; as some Arabian tribes dwelling in Upper Egypt attacked the two monasteries of Abba Paul and Abba Anthony, demolished them, killed all their monks, and used the monasteries' books and manuscripts whenever they needed fuel for their fire. Up till now, the traces of fire are apparent on the walls despite the efforts to wash away the atrocities of the invaders, who did not care for the sanctity of the aged, the hermit, or the texts which urged men to virtue.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 200
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Culture and Views

The Western Church celebrates st. Methodius (Eubilis) on the 20th of June and on the 18th of September. St. Methodius became the bishop of Olympus in Lycia in the southern part of Asia Minor, then became the bishop of Patara. He has martyred in the year 311 AD in Chalcis in Greece. He was forgotten or disregarded by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea, probably because he opposed Origen. This saint was not the same as Methodius, the bishop of Petaris in Syria or the bishop of Phoenicia, who was martyred in Syria.

His Culture and Views:

St. Methodius seemed to have read Plato's works and admired his dialogue style since he authored his essays using the same method. He opposed Origen's views about the prior existence of the souls, the resurrection of the bodies with the spirit, and that the body is a prison for the soul.

His Martyrdom:

According to St. Jerome, St. Methodius received the crown of martyrdom during the last days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284- 305 AD). However, others insisted that he was martyred at the time of Emperors Decius (249-251 AD) and Valerian (253-260 AD) in Chalcis in Greece. Yet, other scholars dismiss the idea of St. Methodius early martyrdom, on account of that he was briefly mentioned by Eusebius of Caesarea (265-339 AD), as being one of his contemporaries.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 201
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

His Writings:

St. Methodius drew his fame from the many articles he wrote, among which were:

1. ‘On Virginity’ (Symposion e peri hagneias): It is a dialogue about commending the virginity. This dialogue ended with a long hymn sung by Thekla, and its verses were arranged in alphabetical order. It is considered as one of the earliest Christian hymns. He quoted from Psalm forty-five, saying: “The bride will sit at the right hand of Christ, adorned with gold.” This work is his only writing, which has been left complete. It revealed his admiration of Plato in following his dialogue style, from which he quoted not only some of its verses but also the idea of the work as a whole. Plato, in his work, commended love, while Methodius commended glories of virginity.

2. ‘On the Resurrection’ (Aglaophon e pen tes anastaseos): This article was lost, but many quotes from it remained in the work of Epiphanius of Salamis (315-403 AD) [Against the Heresies: 64], Photius of Constantinople (858-886 AD) [Codice 234] and John of Damascus (675-749 AD) [On Holy Images: Sermon 2]. In this work too, Methodius followed the Platonic dialogue style to refute Origen and his followers, who denied the resurrection of the material body, and believe that it was enough to say that what would resurrect is an adorned and glorified form of that body. In heaven, our bodies will be spiritual, and according to St. Paul the Apostle: "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corin. 15:44), and, "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; nor does corruption inherit incorruption" (1 Corin. 15:50). According to them, the man initially was in Paradise, namely in the 3rd heaven (2 Corin. 12), in a spiritual body, then having fallen, he was brought down to earth, where God provided him with a leather cover, namely, he got the material body as a punishment. Such a substantial body is the source of temptations and trials of the soul, and without it, the soul could not sin. Then, when we resurrect, we would be where there is no place for crime, we would be like angels, free from the body, which represents a burden on the soul. St. Methodius responded to that in his dialogue by saying that the body is a tool in the hand of the soul to use for doing good or doing evil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, pp. 201–202
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

Then, when we resurrect, we would be where there is no place for crime, we would be like angels, free from the body, which represents a burden on the soul. St. Methodius responded to that in his dialogue by saying that the body is a tool in the hand of the soul to use for doing good or doing evil. When the Holy Bible says that we shall be like the angels of God, this did not mean that we shall be without bodies, but we shall be like the angels in their incorruptible and unchangeable nature.

He also said that by death, God did not plan to change us from what He intended for us when He created us. He is like a sculptor who would re-knead his hand-work when he finds it getting out of shape. He would re-knead it in such a way to conform to what he had for it in his mind originally. In the same manner by death, God would transform us to be free from the corruption of sin.

It was a bold dialogue in the house of a physician by the name Aglaophon in Patara. In that dialogue, Methodius confirmed the resurrection of the body, being a partner of the soul in her strife, to share in her glory, and he indicated that it was not another spiritual body, but he mentioned that this resurrected body would enjoy a heavenly renewal. He said about Christ: “He became a True Body and died a True Death, and not just in appearance, to show that He was the First of those who resurrected from death, to turn what is earthly to heavenly, and what is mortal to immortal.”

Methodius said that at the beginning, the man was immortal, body and soul, that death and the separation of the soul from the collection were the results of the envy of Satan, and that the goal of Christ's Redemption was to rejoin what was separated by Satan.

3. St. Jerome (347-420 AD) mentioned in his book: ‘Of Illustrious Men’ (sec 83), and in his two Letters 48 and 70: that Methodius argued very well in refuting Porphyry's fifteen letters which were written against the Christians.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 203
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — Of His Words

Of His Words:

• The church grows daily in stature and beauty through her cooperation and unity with the Logos, who descends to us to this very day and keep on descending in the commemoration of His passion. • No one should be lazy in welcoming the King; otherwise, he would be deprived of the beauty of the participation in the wedding. I wish no one among us would welcome Him with an ugly face, lest he would be condemned as an evildoer who refrained from receiving the King. Let us come to Him with gladness, receive Him with joy, and hold fast to our banquet with faithfulness. • I keep my soul pure for You, O Bridegroom. I would carry for You a lighted lamp and march to receive You.

[Dr. A. Rustom: The Church Fathers in the First Three Centuries] [H. Wace & W. Piercy: A Dictionary of Early Christian Biography, 1999]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 202
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

3. St. Jerome (347-420 AD) mentioned in his book: ‘Of Illustrious Men’ (sec 83), and in his two Letters 48 and 70: that Methodius argued very well in refuting Porphyry's fifteen letters which were written against the Christians.

4. St. Jerome also mentioned another work for Methodius. It is called ‘The Diviner,’ which was addressed against Origen, although it is now lost. It has the same title used by Ostatheos in his book; he wrote to refute Origen, who believed that the soul of Samuel the Prophet was under the control of the devil and that it was recalled by the diviner using sorcery. The response of Methodius was very different from that of Ostatheus, in which Ostatheus believed that the soul of Samuel was indeed called.

5. Socrates [The Ecclesiastical History 6:13] mentioned another work by Methodius, called ‘Xeno,’ which, according to some, was the same work referred to by Photius.

6. ‘On the Created Objects’: Some quotations from this work were kept by Photius, in which he refuted the Origen teachings, which called the eternity of the world. This teaching assumed that if God is eternal, then He was always the Almighty Creator, and at no time, He was not the Creator, and, since there is no Creator without creation, therefore, they concluded that there was creation since eternity. This Methodius work, too, came in the form of dialogue that responded to all those wrong assumptions.

7. ‘On the Freedom of Will’: A discussion to confirm that the will of man is free and responsible for his actions. It was most probably addressed against the followers of Valentinus and the Gnostics.

8. Lost works: Such as ‘On the Martyrs,’ ‘Interpretation of the Book of Genesis,’ and ‘Interpretation of the Song of Songs.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dionisius, the Bishop, p. 594
passages.text:
Saint: DIONISIUS, THE BISHOP (The martyr)

This saint was a bishop on ‘Corinth’ and was martyred in the days of Emperors ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) and ‘Maximian’ (286-305 AD) after being viciously tortured for the sake of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Finally, his head was cut off by the sword, and he received the eternal crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 23 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Philoromus, p. 452
passages.text:
Saint: PHILOROMUS (The martyr)

St. Philoromus was one of the prominent people of the city of Thmuis (Tell el-Timai) on the east side of the Nile delta in Egypt. He was a Christian military tribune, and he defended St. Philaeas, the bishop of his city when he rejected the appeals of his relatives and friends in trying to save him. Then, they both offered themselves to death and were martyred in the year 303 AD, during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). So they earned immortal palms from God. With them was crowned with martyrdom a countless multitude of the faithful of the same place, who followed the example of their pastor. The western church celebrates him on the 4th of Feb.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 390]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mucius, pp. 259–260
passages.text:
Saint: MUCIUS (The martyr)

St. Mucius (Mocius) was a Christian priest who was martyred in the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). His biography indicates that he was a prominent sermon-giver who preached in Amphipolis in Macedonia.

It happened that during the feast of god Bacchus (Dionysus), this saint dared to cast on the ground whatever was on the idol's Altar with all their sacrifices. When the pagans wanted to kill him, the governor arrested him instead and brought him to trial. The judge condemned him to be burned alive. There in the fiery furnace, the saint was seen walking unharmed in flames, along with three strangers. Later on, the saint was sent to Heraclea, where he was tortured by the hinbazeen. Then, he was cast before hungry wild beasts, but they refrained from touching him. He was finally sent to Byzantium (Constantinople), where his head was cut off by the sword in the year 304 AD.

[Butler: May 13] [Hieromartyr Mocius, the Presbyter of Amphipolis in Macedonia: The Orthodox Church in America (On the Internet)]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Porphyrios, p. 479
passages.text:
Saint: PORPHYRIOS (The martyr)

The Synaxarion of the 3rd of Baramhat mentions another martyr with a similar name Porphyrios (Porphyry). Most probably, this saint was martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). He was a rich man of the city of Banias, who loved the poor and visited those imprisoned. On seeing the governor walking in front of his house, he proclaimed his Christian faith and ultimately received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Marcellus, the Bishop, pp. 55–56
passages.text:
Saint: MARCELLUS, THE BISHOP (The martyr) — Emperor Theodosius the Great Spreads Christianity

Emperor Theodosius the Great Spreads Christianity:

In the year 380 AD, the righteous Emperor Theodosius the Great (379-395 AD) planned on spreading Christianity all over the Roman Empire. The emperor sent a decree which urged everyone to confess the true Christian Faith taught by the popes of Rome and Alexandria. Eight years later, the emperor sent his deputy to Egypt, Syria, and Asia Minor, to make sure that the imperial order to destroy all the pagan temples was carried out in the whole Empire. This action naturally provoked the anger of the pagans.

When the imperial deputy arrived at Apamea in Syria, he sent soldiers to destroy the city's temple of the god Zeus. However, because the temple was huge and was very well built, the soldiers were unable to destroy it. The bishop of the region who was called Marcellus was observing what the deputy was trying to do, and he suggested to him to take his men to his next assignment and to leave the responsibility of destroying the temple of Zeus to him. On the next day, a contractor came to see bishop Marcellus and agreed with him to do the job if he would be paid double. The bishop approved, and the man and his workers started to dig underneath the main foundations of the temple, which caused the whole building to collapse. Bishop Marcellus repeated the same approach in destroying all the other temples.

Then, bishop Marcellus and his people reached a temple that the pagans decided to defend to their last man. So, while the bishop was trying to hide from the arrows aimed at him, some of the pagans charged against him and managed to throw him into a fire pit. In that way, he received the crown of martyrdom in the year 389 AD.

When his sons – as he was a married man – decided to avenge the death of their father, the pious governor stood in their way saying: “It is more befitting for you to rejoice that God found your father worthy to die for His sake.”

[Butler: August 14]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Olympas, the Apostle, p. 319
passages.text:
Saint: OLYMPAS, THE APOSTLE

St. Olympas (meaning "Heavenly" in Greek) was one of the seventy apostles who were sent by the Lord to preach the Word. He was a Roman Christian whom St. Paul the Apostle saluted (in Romans 16:15) around 65 AD. He was also called Paul, and he was the one who served the disciples, carried some of the epistles of St. Peter the Apostle to the Gentiles, entered with him into Rome, where he preached and taught many. When St. Peter was martyred, this apostle was the one who took his body off the cross, shrouded him, and took him to the house of one of the believers. Then, someone reported him to Emperor Nero (54-68 AD) of being one of the disciples of St. Peter. When Nero called him for questioning, he confessed before him that the Lord Jesus Christ is the true God. Nero brutally tortured him, then asked him how he would like to die, to which the saint replied: “I want to die for the sake of Christ, but it is up to you to kill me in whatever way you choose.” The emperor ordered to crucify him upside down the way his mentor died, and in this way, he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion of 6th Abib]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS (The martyr)

St. Hesychius (Esychius), an officer in the imperial court in Antioch, during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, was condemned to death by drowning in the river Orontes because he refused to sacrifice to the idols. This martyrdom took place most probably in the year 297 AD.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Hesychius (15) (Esychius), Vol. III, p. 10]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius, the Monk, p. 252
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS, THE MONK, ST.

St. Hesychius was a saintly monk who lived in the 4th century AD. He was a faithful disciple of his mentor St. Hilarion, whom he accompanied in his travels from Palestine to Egypt. After St. Hilarion's reputation reached its peak in Gaza, he intended not to stay or to go back to Gaza, and he sailed secretly to the island of Sicily. For three years, Hesychius kept searching for the whereabouts of his mentor. Not finding him in the wilderness or the ports of Egypt, he searched for him in Greece. There, he heard about a saintly monk in Sicily who performed miracles. So, he set out to that island and cast himself on the ground, shedding tears on the feet of his mentor.

Wishing to enjoy a life of seclusion, the mentor and his disciple went to Dalmatia and from there to the island of Cyprus. Two years later, St. Hilarion sent Hesychius to Palestine to visit and follow up on the condition of the brethren there and to inspect their old monastery near Gaza. When he returned, he found his mentor disturbed by the frequency of the visitors, and planning to flee to another location. However, being too advanced in age, he managed to convince him to go deeper into the island to enjoy more seclusion. There, they lived until eventually St. Hilarion reposed, leaving his Holy Bible and some clothes to his disciple. After some time, Hesychius carried the relics of his mentor to Palestine, despite the objection of the inhabitants of the island. There, it was received by the multitudes of monks and people with hymns of praise. He was buried in the monastery he built-in Majuma. A few years later, Hesychius himself reposed.

[Baring-Gould: October 3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amphilochius, the Bishop of Iconium, pp. 165–166
passages.text:
Saint: AMPHILOCHIUS, THE BISHOP OF ICONIUM, ST.

St. Amphilochius lived in the fourth century AD and was a close friend to St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory the Theologian, and St. Gregory of Nyssa.

He was born in Caesarea of Cappadocia between the years 340 and 350 AD He was raised to love the knowledge and culture, and he was characterized, beside his noble origin, with justice and wisdom. He succeeded his father in his work as a lawyer in Constantinople in the year 364 AD. Then, he became a judge and became known for his clean hands and integrity. His friend St. Gregory kept urging him to give more of his time to the study the Holy Bible, worship, and ministry, but he felt that he would rather minister to God through his loyalty and in doing his job as a judge with integrity.

He passed through a severe trial when he was unjustly accused of getting a bribe to acquit a guilty man. When St. Gregory, the Theologian hastened to write to the imperial palace in Constantinople to proclaim the innocence of his friend, his intervention was well received, and the saint came out of the trial with more honor. But the more significant benefit of that trial was his perception of the importance of the counsel of his old friend, who kept on urging him to dedicate himself to the ministry of God. He decided to forsake his job in the year 367 AD and to live as a hermit in his own house. He devoted his life to concentrate on the study of the Holy Bible, contemplation, spiritual worship, asceticism and taking care of his sick father in his old age.

Amphilochius took St. Basil the Great as his friend, spiritual mentor, and a guide of his life. There were so many messages exchanged between them, although Amphilochius used quite a bit of caution, to avoid being recommended for a pastoral position. God called him to be ordained as a bishop in the year 374 AD on the city of ‘Iconium’ in the region of ‘Lycaonia,' which was named ‘The second Pisidia.' It seemed that he consented to get ordained as a bishop through the pressure of St. Basil the Great, as it was obvious in the message from the later to him, saying: “God, who, in every generation, chooses the blessed man in whom He is well pleased, reveals the vessels of his choice, and uses them to minister to his saints. He is the One who catches you in the net of His grace, from which you cannot escape, despite your attempts to do so, not to escape from us, but from the call, God addressed through us… So, He brought you over in the middle of ‘Pisidia’ to captivate to the Lord those who were previously captivated by the devil, and to bring them out of the depths of darkness to light, according to His will."

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Domadius, the Syrian, pp. 631–632
passages.text:
Saint: DOMADIUS, THE SYRIAN (The martyr) — Receiving Faith

Receiving Faith:

This saint was raised in Persia, where he was taught astrology. He had a strong desire to be a Christian. So, it happened that in the market place, he met with a Persian monk called ‘Aughalis,’ from whom he learned the way to God. He was so jubilant that he kept teaching his household the way to faith. Then, he got baptized.

His Monastic Life:

Later on, he went to a monastery and became a monk. He lived a great ascetic life that brought on him the envy of some brethren. When he sensed what was happening, he left them and went to the monastery of St. ‘Sergius,’ where he became a disciple to one of their hermits for ten years. During all that time, he ate nothing cooked.

His Simplicity and Purity:

After that, he was ordained as a deacon. And, while he was ministering with the saintly hermit at the altar, he saw a lovely white dove that came on the altar. Thinking that it was an earthly dove and fearing for the vessel, he kept waving at it with his head and hands. After praying the Mass, when the priest asked him why he was so disturbed during the Liturgy, he told him what he had seen. The priest asked him to let him know if he would see it again. The next day, during Mass, the deacon saw it again, and alerted the priest: “There it is Father.” Looking and seeing nothing, the old priest cast himself before the Lord, raising tearful prayers, day and night, until he was found worthy of seeing that dove, which he came to know was a symbol of the Holy Spirit. He did not say anything to St. ‘Domadius’ to spare him from being overcome with pride. However, he told the story to the bishop, who ordained ‘Domadius’ as a priest.

When his fame spread and reached the Patriarch of that time, he planned to visit him. On hearing about it, the saint fled to the church of St. ‘Cosman,’ and dwelt next to it for some time, feeding only on the herbs of the ground.

His Martyrdom:

God performed so many miracles through this saint. When Emperor Julian the Apostate (360-363 AD) came out to fight the Persians, he passed by the cave of this saint. When he was told about his story, he ordered his men to stone him and his disciples to death; they left a great heap of stones on top of their cave.

Several years later, God allowed for his relics to be discovered; and a church was built in his name. God allowed for so many miracles to continue happening in that church.

[The Synaxarion: 25 Abib]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Euthymius, the Great Abbot, p. 89
passages.text:
Saint: EUTHYMIUS, THE GREAT ABBOT

Abbot Euthymius was born in Melitene in Armenia in the year 377 AD, where he was ordained as a priest and became an Abbot on a gathering of monks. On reaching 30 years old, he immigrated to Palestine, where he lived as a hermit in several places, mostly in caves. Finally, he settled down in a desolate town between Jerusalem and Jericho, where he was surrounded by many monks whom he guided, yet not at the expense of his way of seclusion.

Abbot Euthymius was one of the early great Father monks of Palestine and had a significant influence on the Nomads there. It happened that he healed a paralyzed son of one of their chiefs. And, he also had quite an impact on Empress Eudocia (401-460 AD), the widow of Emperor Theodosius II (402- 450 AD), who came to seek his counsel in particular issues. He finally reposed in Palestine on the 20th of January, 473 AD.

[The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, p. 123] [A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Euthymius (4), Vol II; p. 398-400]

records.question: How did St. Moses the Black meet his sister Sarah, who was martyred with him?
records.answer:
St. Moses the Black and his sister Sarah were born to wealthy Christian parents. After their parents passed away, St. Moses intended to become a monk after giving his sister in marriage and handing their whole wealth to her. However, Sarah told him that she also wanted to become a nun, and they agreed to both pursue the monastic life. They distributed all their wealth to the poor and needy. St. Moses brought Sarah into a house of virgins, and he joined a monastery near Alexandria. For the following ten years, they did not see one another.

When Emperor Decius incited persecution against Christians, St. Moses sent to his sister to bid her farewell and to inform her of his decision to be martyred for Christ. Sarah sought permission from her mother-superior, received blessings from her sisters, and joined her brother on his way to Alexandria. There, they both confessed the Lord Jesus Christ together, were tortured, and then beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom [1][2].
