Wherefore the Body of Christ gives life to all who partake of It. For it expels death, when It comes to be in dying men, and removes corruption, full in Itself perfectly of the Word which abolishes corruption.”

“And do not doubt that this is true, since He Himself plainly says, ‘This is My body … This is My blood:’ but rather receive in faith that Saviour’s word; for He, being truth, cannot lie.”

“Let them then, who of their folly have not yet admitted the faith in Christ, hear, Except ye eat the Flesh of the Son of Man and drink His Blood, you have no life in you (John 6:53). For wholly destitute of all share and taste of that life which is in sanctification and bliss, do they abide who do not through the mystical Blessing receive Jesus. For He is Life by Nature, inasmuch as He was begotten of a Living Father (John 6:57): no less giving life to His Holy Body also, being in a manner gathered and ineffably united with the all-quickening Word [Logos].”

St. Augustine says, “He said that He was to ascend into heaven, of course, whole: ‘If you see the Son of Man ascending to where He first was.’ certainly then, at least, you will see that not in the manner you suppose does He dispense His body; certainly then, at least, you will understand that His grace is not consumed by tooth-biting.”

He also says, “He is Himself the Bread which came down from heaven; but Bread which refreshes the failing, and does not fail; Bread which can be tasted, cannot be wasted. This Bread did the manna also figure. Wherefore it is said, ‘He gave them the bread of heaven, and man ate the bread of the angels’ (Ps. 77:24–25 LXX). Who is the Bread of heaven, but Christ? But in order that man might eat Angels’ Bread, the Lord of Angels was made Man. For if He had not been made Man, we should not have His Flesh; if we had not His Flesh, we should not eat the Bread of the Altar. Let us hasten to the inheritance, seeing we have hereby received a great earnest of it. My brethren, let us long for the life of Christ, seeing we hold as an earnest the Death of Christ.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q807 “How does the eucharist support the unity of the faithful together?”, p. 607
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 807. How does the eucharist support the unity of the faithful together?

St. John Chrysostom says, “We have partaken of a spiritual table, let us be partakers also of spiritual love. For if robbers, on partaking of salt, forget their character; what excuse shall we have, who are continually partaking of the Lord’s body, and do not imitate even their gentleness? And yet to many, not one table only, but even to be of one city, have sufficed for friendship; but we, when we have the same city, and the same house, and table, and way, and door, and root, and life, and head, and the same shepherd, and king, and teacher, and judge, and maker, and father, and to whom all things are common; what indulgence can we deserve, if we be divided one from another?”

Notes: [1574] St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 32.10 (NPNF II/10:213).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q770 “Why do we mix the wine with water in the chalice?”, p. 583
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of the Eucharist — 770. Why do we mix the wine with water in the chalice?

When the Lord was pierced in His side, blood and water came out. St. Augustine believes that mixing the Eucharistic blood with water indicates that water is a symbol of humanity which partakes in Christ’s suffering.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q780 “Who transforms the offerings into the body and blood of Christ?”, p. 593
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of the Eucharist — 780. Who transforms the offerings into the body and blood of Christ?

St. John Chrysostom says, “Until now, Christ, who is attached to us, prepares the table Himself and sanctifies it. For it is not man who transforms the offerings into His body and blood, but Christ Himself who was crucified for us. The priest utters the words, but God's power and grace accomplish the sanctification. Christ says, ‘This is My body,’ and the offerings are sanctified.”

Notes: [1524] Cf. Catena Aurea.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q776 “What is the role of this banquet in the lives of those who partake of it?”, pp. 585–586
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of the Eucharist — 776. What is the role of this banquet in the lives of those who partake of it?

First: Openness towards others. As the believer enjoys this banquet, he in turn desires to invite others to it. St. Jacob of Sarug says, “The King’s bride went out on the paths of the world to gather all peoples in order to delight them … She stood in the marketplaces and the corners of the earth to invite the assemblies and the crowds to the banquet.”

He also says, “Who is capable of sacrificing the Son before His Father, if He had not offered Himself from before His sufferings? Our Lord is the High Priest and the perfect sacrifice and therefore, He offered Himself before His Father … He died, but while being dead, He was alive. He is the Priest and the Sacrifice. Comprehending this mystery is beyond debate. He taught them to drink from the Cup of His blood and to make the nations, countries and the world drink from it … He sealed with His blood the new covenant, which He instituted for the remission of sins for the whole world.”

Second: Caring for the poor. St. John Chrysostom says, “These words let us also listen to, all of us, as many as in this place approach with the poor to this holy Table, but when we go out, do not seem even to have seen them, but are both drunken and pass heedlessly by the hungry; the very things whereof the Corinthians were accused.”

Third: Walking in the spirit of unity and love. St. John Chrysostom says, “And what do they become who partake of it? The Body of Christ: not many bodies, but one body. For as the bread consisting of many grains is made one, so that the grains nowhere appear; they exist indeed, but their difference is not seen by reason of their conjunction; so are we conjoined both with each other and with Christ … Wherefore also he adds, ‘for we all partake of that one bread’ (1 Cor. 10:17) … why do we not also show forth the same love, and become also in this respect one?”

St. Augustine also says, “In this loaf of bread you are given clearly to understand how much you should love unity. I mean, was that loaf made from one grain? Were there not many grains of wheat? But before they came into the loaf they were all separate; they were joined together by means of water after a certain amount of pounding and crushing. Unless wheat is ground, after all, and moistened with water, it cannot possibly get into this shape which is called bread. In the same way you too were being ground and pounded, as it were, by the humiliation of fasting and the sacrament of exorcism. Then came baptism, and you were, in a manner of speaking, moistened with water in order to be shaped into bread. But it is not yet bread without fire to bake it.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q771 “How can we prepare ourselves to receive the body and blood of the Lord?”, pp. 583–584
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of the Eucharist — 771. How can we prepare ourselves to receive the body and blood of the Lord?

The believer should examine his conscience before God and purify it through repentance. The Apostle says, “Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgement to himself, not discerning the Lord's body” (1 Cor. 11:27–29).

records.question: confession
records.answer:
Confession in the Coptic Orthodox Church involves several key aspects:

1. **Purpose and Necessity**  
   Confession is necessary to encounter God, the Physician of our souls, and to experience His love through acknowledging our sins and weaknesses. A true believer does not distinguish between big and small sins but seeks to be an icon of Christ and an unblemished steward of heaven. Confession is both a private repentance before God and a public confession before the Father of Confession (the priest), following the example of early Christians who confessed to John the Baptist and the apostles [2].  

2. **Authority to Forgive Sins**  
   Christ gave His disciples the authority to forgive or retain sins after His resurrection, breathing on them and saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:21–23). This shows the continual need for repentance and confession in the Church [3].  

3. **Role of the Father in Confession**  
   The Father in confession (priest) acts as a spiritual mentor responsible before God for the believer. Confession is a form of discipleship, where the believer learns from the spiritual experiences of the Father in confession, following his example in faith, struggle, and watchfulness [4]. Even those who know Scripture well need discipleship and instruction from elders to avoid self-sufficiency and to grow spiritually [5][13].  

4. **Process and Effects**  
   Confession begins with repentance in private and is followed by confession before the priest. This leads to a transformation of life, both internally and externally, acknowledging God’s love and grace that can transform the heart from corruption to incorruption [1].  

5. **Tears of Repentance**  
   Tears in confession express sorrow for sin and open the soul’s spiritual sight, allowing the person to see God’s beauty and hate sin. These tears intercede before God, giving the soul boldness, hope, and confidence in the Savior, renewing the soul’s inner beauty [11][14].  

6. **Concealing Sins and Clear Conscience**  
   Concealing sins is discouraged; the Lord says, “For there is nothing covered that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26). If a person claims their conscience is clear but is unaware of sin, they should trust those who can see their spiritual state more clearly [6][10].  

7. **Relation to Forgiveness**  
   The soul can be convinced of God’s forgiveness by believing in the role of Christ and the mercy and justice of God, as taught by the Apostles and Prophets [8].  

In summary, confession is a vital sacrament and spiritual practice in the Coptic Orthodox Church, involving repentance before God and confession before a priest, leading to spiritual transformation, discipleship, and assurance of forgiveness. It is both a personal and communal encounter with God’s mercy and healing [1][2][3][4][5][6][8][10][11][13][14].

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q730 “What are the important obligations of the believer who repents?”, pp. 558–559
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 730. What are the important obligations of the believer who repents?

First: He or she thanks God for His blessings, His mercy, and His salvation, so that he may have the boldness to seek forgiveness.

Second: To admit that he is a sinner and unable to enjoy the holy life without God’s mercy and free grace.

Third: To be merciful to those who sin against him and to forgive them, so that the Savior may open for him the way of salvation.

Fourth: The believer’s focus on heaven, his anticipation of the eternal wedding and his love for others, elevates all his inner being as on the wings of the Holy Spirit so that the person may know the heavenly Bridegroom, who prepares for him eternal glory. He also acknowledges his weaknesses, and the grace of God that is capable of transforming the heart from corruption to incorruption and from an earthly heart to a new heaven, and from humans to angels.

Repentance to God and confession before Him in our private rooms and in the presence of a priest are the beginning of a change in one’s way of life, both at the inner level as well as the external behavior. It is a transformation in which we acknowledge the richness of

God’s love, and hence offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, in which we acknowledge our

weaknesses and wickedness, confident in His salvific work and His ability to raise use from corruption to an angelic life that is acceptable to the Father. This is how are continuously cleansed in the spirit of hope. “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:23).

St. John Chrysostom says, “Repentance is the evangelical path through which the soul passes to the kingdom,” and, “Therefore, beloved, when you commit sin, do not wait for another man to accuse you but, before you are accused and indicted, you yourself condemn what you have done. Then, if someone accuses you later on, it is no longer a matter of your doing the right thing in confessing, but of your correcting the accusation which he makes … Peter certainly sinned gravely in denying Christ. But he was quick to remind himself of his sin and, before anyone accused him, he told of his error and wept bitterly (Matt. 26:69–75; Mark 14:66–72). He so effectively washed away his sin of denial that he became the chief of the apostles and the whole world was entrusted to him.”

Notes: [1438] St. John Chrysostom, Discourses against Judaizing Christians 8.3.3–4 (FOTC 68:213–214).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q743 “Is it necessary to repent before God in our private rooms, and then again in the presence of the Father of Confession?”, p. 565
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 743. Is it necessary to repent before God in our private rooms, and then again in the presence of the Father of Confession?

The goal of confessing our sins is to encounter God, the Physician of our souls. Whoever does not feel his weakness or sins, will never feel the need for the heavenly Physician and will not therefore experience God’s love. Many times, we consider ourselves righteous, since we do not commit any dangerous sins that hurt others. A true believer, however, does not differentiate between big sins and trivial sins, since what truly concerns him is to be the icon of Christ, the Holy One’s ambassador, and an unblemished steward of heaven.

St. Basil the Great says, “it seems necessary that sins be confessed to those entrusted with the stewardship of the Mysteries of God (cf. 1 Cor. 4:1). For thus also those who repented of old are found to have confessed their sins before the saints. For it is written in the gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (cf. Matt. 3:6; Mark 1:5) and in the Acts of the Apostles, to the apostles, by whom they were also baptized (cf. Acts 2:37).”

He also says, “On the other hand, where sin is concerned, be your own accuser (Prov. 18:17), and do not wait for others to make the accusation. Thus, you will be like a just man who accuses himself in the first speech made in court, or like Job who was not deterred by the crowd of people in the city from declaring his personal guilt before all (Job 31:34).”

Notes: [1444] St. Basil of Caesarea, The Rule of St Basil in Latin and English: A Revised Critical Edition, trans., Anna M. Silvas (Collegeville, Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2013) Q. 21: p. 129. [1445] St. Basil of Caesarea, Of Humility (FOTC 9:485).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q729 “What was Christ’s commandment to His disciples when He appeared to them after His resurrection?”, p. 558
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 729. What was Christ’s commandment to His disciples when He appeared to them after His resurrection?

He said to them, “‘As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.’ And when He had said this, He breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.’” (John 20:21– 23). He gave them this authority to show them that the world always needs repentance and confession so that the believers may never cease to confess the Lord’s blessings as well as the fact that they are sinners and hence offer repentance every time they pray the Lord’s prayer, “Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.” Therefore, Christ who is risen from the dead, calls them to be merciful with the people that the Lord may be merciful with them as well.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q761 “Is discipleship necessary?”, pp. 574–575
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 761. Is discipleship necessary?

Christianity exists wherever discipleship is, but is weakened and becomes dry, heavy, and fictional when discipleship is lost. That was why when the Lord ordered the disciples to preach, He said, “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19–20). The Lord commanded them to prepare a new generation of disciples who will live as they lived, emphasizing the fact that discipleship is the primary method of teaching and the keeping of the commandments. Through discipleship, the disciples are filled with the Spirit of the Lord and Christianity is passed on from one generation to the next. For this reason, Christians were called “disciples,” and were first called Christians in Antioch (Acts 11:26). Perhaps, this was out of mockery from the pagans, by attributing to them the crucified Christ.

Since we are “Christians,” let us also acknowledge that we are “disciples.” I am not thus saying that we are all apostles or shepherds but that every Christian ought to be characterized by discipleship to our Lord Jesus at the hands of his or her mentor. The sacraments of baptism and repentance both fulfill that role through the sponsor and the Father in confession who are both responsible before God for the believer.

Confession, according to this concept, is the discipleship of a new generation that lives

by the spirit of their fathers the saints, for Christ the Lord. It is a union between the confessor, the Father in confession and Christ; not just for a certain time of the week, but continuously. A father gathers his children and delights in regularly meeting them, not just physically but also spiritually in his private prayers or on the altar. The son and daughter then love their father, pray for him, follow his example, and consult him in everything, to learn from his spiritual experiences in struggling against sin so that they may follow his example too, his faith, struggle, and watchfulness.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q762 “Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!”, pp. 575–576
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 762. Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!

(Acts 9:6) So He sends him to an older man, and thinks good to have him instructed by his teaching rather than His own, lest what might have been rightly done in the case of Paul might set a bad example of self-sufficiency, if each one were to persuade himself that he also ought in like manner to be trained by the government and teaching of God alone rather than by the instruction of the Elders. And this self-sufficiency the apostle himself teaches, not only by his letters but by his acts and deeds, ought to be shunned with all possible care, as he says that he went up to Jerusalem solely for this reason to communicate in a private and informal conference with his co-apostles and those who were before him that Gospel which he preached to the Gentiles, the grace of the Holy Spirit accompanying him with powerful signs and wonders: as he says And I communicated with them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles lest perhaps I had run or should run in vain. (Gal 2:2) Who then is so self-sufficient and blind as to dare to trust in his own judgment and discretion when the chosen vessel confesses that he had need of conference with his fellow apostles. Whence we clearly see that the Lord does not Himself show the way of perfection to anyone who having the opportunity of learning despises the teaching and training of the Elders, paying no heed to that saying which ought most carefully to be observed: Ask your father and he will show it to you: your Elders and they will tell you. (Deut. 32:7).”

Notes: [1469] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 2.14–15 (NPNF II/11:315–316).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q754 “What is our stance on those who conceal their sins?”, pp. 570–571
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 754. What is our stance on those who conceal their sins?

St. Basil the Great responds, “What shall we do about him who claims that his conscience does not condemn him for the sins he is committing. Thus, the question here is specific to him who speaks to someone about repentance, while the hearer conceals his sins. It is fitting for us to remind him without aggression with the words of the Lord: ‘For there is nothing covered that will not be revealed’ (Matt. 10:26); ‘For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ (Matt. 12:34).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q697 “How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?”, pp. 530–531
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 697. How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?

Our hearts are also filled with longing for the second coming of Christ who ascended to the east and will return in the same way (Matt. 24:27, Acts 1:11), crying out with St. Methodius of Olympus: “Let us all hurry towards the east, let us be clothed in white garments and let us hold in our hands our lanterns.”

Note that this rite consists of two parts: facing the west to renounce Satan; and then facing the east to accept Christ. This was the clear and central principle found in all baptism liturgies in the early Church. Confessing the faith has a central theological importance in baptism.

First: Christian baptism was referred to as baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 8:16; 19:5) where the candidate for baptism, or his sponsor in the case of infants, confesses their faith in our Lord Jesus the Savior. Then, the person can approach the mystery of the cross and may partake in His burial and resurrection. Therefore, the confession of the crucified Christ who rose from the dead is the cornerstone of all the creeds used in baptism since the beginning of the Church, as the apostle says, “that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). The apostle considers this the cornerstone of the faith he received: “For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4). Pagans knew this, which is why their concern was to oblige the faithful to renounce Christ.

Second: Since baptism is the gate by which one becomes a member of the Church, the confession of faith is the cornerstone on which the Church is built and is the reason for her existence.

Third: The confession of faith is an entry into a divine covenant or like a signed contract with God and is kept in a book in heaven. St. Theodore of Mopsuestia says of this: “We establish agreements and covenants with our Lord God by confessing the faith. By the mediation of the priest, we are prepared to enter His house, to see Him, to know Him and for Him to dwell within us that we may be counted among the citizens of that city and are counted trustworthy.” Again, he says, “By confessing the faith, you associate yourself with God by the bishop and you enter into a covenant in which you declare that you will be persistent in seeking the love of the divine nature.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q749 “How can the soul be completely convinced that God forgives its sins?”, p. 568
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 749. How can the soul be completely convinced that God forgives its sins?

St. Basil the Great answers, “She notices within herself this tendency that says: ‘I hate and abhor lying’ (Ps. 119:163). When God sent His only Son for the forgiveness of our sins, He forgave us as long as we believe in His role. David the Psalmist sings of mercy and justice (Ps. 101:1), testifying that God is merciful and just (Ps. 115:5), so it is very important for the words of the Apostles and Prophets that pertain to repentance to be entwined within us, and also their words about God’s righteous judgments and His perfect mercy in the forgiveness of sins.”

Notes: [1452] St. Basil of Caesarea, Regulae brevius tractatae 12.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q731 “Should someone who lives in sin constantly be in tears and fear? And with what hope must this person approach the Lord?”, pp. 559–560
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 731. Should someone who lives in sin constantly be in tears and fear? And with what hope must this person approach the Lord?

The path of repentance takes the believer away from sin. Our Christ draws him back, speaks to him and gives him life so that he may see His great divine glory by His grace.

St. Basil the Great says of the soul, “In the first place, it ought to hate its former reprehensible life, and shudder and be repelled at the very memory of it; for it is written: Iniquity I hated and abhorred, but your law I have loved (Ps. 118:163 LXX). Second, let it use the dread of eternal judgment and of everlasting punishment as a teacher, that it may gain a livelier fear, and let it acknowledge a season of tears through repentance, just as David taught in the sixth psalm (Ps. 6:6–8 LXX), that the purification of its sins can be achieved through an abundance of tears in the blood of Christ by the power of his mercy and the multitude of God’s compassions, who said: Although your sins be as crimson, I will make them white as snow; although they be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool (Isa. 1:18). After it has received the power and the capacity to please God, it says: You have changed my lamentation into joy for me, you have torn away my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, that I may sing psalms to you in my glory (Ps. 29:11–12 LXX). And so it draws near to the Lord singing psalms and saying: I will extol you, Lord, since you have upheld me and have not let my enemies rejoice over me (Ps. 29:2 LXX).”

Notes: [1439] St. Jacob of Sarug, On Repentance. [1440] St. Basil of Caesarea, The Rule of St Basil in Latin and English: A Revised Critical Edition, trans., Anna M. Silvas (Collegeville, Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2013) Q. 117: p. 203.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q755 “What if a person says, “my conscience is clear”?”, p. 571
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 755. What if a person says, “my conscience is clear”?

St. Basil the Great answers, “A similar thing happens to physical sicknesses. There are many diseases that are not felt by those who have them, yet they trust the physician’s diagnosis more than their own feeling of sickness. So also, for spiritual sickness, namely, sin. If one is unaware of his sin but does not condemn himself, he ought to trust in those who can see his case clearer. This is explained by the holy Apostles who though they were very much attached to the Lord, when they heard the Lord telling them that, ‘one of you will betray Me’ (Matt. 26:21), they preferred to trust in His word and yielded to His declaration, saying: ‘Lord is it I?’ (Matt. 26:22). St. Peter teaches us, that even though he was zealous in his humility, he refused His Master, Lord and God’s ministry (in washing his feet) and so he heard the words: ‘If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me’ (John 13:8), and he was thus convinced of this truth and so said: ‘Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!’ (John 13:9).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q735 “What is the role of the tears of repentance in our lives?”, pp. 561–562
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 735. What is the role of the tears of repentance in our lives?

The first thing that sin does is to destroy one’s spiritual (inner) sight so that he loses his sight of God the Lover of humanity and the acknowledgment of the corruption he is in. Through love, the tears of repentance flow and the Lord opens the person’s sight as He did with the man born blind who washed in the pool of Siloam (John 9). Through tears, we see the divine beauty and cannot tolerate the uncleanness and corruption of sin.

St. Jacob of Sarug says, “Repentance requires me to offer her tears, for they are much loved by her. When the soul commits sin, sin destroys the soul’s love and distorts her vision, so that she does not weep for her corruption … If the soul fixed her eyes on God, regret comes quickly and opens the closed doors. She sees how abhorrent the sin she committed was and sees her weaknesses which she could not see when she committed it.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q698 “What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?”, p. 532
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 698. What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?

I renounce you. I renounce you.”

Then the priest breathes three times into the candidate’s face while saying, “Come out, O unclean spirit.” After that, the candidate looks towards the east and raises his hand to repeat after the priest: “I confess You, O Christ my God, and all Your saving laws, and all Your living service and all Your life giving works.”

Then the priest will teach him or her the faith as follows: “I believe in one God, God the Father the Pantocrator and His only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit the Giver of Life, and the resurrection of the flesh and the one, only, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. Amen.”

Then the candidate and/or sponsor are asked if they believe three times, to which they respond, “I believe” each time. All this occurs before they are baptized in the water.

Notes: [1358] Origen, Commentary on the Gospel of John (Books 13–32) 32.16 (FOTC 89:345).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q762 “Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!”, pp. 575–576
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 762. Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!

In our intellectual and elitist age this kind of objection reveals how many Christians are spiritually lukewarm. Many of our Christian youth memorize many passages from scripture, but are content merely to study and memorize them without putting them into action; without living, tasting, and experiencing them. We live in an era where everyone competes to become a teacher and not a disciple, to convict others for their sins while hiding their own personal sins and ignoring scripture itself, which although it teaches that wisdom comes from the Holy Spirit, emphasizes the importance of discipleship to the Father in confession, to live with him in Christ.

Scripture testifies that when Saul of Tarsus met the Lord, he immediately asked him: “What do you want me to do?” The Lord’s response was to direct him to a spiritual father, Ananias (Acts 9:12). Samuel, great among the prophets, was more attentive to God’s voice than Eli the priest, yet Samuel learned and was trained at his hands (1 Sam. 3:10). Cornelius, to whom the Lord proclaimed the acceptance of his charities and prayers through an angel, was not guided by the angel but was commanded to call Peter the Apostle to guide him (Acts 10:5).

Abbot Moses says, “The Lord did not of Himself instruct by the method of a Divine colloquy the lad Samuel, when chosen for judgment, but suffered him to run once or twice to the old man, and willed that one whom He was calling to converse with Him should be taught even by one who had offended God, as he was an old man, and preferred that he whom He had deemed worthy to be called by Him should be trained by the Elder in order to test the humility of him who was called to a Divine office, and to set an example to the younger men by the manner of his subjection.

“And when Christ in His own Person called and addressed Paul, although He might have opened out to him at once the way of perfection, yet He chose rather to direct him to Ananias and commanded him to learn the way of truth from him, saying: Arise and go into the city and there it shall be told you what you ought to do. (Acts 9:6) So He sends him to an older man, and thinks good to have him instructed by his teaching rather than His own, lest what might have been rightly done in the case of Paul might set a bad example of self-sufficiency, if each one were to persuade himself that he also ought in like manner to be trained by the government and teaching of God alone rather than by the instruction of the Elders.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q736 “What boldness do the tears of repentance give someone before God?”, p. 562
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 736. What boldness do the tears of repentance give someone before God?

Joyful tears that are full of hope and confidence in the Savior, intercede for the soul before God so that her hidden voice may be heard, and her broken evil will may be transformed to a good will. If sin destroys holy thoughts and buries them in the dust, the tears of repentance intercede before Him who is the Resurrection that He may revive the soul and that it may be strengthened in the Lord, experiencing the words of the prophet: “Let the weak say, I am strong” (Joel 3:10). The soul renews her inner beauty and hears the voice of her Beloved saying, “You are all fair, my love, and there is no spot in you” (Song. 4:7).

St. Jacob of Sarug says, “O repentance … the sound of your agony comes to God … pursuers hurled me with arrows of sin. Like a spear, sin is lodged within me. It is good for you, O my soul, to weep for those, for there will be a good reward for your overflowing tears.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q527 “Does the Church have the authority to forgive sins?”, p. 416
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Church: House of Salvation — 527. Does the Church have the authority to forgive sins?

The early Church considered herself a “congregation of saints” and attributed the authority to forgive the sin to God alone. Origen says, “Moreover, just as the sun and the moon enlighten our bodies so also our minds are enlightened by Christ and the Church.”

Notes: [1062] A. Harnack, Lehrbuch der Dogmengeschichte (4 ed. rev.) (Tubingen: J. Mohr, 1909): p. 439ff; and Ernest Latko, Origen’s Concept of penance (Laval,1949): p. 69. [1063] Origen, Homilies on Genesis 1.7 (FOTC 71:55).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q744 “Why does God the Lover of humanity use different ways of chastisement?”, pp. 565–566
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 744. Why does God the Lover of humanity use different ways of chastisement?

God reveals His love and providence not only when He forgives, but also when He disciplines. When He chastises like a Father, He elevates us from pampered infancy to maturity. Without discipline, we may not feel the seriousness of sin, nor struggle to live a life of holiness. Therefore, we would lose our victory and heavenly crown.

St. Basil the Great says, “We should learn, then, that it is because we have turned away from the Lord and disregarded His ways that God has inflicted these wounds upon us. He does not seek to destroy us, but rather endeavors to turn us back to the right way, just as good parents who care for their children are stern and rebuke them when they do wrong, not because they wish them harm, but rather desiring to lead them from childish negligence and the sin of youth to mature attentiveness.”

He also says, “How long will we not obey Christ who calls us to His heavenly kingdom? … This is the time of repentance and that is of receiving the reward. This is the time of toil and labor and that is of receiving the wages. This is the time of patience and that is of comfort.”

Notes: [1446] St. Basil of Caesarea, “In Time of Famine and Drought” 2, in On Social Justice (PP 38:75).

records.question: St Bishoy
records.answer:
Saint Abba Bishoy was born around 320 AD in the village of Shansa in El-Menufyia governorate. He was one of six brothers, raised by their mother after their father died young. An angel appeared to his mother, indicating that Bishoy was chosen by the Lord to serve Him all his life, despite Bishoy’s frail body, because "My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9) [1].

At age 20, in 340 AD, Bishoy went to the wilderness of Scetis (Shiheet) and became a disciple of Abba Bemwah, who was a disciple of St. Macarius the Great. He worshipped in seclusion for three years without leaving his cell, growing in virtue and love for God [1][9].

After Abba Bemwah’s death, Bishoy and Abba John the Short prayed for guidance. An angel told them John should remain in that place, so Bishoy left and dug a cave two miles away. He practiced intense prayer and fasting, tying his hair with a rope to keep awake in prayer, fasting all week and eating only on Saturdays. He memorized much of the Bible, especially the Book of Jeremiah, earning the nickname "Bishoy the Jeremian." He valued manual labor as part of spiritual life and rejected wealth, telling a rich man to give gold to the poor instead of monks [9].

Bishoy had a close fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ, who appeared to him several times, encouraging him and promising to sustain monks who love one another and keep His commandments. Once, the Lord appeared surrounded by angels, and Bishoy washed His feet with water from a basin. After the Lord ascended, Bishoy drank from that water and left some for his disciple, who was slow to drink it; when Bishoy checked later, the basin was empty [5].

Bishoy was known for his humility and love for the salvation of all souls. He had a disciple named Isaac who fell into Judaism through seduction by a Jewish woman. Bishoy prayed and fasted for Isaac’s return, and God saved him [7].

In 407 AD, when Berbers attacked Scetis, Bishoy fled to Ansena, living on a mountain near Sheikh Abbadah. There he formed a close friendship with St. Paul of Tamouh, and they prayed not to be separated in death, which God granted. Bishoy died on 8 Abib 417 AD at age 97 and was buried near Ansena. Later, his and St. Paul’s bodies were moved to the Monastery of Abba Bishoy in the Natron Valley [2].

Bishoy’s body is said to be incorrupt, a blessing given by the Lord after Bishoy carried Him in the form of an old man whom other monks ignored. The Lord told Bishoy his body would never decay [3].

Bishoy also had an encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian, where God granted them mutual understanding despite speaking different languages, and they spent a spiritually rich week together [8].

Emperor Constantine once appeared to Bishoy in vision, expressing a wish to have become a monk after seeing the honor and glory of the monastic life [8].

In summary, St. Abba Bishoy is remembered for his ascetic life, deep prayer, love for God and souls, miraculous fellowship with Christ, and enduring spiritual legacy in the Coptic monastic tradition [1][2][3][5][7][8][9].

If you want to know about other saints named Bishai or Bishoy, such as St. Bishai the martyr or St. Bishai the hermit, please ask.

retrieval.query: Who was St. Bishoy?

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — In Scetis (Shiheet)

Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it and reign with power and dominion!

St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El- Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them up. One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: ‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life.’” She answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9).

In Scetis (Shiheet):

Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple of Abba ‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 361–362
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Forsaking Scetis

Forsaking Scetis:

In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John the Short’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “Do you fear death, O man of God?” He answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell because of me!”

St. ‘John the Short’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba ‘Anthony’ where he reposed. Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain. There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose, and God granted them their wish.

St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. ‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints' bodies and buried them together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El- Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

They are now in the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy’ in the Natron Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren greatly rejoiced, and all of them set forth toward the mountain. The saint, because of his old age, was at the rear. There, he encountered an older man overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passingby monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he did carry him and walked without feeling any labor. However, the older man started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself. He then looked at Him and said: “The heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the earth; how can a sinner like me carry You?” To this, the Lord Jesus Christ smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration up to this very day. Once the brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus;

Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on a friendship level. He used to see Him, to talk with Him, and to enjoy His Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persistent in his great ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and behold, I shall always be with you!”

Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored at all!”

A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: “Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My commandments; I shall save him from all temptations!” He then blessed him and ascended.

Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted him and blessed him. The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with water in a basin, then the Lord ascended. St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water and left a portion for his disciple. The saint sought from him more than once to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai of Antioch, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI OF ANTIOCH, ST. (The martyr)

‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was ordained as a priest because of his piety. His brother and his mother went to Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to take care of their bodies. Then, he felt the longing to partake in their crowns. So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies.

The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: ‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Love for the Salvation of All Souls

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls:

Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted to Judaism and lived with her. When he happened to encounter some monks, he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something?” They answered in the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?! Nobody can overcome the tricks of Satan in women, except that one whom God is with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God saved him, and he came back and repented.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 360–361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian

An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian:

By a Divine arrangement, Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian’ came once to meet with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. ‘Bishoy’ talked in the Coptic tongue; the later sought from God to give them both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monastic experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’

After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. ‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother started to run to catch him. St. ‘Bishoy’ called him and said he would never be able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’

Emperor Constantine visited Him:

St. ‘John the Short’ once went to visit his friend St. ‘Bishoy,’ and while he was still outside his cell, he heard him talking to someone inside. Knocking on the door and entering, he found no one with the saint. Asking him with whom he was talking, he answered: “Emperor Constantine came to visit me and told me: ‘I wish I have abandoned my kingdom and became a monk; for I did not imagine how the monks enjoy such an honor and great glory. I see how those who depart were carried by the wings of eagles; and how they were received with great honor in heaven.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 358–359
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Life in Seclusion

Life in Seclusion:

When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the guidance of God. An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the Short’ should remain alone in that location. In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left the place forsaking his friend, and dug for himself a cave near the southern rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

His Strife:

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it. Then, he used to tie the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his heart; that it was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’

He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. He believed in the saying: “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.” (2 Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai Anoub, p. 355
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI ANOUB, ST. (The martyr)

He was a soldier in the days of ‘Cyprian,’ the governor of ‘Atrib’ (now Banha). When Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) stirred up persecution on the Christians, this soldier came forward and proclaimed his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He was arrested, and the governor tortured him, but when he did not forsake his faith, or deny his Christ, his head was cut off in ‘Matarieh’ in the region of ‘Ăin-Shams;’ a suburb of Cairo, on the 19th of Paona.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 356–357
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

The story of this saint reveals the fantastic plan of God for the salvation of every soul; how He uses every tool to draw them to Him, and how He sets them on the highest level if they receive His call and respond to it.

This saint, also (called ‘Peter’), was born in the village of ‘Epsona,’ a suburb of ‘Akhmim.’ In his youth, he walked in an evil path; but God did not leave him there but allowed for him to fall ill, and in a night vision, He revealed to him the place of the eternal sufferings which he was heading to. He bitterly wept, and raised his eyes to heaven and cried out: “My Lord and my God! If

you heal me of this illness; I shall repent, return to You and worship You

with all my heart.” ‘Bishai’ (Peter) was healed, and he did not forget his promise to the Lord, but he was inflamed in his heart with an intense longing to experience the monastic life. He forsook the sheep he was shepherding, and set forth to the monastery where he met with St. ‘Bigol,’ the uncle of St. ‘Shenouda’ (who was to become the Archimandrite in Mount Adriba).

His Monastic Life:

God used the illness to bring that young man out of the covetousness of the body, which would destroy the soul. Once he tasted the real spiritual life, his heart got filled with so much joy to set forth firmly and be willing to do so many labors enduring daily so many harsh sufferings with a joyful heart.

He lived with St. ‘Bigol’ in a fantastic friendship, partaking together in monasticism and worship without ever getting bored, watching the nights, and opposing the temptations of the devil.

God granted him an exalted capability beyond the limits of human endurance; he used to fast, in a way that defied imagination, for a whole month not tasting anything, and by a fantastic Divine allowance, he would stand the entire night praying. God, in His love, granted him to have the deeds of other people revealed before his eyes, which he used to support them on the life of true repentance. Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef Ĥabib, the Deacon, pp. 364–365
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF ĤABIB, THE DEACON

After the Holy Liturgy and the rites of ordination, he went back to his work. He submitted his resignation on the same day in order to dedicate all his time and effort to a better activity.

When Fr. Bishoy came back from the Syrian Monastery in the Natrun Valley after the 40 days the new priest has to spend after his ordination; he found Yousef Ĥabib had dedicated himself to serve, day and night, in that new church of St. George in the district of Sporting in Alexandra. He took upon himself, without being asked by anyone, to support Fr. Bishoy at the beginning of his ministry in a new church that had no deacons, cantor, or ministers. Yousef Ĥabib was a first-class ecclesiastical man who elaborately knew by heart all the Church hymns and sang them with the spirit of prayer in a very touching voice. With that beginning, Yousef Ĥabib became the teacher of the Church’s young men and boys and let them absorb the spirit of the Fathers. He raised them on the love of the church and her hymns. Then, when the church came to have a cantor, her beautiful choir of deacons and her affairs started to settle down. Yousef Ĥabib withdrew himself in humility and self-denial and shifted his whole effort towards a new field to revive our ecclesiastical heritage.

Yousef Ĥabib, for a long time, has been fond of the biographies of the Saints, in particular of those whose fragrant life stories had not been published before. He started to travel to the desert monasteries to search in their libraries treasures about what was hidden, and he brought to light tens of biographies and rare stories. He also used to research in the libraries of the Coptic Museum and the library of the Patriarchate, etc. He even purchased a permanent train travel permit to go back and forth to Cairo twice a week for that purpose. He used to translate, research in the biographies of the Saints and their sayings, then returned home to publish them in small booklets, to the benefit of ministry, and for the improvement of the souls.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidhom Bishai, p. 144
passages.text:
Saint: SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr)

On the 17th of Baramhat in the year 1561 AM (25 March 1844), the Coptic Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Sidhom Bishai.

Sidhom Bishai was a trader of wood in the city of Alexandria. He used to go twice every year to Damietta to purchase lumber, which was imported through its harbor. Being an archdeacon who loved the old churches, Sidhom Bishai on hearing that the wooden roof of St. George el-Muzaĥem Church in the town of Basat in the district of Sherbin had collapsed; he took on himself the responsibility of repairing the damage done and provided a full ship load of wood for that purpose. At the same time, during his visits to Damietta, he used to attend the Holy Liturgies in St. George Church. One time, it happened that a non-Christian stroked shoulder against him on his way to the church aiming to block him from going to the Church. But, seeing how muåallem Sidhom Bishai paid little attention to that evil man, he was provoked to anger and paid some street boys to insult him. Then, it happened that the Mofti of the town was passing by; and these boys falsely accused Sidhom Bishai of insulting Islam, its “Prophet” and the “Quran.” Those false accusations, finding the expected fertile soil in the Moftis ears; he chose two of equally evil people around as witnesses. Through these people, they rigged the case against muåallem Sidhom Bishai. He was then 40 years of age, well known for meekness, kind-hearted and loving for all, not at all expected to utter what they falsely claimed that he has done.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Boulus El-Booshy, pp. 376–377
passages.text:
Saint: BOULUS EL-BOOSHY, ABBA — Bishop of Babylon

Bishop of Babylon:

He is considered one of the most prominent Coptic scholars of the 13th century AD. He was born in ‘Boosh,’ part of ‘Beni-Suef’ governorate. He became a monk in a monastery in the province of ‘Fayyum’ along with ‘Dawud ibn Laqlaq’ who, later on, became the 75th Pope ‘Kyrillos ibn Laqlaq’ (1235- 1243 AD). The 20th century Dutch Orientalist fr. ‘Jacob Moyzer’ described this saint, saying: “He was an honest man, who loved his congregation, stayed away from political issues; cared only for his church. A revered scholar, long-suffering in what concerned the religious knowledge, a priest in whose heart inflamed the zealously of ‘Paul the Apostle.’ An able interpreter and commentator on the Divine sayings, to reveal their vagueness and to solve their problems. He was an eloquent religious speaker who raised the hearts of his audience to such a high level. He was a talented debater, with a sharp mind full of strong views and answers, as the soft five stones in the sac of the young man ‘David’ when he confronted ‘Goliath.’”

He was a candidate for the papacy, along with two stubborn competitors: archdeacon ‘Abu-Shaker Butros’ of the ‘hanging church’ and ‘Dawod ibn Laqlaq.’ After a scorching battle, the church was split into many parties. Abba ‘Boulus el-Booshy’ was not interested in the throne of St. Mark, and we find him instead occupied in helping his good friend ‘Dawud ibn Laqlaq’ in writing his book on “The Religious Roots and Rebuttal for the Apostatized from Faith.” However, ‘Dawud ibn Laqlaq,’ on the other hand, was so enthusiastic about that post. So, he inflamed the atmosphere of the papal election, in such a bad way that the throne remained vacant for 19 ½ years. During that time, the great majority of the bishops reposed, except for three. Finally, the battle ended with the election of ‘Dawud’ by the name of ‘Abba Kyrillos’ in June 1235 AD. However, his papacy was so filled with mistakes that brought upon the church many troubles; despite what he was characterized with knowledge and understanding. The church laws he set, and his work “The Book of Confession,” known as ‘The Book of the Teacher and the Student;’ would testify to his scholastic capabilities; even though abba ’Boulus el-Booshy’ has helped him in these projects.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidhom Bishai, p. 146
passages.text:
Saint: SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr) — Raising the Cross in Public

They brought him to the Church, where they prayed on him, then buried his body in a unique tomb on the land of the Church, which was originally a cemetery for the Copts. On the night of his burial, a shining pillar of light was seen over his tomb and so many people took ashes from his tomb for the blessing.

Finally, the relics of St. Sidhom Bishai were moved to St. George Cathedral in Damietta. And, it happened that in the year 1848, they intended to widen the church, so they had to move the body of the martyr to a special place on the south-west side of the Church, next to that of muåallem Banoub Farag and all the rest of his family. There, it remained until the year 1986. The feast of his martyrdom was continuously celebrated; until the day the Lord, intending to honor His Saint; the committee of the Church decided to move his blessed body with a grand celebration into a particular tomb in the court of the Church, in the days of the 116th pope Abba Kyrillos VI (1959-1971). One of the toes of the right foot of the Saint was placed in a tube in St. Mary Church in Dayrut.

The Wonders of God through the Saint:

Many signs appeared from the body of this saint, among which was that a rosary which was found in the hand of the saint after moving him, was offered to the bishop Abba Aghabius, who carried out the consecration of the blessed body. To get its blessing, a brother borrowed it from the bishop, but intending in secret to cut a portion of it, St. Sidhom Bishai appeared to him, unknown to the man and ordered him to bring it back; and so he did, confessed and got absolution.

It happened once that a priest, while sick, came to receive the blessing of the martyr, and on leaving, before he reached the door of the Church, he was completely healed of his illness. Many other miracles were performed with so many visitors of the city and the Church.

[The Synaxarion: 17 Baramhat]

Notes: [1] The ‘Mofti’ is a Muslim scholar who interprets the Shariåa Law…

records.question: Anthony the Great
records.answer:
St. Anthony the Great, also known as the Father of the Monks and the Founder of the Monastic Movement, was born around the year 251 AD in the village of Komn Al-Aros (Qiman El-Arous) in Egypt to wealthy parents [3][4]. After his father's death, he was deeply moved by the mortality of the world and, in 269 AD, upon hearing the Gospel invitation to perfection (Matthew 19:21), he sold his possessions, gave the proceeds to the poor, and dedicated his life to worshipping God [3][4].

He initially lived near the Nile in strict asceticism and prayer but later moved to the inner wilderness around 285 AD, dwelling in a cave on Mount Al-Kalzam near the Red Sea, where he practiced seclusion and battled demonic temptations [3]. He is credited with founding the monastic order of seclusion, emphasizing a life of solitude, prayer, and manual labor, which he learned from an angelic vision instructing him to weave palm leaves and pray [2][3].

Though he loved seclusion, St. Anthony did not isolate himself from the Church; he supported the Christian community, including Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, and visited Alexandria to aid martyrs and confessors [2][4][8]. He lived a long life, reaching 105 years, and was known for his cheerfulness and spiritual strength despite being illiterate [2][5].

St. Anthony's teachings included the importance of love for one's neighbor, discernment in asceticism, and obedience, which grants authority over wild beasts [5]. He overcame Greek philosophers by the purity of his heart and was a spiritual guide to many, including St. Hilarion and St. Serapion [6][7].

He died in 352 AD, and his legacy continued through his disciples and followers, who revered him as a model of monastic life and spiritual perfection [4][9].

This summary is based on the supplied passages; details about his early life, specific miracles, or broader historical context beyond these sources are not covered here.
