passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Church: The Kingdom of God — 471. What do we mean when we say that the Church is Catholic (universal)?

We are not referring here to a particular denomination. Rather, we mean that the Church is able, by the grace of God, to spread in many countries who accept the Orthodox faith and to be in Christ Jesus, enjoying their membership in the Church that extends from Adam to the end of the ages. Origen says that we will be astonished on the great day of the Lord when we see little children who are considered heroes, and unknown individuals among those who were considered to be saints more than many priests, servants, and missionaries.

The Church of the New Testament bears the title of universal or “catholic”: “where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcised nor uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. 3:11), since the Church includes members from all nations and peoples. Origen tells us about the universality of the Church, which is the continuity of the apostolic era, as her members preach to others as faithful apostles of Christ. He speaks in a very realistic manner of the “Teaching of the Apostles,” who, like the prophets of the Old Testament, were inspired by the Holy Spirit. He directs this definition of the apostolic continuity, against the separation of a single apostle from the apostolic community.

Notes: [947] Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles) 4 (ANF 4). [948] Jaroslav Pelikan, The Christian Tradition, 1. The Emergence of the Catholic Tradition (100-600) (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1971): p. 112.

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › (c) Exposition of the Creed — 140. What does it mean for the Church to be “catholic (universal)”?

In the water of baptism, the Holy Spirit expels the spirit of division. The Church of Christ, the One Lord, should have one faith and one Holy Spirit, working within her, despite her diverse languages and cultures. No social barriers can deprive a genuine believer from being a member in the universal Church. Multilingualism and multiculturalism cannot negate the universality of the Church.

This universality is deeply felt by every believer. The Holy Spirit sanctifies the soul, body, mind, emotions, and all the talents and gifts of the believer. Not even death is able to overcome this characteristic of the Church, for the faithful who have departed become a for us cloud of witnesses that is not far from us, nor estranged from us. The apostle Paul says, “Therefore we also, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses …” (Heb. 12:1). He also says, “raised us up together” (Eph. 2:6). Thus, the risen life has become ours in Christ Jesus. We are one — the departed with those who still struggle on earth — together with the generations yet to come. We are one family, one sanctified bride of the heavenly Bridegroom.

Whenever we see divisions within the human community, or the human family, then with a heart set aflame with love we ought to plead with the Holy Spirit to work in people’s hearts, that we might fulfil the words of the apostle Paul: “Endeavoring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all. But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:3–7).

The Eleventh Article: “We confess one baptism, for the remission of sins.”

Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

Nestorius and his followers criticized the Magi for their worship of the Child Jesus and held that His divinity was parted from Him at the moment of crucifixion.

What impact did the three Councils have on the Catechism of the Christian Sees or

the Universal Church?

All the apostolic Churches — whether Orthodox Chalcedonians, non-Chalcedonians or the Roman Catholic Church — consider these three ecumenical councils as being responsible for clarifying the faith, especially with regard to the Holy Trinity; and for the defense against many of the heresies that appeared in this period. Although there were some small disputes over the language of some expressions, these councils carried on their discussions in a spirit of love and holy zeal for the faith.

As for the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451 A. D., some apostolic Churches hold that it did not introduce anything new, but only explained and clarified the first three ecumenical councils. Our unofficial and official dialogues with the apostolic Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches and the Catholic Church in the late twentieth century brought more openness. All of them came to realize that we are not Eutychians as they had thought; that is, we do not proclaim that His humanity was annihilated within His divinity.

Thus, we achieved positive results together with our Orthodox Chalcedonian brethren.

I recall, for example, that in the first official meeting between the two families, the Chalcedonians refused to call us “Orthodox,” insisting instead on referring to us as the “Ancient Eastern Churches.” After discussions filled with love, the following occurred:

First: After many years of dialogue with a Greek theologian, I asked him: “Do you remember the day when you refused to call us Orthodox?” He smiled and said: “We feel a sense of unity with you, perhaps even more than that which we feel among ourselves, between Orthodox Chalcedonians.”

Second: A well-known priest and dear friend took the initiative of supervising the doctoral thesis for some of Copts in England. He would answer every person who accused St. Dioscorus with heresy by saying: “I have the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon in the Greek language. They witness to the fact that this St. Dioscorus was not accused of heresy, but of insulting the Pope of Rome.”

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › Coptic Art and Symbolism — 636. Are there examples of Coptic crosses found in Coptic monuments and antiquities?

a. A carved stone from the fifth century, now in the Louvre. It contains a Coptic cross (sign of life) that closely resembles the ankh used by ancient Egyptians. As for the alpha and omega, these refer to the divinity of the crucified Lord.

b. A Coptic cross, sign of life, that was depicted with two birds on both sides as a symbol of the people of the Old and New Testaments as they behold the cross as a source of life, under which they take refuge and find comfort.

c. A cross with the nails as in Figure 1.

d. Figure 2 is of Byzantine origin, found in the decorations of ancient Coptic iconostases.

e. Figure 3 is a triangular cross, also known as Botonnee or Trefflee. The four extremities of its arms are triangular and ornamented with trefoils. This type is also used by the Byzantine Church.

f. Figure 4 has three points to each point of the cross as a symbol of the Holy Trinity.

The total number of edges is twelve, representing the twelve apostles and the Holy Trinity’s kingdom in the four corners of the world.

g. Figure 5 was first found in Egyptian houses and then became the sacred heart symbol of worship and adoration in the Catholic Church.

Figure 1 Figure 2 Figure 3 Figure 4 Figure 5

h. Processional Crosses: Socrates the Church historian notes that Empress Eudoxia presented some crosses to the Church, and St. John Chrysostom used them in night processions during praises. These processions were intended to counteract what the Arians were doing. The Coptic Church now uses a gold-plated or silver-plated cross mounted on a long pole carried by a deacon at the front of the procession. Two deacons walk behind him carrying two fans that are plated with gold or silver, during every procession in church or when a bishop is entering the church.

It is important to note that the processional cross usually bears an icon of Christ crucified on one side and the icon of the risen Christ on the other side. In most cases, the procession is done three times around the church and in the third circuit, the deacon shows the other side of the cross to declare that the reason for the Church’s joy is the cross of Christ and His resurrection. The fans are usually shaped like the Cherubim, so that the procession can show that the heavenlies partake with us in our spiritual joy.

Notes: [1246] Johannes Troyer, The Cross as Symbol & Ornament Collected, Drawn and Described (United States: Westminster, 1961): p. 60. [1247] PG. 67:689.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q62 “What is the material of tradition?”, p. 72
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › Holy Tradition — 62. What is the material of tradition?

This is the essence of “tradition.” When we study tradition, we must focus on its contents which include:

a. The message of faith in the Holy Trinity and God’s saving works, and the teaching of it.

b. The acts and words of the Lord Christ.

c. The books of the Old and New Testaments and the experience of the Church Fathers and their understanding of the word of God, etc.

d. The spiritual and behavioral program in Christ Jesus.

e. The pattern of worship: its concepts and order.

f. The canons of the Church and the order of worship, such as prayers, fasting, prostrations (metanoias), feasts, etc., which are practiced in a spiritual manner for the edification of the Church and the growth of every believer’s spiritual life and personal relationship with the Holy Trinity.

passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL MAQAR, THE BISHOP — Patriarch of the Catholics and a Return to the Orthodox Church

Patriarch of the Catholics and a Return to the Orthodox Church:

The Church of Rome raised that bishop to the rank of a patriarch. However, they were genuinely puzzled when they got a surprise that Abba ‘Cyril Maqar,’ who was always studying and researching, returned to his Orthodoxy.

Assuming that Coptic Orthodox Pope ‘Cyril V’ of the See of St. Mark, would not accept him back among his children because of all what he already wrote against the Coptic church; Abba ‘Cyril Maqar’ set forth to Alexandria. There, he met with Abba ‘Vothius,’ the patriarch of the Greek Orthodox Church, and told him about his desire to join his church. The patriarch and his council rejoiced, but the Greek archons and clergy firmly asked him to reject the request.

While being in Alexandria, Abba ‘Cyril Maqar’ wrote a two-part book in French about ‘Origen of Alexandria.’ Once his application to join the Greek Church was rejected, he left to Beirut, Lebanon. There, he kept himself busy with writing. He wrote two essential books in French, which confirmed his complete conviction about the Orthodox Faith: the first he called: “The Divine Basis for the Church Foundation,” in two parts, and the second he shouted: “The Truth, at Last.” Then, he wrote a third book entitled: “We Talk, at Last,” in which he refuted some of what the Catholics published in Egypt.

Eighty Catholic families in Egypt followed their patriarch and rejoined the Coptic Orthodox Church. The most famous of whom was the family of ‘El- A´ter,’ of which ‘Francis El-A´ter’ became the archdeacon of the ‘Botrosiah Church’ built by the family of ‘Botros Ghaly Pasha’ in ‘Abu Roweis.’ It then so happened that some of the Coptic archons encountered the archon ‘Francis El-A´ter’ and spoke about abba ‘Cyril Maqar.’ The next day, they went to meet with Pope ‘Cyril V,’ who once understood the reason for their visit, he instantly said to them: “Inform Francis, that this was my desire from the very beginning, but when you hastened to go knocking on the Greek Church’s door, I preferred to keep away, because of my good relationship with patriarch ‘Vothius.’

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q628 “To what extent were Copts involved in art, especially iconography?”, pp. 479–480
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Iconostasis — 628. To what extent were Copts involved in art, especially iconography?

The Christian faith penetrated into the life of the Copts, even in their eating, drinking, literature, and arts. The Christian symbols and images that were inscribed on their rings, painted on their walls, doors, cups, glasses, plates, and chairs bear witness to this. For instance, in the Coptic Museum in Cairo, there is a Coptic ivory comb from the fifth century, on which appears Lazarus in the shape of an Egyptian mummy on one side, while Christ bearing a cross instead of a scepter, appears on the other side. Besides that, there is another depiction of the healing of the man born blind. On the other side of the comb, there is a Coptic saint enclosed within a wreath supported by two angels.

Egypt was ruled successively by the Greeks, Romans, the Byzantines … etc., who had their own cultures and arts. These rulers had their own districts inside the great cities of Egypt, where they left monuments, which are now mixed with the indigenous ones. In addition to this, the surviving Coptic monuments do not represent the true quality of Coptic art, since the most prized and valuable pieces were ruined or lost in the unceasing waves of persecution, as the historian Al-Makrizi describes. To this effect, K. Wessel says, “At the height of the medieval period, Arab writers described magnificent paintings, those of the shrine of St. Menas for example, were especially famed, but little survives.” We can therefore only get a rough idea of what once was found in abundance in the Churches and Monasteries.

Notes: [1230] Brooklyn Museum, Pagan and Christian Egypt; Egyptian Art from the First to the 10th Century A. D. (Brooklyn Museum, 1941): p. 10. [1231] Klaus Wessel, Coptic Art (UK: Thames and Hudson, 1963): pp. 160–161.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q4 “What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?”, pp. 10–11
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

ii. Paedagogus (The Instructor or Tutor), where Christ urges believers to live a better life, He being the heavenly Guide leading them to heavenly things.

iii. Stromata (Miscellanies), which is incomplete, but in which he stresses that the Christian philosopher can find everything he needs in the Gospel. St. Clement of Alexandria is considered to be among the first to link philosophy to faith. In his view, if God provided the Law to the Jews to lead them to the Savior, so He also provided whatever is true in philosophy to lead the Gentiles to the Savior.

In this way, the saint reveals to us the Christian program of evangelism. We ought not to attack others, but in love and wisdom, we should ask God to teach us how to present His Word, which is capable of satisfying souls and elevating them so that they may taste heaven.

Stage 3: The Alexandrian Fathers and the age of the ecumenical councils.

Whoever studies the first Ecumenical Councils encounters the Alexandrians as Christian thinkers who are heroes of faith and leading thinkers on an ecumenical level. The School of Alexandria played an important role in supporting the leaders of the Church of Alexandria as well as those among the congregation who were passionate about the orthodoxy of the faith and about witnessing to the Gospel of Christ at every opportunity. The Church of Alexandria was not concerned with engaging in temporal politics. Alexandria lived within the Roman Empire, under the rule of Rome, and after that, under the rule of Byzantium, until the conquest of Egypt by the Arabs. What supported them was their spiritual, pious, theological, and biblical focus. The School of Alexandria, with its strength of spirit, deep theological thought, and biblical studies, was the secret behind the strength of the Alexandrian Fathers.

The Alexandrian Fathers did not covet positions of power for personal benefit. Rather, it was the opening up of their hearts full of divine love and the depth of their studies that attracted many people to the School of Alexandria, and to the Egyptian deserts, where they learned their theology and were trained in the ascetic life under the guidance of the monks of Egypt. Since the dawn of Christianity, the Copts were known for their zeal for the orthodox faith, and they played a positive role in resolving many theological issues, both in the East and the West. They did not interfere in the problems of other Churches, nor did they intrude upon them; but with a spirit of love and unity, and through genuinely fraternal relations, they were invited to resolve such problems, or responded through the exchange of messages.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1087 “What are the communal fasts of the Church?”, pp. 239–240
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1087. What are the communal fasts of the Church?

All fasts, even if some of them bear the names of saints, like every worship, are directed to the Lord Christ. Each fast has a particular purpose that touches some aspect of our salvation and spiritual growth in Christ Jesus. The fasts are:

a. Wednesdays and Fridays (excepting the fifty days following the Resurrection and if Christmas or Theophany falls on one of these days).

b. The Paramoun fasts or preparation (before Nativity and Theophany).

c. The Nativity Fast: forty-three days.

d. Jonah’s Fast: three days.

e. Great Lent: fifty-five days.

f. The Apostles’ Fast, from the day following the Feast of Pentecost until the eve of the Feast of the Apostles.

g. The fast of the Assumption of the body of the Virgin Mary: fifteen days.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q792 “What are the main sections of the Coptic Liturgy?”, pp. 599–600
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 792. What are the main sections of the Coptic Liturgy?

The Liturgy can be divided into three services:

a. Offering of the Lamb. The Lamb is chosen from among the offered loaves of bread.

The priest anoints it with wine in the name of the Holy Trinity. The offering of the Lamb was once part of the Liturgy of the Faithful, but just before the fifth century, this rite was moved to the beginning of the Liturgy instead, in order to prepare the congregation for the renewal of their covenant with God by listening to God’s word and partaking of the sacraments. It is the beginning of the journey where the Church acknowledges the cost of following Christ. The Church offers her whole life through Christ, the true Sacrifice. She offers her life as a sacrifice to the Lord who was slaughtered for her, for the Lord accepts no less from His Church than her entire life. Otherwise, the journey becomes feeble if the Church does not pay the cost in full.

b. Liturgy of the Catechumens. Predominantly characterized by preaching and teaching, without ignoring the worship aspect. The catechumens, along with the believers, listen to the readings and the sermon, along with some prayers offered for them by the Church, for God to grant us understanding, wisdom, and faith. Thus, since the early Church, the catechumens enjoyed the Liturgy of the Word or the Liturgy of the Catechumens which prepares one for receiving the holy sacraments. For even when they have received the sacraments of baptism, chrismation, and the eucharist, they remain in need of listening to the word continuously.

c. Liturgy of the Faithful (Eucharist or Anaphora). This service is an act of worship, which includes an educational aspect, where the Church ascends to heaven by the Holy Spirit to be in the presence of God in Christ Jesus.

Notes: [1548] See Fr. Tadros Yacoub Malaty, Christ in the Eucharist. 2nd ed. (Sporting, Alexandria: St. George’s Coptic Orthodox Church, 1973). [1549] Anaphora means to “lift up” for the Church is raised up to heaven through the celebration of the eucharist.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1095 “What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?”, p. 245
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1095. What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?

The Coptic Church calendar is based on the Coptic months, but I will also provide the corresponding dates in the Gregorian calendar, although we should bear in mind that they may move by a day or two in leap years.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q791 “Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?”, p. 599
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 791. Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?

a. The Liturgy of St. Basil the Great. The Coptic Liturgy differs from the Byzantine Liturgy of the same name. This Liturgy is the one that is most often used.

b. The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian. Often used on special occasions and feasts. Prayers of this Liturgy address the hypostasis of the Son. It is not unique in doing so because there are other liturgies with the same style, such as other Egyptian liturgies, three Ethiopian liturgies, the Syrian Liturgy of Saints Addai and Mari, and the Syrian Liturgy of St. Jacob.

c. The Liturgy of St. Cyril (St. Mark the Evangelist). St. Cyril of Alexandria compiled it and edited the older Liturgy of St. Mark; so it came to be named after him. Its use is less widespread than the previous two.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q797 “How do we begin the Liturgy of the Faithful?”, p. 602
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 797. How do we begin the Liturgy of the Faithful?

“The deacon says: Stand with trembling. Look towards the East. Let us attend. The priest says: The Lord be with you all. And the people answer: And with your spirit. Then he says: Lift up your hearts to the Lord. The people say: We have them with the Lord. Then he says: Let us give thanks to the Lord. The people say: You are worthy, O righteous One. Then he begins with suitable prayers as ordained by our fathers the Apostles.”

Notes: [1560] In the Coptic rite of St. Basil’s Liturgy, the deacon says, “Stand in the fear of God …”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1088 “What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 240
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1088. What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

Ancient Egyptians developed their calendar at least as far back as 4240 B. C. The famous Greek historian Herodotus remarks that the Egyptians preceded the Greeks in correcting their calendar by adding an additional five days each year to the standard twelve months of thirty days each.

The Copts inherited an interest in the solar calendar from their ancestors, the Pharaohs, and until today, even illiterate Copts in Egypt still follow and pass on their oral traditions for the reckoning of times, by which they order the agricultural seasons, predict weather conditions, and worship using the liturgical calendar.

The Coptic year, which is of ancient Egyptian origin, is divided into twelve months, each of which contains thirty days, and to which are added five extra days at the end of the year called the “little month” or the Epagomenal days. Every four years, in a leap year, six days are added instead of five. The year is divided into three seasons with each season made up of four months. The first season is the season of the flooding of the Nile; the second is the season for sowing; and the third is the season for harvesting and gathering fruits. This seasonal structure continues to define the Coptic liturgical year in Egypt. It was also used outside of Egypt until the Holy Synod of the Coptic Church issued a decree to combine the prayers of the three seasons into a single unified litany of the air of the heaven, the fruits of the earth, and the waters of the rivers together, since in the diaspora, each land has its own agricultural conditions that are unlike those of Egypt.

Notes: [632] Herodotus. The Histories of Herodotus, trans., Henry Cary (D. Appleton and Company, 1904) 2.4: p. 86.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1091 “What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 242
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1091. What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

The Copts inherited the ancient Egyptian calendar from their ancestors, and with some slight modifications, used it to order their liturgical Church life and their daily affairs, especially agriculture. The Coptic liturgical day begins at sunset, like that of the Jews and the Greeks; and each week consists of seven days, the first of which is the Lord’s Day (Sunday).

In the fourth century, many Copts were martyred, and they therefore considered the reign of Diocletian as a golden age. They set the year in which Diocletian became emperor (November, 284 A. D.) as the first year of their calendar. They introduced the term, “The Year of the Martyrs” (Anno Martyrum), abbreviated as A. M. The scholar Tertullian said, “If the martyrs throughout the world were to be put in one side of the scales and the Coptic martyrs alone were to be put in the other, the latter would outweigh the former.”

Notes: [637] Iris Habib El-Masry, The Story of the Copts: Book 1, (Southern California, U.S.A: St. Anthony Coptic Orthodox Monastery, undated) 1.9.99: p. 100.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q790 “What are the features of Egyptian liturgy?”, p. 599
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 790. What are the features of Egyptian liturgy?

The East in general, and Egyptian Church in particular, still retains the spirit of the apostolic patristic Liturgy. The liturgical texts that are used have not changed very much since the fifth century, which gives the study of the Egyptian liturgy particular importance. In his book “The Early Liturgy,” Father Jungmann says, “especially in the general structure of the Mass, the Oriental rites have kept many primitive characteristics which have disappeared from the Roman rite … Whereas our Mass changes day after day, the Orient constantly repeats the same invariable formulary.” Fr. Dix, the Anglican monk, says, “The main lines of all the Eastern traditions had been reached before the end of the fourth century, and after this the process in all of them is no more than one of adjustment and development of detail. No new principle arose in the fifth century, as it did in the West …”

Notes: [1546] Josef Andreas Jungmann, The Early Liturgy, to the Time of Gregory the Great, trans., Francis A. Brunner (University of Notre Dame Press, 1959): pp. 211, 221. [1547] Dom Gregory Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (Bloomsbury, 2005): p. 546.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q4 “What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?”, pp. 20–21
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

e. Morsi then came to power and imagined could destroy the Church; but he was ousted and imprisoned after only one year since becoming president.

The leaders of the Church were often accused of treason against their country simply because they participated in international Christian conferences.

In brief, the Church never enjoyed freedom to move; but God has always preserved her orthodox faith, that she might work with all her strength to witness to divine truth.

Stage 9: The beginning of the immigration movement and spread of the Copts around the world since 1968.

As a result of the suffering experienced by the Copts during the previous period, many were impelled to immigrate to America, Canada, Australia, and Europe. I must confess personally that my colleagues in the Church and I considered immigration to be a way of escaping from carrying the cross. However, Pope Cyril VI often stated that these families and immigrants were sent by God to the diaspora to spread the gospel of Christ. There are many needs for the Church to fulfill, which I have spoken about on more than one occasion, especially in especially in my book, “The Memoirs of a Priest in the Land of the Diaspora” in two volumes. Now, after over half a century of the immigration movement, I feel the

need to record “The Catechism of the Orthodox Church.”

Notes: [3] See Fr. Tadros Yacoub Malaty, God (COERL, 1994).

[4] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor 1.2 (ANF 2:210).

[5] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Stromata, or Miscellanies 4:6 (ANF 2:413).

[6] St. Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen 1 (ANF 2:174) amended.

[7] Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate, St Mark and the Coptic Church (1968): pp. 25, 62; St. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 36 (NPNF II/3:370).

[8] Fr. Tadros Yacoub Malaty, Introduction to the Coptic Orthodox Church (Sporting, Alexandria: St. George’s Coptic Orthodox Church, 1993) ch. 2: p. 45.

[9] Cyril of Alexandria, Letter I (FOTC 76:15).

[10] Joseph Maurice Faltas, Ta’thir alqidis Athnasyos alrasuli fi alta’lim allaahutii lilkanisat alqibtia — alqidis bulos albushi, vol. 1 (The influence of St. Athanasius’ on the Theological Teachings of the Coptic Church — St. Boulos Al-Boushi, vol. 1) (Arabic, 2011).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1031 “How is our Christ transfigured through the fasting of the Church?”, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1031. How is our Christ transfigured through the fasting of the Church?

The purpose of the fasts of the Church is to entreat the Savior to work in all humanity.

First. In weekly fasts (Wednesday and Friday): On Wednesday, the conspiracy to crucify Christ was hatched. Therefore, the believer fasts to thank God who turns the malice of the evil to the service of salvation. On Friday the believer sees, with St. Jacob of Sarug, Mount Golgotha turned into a wedding mount where Christ offers His bride, the Church, her dowry. Thus, the fasts of Wednesdays and Fridays lead us to the day of the Lord who rose from the dead, early on Sunday morning, so that our hearts rejoice and cry out that the Lord may grant us a resurrected life that prepares us for paradise.

Second. The annual fasts:

During the Nativity Fast [Christmas Fast], the believer does not cease praying for all humanity so that the Baby in the manger (Luke 2:7) may dwell in their hearts, minds, and emotions.

During Great Lent the believer rejoices as he shares in Christ’s fast, in order to celebrate the Christian passover. Every day he prays to the Lord to pass his mind, heart, and emotions over to the heavenly life.

During the Apostles’ Fast, the believer’s heart burns with longing to share with the Apostles in preaching of the gospel of Christ.

During Jonah’s Fast, we pray for non-believers that God may work in them as He did with the people of Nineveh.

During St. Mary’s Fast, we pray that Christ may dwell in our hearts just as the Word of God was incarnate in her womb.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q873 “What is the relationship between asceticism and the ecclesiastical life?”, p. 665
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 873. What is the relationship between asceticism and the ecclesiastical life?

I have spoken often of asceticism in the Coptic Church, its theological understanding, its life of worship, and its behavioral implications. It will be sufficient, then, to add the following few points:

1. The influence of the ascetic life on the Coptic worship is clear. There are many hymns that bring joy to the soul; the Church fasts more than half of the year; her liturgies are centered around waiting for the coming of Christ with an eschatological mindset.

2. The Coptic Church is known for her numerous martyrs, to the extent that some scholars regard the fact that the Coptic Church still exists till our present day as a divine miracle. Entire cities were martyred, and the martyrs faced their persecutors with joy, waiting for their crown of martyrdom.

3. Ascetic and spiritual thought influenced Alexandrian theology, which bears a salvific mindset, so that her theology was centered around salvation (Soteriology). Theology is not about some philosophical ideas for research, as much as it is tasting God’s salvific work in the believer’s life.

4. The ascetic life does not mean being in enmity with the flesh, but rather viewing the flesh as being sacred and a helper for the soul.

5. The ascetic life paved the road to start the ascetic movements in all their forms (solitude, coenobitism, and semi-eremitism). These movements aimed for a life of unity with God, in one form or another. This is why the believers understood solitude not as isolation from people, but as solitude with God. Even if a monk lives in the wilderness alone, his heart is never isolated from the rest of humanity, but he rather bears them with love in his heart, as he prays for them and suffers with their sufferings, longing for the salvation of everyone.

6. Many Egyptian fathers resisted exaggeration in asceticism, especially if done without discernment or wisdom.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q3 “How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?”, p. 7
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 3. How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?

I greatly desired to present a Coptic Orthodox Catechism to reveal our Christian understanding concisely and briefly; particularly because, due to ecclesiastical and political circumstances, our Church was isolated from Western churches in the fifth century A. D. and remained so to a large extent up until the twentieth century, when she was accused by many in the West of adhering to Eutychianism. The Coptic Church, therefore, did not have the opportunity to reveal her true teachings through the writings of her Fathers and her liturgies. Despite the Church’s participation in many international theological conferences in recent years, insisting upon her rejection of Eutychianism, some sources continue to attribute this heresy to our Church, of which the Church is completely innocent and strongly opposes through her liturgies and praises.

In a certain dialogue with the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, theologians were surprised to observe that the liturgies and praises that we enjoy to the present day lack even the slightest hint of Eutychianism, but rather, positively oppose it in a beautifully Christian manner; especially the daily Theotokias and those of the festal celebrations. Some of the theologians observed that they harmonize with the thought St. Cyril, or that perhaps he was their author.

A Greek theologian once asked me whether we use the word “Theotokos” to describe St. Mary and was astonished to learn that it is a term beloved in Coptic texts in every age.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1080 “What is the annual Church cycle?”, p. 226
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1080. What is the annual Church cycle?

This cycle, in fact, subsumes all the days of the year. We celebrate the major and minor feasts of the Lord, the feasts of the Theotokos, the feasts of saints, the commemorations of the consecration of churches, and the annual fasts. Through all of this, we repeat in our depths the words St. Athanasius records in one of his Paschal letters: “‘Our Passover, Christ, is sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5:7). Henceforth the feast of the Passover is ours.”

Notes: [618] St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Festal Letters 19.1 (NPNF II/4:544).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q870 “Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical?”, p. 664
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 870. Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical?

The Coptic Church is known for its ascetic inclinations, not only due to the monastic movement that started in it, but asceticism is also considered one of the essential characteristics manifested in her life as a whole and her worship. These inclinations exist not because asceticism is a goal in and of itself, nor on the basis that the flesh is evil in nature; but rather on a biblical and heavenly understanding: “For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). “Go your way, sell whatever you have and give to the poor … and follow Me” (Mark 10:21, Luke 18:22). “But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

This biblical understanding was found to be sweet by the Copts, whose hearts were inflamed with eternal love.

passages.text:
THE COPTIC ORTHODOX CHURCH & THE CHRISTIAN DOGMAS — 8. DOGMAS AND KNOWLEDGE

They were steadfast and strict concerning the faith they had received (2 Tim. 1:12, 14), and some historians described them with violence, but they were genuinely loving and kind men. St. Cyril wrote to Nestorius, telling him that he would never find a person who loved him like Cyril but never would this love be at the expense of his faith [17] . He hated heresy and error but loved the soul of the heretic and desired his salvation.

The Alexandrian Fathers used theological terms to explain the divine truths and their profound meanings to defend the Orthodox faith against heresies. Still, they were not enslaved to the terms themselves. St. Athanasius, who devoted his life to defending Christ's Godhead, stated that disputes merely about words must not be suffered to divide those who think alike [18] .

It was the duty of the early Church to offer the Christian faith in Greek terms for the Hellenist world. However, some theologians believe that the Church has to express its faith not in Greek terms but in simple words that modern man can accept. Leslie Dewart, a Canadian Roman Catholic philosopher, aims to achieve a "dehellenization" of the Christian faith in God. He feels it is time that the Christian faith took on a form in keeping with the experience of modern man. To do so, it must eliminate the philosophical categories of Greek philosophy, as that philosophy belongs to an ancient past. He states that we have to exclude three terms: Ousia (essence), Trias (Trinity), and Hypostasis (Person)."

a) Concerning the term "ousia" (essence), he says that God is beyond this term. We feel God as "presence" and not as "Supreme Being."

b) Concerning Trias, he says, that it could lead to "Tritheism."

c) He suggests abolishing the term "Hypostasis" in dealing with the Holy Trinity.

The Coptic Orthodox Church is well known as a conservative church, especially in dogma and doctrines. At the same time, it developed not by embracing new doctrines or new "articles of faith," but by explaining the same faith "once given to the saints" (Jude 3) in a contemporary language. records.question: list saints who were martyred in Egypt
records.answer:
Here is a list of saints who were martyred in Egypt according to the sources:

1. Martyrs of Cairo (1389 AD) — men and women who returned to Christianity from Islam and were killed by a Muslim mob in Cairo [1].
2. Basil (martyr) — martyred around 203 AD in Alexandria during the reign of Septimius Severus [2].
3. Martyrs of the Arian Heresy — many bishops and priests exiled and some slaughtered in Egypt during the Arian controversy [3].
4. Martyrs of Mount Sinai — 38 hermits martyred by Arab raiders in Sinai in the 4th/5th century AD [4].
5. Patra (Matra) — martyred around 250 AD during the persecution of Emperor Decius [5].
6. Martyrs of Akhmim — many killed in Akhmim during Diocletian's persecution (284-305 AD) [6].
7. Arsephius and Arkias — martyred in Assiut during the persecution under governor Arianus [7].
8. Martyrs of Atrib — 1,500 believers killed by governor Alexandros in Atrib near the end of Diocletian's reign [8].
9. John of Heraclea — martyred in Egypt under Diocletian, tortured and beheaded near Assiut [9].
10. Haeremon and Ischyrion — martyred during Decius' persecution around 250 AD; Ischyrion was killed on a stake [10].
11. George of Alexandria — martyred under Diocletian, beheaded after severe torture [11].
12. Martyrs of the Serapeum — many Christians killed in Alexandria in 390 AD during pagan riots [12].
13. Salib the Martyr — crucified and beheaded in Cairo during the Mamluk period [13].
14. Ischyion — martyred during Decius' persecution, tortured severely and killed [14].
15. Martyrs of Dandara — 400 martyrs executed near the end of Diocletian's reign [15].
16. Shenouda — martyred by beheading during the early Arab invasion in the 7th century [16].

This list includes the saints and groups of martyrs explicitly mentioned as martyred in Egypt in the sources.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Cairo, pp. 122–123
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF CAIRO

At the beginning of the reign of the Circassian Mamluks (Burji dynasty: 1382-1517 AD) over Egypt, in the year 1389 AD (791 AH), a large number of men and women who were forced earlier to convert to Islam, came into the city of Cairo (El-Fustat) in a vast procession and publicly proclaimed that they have forsaken ‘Islam’ and returned to the fold of the Lord Jesus Christ. They declared that they would never change their position again, even if their necks would be cut off. They kept saying, “We came here to atone for our weak faith and our earlier denial of Christ, and we are ready now to offer our lives on the altar of sacrifice to receive the blessing of martyrdom and the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Muslim mob gathered around them and advised them to return to Islam, but the converted believers daringly refused. The Muslim mob tried to frighten them through the threat of death, but it was in vain. Then, the Muslim mob led many of them, men and women, to a public square before the “School of the ‘King el-Saleĥ,’” and there in front of everybody, they cut their necks one after the other. However, the faith of none of them was shaken. The mob took some women and tortured them, but they also held fast to their faith. So, the mob bared them of their clothes, dragged them to the valley beneath the Citadel, then cut their necks with such viciousness, that many moderate Muslims protested against those atrocities, and turned against the judge who issue such a verdict.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 234]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Basil, pp. 317–318
passages.text:
Saint: BASIL (The martyr)

There are historical accounts about a group of martyrs in Alexandria during the reign of Caesar ‘Septimius Severus’ (193-211 AD). They gained their martyrdom around the year 203 AD. Among those martyrs was ‘Leonides,’ the father of ‘Origen,’ ‘Artyrus,’ ‘Keriacus,’ and ‘Basil.’ We do not know much about those martyrs, except their names.

‘Septimius Severus’ [his name means: the 7th Cruel one], was known at the beginning of his reign for having an open mind and considerable leniency. He disregarded all the previous creeds concerning the persecution of Christians. However, his Syrian wife ‘Julia Domina,’ the daughter of one of the chief priests of the temple of the ‘Mount’ in the city of ‘Homs,’ had a severe role in changing her husband's behavior. She surrounded herself by a group of pagan religious men, and she managed eventually to stir her husband to persecute the church with extreme ferocity. It was as though the fire of persecution remained for a while hidden under the hay, and then suddenly and viciously flared up. In the days of ‘Septimius Severus,’ a multitude of believers received the crowns of martyrdom all over the Roman Empire, and in Egypt in particular. Many Christians were imprisoned, especially those who were dedicated to ministry, rich and poor. The jails turned into churches from which the voice of praise was always heard.

[Cheneau: Les Saintes d’Egypte, Tome 1, pp. 483-6]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of the Arian Heresy, p. 138
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF THE ARIAN HERESY — Among those Exiled were

Among those Exiled were:

• Bishops Amon and Adelphius, who were exiled to the Outer Oasis. • Bishops Muis, senosiris, Pilammon, Plenes, Marcos, and Athenodorus, who were exiled to Amon Oasis (Siwa Oasis), instead of being condemned to be burnt alive. • Bishop Dracuntius, who was exiled to the desert of Qalzam, near city of Suez. • Bishop Philon, who was exiled to Babylon. • Bishops Ammonius, Agathos, Agathodemon, Aplonius, Eulogius, Pavnotius, Apollon, Gaios, Flavius, Dioscorus, Heraclides, and Psain, along with the two priests Hierax and Dioscorus, who were exiled to Aswan. Then, they kept chasing them from one location to another. They forced many of them to toil in the mines and quarries. Also, they slaughtered some of them without any mercy. The bishops of Pentapolis were exiled to the Outer Oasis, while the bishops of Upper Egypt were exiled to Siwa Oasis.

This is not a complete list of the bishops and priests who were tortured or martyred, for the list wrote by Pope Athanasius was unfortunately lost. However, in another document, the names of 90 great priests were included, who were expelled from their churches. Pope Athanasius has advised that all of those who suffered should be honored by the Church on the same level as the blessed saints and martyrs.

[Encyclopedia of the History of the Copts; Part 11, Bk 4, p. 127]

[The Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 245]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Mount Sinai, pp. 128–129
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF MOUNT SINAI

During the 4th/5th century AD, 38 hermits on Mount Saini were martyred in a barbarian Arab (Saracens) raid on their area. Also, a significant number of more hermits in the desert of Raithu (by the Red Sea, about two days travel from the center of Sinai) were slaughtered in the same manner at the hands of those Arab raiders. Among the martyrs was a young 14 years old boy, who was starting a life of great strife in seclusion. When the Arab invaders found him, they threatened to kill him if he would not reveal the location of the older hermits. He told them that he did not fear death, and he was not ready to spoil his life by the sin of betraying his Fathers. Provoked to anger by his answer, they killed the young saint, and he received the crown of martyrdom. The above incidents were documented by St. Nilus of Sinai (died in 430 AD) who wrote the “Works about the Monastic Life” concerning the above slaughters in seven parts, and told about his own life in Sinai, the invasion of the Saracens’ the captivity of his son, etc.

[Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, Vol. 1, 1897, pp. 202-9: January 14]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Patra, p. 377
passages.text:
Saint: PATRA (The martyr)

St. Patra (Matra) was martyred on the 10th day of the Coptic month Mesra, most probably in the year 250 AD, in the days of St. Dionysius the Great, the 14th pope of Alexandria (247-264 AD). When Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) issued a decree committing everyone to worship the idols and to deny the Lord Jesus Christ; St. Patra set forth to the idol temple, removed the golden hand of the idol, cut it into small pieces and distributed the pieces on the poor. Finding out what happened to his idol, the emperor in great anger arrested many people; but the saint daringly came to him on his own, proclaiming that he took the hand and gave its gold to the needy. The governor gave the order to burn him alive, but God sent His angel and saved him. Then, the governor ordered to cut off his hands and feet, and to nail him upside down on a tree. A blind man took some of the blood pouring from his body and put it on his eyes and he had his sight back. Ultimately the saint had his head cut off and received the crown of martyrdom.

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt, p. 103]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Akhmim, p. 118
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF AKHMIM

After the decree of the persecution of the Christians was issued by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), Ariana, the governor of Ansenah made a tour through Upper Egypt to supervise by himself the execution of the imperial orders. Upon arriving at Akhmim on the day of the Holy feast of Nativity, Ariana found out that the Copts were assembled in the Church, with Abba Abadion the bishop of Ansenah, who was delivering to them a sermon of words of grace; because their own bishop Audacius reposed a short time before. Because the Copts were assembled in the Church and did not come to welcome him, Ariana was provoked to evil anger, and he gave the order to kill all those who were in the Church. The blood which was shed on that day ran from the Church to the streets of the city. Hearing about that massacre, those in the other towns and villages, hastened to come to Akhmim, proclaiming their faith. Before the governor Ariana, the fathers and mothers cried out with joy: “We are going to the Kingdom of Heaven,” and presented their children by their own hands to the sword and encouraged them by saying, “Have no fear; it is only moments, and you will be with Your Heavenly Groom.” It was hard to estimate the exact number of those martyrs who were killed in and outside the church on that day.

[Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 190]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Arsephius and Arkias, p. 248
passages.text:
Saint: ARSEPHIUS AND ARKIAS (The martyrs)

These two saints were martyred along with a significant number of believers in the city of ‘Assiut.' It happened when St. ‘Abaskhiroun’ was led to ‘Ansena’ to be tortured by its governor ‘Arianus,’ but because the governor has left to ‘Assiut’ to torture the Christians there, the saint was taken to ‘Assiut’ as well.

With ‘Arianus’ in ‘Assiut,’ there was ‘Maximas’ (most probable governor of Assiut), and the latter ordered that the two brothers ‘Arsephius’ and ‘Arkias’ be tied from behind, whipped then be led to the north of the city. There, they were tightly tied spread-eagle to anchors secured to the ground and left to suffer in agony, hoping that they would eventually submit and burn incense before the idols.

The two brothers endured the sufferings with joy and happiness and refused to burn incense before the idols. The governors were planning to carry them into a furnace of fire, but they found out that they already have died amid their sufferings, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.

[Church of the Virgin St. Mary, Moharrem Bek, Alexandria: The Biography of St. Abaskhiroun, the Soldier; 1977, pp. 23-25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Atrib, p. 122
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ATRIB

At the end of the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), Alexandros, the governor of Towa in the province of Atrib in the Nile Delta, attempted to convince the Copts to worship the idols. When all his trials ended up with failure, he killed 1,500 believers, and they all received the crowns of martyrdom.

[Encyclopedia of the History of the Copts, Part 11, Bk 4, p. 121]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Heraclea, pp. 429–430
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF HERACLEA (The martyr) — In Egypt

This saint was initially from Heraclea in Asia Minor. His father was a governor in the time of Diocletian (284-305 AD). He had a Christian upbringing, and when his father reposed, he was appointed to replace him when he was just twenty years of age. He eventually encountered Diocletian, refrained from worshiping the god Apollo, and rebuked the emperor. The latter cast him in prison, where the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision, encouraged him, and strengthened him.

In Egypt:

In an attempt to lure the saint to his side, the emperor Diocletian sent him to Egypt to collect the taxes for the treasury and to repair the ruined temples of the idols, a chance the saint used instead to break them down altogether.

His Martyrdom:

Later on, the saint was there with governor Keriakos while he was torturing the Christian confessors; and he saw angels placing heavenly crowns on their heads. St. John cried out confessing his Christian faith before the governor, who ordered to put him in chains and to send him to Arianus, the governor of Ansenah , along with the other confessors.

There, he was hanged on the Hinbazeen, scourged so violently that his blood was scattered all over the place; skinned; red-hot nails put on his face; tied to the tail of a wild horse and was dragged with his face down on earth. Finally, he had his hands, feet, and head cut off by the sword in Qusiah close to Assiut on the 4th day of Paona.

[The Martyrdom in Christianity; p. 131]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Haeremon and Ischyrion, p. 423
passages.text:
Saint: HAEREMON AND ISCHYRION, SS. (The martyrs)

The 14th Pope of Alexandria St. ‘Dionysius’ (246-264 AD) in his letter to St. ‘Fabian’ of Antioch about the Egyptian Christians who endured torture during the persecution by Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD); he mentioned that so many of them fled to the Egyptian deserts, where they perished out of hunger, thirst, and wild beasts; while so many others were arrested and sold as slaves. He mainly referred to the name of St. ‘Chaeremon,’ an ancient Bishop of ‘Nilopolis,’ who fled with another person to the Arabian mountains, and they have not been heard from ever since. When the brethren went to search for them, not even their corpses were found.

St. ‘Dionysius’ also referred to St. ‘Ischyrion,’ a representative of a prince in one of the cities of Egypt, who was ordered by his master to sacrifice to the idols; and when he refused to do so, he was tortured, then he was killed on a stake and he received the crown of martyrdom in the year 250 AD.

[Butler: December 22]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George of Alexandria, p. 169
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE OF ALEXANDRIA (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

When the governor knew that it was his nephew George, the one who convinced his daughter to receive her new faith, he put him under arrest. Then, he tortured him fiercely and sent him to Arianus, the governor of Ansena, who tortured him more and finally had his head cut off, and he too gained the crown of martyrdom during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). A deacon, by the name of Samuel, took his holy body, shrouded him with great respect, and took it Manuf in the province of Giza. On hearing about it, his uncle's wife took the body and buried it in Alexandria next to that of her martyred daughter. His relics now are in St. Mark's church in the city of Rashid.

th

[Synaxarion of the 7 of Hator] [OLeary: The Saints of Egypt, pp. 145-146]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of the Serapeum, pp. 139–140
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF THE SERAPEUM

When the 23rd Pope of Alexandria St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), got a decree from Emperor Theodosius I (379-395 AD) to turn the deserted pagan temple of Bacchus into a Christian church, this led the pagans to a great riot. During that time, they killed so many Christians on the streets. The pagan rebels made their headquarters in the temple of Serapis in Alexandria, from which they attacked the Christians. They caught many of them and gave them the choice, either to sacrifice to Serapis or to be killed without mercy. In that manner, they killed so many martyrs. Emperor Theodosius I proclaimed his admiration for the courage and brevity of those saintly Christian martyrs, and to honor them, he forgave those pagans who killed them. However, he issued a decree to destroy all the pagan temples on the land of Egypt. When the emperor’s decree was publicly broadcast, the pagans forsook the temple of Serapis. Then, after the idol was broken down, it was cast into the fire. The pagans imagined that as a result of the destruction of their temple and its idols, the heaven would fall, and a chaos would prevail on the whole land. However, on seeing that nothing changed, many of them proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ.

Those Christian saints were martyred in the year 390 AD, and are celebrated by the Church of the West on the 17th of March. Two churches were built on the same place of the temple of Serapis in Alexandria, which was one of the most important landmarks in the old world.

[Butler: March 17]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John XIII, the 94th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 397–398
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN XIII, The 94th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Salib the Martyr

Salib the Martyr:

One of the famous names of the Coptic martyrs in the days of that revered pope was St. Salib, whose body is still there uncorrupted to this very day. Some of his relics were moved to the monastery of Mar Mina, the Wonder-Maker in Marriott. He received the crown of martyrdom after being crucified on a wooden cross. He paraded on a camel along the streets of Cairo, by an order from the four Muslim judges, yet he remained silent, with the grace of God showing on his face a shining light. Then, he was beheaded while saying, “I lived a Christian, and so I will die.”

The Anguish from the Mamluks:

The rule of the Mamluks in Egypt has lasted for a long time (1250-1517) and was extended to Syria, Cyprus, and Hijaz, and they managed to defeat the Crusaders and the Moguls. At the same time, on the hands of these Mamluk masters, the Egyptians endured every kind of discrimination, injustice, poverty, humiliation, and huge excessive “Jizyah” taxes they had to pay. Besides, the Copts were living in the middle of the Mamluks internal revolutions, riots and disturbances; and they had the most significant share of suffering from their tyranny, through which they crushed the Christian churches and monasteries.

Destruction of the Monasteries and Churches:

Of the most famous monasteries demolished in those days were:  The ‘Quseir (Short one)’ monastery, which used to have icons of the most beautiful portraits of the Virgin St. Mary.  The monasteries of Mar John and Abu-Mina in the cave of Shaqalqil on the top of the mountain looking over the River Nile, in the province of Manfalot.  The Boctor monastery in Abnoub's quarries, the monastery of Abu-Hermina the hermit, the monastery of the Seven Mountains in Akhmim, and the monastery of Abba Besada (Beshada), the Coptic scholar.  The Nohia monastery in Giza. Some historians considered it as the most beautiful monastery and in the best location.  The Isuos monastery, which had a well called Isuos. Its water used to rise in this saint's feast on the 15th of Bashons. This phenomenon gave the Egyptians the idea of constructing a water level monitor for the Nile flood, based on the fact that the level of water in that monastery well conformed to the Nile flood level.  The Yehness the Short monastery on the top of the mountain west of Assiut.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ischyion, pp. 326–327
passages.text:
Saint: ISCHYION (The martyr)

In the days of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD), the Governor of Alexandria was so violent in persecuting the Christians. According to the historian Eusebius, this Governor started his persecution on his own a whole year before the emperor has issued his decree (in the year 249 AD).

The Christians in Alexandria were dragged to court to fall under so many kinds of tortures. It happened that one of those Christians who were on trial started to weaken when he saw those dreadful tools of torture, and he was about to collapse and deny his Christ. However, our Lord Jesus Christ did not forsake him, but all of a sudden, the man saw five soldiers, one of whom was called Ischyion, forcing their way into the court, declaring their conversion to Christianity. This incident drew the attention of everyone to find out what their intention was. They set forth to stand beside the accused Christians, proclaiming that they, too, were also disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The judge and all the audience were amazed to watch such a scene, mainly that those men carried cheerfulness on their countenances, as though they were coming, not to face torture, but to receive joy and crowns. Here, the believer who was on the brink of collapse, felt strength coming over him and got comfortable in his heart. After the judge was starting to exult in his eminent failure, everything changed when the man proclaimed his longing to endure any torture for the sake of his true faith.

When Ischyion began to testify to his Christ and to profess for Him in the court, the judge ordered someone called Arminius to torture that brave soldier by cutting off one member of his body after another. Then, they opened his belly up with a rod. In that way, St. Ischyion was martyred and was followed by his other friends.

[Cheneau: Les Saints d'Egypte; V. 2; p. 109]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Dandara, p. 124
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF DANDARA

On the 16th of Bashons, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of the martyrdom of 400 martyrs in the town of Dandara (on the west bank of the Nile, about 5 kilometers south of the city of Qena). They were executed after suffering many tortures because they were Christians. This happened near the end of the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD).

[The Synaxarion: 16 Bashons]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, pp. 137–138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA (The martyr)

He lived during the 2nd half of the 7th century when the Arab invasion to Egypt has just begun. This saint was raised in a truly Christian way. He observed a lifestyle within God's commandments and guidelines. He did not stop at fasting, prayers and attending masses, but he was also a generous giver to the poor, and always visiting the sick and imprisoned. Some evil people were annoyed by his piety, so they went to the Arab governor, claiming that the saint was mocking their religion. So, they brought him over for questioning. St. Shenouda declared that he believed in Christ, who commanded his followers to love everybody. He explained to the governor that he was just doing that, and he never made fun of any religion. The governor did not accept his reasoning and ordered him to deny his Christ and join Islam. The saint refused to proclaim his pride in being a Christian. The governor put him through so many tortures, which he accepted gladly.

Finally, they beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] [Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, vol. 2, p. 85]
