But with God this cannot be, for He is not composed of parts, passibly and invisibly and simply, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son. This, again is strongly evidenced and proved by divine Scripture. For the Word of God is His Son, and the Son is the Father's Word and Wisdom, and Word and Wisdom is neither creature nor part of Him whose Word He is, nor an offspring possibly begotten. Uniting then the two titles the Scriptures speak of 'Son' in order to herald the natural and true offspring of His essence, and on the other hand that none may think of the offspring humanly, while signifying His essence, it also calls Him Word, Wisdom and Radiance to teach us that the generation was impassible, and eternal and worthy of God [36] .

It is important to look to God not with material sight, for He is not a human being nor a creature. On hearing the titles, "the Father" and "the Son," this does not mean that God was married and brought forth another god, for there is no sex in God's essence. The Father brings forth the Son as the sun brings forth its rays, or the human soul has its mind, or light has its brightness. Even these examples cannot express what is divine. The material view created modern "feminist theology," for women feel discrimination; they ask that God be called by feminist terms, using the word "She" instead of "He" when speaking of God, but God is beyond gender so discrimination is not possible.

7. The unity of the Holy Trinity is unique, not like the mixing of material and liquid nor as the unity of man's soul and body nor as the unity of Christ's Godhead and manhood, because the Three Hypostases have one clear divine Essence. Each One fills the Others and is contained in Them but is distinguished from Them. St. Athanasius wrote,

How can the One be contained in the Other and the Other in the One? 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30, 38). He adds, 'that you may know that I am in the Father and the Father in Me' (John 14:10). Moreover, He has added this again, 'He that has seen Me, has seen the Father' (John 14:9). There is one and the same sense in these three passages. For He who is in this sense understands that the Son and the Father are one and knows that He is in the Father and the Father in the Son, for the Godhead of the Son is the Father's, and it is in the Son. The fullness of the Father's Godhead is the Being of the Son, and the Son is a whole God.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q188 “Does the Son have a will that can contradict the will of the Father?”, pp. 161–162
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Holy Trinity — 188. Does the Son have a will that can contradict the will of the Father?

On the divine will and unity of the Holy Trinity, G. L. Prestige says, “Origen observes that the will of God is present in the will of the Son, and the will of the Son is undeviating from the will of the Father, so that there are no longer two wills but one will, which single will provides the reason for our Lord's assertion that ‘I and the Father are one.’ He repeats that the Father and the Son are two ‘things’ (pragmata) in objectivity, but one in consent and harmony and identity of purpose. Athanasius follows Origen in maintaining the position that there is one will which proceeds from the Father and is in the Son, so that from this fact the Son may be seen in the Father and the Father in the Son.”

G. L. Prestige also says, “As God is one in will, so is He one in operation or ‘energy.’ This doctrine goes back to Athanasius, where it forms part of his proof of the deity of the Holy Spirit. Thus he argues at some length that, since the Father is light and the Son is the radiance from that light, the Holy Spirit, being the agent by the reception of whom mankind receives its enlightenment, must be discernible in the Son; when, therefore, we are enlightened by the Spirit, it is Christ who in Him enlightens us, since St. John has said that it is Christ who is the true light that enlightens every man. Similarly, the Father is the source and the Son is called the river that flows from that source, yet the Scripture says that we drink of the Spirit, because in drinking of the Spirit we drink Christ: and again Christ is the true Son, but it is through receiving the Spirit that we are made sons and have received the Spirit of adopted sonship. So he concludes that there is a holy and perfect triad expressed in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, which contains nothing foreign or derived from an external source; its nature is self-consistent (literally, ‘similar to itself’) and indivisible, and its ‘energy’ is one; for the Father acts invariably through the Word in the Holy Spirit. Thus the unity of the holy triad is preserved, and so one God is preached in the Church, who is over all and through all and in all; over all, as Father, the arche and fount; through all, through the Word; and in all, in the Holy Spirit.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q206 “Is the Holy Spirit separate from the Father and the Son?”, pp. 172–173
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Holy Trinity — 206. Is the Holy Spirit separate from the Father and the Son?

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “The Father through the Son, with the Holy Spirit, is the giver of all grace; the gifts of the Father are none other than those of the Son, and those of the Holy Spirit; for there is one Salvation, one Power, one Faith; One God, the Father; One Lord, His only-begotten Son; One Holy Spirit, the Comforter. And it is enough for us to know these things; but do not inquire curiously into His nature or substance: for had it been written, we would have spoken of it; what is not written, let us not venture on; it is sufficient for our salvation to know, that there is Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit.”

And St. Cyril the Great says, “our salvation [is] the work of One Divinity. And if we must apportion the gifts which are bestowed upon us, or those activities which They display about creation, to each person of the Trinity separately, none the less do we believe that everything proceeds from the Father by the Son in the Spirit.”

Notes: [413] St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 16.24 (NPNF II/7:121) amended. [414] St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel of St. John, Volume 2 10.2 on John 15:1 (LFHCC 48:364–365; PG 74:333–336).

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — THE TRINITARIAN DOGMA AND THE BIBLE (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd)
passages.text:
GOD: The Coptic Orthodox Church & The Dogmas — THE TRINITARIAN DOGMA AND THE BIBLE

The Trinitarian dogma is the first of all biblical dogma [24] . The Holy Trinity is referred to at Jesus' baptism (John 1:27-33). Our baptism too is performed in the name of the Three Hypostases, according to St. Matthew (28:19). St. Paul's benediction enumerates them in 2 Cor. 13:14. The Three are spoken of in John 14:16; Eph. 2:18; 1 Pet. 1:21, 22; etc. The works and the titles of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit declare Their divinity as we will later see. After light was thrown on the nature of God by New Testament revelation, Christians began to see that in the Old Testament there is not much light thrown upon God, which points to His tri-hypostases. One of them is the Trisagion (holy, holy, holy) of Isaiah's vision in 6:3, when coupled with the "who will go for us?" in 6:8. Another is the plurality of persons (hypostases), possibly implied in the plural "Elohim" (God), often used, even in the Deuteronomy 6:4 "unity" passage; and certainly suggested in such passages as "let us make man in our image" (Gen. 1:26) and "let us go down, and there confound their language" (Gen. 11:7).

Truly, in the Old Testament, the dogma of the Trinity was not clear, for the Jews were surrounded by many nations who worshipped idols, and they themselves sometimes worshipped the false gods of their neighbors. Certainly if God had revealed this dogma openly they would have misunderstood it and believed in polytheism. Moreover, there was no need to accept this dogma before the Incarnation of the Word of God and the descent of the Holy Spirit on the Church.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q192 “How do the Hypostatic characteristics constitute the divine essence?”, p. 166
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Holy Trinity — 192. How do the Hypostatic characteristics constitute the divine essence?

Hypostatic characteristics reveal the relationship between the three Hypostases —that there is no separation between any one and the other two — while at the same time clearly distinguishing each Hypostasis. It cannot be said that the Father is a Son or a Holy Spirit, etc. That would be to fall into Sabellianism, the heresy of Sabellius, which claimed that God the Father Himself appeared by taking the form of the Son to perform the work of salvation, and takes the form of the Holy Spirit in the performance of baptism. In Sabellius’ view, the three Hypostases are nothing more than three modes of appearance of a single Hypostasis.

In saying that there are three Hypostases in one essence, we are certainly not saying that each Hypostasis is one part, which, put together with the other parts, makes up the one divine essence. Each Hypostasis is complete in itself — not a part of an essence — and inseparable from the other two distinct Hypostases.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q204 “Why did some Fathers use the expression: “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son?””, p. 172
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Holy Trinity — 204. Why did some Fathers use the expression: “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son?”

This expression confirms that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father eternally, just as the Son is born of Him eternally. When they say “through the Son,” they do not mean that the Son is inferior to the Father, but that the Spirit proceeds from the Father as a divine Hypostasis and is sent by the Son to give enlightenment and knowledge of divine mysteries; so that by Him, we enjoy the perfection of His work of salvation through our continuous sanctification and renewal.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q187 “How can we understand the oneness of the Holy Trinity?”, p. 161
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › The Holy Trinity — 187. How can we understand the oneness of the Holy Trinity?

Everything is arranged, therefore, according to its power and merits. There is one Power from whom are all things, one Offspring through whom are all things, and one Gift of perfect hope. Nor will anything be found wanting to a perfection so great within which there is found in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: infinity in the Eternal, the form in the Image, and the use in the Gift.”373

Notes: [371] St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Four Discourses Against the Arians 3.23.5 (NPNF II/4:395–396). [372] St. Athanasius of Alexandria, The Letters of Saint Athanasius Concerning the Holy Spirit to Bishop Serapion, trans. C. R. B. Shapland, (Epworth Press, 1951), Epistle 1:14: pp. 93–94.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: THE ORTHODOX CONCEPT: TRADITION AND ORTHODOXY — TRADITION AND COUNCILS (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-yspaf)
passages.text:
THE ORTHODOX CONCEPT: TRADITION AND ORTHODOXY — TRADITION AND COUNCILS

In the 1 st century, the apostles assembled together in Jerusalem (Acts 15) to study the problem of accepting the Gentiles in the new faith and to give a Church decision matching Christ’s mind. It is the responsibility of the church Fathers to assemble in local or ecumenical councils to study the needs of the present church and to preserve its traditional life through new circumstances. They do not give individual but collective opinions. They assemble under the guidance of the Holy Spirit in one mind to satisfy their people’s needs. For example, they must study how to explain the church doctrines and dogmas to modern man and how to strengthen their people against every heresy or materialistic philosophy. They also discuss the pastoral and preaching needs and the church ecumenical role, etc....

In other words, it is the Fathers’ responsibility to preserve the Church’s traditional role as an active life with its spiritual effects, both locally and ecumenically.

records.question: Give me a short summary of the life of St. Moses the Black
records.answer:
St. Moses the Black was born between 330 and 340 AD, likely from a Barbarian tribe, and lived a life of extreme evil, becoming a gang leader involved in robbery and murder [1]. He experienced a profound conversion after hearing a voice urging him to meet the monks of Scetis, where he met St. Isidore, confessed his sins, and was guided to repentance and baptism by Abba Macarius the Great [1][3]. He became a monk, enduring intense spiritual struggles and ascetic practices, and was eventually ordained a priest by Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD) despite initial rejection due to his past [2][3][5].

St. Moses was known for his humility, love, and miracles, and he taught forgiveness and mercy among the monks [2][4]. He was martyred in 408 AD when Barbarians attacked the monastery; he and seven brethren were killed, and he is remembered as the first martyr of Scetis [4]. His life earned him three crowns: for love and asceticism, monasticism and priesthood, and martyrdom [4]. He left many spiritual teachings emphasizing repentance, humility, and love for neighbors [7][15].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 249–250
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

Not much is known about the past of St. Moses the Black before his repentance. He was most probably one of the Barbarian tribes. His life was so evil that it was said that there was no sin he did not commit. He was born between the years of 330 and 340 AD. It seems that he was a slave of a head of a tribe that worshipped the sun, but because of his extreme evil nature, his master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become the head of an evil gang.

Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ:

Even though an extreme evil-doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking from it to proclaim itself to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened to meet with St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells) coming out of his cell and heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: “What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “I heard that you are a good servant of God. Therefore, I escaped and came to you to let God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins and my great evils.”

St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he has been. Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to contemplate.

For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a loud voice, he confessed all his evil crimes again, with such contrition of heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 252–253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Ordained as a Priest

Ordained as a Priest:

Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: “Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said to him: “There you became all-white Moses.” He responded by saying with humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.”

His Virtues:

He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, but it happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.

Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticism, he was granted by God to perform miracles and signs.

A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from going. When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the wilderness.

Moses stood in the church and confessed publicly about all his sins and evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became allwhite. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would leave it, all evil will come back to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your feet.”

His Strife:

St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macarius to find for him a secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept counseling him to stand fast until the devil would get tired of him. He gave him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it.” Father. Abba Isidore took him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Virtues

When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a week. During that week, some guests came to visit Fr. Moses. He prepared food for them to eat. On seeing smoke rising from his cell, the brethren said to one another: “Look, Moses has broken his fast and is preparing food for himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they said to him: “Father Moses! You have disregarded the commandment of men, but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”

His Martyrdom:

Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” He told them: “There, they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred monks. Then, he hastened to come down and ran forward to receive his crown of martyrdom.

So, Abba Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, when he was seventy-five years old (or eighty-five). He earned three crowns: the 1st for love and intense asceticism, the 2nd for monasticism and priesthood, and the 3rd for martyrdom. He was counted the first martyr in the Scetis, and he had so many great teachings. His body was kept along with that of his spiritual guide Abba Isidore in one tube at the Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 251–252
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Strife

There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly angels, about whom the saint said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and returned to his cell.

Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks at night, take their water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to move, until some brethren happened to come to the well, and they carried him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he regained his ability to move.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and carried them to the church. When the thieves realized that he was Moses, who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.

Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. Abba Isidore told him that, to keep him from thinking that by his ascetic efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual repentance, God would fight on our behalf.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, p. 258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands

If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take the monk to the nearest location of the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.

Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not having a steady residence, teaching, preaching, and converting multitudes to Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in the year 372 AD.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

[Baring-Gould: February 7]

Notes: [2] These tribes were known by the name ‘Saracens’… It is worth mentioning that the name ‘Saracens’ was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 254–255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6)” • Then, the brother asked: “If a man beat his servant for something wrong he did, what should the servant say?” The saint answered: “If he was a good servant, he would possibly say: ‘Have mercy on me, for I made a mistake.’ Thus, he would blame himself and draw the mercy of his master.” • In general, a man should never condemn his neighbor. When in the Old, the hand of God came heavy on the firstborn of the Egyptians, there was no house without a dead son in it. For us, it meant that we should concentrate on our sins and not worry about those of our neighbors, for it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor.

To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad about his neighbor, because it would make you fall in condemnation. Do not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This would bring you peace.

[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria- Diocese of Los Angeles] [Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of OrthodoxWiki]

[Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of Wikipedia]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, pp. 255–256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.

Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to spend the night at her place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.

[The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Confessor, p. 257
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE CONFESSOR

This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, at the start of the heresy of Novatian. The rest of the confessors were: Fr. Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the system and wrote another message to Cyprian.

After spending about a year in prison (eleven months and few days), St. Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views as unorthodox.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948]

[Baring-Gould: November 25]

Notes: [1] ‘Novatian’ was a Roman bishop and theologian of the 3rd century who took a strict position on readmission of apostates during the persecutions at the time…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, pp. 257–258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — The Tribes of Saracens

The Tribes of Saracens:

The Arabian tribes populating the area of Rhinoclura in-between the eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes joined forces together and formed one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.

Choosing Moses as a Bishop:

Those Christian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be their bishop. Then, when Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those united tribes.

Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands:

On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then, St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, p. 255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went deep in the wilderness and lived for thirty-five years in a spot having olive and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended the wild beasts.

His Multiple Falls and Repentances:

Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the devil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, pp. 240–241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — The Bitterness of Anguish

St. Moises (Moses) was one of the prominent fathers and saints of the church in the 8th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.

St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Scetis, where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox faith. He used to spend most of his time in worship, that it was said that he did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

The Bitterness of Anguish:

During his bishopric, the Umayyad rulers of Egypt subjected the Copts to extremely severe persecutions, and great anguish dwelt upon the church. The bishops returned to their monasteries to concentrate on prayers and fasts, imploring God to lift that anguish. However, St. Moises remained among his people to encourage them and to keep them holding fast to their faith against the snatching wolves. St. Moises also got the grace to perform miracles and signs, healing sicknesses, as well as the grace of prophecy.

Due to these intolerable persecutions at the time, the number of Copts who converted to Islam reached 24,000 persons. When some archons came to seek from St. Moises to pray to the Lord to lift the anguish from His people, he told them: “My children, be assured that the governor who is persecuting you will perish within this month,” and this was what did happen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — Imprisoned along with the Pope

Imprisoned along with the Pope:

The last of the Umayyad caliphs Marwan ibn Muĥammad (Marwan II: 744-750 AD), arrested the 46th Pope of Alexandria, St. Khael I (743-767 AD). Bishop Moises stayed in the company of the pope, and he longed to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When the soldiers brought them to the tent of Marwan, they forced St. Moises on his knees, raised his feet, and beat him with bronze clubs on his sides and neck. His tormentors were seeking from him a bribe to set him free. The saint did not utter a single word, for he did not understand their Arabic language. When Marwan gave the order to cut the head of Pope Khael I, and the swordsman led him to the place of execution, St. Moises ran after him, despite the attempts of the swordsman to keep him away. An angry soldier intended to kill him if it was not for some officials who did not let him do it. Then, he was cast in prison along with Pope Khael I, and their feet were placed in chains, among many others. However, St. Moises prophesied that they would eventually come out safe from that prison, which was realized when Marwan was defeated by the Abbasids dynasty.

His Prophesy concerning the Umayyad Caliphate:

During the revolt of the Coptic Bashmurians (Coptic rebels) due to the intolerable Umayyad persecution, St. Moises disciple asked him a question concerning when that calamity would come to an end, the saint prophesied: “God will not forsake His church to the end, but He will save her, and this caliphate (of Umayyad) will vanish and be replaced by some other.” This prophecy was realized in 750 AD when the Umayyad dynasty was replaced by the Abbasids.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

Abba Moises continued to accompany Pope Khael I, faithful to him and to the church all along during the bitter tribulations. Then, when he completed his strife and was in a right old age, he had a short illness and knew the time of his departure. So, he called his congregation, blessed them, commanded them, and asked them to pray for him. They all wept and asked him to remember them before Christ. He stretched out his hand, prayed, bid them farewell, and departed in peace.

The Church of Saint Mina in Marriott:

Bishop Moises was with pope Khael I when the Chalcedonians (Melkites Byzantine Christians) tried to take possession of the great church of St. Mina in Marriott to take away its marble pillars and adornments. They bribed the caliph Marwan II and asked him to issue an order to Ăbdel Malek ibn Mousa, the governor of Egypt, to give them the possession of St. Mina's church in Marriott. When the decree was delivered to Ăbdel Malek, he held a council under a judge by the name of Ăyssa to decide who had the possession of that church, and he asked the two parties to defend their rights before him. Here, Pope Khael I asked the most prominent of his bishops and archons, including St. Moises, to attend the governor's council. Still, as the Chalcedonians bribed the judge, he took the stand against the Orthodox Copts and refrained from listening to their defense. Some archons suggested paying a bribe to the judge to take their side, but St. Moises rejected such a counsel, saying that it would not befit for the pope or the bishops to pay bribes to anyone, and he prophesied that God would never forsake them. Then, when judge Ăyssa was about to write his verdict in favor of the Chalcedonians, he was fired from his position and was replaced by another judge called Abu el-Ĥuseiny, who happened to be just and honest. The new judge issued his verdict in favor of the Copts, and the Copts kept St. Mina church in their possession.

The church celebrates him on the 11th of Mesra.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 57]

[The Synaxariun: 11 Mesra] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Kha’il I, by Subhi Y. Labib, pp. 1410-2]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 253–254
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

Of his Sayings:

• To a brother in the Scetis who sought from him a word of encouragement, he said: “Go and sit in your cell, it will teach you everything.” • The man who flees from the world is like ripe grapes, but he who dwells among the distractions of men is like sour grapes. • If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I promise you that the Barbarians would never come here, but if we do not, this place will soon become desolate. • According to Fr. Poemen, Fr. Moses was once asked: “How can a man become like dead to his neighbor?” The older saint said to him: “Unless a man keeps in his heart that he has been three days in the grave, he will not be strong enough to do that.” • It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbor, and he should not condemn him in anything. • It is good for a man to die to every work which is evil before he departs from the body, so as not to offend anyone. • Unless a man feels in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not listen to him. A brother asked him about the meaning of that, and the saint said: “Whoever focuses on his sins, would never see those of his neighbor.” • Unless your prayers conform to your behavior, your struggle would not be of any benefit. When the saint was asked to explain, he said: “We should apply what we pray about, for when man forsakes his own will, he reconciles with God and God will listen to his prayers.” • A brother asked him: “What would help the man in his every endeavor?” He answered him: “God is the One who helps, for it is so written: "God is our refuge and strength. A very present help in trouble" (Psalm 46:1).” • When the brother added: “What then is the benefit of fasting or spending sleepless nights, father?” The saint answered: “These practices make the soul meek and humble, for it is written: "Look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins" (Psalm 25:18). So, once the soul reaps the fruits of these practices, God would have compassion on her.” • Then, the brother asked: “What will man do with every temptation he encounters or every evil thought coming to him?” The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?"

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises and his Sister Sarah,, pp. 239–240
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES AND HIS SISTER SARAH, (The martyrs) — Their Martyrdom

These two saints were born to wealthy Christian parents. When their parents passed away, St. Moises (Moses) intended to become a monk after giving his sister Sarah in marriage and handing their whole wealth to her. However, when he discussed the idea with his sister, she responded to him by saying: “If you get married first, then I would follow suit.” He told her: “I have committed so many sins, which I intend to atone for by leading a monastic life, for I cannot get married and care for my salvation at the same time.” She answered him: “How would you cast me in the snares of this world, and care only for your salvation?” Then, he answered her: “Whatever you choose will be yours.” She responded: “All that you would do, I shall also do, for we are of one father and one mother.” Then, they distributed all their wealth to the poor and the needy. St. Moises brought his sister Sarah into a house of virgins, and he joined a monastery near Alexandria, and for the following ten years, they did not see one another.

Their Martyrdom:

Then, when Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) incited persecution against the Christians, in the days of the 14th Pope St. Dionysius the Great (246-264 AD), so many believers were martyred. At that time, St. Moises sent to his sister to bid her farewell, and let her know of his decision to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. She hastened to her mother-superior, sought to be released, got the blessings of her sisters, and joined her brother on his way to Alexandria. There, they both confessed together the Lord Jesus Christ, and after being tortured by many tools, they had their heads cut off by the sword, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Mesra]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1070 “What tunes are used by the Coptic Church in her worship?”, pp. 216–217
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Church Hymns605 and the Heavenly Mindset — 1070. What tunes are used by the Coptic Church in her worship?

There are five tunes that the Church uses in worship:

a. The Annual tune. Used on regular days throughout the year.

b. The Hosanna tune [Arabic: Sha’aniny]. Used on Palm Sunday when the multitudes, children, and infants welcomed the Lord Christ as He entered Jerusalem. “Hosanna” is a Hebrew word that means “save us.” The Lord Christ entered Jerusalem as the Lamb of God who carries the sin of the world, offering Himself as a sacrifice on the cross. It is also used on the Feasts of the Cross.

c. The Paschal tune. Used in Passion Week, it expresses a kind of awe of the crucified and risen Lord who grants the soul peace. The mystery of this tune lies not in asceticism in food and drink, but rather in the desire to repent from sins. Some call it the “Mournful tune” [Arabic: Hazainy] but this term was not known to the Church of the first five centuries.

d. The Kiahk tune. Used in the month of Kiahk, in which we remember St. Mary, to whom the Archangel Gabriel announced the incarnation of the Word by the work of the Holy Spirit who would descend upon her and prepare her for the fulfilment of this annunciation. We, too, in the Nativity Fast, proclaim our longing to fix our eyes on His kingdom that is within us (Luke 17:21), yearning for the Word of God to be formed in all humanity, that we may all become a heavenly bride for the heavenly Bridegroom. During this month of Kiahk, the Church proclaims her joy at the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ: this birth that elated the inhabitants of heaven as He revealed to them the mystery of His divine wisdom for the salvation of faithful humans.

e. The Joyful Tune. Used for major and minor feasts of the Lord, as well as during the Holy Fifty Days after the Resurrection, the period from Nayrouz (the Coptic New Year) to the Feast of the Cross, and from the Feast of Nativity (Christmas) to the Feast of the Circumcision. Our souls exult in the salvific work of the Lord Christ; whether in His birth, transfiguration, resurrection, or ascension to heaven. This work is strongly evident in the lives of the martyrs whom we celebrate from the day of Nayrouz to the glorious Feast of the Cross each year.

Notes: [607] Cf. David Arida’s Hymnology.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1068 “Why do we cherish Coptic Church Hymns? Is it permissible to translate them into the language understood by the people?”, pp. 214–215
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Church Hymns605 and the Heavenly Mindset — 1068. Why do we cherish Coptic Church Hymns? Is it permissible to translate them into the language understood by the people?

First: Our pride in our Coptic Church Hymns does not mean that we should belittle or ignore the Church Hymns of other traditions, such the Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, or others. At the same time, we must consider those faithful who participate in worship, and we must make the effort to translate these Church Hymns into the languages spoken by the local people, as currently happens in the diaspora.

Second: The ancient pharaohs believed in a kind of heavenly afterlife in another realm, although this belief was corrupted by some errors. Thus, the children of the pharaohs, the Copts who were attracted to the Christian faith, adopted pharaonic melodies and gave them a deep and heavenly tint. Some people even say that they “baptized” these melodies. Also, some of the Church Fathers eliminated the heresies that troubled the Church through songs and Church Hymns for the congregation that employ expressions that communicate the true faith.

Besides all this, the Copts were inflamed with love for heaven and quiet worship. The large number of vowels in the Coptic language gives it a kind of sweetness and flexibility in hymnology. I recall, for example, that a young man, an army officer, was staying with a non-Christian officer in a tent in the desert of Marsa Matruh. As he was washing his face one morning, he was humming one of the Church Hymns from the Holy Week. His colleague asked him, “What is that beautiful song?” The Christian asked him, “How does it make you feel?” He responded, “It has a sad tune, but it gives peace to whoever hears it.” He then asked the Christian to sing it with words, and the non-Christian felt an amazing peace.

A man in New Jersey told me he had a little boy who had not yet learnt to speak, whom he was taking to the Pascha prayers. After several days, he found him humming the hymn of “Thine is the power” from Holy Week, without being able to pronounce a word of the hymn.

Third: We cannot deny that when the early [Coptic] Church spread to Ethiopia it did not force them to adopt the simple musical tradition of the Copts, even if some Ethiopians enjoyed our Coptic Church Hymns. Also, during conferences with our beloved [Christians] of other denominations, some of our bishops and priests liked some hymns from other traditions so much — Syrian tradition, for example — that they began to sing them in their own time and in their private prayers.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q791 “Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?”, p. 599
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 791. Which eucharistic Liturgies does the Coptic Church currently use?

a. The Liturgy of St. Basil the Great. The Coptic Liturgy differs from the Byzantine Liturgy of the same name. This Liturgy is the one that is most often used.

b. The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian. Often used on special occasions and feasts. Prayers of this Liturgy address the hypostasis of the Son. It is not unique in doing so because there are other liturgies with the same style, such as other Egyptian liturgies, three Ethiopian liturgies, the Syrian Liturgy of Saints Addai and Mari, and the Syrian Liturgy of St. Jacob.

c. The Liturgy of St. Cyril (St. Mark the Evangelist). St. Cyril of Alexandria compiled it and edited the older Liturgy of St. Mark; so it came to be named after him. Its use is less widespread than the previous two.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1071 “Why are Church Hymns sometimes chanted in an abbreviated short tune and sometimes in a long tune?”, p. 217
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Church Hymns605 and the Heavenly Mindset — 1071. Why are Church Hymns sometimes chanted in an abbreviated short tune and sometimes in a long tune?

In the early Church, there were no churches in some villages, and many people would attend their nearest church from sunset on Saturday until the morning or dawn of Sunday to participate in the divine liturgy. The faithful would praise throughout their journey from their village to the church in town, and also after evening Vespers until the beginning of Matins in the morning, so that those present would not be distracted with temporal matters. Longer tunes were clearly useful in these circumstances. But the Church arranges worship according to the circumstances of her people.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q792 “What are the main sections of the Coptic Liturgy?”, pp. 599–600
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 792. What are the main sections of the Coptic Liturgy?

The Liturgy can be divided into three services:

a. Offering of the Lamb. The Lamb is chosen from among the offered loaves of bread.

The priest anoints it with wine in the name of the Holy Trinity. The offering of the Lamb was once part of the Liturgy of the Faithful, but just before the fifth century, this rite was moved to the beginning of the Liturgy instead, in order to prepare the congregation for the renewal of their covenant with God by listening to God’s word and partaking of the sacraments. It is the beginning of the journey where the Church acknowledges the cost of following Christ. The Church offers her whole life through Christ, the true Sacrifice. She offers her life as a sacrifice to the Lord who was slaughtered for her, for the Lord accepts no less from His Church than her entire life. Otherwise, the journey becomes feeble if the Church does not pay the cost in full.

b. Liturgy of the Catechumens. Predominantly characterized by preaching and teaching, without ignoring the worship aspect. The catechumens, along with the believers, listen to the readings and the sermon, along with some prayers offered for them by the Church, for God to grant us understanding, wisdom, and faith. Thus, since the early Church, the catechumens enjoyed the Liturgy of the Word or the Liturgy of the Catechumens which prepares one for receiving the holy sacraments. For even when they have received the sacraments of baptism, chrismation, and the eucharist, they remain in need of listening to the word continuously.

c. Liturgy of the Faithful (Eucharist or Anaphora). This service is an act of worship, which includes an educational aspect, where the Church ascends to heaven by the Holy Spirit to be in the presence of God in Christ Jesus.

Notes: [1548] See Fr. Tadros Yacoub Malaty, Christ in the Eucharist. 2nd ed. (Sporting, Alexandria: St. George’s Coptic Orthodox Church, 1973). [1549] Anaphora means to “lift up” for the Church is raised up to heaven through the celebration of the eucharist.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q800 “What does the Church focus on during the partaking of the Holy Mysteries?”, pp. 603–604
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 800. What does the Church focus on during the partaking of the Holy Mysteries?

While partaking of the Holy Mysteries, the Church is concerned with praise in the spirit of the Bible. The Church used to warn against the songs that heretics composed to spread their corrupt teachings. This is what Arius and his followers did. It was said that because the music of these songs was so attractive, the people liked it and used to sing it in public markets. This drove St. Athanasius and those who were working with him to compose alternative hymns, to preserve the true faith.

“Those who sing on the altar should not sing as to show off their voices, but in wisdom. They should not sing anything but the Psalms (or anything outside of Scripture). And if some of them sang something that they composed themselves or something that they heard from others that is not written in the Psalmody, let them be cast out. If the readers read from foreign books and defiled the ears of the congregation, let them be cast out.”

Notes: [1564] Monastery of the Syrians, St. Basil the Great: His Life, Asceticism, and Church Canons (Arabic) (St. Mary’s Monastery (Deir al-Sourian), 2003): p. 545.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1069 “Are rites and Church Hymns necessary in the Church? Do they impact on our salvation and eternity?”, pp. 215–216
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Church Hymns605 and the Heavenly Mindset — 1069. Are rites and Church Hymns necessary in the Church? Do they impact on our salvation and eternity?

Third: A beloved brother from East Brunswick wrote, “The hymns and rites of the Church are powerful and beautiful instruments that make us cling to God and allow us a glimpse of the heavenly life. The Fathers used various musical tunes and rites during the different seasons of the Church — whether feasts or fasts — that allow us to experience the spirituality of the prayers and mysteries of our worship.

“This is especially evident in the rite of Bright Saturday (Apocalypse Night) when the faithful gather together and keep vigil all night by the tomb of Christ, bearing witness to the victory of the Cross over the darkness of the abyss. In the first prayer that the priest chants at the royal door of the sanctuary, next to the tomb, he sings Psalm 151: “I was small among my brothers.” The Church is explaining to her children who are practicing the rites of Bright Sunday that although the appearance of the cross shows Christ’s weakness as He submits Himself to death, it is He who destroyed death. Then the believers stand up and walk in a procession around the church, holding candles to announce that Christ is the light that dispels darkness. Every moment of this night is a living lesson that inflames the hearts of the faithful and strengthens their faith. We proceed from all the stories of salvation (Susanna, the three youths in the furnace of fire, Daniel in the lions’ dens, etc.) to wonderful hymns that proclaim the power and divinity of Christ; like the melody of Agios Athanatos Nai Nan, which means, ‘Holy Immortal, have mercy on us,’ until we reach heaven through the readings and hymns of the Book of Revelation. This is how the Church sets out with her children from the tomb of Good Friday to the heavenly Jerusalem, and the celebrations of the Resurrection.”

This is an example of the beauty of the rites, the readings, and the Church Hymns of Bright Saturday. In the chapter on the “Coptic Calendar,” I will talk more about Church Hymns, rites, and readings, and how they disclose the meaning behind each occasion that pertains to our salvation, spiritual growth, and the living testimonies to the work of the Holy Trinity for the sake of our eternity.

Notes: [606] See Deacon Mina Azer’s English article on Church Hymns.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1095 “What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?”, p. 245
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1095. What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?

The Coptic Church calendar is based on the Coptic months, but I will also provide the corresponding dates in the Gregorian calendar, although we should bear in mind that they may move by a day or two in leap years.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q652 “What other utensils are used?”, pp. 492–493
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Holy Utensils — 652. What other utensils are used?

a. A small box for incense, usually made of silver or carved wood.

b. The ewer and basin that are used for washing the hands of the priest during liturgical services.

c. The basket of the oblation is a small basket in which the holy bread is placed, one of which the priest chooses as the “Lamb” to become the Body of Christ.

d. Musical instruments: Coptic hymns, first and foremost, rely on the one natural instrument: the human voice. However, we use some primitive instruments such as the triangle and cymbals.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1077 “What is the daily Church cycle?”, p. 225
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1077. What is the daily Church cycle?

d. The Ninth Hour (None): At this hour, we remember the acceptance of the righthand thief and the death of Christ in the flesh. It is an apostolic tradition, for the apostles Peter and John went to the temple to pray at the time of the ninth hour (Acts 3:1).

e. The Eleventh Hour (Sunset, Evening, or Vespers): At this hour, we remember the taking down of the body of Christ from the cross. We also thank God that we have completed the day in His care, for His gifts, and for all He has done for us and within us, while confessing our failures.

f. The Twelfth Hour (Compline or Before Sleeping): At this hour, we remember the burial of the body of Christ and we also remember that we too must one day fall asleep and depart from this world. We also pray that we may find rest in our sleep without disturbance or terrifying illusions.

g. The Midnight Prayer: We receive this prayer from saints Paul and Silas (Acts 16:5). The psalmist says, “At midnight I will rise to give thanks to You, because of Your righteous judgments” (Ps. 119:62). At this hour, we remember the second coming of Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, on the clouds. Just as we start the day with the joy of the Resurrection, we conclude it at midnight with the joy of encountering the Heavenly Bridegroom. Thus, every day becomes a joyful feast, for we consider the Lord to be our eternal feast.

Notes: [617] St. Basil of Caesarea, The Long Rules Q. 37 (FOTC 9:311).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1091 “What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 242
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1091. What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

The Copts inherited the ancient Egyptian calendar from their ancestors, and with some slight modifications, used it to order their liturgical Church life and their daily affairs, especially agriculture. The Coptic liturgical day begins at sunset, like that of the Jews and the Greeks; and each week consists of seven days, the first of which is the Lord’s Day (Sunday).

In the fourth century, many Copts were martyred, and they therefore considered the reign of Diocletian as a golden age. They set the year in which Diocletian became emperor (November, 284 A. D.) as the first year of their calendar. They introduced the term, “The Year of the Martyrs” (Anno Martyrum), abbreviated as A. M. The scholar Tertullian said, “If the martyrs throughout the world were to be put in one side of the scales and the Coptic martyrs alone were to be put in the other, the latter would outweigh the former.”

Notes: [637] Iris Habib El-Masry, The Story of the Copts: Book 1, (Southern California, U.S.A: St. Anthony Coptic Orthodox Monastery, undated) 1.9.99: p. 100.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1088 “What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 240
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1088. What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

Ancient Egyptians developed their calendar at least as far back as 4240 B. C. The famous Greek historian Herodotus remarks that the Egyptians preceded the Greeks in correcting their calendar by adding an additional five days each year to the standard twelve months of thirty days each.

The Copts inherited an interest in the solar calendar from their ancestors, the Pharaohs, and until today, even illiterate Copts in Egypt still follow and pass on their oral traditions for the reckoning of times, by which they order the agricultural seasons, predict weather conditions, and worship using the liturgical calendar.

The Coptic year, which is of ancient Egyptian origin, is divided into twelve months, each of which contains thirty days, and to which are added five extra days at the end of the year called the “little month” or the Epagomenal days. Every four years, in a leap year, six days are added instead of five. The year is divided into three seasons with each season made up of four months. The first season is the season of the flooding of the Nile; the second is the season for sowing; and the third is the season for harvesting and gathering fruits. This seasonal structure continues to define the Coptic liturgical year in Egypt. It was also used outside of Egypt until the Holy Synod of the Coptic Church issued a decree to combine the prayers of the three seasons into a single unified litany of the air of the heaven, the fruits of the earth, and the waters of the rivers together, since in the diaspora, each land has its own agricultural conditions that are unlike those of Egypt.

Notes: [632] Herodotus. The Histories of Herodotus, trans., Henry Cary (D. Appleton and Company, 1904) 2.4: p. 86.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1076 “What is the Coptic Church calendar cycle?”, p. 224
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1076. What is the Coptic Church calendar cycle?

The Church calendar contains different joyful cycles: on a daily, weekly, monthly, and annual basis.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q790 “What are the features of Egyptian liturgy?”, p. 599
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 790. What are the features of Egyptian liturgy?

The East in general, and Egyptian Church in particular, still retains the spirit of the apostolic patristic Liturgy. The liturgical texts that are used have not changed very much since the fifth century, which gives the study of the Egyptian liturgy particular importance. In his book “The Early Liturgy,” Father Jungmann says, “especially in the general structure of the Mass, the Oriental rites have kept many primitive characteristics which have disappeared from the Roman rite … Whereas our Mass changes day after day, the Orient constantly repeats the same invariable formulary.” Fr. Dix, the Anglican monk, says, “The main lines of all the Eastern traditions had been reached before the end of the fourth century, and after this the process in all of them is no more than one of adjustment and development of detail. No new principle arose in the fifth century, as it did in the West …”

Notes: [1546] Josef Andreas Jungmann, The Early Liturgy, to the Time of Gregory the Great, trans., Francis A. Brunner (University of Notre Dame Press, 1959): pp. 211, 221. [1547] Dom Gregory Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (Bloomsbury, 2005): p. 546.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q797 “How do we begin the Liturgy of the Faithful?”, p. 602
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › On the Main Features of the Coptic Liturgy — 797. How do we begin the Liturgy of the Faithful?

“The deacon says: Stand with trembling. Look towards the East. Let us attend. The priest says: The Lord be with you all. And the people answer: And with your spirit. Then he says: Lift up your hearts to the Lord. The people say: We have them with the Lord. Then he says: Let us give thanks to the Lord. The people say: You are worthy, O righteous One. Then he begins with suitable prayers as ordained by our fathers the Apostles.”

Notes: [1560] In the Coptic rite of St. Basil’s Liturgy, the deacon says, “Stand in the fear of God …”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1079 “What is the monthly Church cycle?”, p. 226
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1079. What is the monthly Church cycle?

Every month is sanctified by our monthly commemoration of St. Mary the Mother of God, the Theotokos, on the 21st of each Coptic month. We look up to St. Mary as a living role model for the faithful and the First Citizen of the Church of the Lord Christ, learning from her to live as those who carry the Lord Christ wherever they go; He who establishes His kingdom in our depths.

On the 29th of every Coptic month, we commemorate the annunciation, nativity [or Christmas], and resurrection of Christ (except for the months of Tobe and Meshir). With these commemorations, the believer is dissolved into love through his union with the Savior every hour, every day, every week, and every month.

And we commemorate the chief of the army of the Lord, Archangel Michael, every 12th day of the Coptic month. Thus, the believer feels that he is a good soldier of our Lord Jesus (2 Tim. 2:3) and that he has joined the ranks of the heavenly powers.

This is the happiness of the believer and his continual joy on a daily, weekly, monthly, and annual basis.
