passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1084 “What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?”, pp. 236–237
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1084. What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?

In addition to the monthly commemoration of the Virgin Mary on the 21st of every Coptic month, we celebrate the following feasts:

a. The annunciation of her birth (7th Mesore / 13th August). On this feast we celebrate the conception of St. Mary, the living ark of the covenant, the dwelling of the Most High, and the second heaven.

b. Her birthday (1st Pashons / 9th May). Copts usually commemorate the day a saint passed from this world; their martyrdom or departure to paradise — but they insist on honoring St. Mary on her the day of her birth as a joyful day.

c. Her entry into the temple (3rd Kiahk / 12th December). We learn from the tradition of the Church that St. Mary’s life was consecrated to God in fulfillment of her mother’s vow, for she had vowed to consecrate her firstborn — whether a son or a daughter — to serve the Lord all the days of his or her life.

d. Her departure (21st Tobe / 29th January).

e. The revealing of the assumption of her body (16th Mesore / 22nd August). This feast is preceded by the fifteen-day fast of St. Mary.

f. The consecration of the first church in her name at Philippi (21st Paone / 28th June). This feast also coincides with the commemoration of the Virgin’s miracle of melting iron in the city of Bartus.

g. The apparition of the Virgin Mary above her church in Zeitoun (24th Paremhotep / 2nd April). This apparition is considered unique among the whole history of Marian apparitions. It began on 2nd April 1968 and was repeated on most days for hours at a time and for many months. These apparitions appeared above the domes of the Church of St. Mary and were seen by several hundred thousand people, of all ages and positions, Christians and Muslims. Every night, the people would gather around the church, pray, and praise God, waiting to see the dazzling spectacle of St. Mary standing above one of the domes. She was seen kneeling before the cross, or at other times, carrying the baby Jesus. These apparitions were accompanied by the apparition of birds in the form of doves. Among the fruits of these apparitions were the repentance of many and the occurrence of countless miracles.

Notes: [624] Jerome Palmer, Our Lady Returns to Egypt (Culligan Publications, 1969): p. 1.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — ST. CYRIL AND NESTORIUS (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — ST. CYRIL AND NESTORIUS

These letters came to the notice of Nestorius, stirring him to great wrath, and he engaged one Photius to answer them. He wrote to the court of Constantinople, trying to enlighten and win the support of the Emperor and the princesses who exercised so much influence on the mind and heart of Theodosius II.

Cyril sent letters to Nestorius in which he explains the nature of Christ, as the Incarnate Son of God, one Person, and declared St. Mary’s right to be called “ Theotokos .” In his second letter to Nestorius (February 430 CE) he writes:

We do not mean that the nature of the Word was changed and became flesh, or that it was transformed into a complete human being consisting of soul and body. But rather, we affirm this, that the Word, hypostatically united to Himself flesh, animated with living soul, in a manner mysterious and inconceivable, and became man, and was called Son of Man. Yet not merely by way of divine favor or good will, nor again by the simple assumption to himself of a human person, and that while the natures which were joined together to form a real unity were diverse, one Christ and Son came from both of them -- not implying that the difference between the natures was abolished through their union, but that instead Godhead and manhood have given us the one Lord, Christ and Son by their mysterious and inexpressible unification. He was not at first born as an ordinary man of the holy Virgin, and then the Word simply descend ed upon him, but having been made one with the flesh from the very womb itself, He is said to have submitted to a birth according to the flesh, as appropriating and making his own the birth of his own flesh... Thus, we confess one Christ and Lord, not “worshiping” a man “along with” the Word but worshiping one and the same Christ because the body of the Lord is not alien from the Lord, with which body also he sits with the Father himself... But if we reject this hypostatic union either as impossible or unseemly, we fell into the error of making two sons... Thus, shall we find the holy Fathers to have held. So, did they make bold to call the holy Virgin “Theotokos.” Not as though the nature of the Word’ or His Godhead had its beginning from the holy Virgin, but inasmuch as His Holy Body, endued with a rational soul, was born of her, to which Body also the Word was hypostatically united, on this account He is said to have been born after the flesh. [472]

Afterward a local council was held in Alexandria and a syndical letter was sent to Nestorius, clarifying the same doctrines mentioned in Cyril’s letters, concluding with “The Twelve Articles or Anathemas.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q101 “What did our Fathers of the Middle Ages transmit to us?”, p. 106
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › (b) Regarding the Coptic Orthodox Creed — 101. What did our Fathers of the Middle Ages transmit to us?

The libraries of Europe overflow with medieval manuscripts from Egypt, in both the Coptic and Arabic languages, that reveal the theological richness of the Coptic Church of the Middle Ages. This motivates me to present a sample of their writings about the Creed.

Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis, a priest from Manyat Bani Khusib (now called Minya), who died in 1357 A.D., has an exposition of the Creed in about fifty large manuscript pages attributed to him. He wrote this at the request of Anba Gabriel, the bishop of Qus, in reply to a Jewish person who criticized the Creed saying, “Where did you get this text? And why have you inscribed it among the books of the church?” Thus, the book contains a collection of texts from the Old Testament to substantiate each of the Creed’s clauses.

This work differs in its aims from other medieval Coptic expositions of the Creed: those of Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (around 940 A.D.); and a commentary at the beginning of the second chapter of Abu al-Barakat ibn Kabar’s work titled Mișbâḥ al-ẓulma wa-îḍâḥ alkhidma (The Lamp in the Shadows and the Illumination of Service, about 1310 A.D.). Abu al-Barakat quotes mostly from the New Testament. The Rev. Dr. Samir Khalil says that “the three Coptic commentaries complement each other in a felicitous manner.”

A summary of the text of Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis’ exposition:

1. We believe in one God: he cites the Torah (2 quotations), Isaiah (2 quotations), Jeremiah, and the Gospel (2 quotations; these are the only quotations from the New Testament).

2. The Father almighty, [Pantocrator] of all things visible and invisible: quotations from Zechariah (2), Nahum, and the books of Kings.

3. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten, born of the Father before all ages: quotations from Isaiah (2), David, Solomon (2), and Micah.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q536 “How can the Church be a virgin?”, p. 423
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Eminence of the Church — 536. How can the Church be a virgin?

St. Augustine says, “Do you want to know how the church could be a virgin? Listen to Paul the apostle, listen to the zealous friend of the Bridegroom when he says: ‘But I fear, lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ’ (2 Cor. 11:3). As though the serpent, namely Satan, has defiled Eve’s purity and destroyed the virginity of her heart. So it is that we should not accept the devil’s deception and fall into evil desires and lose the virginity of our hearts.”

He again says, “If you would ask: ‘if the church is Virgin, how could she beget children?’ I will respond that she is a virgin but also begets children. She is likened to Mary who gave birth to Christ. Did Saint Mary not give birth to a child while remaining a virgin? So it is that the church begets children while remaining a virgin. She gives birth to Christ for whoever is baptized becomes His members.”

“The church is like Mary; her perfection was never defiled, and her fertility was never corrupted. What Mary was made worthy of in the flesh, the church received it spiritually. The only exception to that is that Mary gave birth to one son (Jesus Christ) but the church gave birth to many children for them to be gathered together in the one body in the one (Christ).”

Notes: [1089] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons 213.7 (FOTC 38:127). [1090] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons 195:5 (FOTC 38:42).

The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — POPE CYRIL THE GREAT AND NESTORIANISM

On 22 June 431 CE, the Third Ecumenical Council was held in Ephesus at the behest of Emperor Theodosius the Lesser. It was attended by 200 Bishops and St. Cyril the Great, Pope of Alexandria, chaired the council. The council convened to try Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, for he divided Christ into two separate persons: The Son of God and the Son of Man. St. Cyril stressed the unity of the Godhead and manhood without mixing or mingling. He also emphasized the title Theotokos ("The Mother of God") for St. Mary in order to clarify that Who was born from her is truly God the Incarnate Word and not an ordinary man on whom the Godhead descended subsequently.

The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE THEOLOGY OF ST. CYRIL

[521] Similarly the conception of Christ as the second Adam inaugurating a new, regenerated race of humankind demanded, he thought, [522] a much more intimate union of the Word with the flesh than Nestorius postulated [523] .

3 - The Hypostatic Union and the Nestorian Dualism

Cyril repeatedly confirms the Hypostatic Union as the opposite of the Nestorian Dualism. He did not hesitate to say that we are left in ignorance, and that at bottom the unity of Jesus Christ exceeds our comprehension and is unspeakable. [524] He teaches that the union began with the conception of Jesus. It is not a man who was born of Mary, but the Word of God according to the humanity. " For there was not born of the Holy Virgin, first an ordinary man, into whom the Word afterwards came down, but having united Himself (to the flesh) in the womb (of Mary) the Word was born according to the flesh, ascribing to Himself the birth of a flesh that is His own ." [525]

He confirmed that in the “union” humanity is not a ‘‘person,” not because He was an incomplete man, but because humanity does not exist apart. It does not exist by itself, nor does it belong to itself, for it belongs to the Word, who has made it His own. [526]

4 - The Hypostatic Union without Confusion

Cyril affirms that this hypostatic Union of the two natures had been realized without mixture or change or confusion ( synchysis ). He states:

Following in every point the confessions of the Holy Fathers, which they have drawn up under the guidance of the Holy Spirit speaking in them, and keeping close to their intentions taking the royal highway as it were, we affirm that the very Only-Begotten Word of God, begotten of the very substance of the Father... For our salvation came down, and of His condescension emptied Himself, and became Incarnate and was made Man having taken flesh of the Holy Virgin, and made it His own from the womb. He vouchsafed to be born as we, and came forth as a human being from a woman, without abandoning what He was, but remaining, even when He assumed flesh and blood, what He was, God in nature and in truth.

records.question: Who was St. George the Cappadocian?
records.answer:
St. George the Cappadocian was a martyr who most probably lived during the time of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), though some Coptic manuscripts suggest he lived earlier, during the reign of a pagan king of Persia named Dadianus, who controlled Cappadocia [1]. He was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor to pious, wealthy parents of noble origin: his father Anastasius was the governor of Melitene in Cappadocia, and his mother Theobesta (Theognosta) was the daughter of the governor of Lydda in Palestine [1][2].

His father was a faithful Christian who was beheaded when George was about fourteen years old, which inspired George with divine love to become a martyr himself [1][2]. After his father's martyrdom, his mother took George and his siblings to her homeland Diospolis in Palestine [2].

George was made a cavalryman by Prince Justus, who succeeded his father as governor and was a God-fearing man. George excelled in military skills and courage, becoming a leader of 1,000 warriors, then promoted by the emperor to leader of 5,000 warriors with the title "Prince George the Roman" at about twenty years old [2][4].

When the emperor issued a decree to persecute Christians, George publicly tore it up and prepared joyfully for martyrdom. Despite the emperor's attempts to seduce and torture him over seven years, George remained steadfast in faith, performing miracles such as drinking deadly poison without harm, causing wooden chairs to blossom, and raising the dead to life [4][8].

Eventually, the emperor ordered George's execution by beheading on the 23rd of the Coptic month of Baramhat, fearing a public revolt due to the miracles performed through him [3][4]. The empress also converted to Christianity through George's prayers and was martyred [3].

The icon of St. George symbolizes the Church (represented by a young girl), the dragon as Satan, the spear as the Cross of Jesus, and the defeat of the dragon as the triumph of faith over evil [3].

In summary, St. George the Cappadocian was a noble-born Christian military leader and martyr, renowned for his courage, miracles, and steadfast faith during intense persecution [1][2][3][4][8].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Capaducian, pp. 169–170
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) — Time of His Martyrdom

Time of His Martyrdom:

Saint George was most probably considered as the Prince of Martyrs in the time of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). He led a revolt in the province of Cappadocia against the persecution decree of the Christians. However, the majority of the Coptic manuscripts did refer to this saint as a martyr who lived in an era before Diocletian time. He lived during the reign of a pagan king of Persia called Dadianus, whom the province of Cappadocia was under his control. This version would be in agreement with what was documented in the biography of the martyr George of Alexandria, where he was born after his father attended the feast of the consecration of the church of St. George, the Cappadocian in the city of Lydda in Palestine. Some of the Coptic manuscripts did not assign his era, but only mentioned that its events happened “in the old,” probably meaning before the time of Diocletian.

His Upbringing:

This saint was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor, to pious, wealthy parents of noble origin. His father was Anastasius, the governor of Melitene in Cappadocia, and his mother was Theobesta (Theognosta), the daughter of the governor of Lydda in Palestine. His father was said to be a pious man, faithful to God and the king, that he was so loved by the king to make him one of his entourage who accompanied him wherever he would go, but when he discovered that Anastasius believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, he gave the command to cut off his head. This happened when his son St. George was only fourteen years of age. Anyhow, St. George came as a fruit of a holy seed, buried in a holy land, to provide to the church, as well as to the celestials, what brought pleasure to their hearts. The martyrdom of his father governor Anastasius did not break the souls of his family but inflamed the heart of his blessed son George with the fire of the Divine Love to make him a martyr for the Lord, as well. After the martyrdom of her husband, governor Anastasius, Theobesta took her children: George, Casset, and Madrona, and she set forth to her homeland Diospolis in Palestine.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Capaducian, p. 170
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) — His Upbringing

The martyrdom of his father governor Anastasius did not break the souls of his family but inflamed the heart of his blessed son George with the fire of the Divine Love to make him a martyr for the Lord, as well. After the martyrdom of her husband, governor Anastasius, Theobesta took her children: George, Casset, and Madrona, and she set forth to her homeland Diospolis in Palestine.

Prince George the Roman

After the martyrdom of governor Anastasius, a prince named Justus replaced him. He was a God-fearing man who loved the Lord Jesus Christ. Hence, he did well to the household of Anastasius, the martyr, and made the young man George a cavalryman to prepare him for a military career. George surpassed all his peers on every aspect and showed rare courage that he soon became a hero whose fame spread all over Palestine and was promoted to a leader of 1,000 warriors. The prince sent him to the emperor with a message that revealed his achievements and sought from the emperor to grant him the rank of a prince. There, the emperor was very impressed by him and gave him the title: Prince George the Roman. He made him a leader of 5,000 warriors and gave him a blonde horse of the rarest kind to show how he was pleased with him. All loved George, and his noble characters, prudence, and his stature that would project his courage in battle qualified him to become the highest commander in the army. He was still twenty years of age at that time, and his mother also reposed in the Lord shortly after.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Capaducian, pp. 173–174
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) — In the Royal Palace

In the Royal Palace:

After such a multitude of Divine miracles performed by God through the saint, the emperor felt so ashamed, he took the young man George to his palace, in a final round of seduction. There, the empress heard him praying and sought from him to explain his faith to her, and God opened her heart up, and the Spirit of God led her to faith. The empress started to admonish her husband, the emperor, saying: “I told you not to go against those of Galilees, for their God is strong!” Perceiving that she was seduced by the saint to faith in the Lord, the emperor gave the order to comb her body with an iron comb, then to cut her head off.

On her way to the place of execution, the empress asked the saint, how she would go to death without being baptized. The saint told her not to worry, for shedding her blood for the faith in Christ would be a Holy Baptism in itself, which would open the gates of Paradise before her. On hearing those words, the empress exultantly approached her martyrdom, saying: “O Lord, as I left the gates of my palace wide open, I pray to You not to close the gate of Your Paradise before my face, but open it the way You did for the right-hand thief on the Cross.” The empress had her head cut off, and her soul set forth to Paradise to enjoy the company of Jesus Christ, her Savior.

The Martyrdom of St. George:

The emperor finally gave the order to cut the head of St. George off because of his fear that a possible public revolt against him would erupt due to all God's works through His saint. This took place on the 23rd of the Coptic month of Baramhat.

About the Icon of St. George the Roman:

It carries the following symbolic meanings:  The young girl in the icon refers to the church that looks at her martyred children with joy and appreciation.  The dragon refers to Satan, who moves the evil world against faith.

 The spear refers to the Cross of Jesus, the Lord of Glory, that grants the conquest.  The defeat of the dragon refers to the defeat of evil and its initiator (Satan)

by the power of faith.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Capaducian, p. 171
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) — The Love of the Governor for Him

The Love of the Governor for Him:

Justus planned to select George to be wed to his only daughter, the little pure princess who feared God. He revealed his intention to Theobesta, the mother of George, before she died, and she was immensely exultant to hear it. He also appointed George as his deputy on all his possessions. However, Justus had to postpone the wedding because of the young age of his girl, unaware that God prepared something more significant for the young man.

The Zeal of Prince George:

When George heard that the emperor had gathered an assembly of seventy of his governors and proclaimed his intention to wipe out Christianity from the face of the earth, he readied himself to confront the persecution. He planned to make his religion known to the emperor and sold all that he inherited from his father, including his clothes and his house furniture, and gave the entire proceeds to the poor. Then he released all his slaves, and when the emperor issued his decree, George took it and tore it off in public before multitudes of people, and he prepared himself for martyrdom with joy.

Before the Emperor:

Then, they led him before the emperor, who started by talking to him nicely, promising him with extraordinary gifts. However, the young man utterly disregarded all these promises. On failing to seduce him, the emperor tortured the saint for an extended period. He kept torturing him for a whole seven years period. During that time, God's hand supported him and made him a tool to bring a multitude of souls to the true faith. During being tortured, St. George died three times, and God kept raising him to be glorified in him, and amid his suffering, He made him enjoy heavenly visions to support him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George of Alexandria, pp. 168–169
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE OF ALEXANDRIA (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

St. George (Gawargios) was born to wealthy pagan parents. His father was a merchant in the city of Alexandria, and the family had no children. Then, once he traveled to the city of Lydda in Palestine, where it happened that the people there were celebrating the feast of the consecration of the church of the martyr St. George the Cappadocian. He was quite impressed and moved by the awesome celebration and with the church hymns, and when he listened to the biography of the martyr, he so loved the Christian faith that his soul was happy, and he sought to be baptized. The saint's father prayed to God that through the intercession of the great martyr, he would be granted a son. On returning home to Alexandria, he narrated to his wife what he encountered, and she believed as well and got baptized. God received their supplications and granted them a boy whom they called George. The child was raised in a pious atmosphere, loved the church, and had compassion on the poor and the needy. When he reached the age of twenty-five years, his parents departed to heaven.

With His Uncle Armenius's Daughter:

After the death of his parents, his uncle Armenius, the governor of Alexandria, took him under his care. The uncle had a kind-hearted daughter, she happened to go for a picnic with some of her girlfriends, and they passed by a monastery outside Alexandria. She was very impressed to hear the monks praising God with sweet hymns. On coming back home, she inquired from her cousin George about what she heard, and he told her that it was Divine Christian praises sung by monks, who forsook the world to practice angelic lives. The young man then talked to her about the faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, eternal life, and the endless suffering. She was so impressed with what she heard that she accepted belief in the Lord Jesus.

Getting to know about what happened to his daughter, her father governor Armenius attempted first to lure her into changing her mind, and she did not, then he threatened her. Yet, she, in complete love for her Lord Jesus Christ, was ready to deliver her own life as a sacrifice to God. So, her cruel father cut her head off, and she gained the crown of martyrdom.

passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, BISHOP OF CAPPADOCIA

This St. Theodore (Tadros), apparently was a shepherd before he was ordained as a bishop on Cappadocia. Even though he was freshly ordained and just got acquainted with St. Gregory of Nazianzus (329-390 AD), he was assigned to urge St. Gregory to shepherd the Orthodox congregation in Constantinople. St. Gregory wrote him in response [Letter# 222], to tell him about what he did. He told him also about the insults that came on him from the bishops of that region. He also apologized about what happened to him, being new in his bishopric.

[Smith and Wace, Vol. 4, p. 932]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Deacon, p. 174
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE DEACON

He was a contemporary of the 42nd Pope of Alexandria, St. Simeon I (692- 700 AD). After the departure of that pope to heaven, he was sought by some to be worthy of sitting on the Seat of Alexandria, although because he was not in the rank of priesthood, he was not selected for the papal seat. This did not bother him, and he continued to serve diligently and faithfully in his church, and eventually, he got the priestly rank. While dedicating all his energy to ministry, he managed to document the biographies of the popes of Alexandria. When he was residing in the monastery of Prince Tadros in Ablag, he started to write the journal of the 24th Pope St. Cyril I, the Pillar of Faith (412-444 AD). Then, he followed it by his successors, until he reached the biography of the 43rd Pope St. Alexandros II (704-729 AD), who was leading the Coptic Church at that time. This pope at that period was residing in the monastery of Abba Macarius the Great in the Scetis. Fr. George gave a good account of the political events through which Egypt was passing, as well as the civil rulers who governed the land. He covered almost four centuries, from the 4th to the 8th century, during which twenty Alexandrian popes sat on the throne of St. Mark.

[Iris Habib El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church – Bk 2, p. 328]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George, the Capaducian, pp. 171–172
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) — More durable than Magic or Poison

More durable than Magic or Poison:

Among the tortures that St. George was exposed to was that the emperor brought a famous magician named Athanasius, who prepared a highly deadly poison and gave it to the saint to drink. By faith, the saint drank it, and it did him no harm. Right away, the magician declared his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. The angry emperor gave the order to squeeze the saint by a press with sharp iron teeth until he gave his last breath, but the Lord Jesus Christ raised him from death, and a multitude of those who watched him tortured, died and getting raised from the dead, declared their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and their readiness to be martyred for His sake.

With the emperor, there were several governors among the spectators. Those governors sought to test the saint, so they asked him to make their wooden chairs blossom with leaves, flowers, and fruits. By the saint's prayer, their request was granted. The governors were genuinely astonished, and they took him to the cemetery and sought from him to raise some of the dead. The saint prayed to the Lord, and few of the dead were raised to life, testified to the salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ, and then went again to sleep.

In the Temple of Idols:

Trying to seduce the saint, the emperor talked again to him nicely and tried to tell him how his heart was bleeding on seeing him suffering, how he was so dear to him to let him have the highest position in the State. Thus, St. George did not refuse the emperor's request to go with him to the temple of the idols. The emperor thought that the young man would have a change of heart, and he would burn incense before the idols to qualify for becoming his son-in-law, as promised. The emperor headed to the temple, in a crowd of his officials and a multitude of people, where George stood before the statue of the idol Apollo and cried out: “Are you a god, to whom I should offer a sacrifice?” The idol answered back with a loud voice: “No! I am not a god!” The saint made the sign of the Cross, and all the idols in the temple fell and got broken into pieces. On seeing that, the people cried out, seeking death to the enemy of their gods. Feeling great shame, the emperor returned with a bitter soul back to his palace.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George of Alexandria, p. 169
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE OF ALEXANDRIA (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

When the governor knew that it was his nephew George, the one who convinced his daughter to receive her new faith, he put him under arrest. Then, he tortured him fiercely and sent him to Arianus, the governor of Ansena, who tortured him more and finally had his head cut off, and he too gained the crown of martyrdom during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). A deacon, by the name of Samuel, took his holy body, shrouded him with great respect, and took it Manuf in the province of Giza. On hearing about it, his uncle's wife took the body and buried it in Alexandria next to that of her martyred daughter. His relics now are in St. Mark's church in the city of Rashid.

th

[Synaxarion of the 7 of Hator] [OLeary: The Saints of Egypt, pp. 145-146]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Phocas, the Gardner, pp. 461–462
passages.text:
Saint: PHOCAS, THE GARDNER (The martyr) — His Courage

His Courage:

In the morning, he went to his guests and told them that Phocas was around and ready for them to arrest him whenever they decide. When they asked him where he was, he answered them: “He is here! I am the man you are looking after.” Amazed at his love, generosity, courage, and steadfastness; the soldiers were shocked and did not know what to do. On seeing that, Phocas indirectly encouraged them and told them that he would consider his death for the sake of Christ, as the most excellent service they could offer him. After getting over their confusion, they cut his head off, and the Christians eventually built a great Church to carry his name. God granted him the gift of performing wonders through his relics, that he was called Thaumaturgus (Miracle-maker). His body was moved to Constantinople in the days of St. John Chrysostom, who gave a sermon on occasion. A monastery was also built on the same location.

It was said that part of his relics was moved to the church of the apostles in Vienna. St. Phocas is beloved by the Greek sailors, who are counting him as a partner in their meals, and used to put aside a part of the price of their food in his name and distribute it among the poor once they land safely ashore. The contemporary Greeks celebrate him on the 22nd of July and the 22nd of September. St. Gregory the Nazianzus called him The Renewable Disciple of Christ.

[Baring-Gould: September 22]

[Butler: July 3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Fr. Theognostus, p. 278
passages.text:
Saint: THEOGNOSTUS, FR.

He was a priest from Alexandria, who was sent as a deputy of the 24th Pope Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to Constantinople, along with Fr. Sharmocinus the priest and Liontius the deacon [Cyril: Letters 37, 41]

[Smith & Wace; Vol 4, p. 990]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Nectarius, Patriarch of Constantinople, pp. 271–272
passages.text:
Saint: NECTARIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE, ST. — Opposing the Arians

In the year 381 AD, when St. Gregory of Nazianzus (329-390) resigned after a short reign as the patriarch of Constantinople, he was succeeded by St. Nectarius. St. Nectarius was from Tarsus in Cilicia, and being chosen for the patriarchate has an exciting story. While the Second Ecumenical Council was being held in Constantinople, Nectarius planned to visit his family in Tarsus. So, he went to see Abba Diodorus, the bishop of Tarsus, who was attending the Council, to ask him if he wished to send any letters to Tarsus. During that encounter, Abba Diodorus was so impressed by Nectarius conduct and attitude, that he suggested to abba Meletius, the bishop of Antioch, that Nectarius was fit to succeed St. Gregory on the throne of Constantinople. Although Abba Meletius laughed at the idea, yet the name of Nectarius was added to the list of candidates presented to the emperor to choose from. To the amazement of all, Emperor Theodosius I (379-395 AD) wanted Nectarius, who was not even baptized yet; and it was said that he was married and had a son. However, the bishops' Council approved that choice; and Nectarius was baptized, and then ordained.

Opposing the Arians:

Abba Nectarius sat on the throne of Constantinople for sixteen years, during which he unceasingly opposed the Arians. For that reason, the Arians dared to burn his house in the year 388 AD, when a rumor spread that the emperor in Rome has died. St. Nectarius reposed on the 27th of September 397 AD, and he was succeeded by St. John Chrysostom (397-407 AD).

[Baring-Gould: October 11]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, pp. 480–481
passages.text:
Saint: CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE (The martyr) — His Upbringing

A great transformation occurred in his life, as he says:

“Once I got baptized, I was cleansed from my sins by the water of the Holy Baptism, and a light from heaven poured into my repentant heart, to dissipate the doubts, to open the windows and to lift the darkness.

What I used to see severe, I see now easy. What I thought was impossible became a reality. I came to see my past life as earthly and carnal, but now, I am born from the water and Spirit; this is the work of God.”

After baptism, St. ‘Cyprian’ made four critical decisions: 63e sold most of his possessions and distributed their proceeds on the poor and the needy, keeping only what was needed for his family. 64t about the age of 46 years, he vowed the life of virginity after getting the approval of his wife. He also brought his wife to the elderly priest ‘Caecilius’ along with their children, leaving with them enough wealth to live on. He loved virginity as a sign of his longing for the Divinities and his desire for getting to the end of this world and for the enjoyment of the life to come with the heavenly hosts, and also as a practical protest against the defiled ethical corruption which was highly spread at his time. 65enying the worldly studies, he concentrated on the study of the Holy Bible daily, and cared for the writings of the scholar ‘Tertullian.’ The saint said about himself that after he was baptized, he despised the human eloquence and the adornment of words, although his writings testify about his natural rhetoric. 66e dedicated his talents to the ministry of the kingdom of God; and through developing his system of stenography, he managed to record very accurately the views of 87 bishops who attended the council which he held in the year 326 AD, concerning the repetition of the baptism done by the heretics.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Capreolus, Bishop of Carthage, p. 389
passages.text:
Saint: CAPREOLUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

St. ‘Capreolus’ was the bishop of Carthage (in Tunisia, Africa). His name in history is connected to the ‘Council of Ephesus’ held in the year 431 AD. Unable to attend the council because of the attacks of the barbarian ‘Vandals,’ the bishop, in his zeal for the upright doctrine, dispatched an elaborate letter in defense of the proper faith, both in Greek and Latin. His letter was read in the council, along with two other letters from the pope of Rome St. ‘Celestine I’ (422-432 AD), and from the 24th pope of Alexandria St. ‘Cyril’ (412-444 AD). When St. ‘Capreolus’ letter was read, St. ‘Cyril’ commented: “This is what all of us are saying, and it is the wish of all of us.” ‘Capreolus’ letter was included among the documents of the council.

This bishop reposed on the 20th or the 30th of July of the year 435 AD.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biographies, Vol. I, p. 400]

Notes: [1] This letter is still in existence…

passages.text:
Saint: GORGONIUS (The martyr)

St. Gorgonius was an officer in the army of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) in Nicomedia and was condemned to death, along with a fellow officer, named Dorotheus, because they protested against the persecution of a Christian by the name of Peter Cubicularius. After his martyrdom, his body was buried in the city of Rome.

[Butlers Lives of the Saints: September 9]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, pp. 480–481
passages.text:
Saint: CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE (The martyr) — His Upbringing

St. ‘Cyprian’ (Cyprianus) is considered the 2nd most crucial western theologian after the scholar ‘Tertullian’ (160-220 AD). St. ‘Jerome’ wrote about him in his book ‘On Illustrious Men’: “He was used not to let any day pass without reading some of the writings of ‘Tertullian’ and to say to his disciple: ‘Give me the knowledge;’ by which he meant ‘the writings of the scholar Tertullian’.”

St. ‘Cyprian's’ deacon ‘Pontius’ who shared his exile until the day of his death, left a notable volume about his biography, which was written directly after his martyrdom.

His Upbringing:

The saint was born in ‘Carthage,’ the capital of Northern Africa on the gulf of ‘Tunisia.’ His full name was ‘Thaschus Caecilius Cyprianus,’ and he was born around the year 205 AD to a pagan noble family. His father was one of the most prominent judges in the city.

He was appropriately educated according to the standards of his time and his high social status. He was particularly versed in logic, philosophy, and rhetoric. He got married and had children. Early in his career, he became a famous rhetoric speaker and a teacher of oration and rhetoric. It seemed that at this stage of his life, he plunged in abomination, like all the youth at his time, but when the Divine grace touched his heart, he was awakened and realized the corruption which consumed humanity on the level of individuals, congregations, and governments. So, he came to proclaim Christianity in the hands of an elderly priest called ‘Caecilius’ in ‘Carthage’ around the year 246 AD, and he joined the rows of the catechumen.

He got the Sacrament of Baptism on the hands of that priest, whom he so loved, to add his name to be called ‘Caecilius Cyprianus.’ A great transformation occurred in his life, as he says:

“Once I got baptized, I was cleansed from my sins by the water of the Holy Baptism, and a light from heaven poured into my repentant heart, to dissipate the doubts, to open the windows and to lift the darkness.

records.question: Who was St. Mina the Wonder-Maker?
records.answer:
St. Mina the Wonder-Maker was a famous Egyptian martyr born around the year 285 AD in the town of Nikiu (Nakiyos) in the district of Menuf in El-Monufyia governorate on the Nile delta. His father, Eudoxius, was the governor of the city, and his mother, Euphemia, had no children until she prayed before the icon of the Virgin St. Mary, who promised her a son. Euphemia conceived and gave birth to Mina, whose name means "Amen," and his birth was celebrated by the whole city [1].

St. Mina was educated with an Evangelic spirit and love for the Holy Bible by his father. After his parents died when he was young, he inherited wealth and spiritual blessings. At fifteen, he was appointed an officer in the army in ancient Africa (Algeria). When the decree of Emperors Diocletian and Maximian in 303 AD ordered idol worship, Mina distributed his wealth to the poor and left the military to live as a monk in the wilderness [2].

After five years of monastic life, he desired martyrdom and was promised by a heavenly voice that he would receive three immortal crowns: for virginity, monastic life, and martyrdom. His name would become famous among martyrs, and many would come to worship in a church built in his name [2].

St. Mina publicly proclaimed his Christian faith during a pagan celebration, which led to his severe torture by the governor. Despite brutal tortures, he remained steadfast, praising God and refusing to renounce his faith. He was imprisoned, comforted by a vision of Christ, and eventually martyred by beheading around the year 309 AD at the age of twenty-four. His body was miraculously preserved from burning and was buried with honor [3][8].

After his martyrdom, his tomb became a site of many miracles and healings. His relics were moved to Marriott, where many came to seek healing through his prayers. Churches were built in his honor, including one by Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic and later expansions supported by Emperor Arcadius. His monastery flourished and was renewed in modern times under Pope St. Kyrillos VI [6][10][11].

St. Mina's spiritual influence extended far beyond Egypt; seven monks from his monastery preached the Gospel in Ireland, and his name is still remembered there. His relics and artifacts are found in many countries, and his prayers continue to be a source of healing and support for the faithful [6][5].

An icon from the 5th century in the Louvre Museum depicts Christ placing His hand on St. Mina's shoulder, symbolizing the church's view of the saints as channels of God's compassion and friendship. Even centuries after his martyrdom, St. Mina is believed to work for the kingdom of heaven, supporting church leaders and believers [4].

In summary, St. Mina the Wonder-Maker was a young soldier turned monk and martyr, renowned for his steadfast faith, miraculous intercessions, and enduring spiritual legacy in the Coptic Orthodox Church [1][2][3][4][5][6][8][10][11].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 230–231
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — The Son of the Promise

This St. Mina is the most famous of the Egyptian martyrs. He became so well-known in and outside of Egypt, because of the so many wonders, performed by God through his prayers, up to this very day.

St. Mina was born around the year 285 AD in the town of Nikiu (Nakiyos) in the district of Menuf in El-Monufyia governorate on the Nile delta. His father, Eudoxius was the governor of the city, and his grandfather Plondionus was also governor before him. Because Eudoxius had an excellent reputation and was loved by everybody around him due to his piety and virtues, his brother Anatolius was envious of him. He brought charges against him before Caesar Carinus (283-285 AD). However, the Caesar wanted to gain the favor of both men, so he sent Hypatus the leader of his army, with an order to appoint Eudoxius as a governor on ancient Africa (Algeria), in place of its governor who passed away, and he asked Hypatus to accompany Eudoxius and his family on the trip and make sure that everything was for them in their new residence. The people of Nikiu were unfortunate to lose Eudoxius, while his brother Anatolius showed remorse on what he has done.

The Son of the Promise:

St. Mina's mother, Euphemia, had no children, and one day, she went to the church on one of the feasts of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God, at Atrib on the 21st of Toba. She saw the children in the church wearing their beautiful clothes with their parents. She heaved a sigh and wept before the icon of our Lady St. Mary, imploring her to intercede for her before her beloved Son, so that He would give her a son. A voice came from the icon saying, Amen. She rejoiced in what she had heard and realized that the Lord had heard her prayers. When she returned to her home and told her husband about it, he replied: “May God's Will be done.”

Euphemia conceived and gave birth to the son of her prayers, promised to her by the Lord Jesus, whom she called Mina, meaning ‘Amen.’ The whole city rejoiced for his birth, and his father Eudoxius, the governor, released many prisoners and gave away many donations in celebration.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 231–232
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

His father cared to educate him with an Evangelic spirit about all the church teachings. He planted in him the love of the Holy Bible and the right knowledge, with the mood of worship and the pious behavior. Then, his father passed away when Mina was only eleven years old, followed by his mother when he was fourteen years old. The saint inherited from them a significant wealth and much spiritual blessings and honor.

A year after the repose of his mother, when he was fifteen years old, he was appointed an officer in the army in the regiment of ancient Africa (Algeria), for the high regard they had for his departed father.

Becoming a Monk:

In the year 303 AD, when a decree was issued by the two evil Emperors Diocletian and Maximian (284-305 AD) ordering everyone to worship and offer sacrifices to the idols, the officer Mina distributed his wealth on Jesus' little brethren and decided to dedicate all his time and energy to the kingdom of God. He abandoned the military service after three years and set forth to the wilderness to worship God, which he was longing to do for some time.

Then, it happened that after five years in his monastic life, Mina saw while praying the martyrs were being crowned by the angels and carried by them to Paradise, with their shiny countenance more splendid than the sun. Desiring to become a martyr, he heard a voice from heaven, saying: “Blessed you are Abba Mina, for you are called for piety since your childhood. You will get three immortal crowns: one for your virginity, one for your monastic life, and the third for your martyrdom. Your name will be famous among the martyrs, for I shall make men of every tribe and tongue come to worship Me in your church, which will be built in your name, and above everything else, you will get an indescribable glory in My everlasting kingdom.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, p. 232
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — In the Celebration Arena

In the Celebration Arena:

Forsaking the wilderness, Mina set forth to the city in his monastic attire. On that day, there was a big pagan celebration for the gods. The saint's soul felt bitterness on seeing such a high number of lost souls getting into the celebration arena. He cried out in a loud voice, proclaiming the longing of the True God to see all of them getting to know His love and Salvation. He quoted the prophetic words: “I was found by those who did not seek Me. I was made manifest to those who did not ask for Me.” (Isaiah 65:1; Romans 10:20). The multitudes and the spectators were amazed to see such a daring scene, and an impressive silence dwelt on the place. The governor wondered how someone dared to interrupt the celebration of the gods. In the meantime, some of the military people recognized Mina and informed the governor about his past position. So, he asked the saint: “Why did you desert your military service, and how come you proclaim that you are a Christian?” The saint answered him: “Yes, I am a soldier, but I decided to serve my Lord Jesus Christ to please His Holy Name.”

At that point, the angry governor decided to punish the saint. So, he ordered the leader of his officers to put the saint in the hinbazeen, which tore off his flesh and exposed his bones. In the meantime, that leader kept asking the saint sarcastically if he was in pain. The saint responded by saying: “Your tortures are my investment which prepares for me the crowns before Christ, my King, and God.” Then, they dragged him over a platform made of sharp iron nails until the rest of his flesh was torn apart. Afterward, they rubbed his wounds with rough fabrics and burned his sides by flames for two hours. However, the Lord relieved all his pains that nobody heard him moaning.

They also hit the saint's mouth with rods until his teeth were broken, all that while he kept giving thanks to God, and considering himself unworthy to be reproached for the sake of His Holy Name.

When the leader failed to make the saint change his stand, he sent him sailing back to the governor with a report about all that happened. While sailing with the soldiers on board of a boat, the saint heard a voice from heaven saying: “Do not have fear, O My beloved Mina, for I shall always be with you wherever they take you.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, p. 236
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — The Icon of St. Mina

The Icon of St. Mina:

In the Louvre Museum in Paris, there is a Coptic icon from the 5th century, in which we see the Lord Jesus Christ puts His blessed hand on St. Mina's shoulder in exalted amiability. Such an icon reveals how the church views the saints, through whom we get to recognize the elevated compassion of God and His longing toward the believer to set with Him a covenant of love and friendship on an everlasting level.

An Unceasing Action:

My dear friend (Ĥ. Y.), who was also a friend of Pope St. Kyrillos VI, since he was a monk in Old Cairo, told me the following story:

“One evening in the monastery of St. Mina in Marriott, when the only persons attending the church with the pope were just two or three people, during the vesper I noticed that the pope was laughing while he was alone in the sanctuary. At the end of the prayer, I hastened toward the pope and told him: ‘I never saw you laughing in the sanctuary. Would you please tell me what you have seen.’ After much reluctance, he told me: ‘You know the intense tribulation we are living through these days. I was complaining to God that, because of such bitter anguish, I am not able to resolve any problems for His children, but right away, St. Mina appeared to me and pocked my belly with his finger, saying: ‘You think that you are alone!? We are all working together with you. Do not despair.’ For that reason, I laughed!” After more than seventeen centuries since his martyrdom and departure from this world, St. Mina's heart, full of love, still works for the kingdom of heaven, to support so many: patriarchs, bishops, priests and the members of the congregation. Indeed: "Love never fails" (1 Cor 13: 8).

[The Church of St. ‘Mina’ in Fleming: Mar Mina, the Wonder-Maker, 1963]

[The Church of St. George in Sporting: The Egyptian Martyr Mina, 1974]

Notes: [1] From a biography of St. Mina found in a Coptic manuscript (893 AD) called “Encomium” kept in P. Morgan library in NY.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 235–236
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — Monuments of the era of St. Mina

Monuments of the era of St. Mina:

In the German city of Frankfurt, there is a museum that is wholly dedicated to St. Mina. The reason behind that was the German scholar bishop Carl Maria Kaufmann (1872-1951), who discovered the location of St. Mina's ancient city in Marriott in the year 1906/1907, managed to take back with him to Germany about 100 large size boxes full of beautiful artifacts, crowns of marble columns, etc. After that discovery, the museums of the whole world moved to take some of St. Mina's monuments, but Kaufman got the best of it. Some German researchers kept working on the location until 2013 through an assignment by the German Museum of antiquities in collaboration with the Coptic Museum of Cairo, to carry out new and elaborate excavations.

The departed Coptic scholar Banoub Ĥabashy moved a lot of St. Mina's antiquities to a section of the Graeco-Roman Museum in Alexandria, and he called that section: [The Coptic Museum in the era of St. Mina.]

An Ecumenical Love:

The heart of St. Mina was full of love for God, and he kept working, even after his martyrdom. Many sick people from all over the world came to get the blessing of his prayers and to get healed from their sicknesses. They went back home with holy water in small clay flasks (ampoules) on which his name and picture were engraved. These ampoules are still found in many countries far apart, like Colon and Heidelberg in Germany, Marseille in France, Dalmata in Yugoslavia, Milan in Italy, Dengela in Sudan, Jerusalem and parts of England.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 234–235
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — His Spiritual Effect

His Spiritual Effect:

St. Mina has been martyred over 1,700 years ago when he was twentyfour years old, but his fragrant life and prayers still have their miraculous effect on so many. At the beginning of the 5th century, the hearts of many young men flared with God's love, sold all their possessions, and set forth to St. Mina's holy tomb to practice the monastic life and establish his monastery in Marriott.

The history testifies that seven monks of the St. Mina Monastery preached the Gospel to Ireland and built the first church there in the name of St. Mina. The Irish Church still keeps in its prayers up to this very day, a litany for the Coptic fathers who carried to them the torch of faith. According to the historical accounts of that area, the great city of St. Mina went through several stages of ups and downs, flourishing and looting. During the papacy of the 52nd Pope Yusab I (831-849 AD), St. Mina's cathedral was ransacked, and most of its marble columns were stolen. However, its monastery came to flourish again in the era of the 55th Pope St. Shenouda I (859-880 AD).

It is believed that the eventual demise of the first great city of St. Mina took place around the end of the 13th century AD. Then, in the era of Pope St. Kyrillos VI (1959-1971), the new monastery of Mar Mina was built, and another wave of monastic renaissance started anew in Marriott.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Bishop, pp. 228–229
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE BISHOP (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

This St. Mina lived in the 8th century AD and became the bishop of Tamai el-Amdid in Sinbellawein. His father was from Samannud. He was the only son of God-fearing parents, who were known to practice a monastic style of prayers and fasting, which made them famous all around the area. His parents forced him to get married, but he got his bride's consent to keep their virginity. They practiced so many worships like those performed by the monks, they put on sackcloth and spent most of their nights in prayers and in reading the Bible.

His Monastic Life:

St. Mina longed for monastic life, so he said to his wife: “It is not befitting of us to practice a monastic life while being in the world.” On having her approval, he set forth to the monastery of Abba Anthony in the eastern desert, to be as far as he could from his parents. They diligently searched for him for a while, and then they stopped. From there, he went to the monastery of St. Macarius, in the wilderness of the Scetis accompanied by Abba Khael (who eventually became the 46th Pope on the See of Alexandria: (743-767 AD). There, they both started their monastic life, in the days of the two shining stars St. Abram and St. Gawargi. St. Mina became a disciple of these two saints and had the benefit of their vast knowledge, imitated their worship, and grew in the angelical work, more than many other fathers. Satan envied him for his strife, and he severely struck him in his legs, that he was left bedridden on the ground for two months. Then, he was healed by the power of the Lord Jesus Christ.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 232–233
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — In the Celebration Arena

When the leader failed to make the saint change his stand, he sent him sailing back to the governor with a report about all that happened. While sailing with the soldiers on board of a boat, the saint heard a voice from heaven saying: “Do not have fear, O My beloved Mina, for I shall always be with you wherever they take you.”

The governor put him in jail together with so many other believers. The saint kept consoling them and encouraging them. There, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself appeared to him and comforted him, then ascended to heaven.

The Saint's Martyrdom:

On the next day, the governor brought him up before the court of justice; started to treat him tenderly to bring him to his side, then when he failed, he threatened him with death. The governor ordered his men to scourge the saint with oxtails. Then, they tried to sow him with a sharp iron saw, but the saw melted like wax. Finally, the governor ordered to cut his head off by the sword. In the arena of martyrdom, the saint knelt, and after raising his hands in prayer toward heaven, the swordsman struck him with the sword. St. Mina was martyred on the 15th of Hator, around the year 309 AD, when he was twenty-four years old. The soldiers ignited a fire to burn his body. However, it remained three days and three nights in flames without being burned. Some believers came, took his body, shrouded it with precious fabrics, and buried him with honor.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Monk, pp. 229–230
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE MONK (The martyr)

This saint was born in a village around Akhmim to Christian parents who lived on farming. Since his youth, his heart longed toward asceticism. He became a monk in one of the monasteries of Akhmim, where he dwelt, fasting every two days and practicing asceticism in his food and drink. Then, he moved to El-Ashmonein, where he stayed in a monastery for sixteen years, during which he never left the monastery. When the Arabs ruled the country (after 640 AD), he heard that they denied that God has a Son from His nature and essence, and equal with Him in Eternity. This denial of faith was painful to the saint, so he took permission from the Abbot of the monastery and went to El-Ashmonein.

He came before the commander of the Arab camp and asked him: “Is it true that you say that God has no Son from His Nature and Essence?” The commander replied, saying: “We deny that saying about God and reject it. ” The saint told the Arab commander that it should only be rejected if His Son was born through parental procreation, but we believe that the Lord Jesus Christ is God from God and Light from Light. The commander replied: “In our faith, this is blasphemy. ” The saint told him that the Bible says: "He who believes in the Son has everlasting life, and he who does not believe in the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him. " (John 3:36)

The commander became enraged at this and ordered his soldiers to cut the saint into pieces and to throw him into the river. The believers gathered the parts of his body, shrouded it, and buried it. They arranged a commemoration to celebrate the martyrdom of St. Mina the Monk on the 17th of Amshir.

[The Synaxarion: 17 Amshir]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, pp. 233–234
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — The Body of St. Mina

The Body of St. Mina:

After a few years from St. Mina's martyrdom, some of the Barbarians came from Eastern Libya and attacked the city of Marriott. Athanasius, the army commander, was asked to take his troops and defend that area. He used to be a very close friend of St. Mina when they were together in the army. So, he decided to take the body of the saint along with him. The soldiers uncovered St. Mina's tomb, a great light came out, before which they fell on the ground worshipping the God of St. Mina. While sailing with the body on a boat toward Alexandria in their way to Marriott, fierce marine beasts attacked them, but fire came out of the body and scared them away.

After arriving at Alexandria with the body loaded on a camel, they marched to Marriott, and they defeated the Barbarians, and on their way back, the camel refused to get up to go with them, despite striking it very hard. They loaded the saint's body on another more robust camel, but it refrained from moving, as well. When this was repeated, the prefect Athanasius perceived that it was the will of the Lord for the body to stay in Marriott.

The Lord Jesus Christ Reveals the Location of the Body:

Around the period (320-325 AD), according to the 48th Pope of Alexandria St. John IV (777-799 AD), a lame boy who was living in a village near the place where the body of the saint was buried, happened to crawl out of his village, and when he saw a brightly lit lamp at a distance, he kept crawling toward it, when he got there, he fell asleep, from exhaustion. The next morning, when the worried parents of the lame boy found him, they kept screaming at his face. However, they were amazed to see him jump and run away from them. The healed boy told the people in the village about what he saw. People came to the tomb, and they saw the splendid light coming out of it. Multitudes of people came to the saint's tomb to enjoy many wonders that God performed through the prayers of St. Mina.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Wonder-Maker, p. 234
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) — Healing of the Emperor's Daughter

Healing of the Emperor's Daughter:

Sometime later, a shepherd who was attending to his flock outside of the city had a sheep inflicted with skin disease. Then, it happened that the inflicted sheep went down into a nearby swamp, then came out and rolled over into the dirt, and it was instantly healed. Incredibly amazed, the shepherd brought over all the inflicted sheep into the swamp, then let them roll over in the dirt to be repaired in the same fashion. Soon enough, the news spread around and reached the emperor of Constantinople, whose only daughter was inflicted with leprosy. He sent her with a large entourage to Egypt to be healed in that fantastic location. In that spot, the saint appeared to her in a dream, instructed her to have that location dug few meters deep to find his relics. So, she did, and she was instantly healed. Her father built a small church on that spot in the name of St. Mina, which was consecrated on the 15th of Paona.

In (363-373 AD), the 20th pope of Alexandria St. Athanasius, the Apostolic (328-373 AD), built a church in that location, and he placed the holy relics of St. Mina in a special chamber beneath the Altar. Then, the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD) wrote to Emperor Arcadius (E: 383-408 AD), the son of Emperor Theodosius the Great (379-395 AD), to ask for his help because St. Mina's church became too small to accommodate the multitudes of visitors. The emperor responded and helped him in building a sizeable beautiful church, in the form of an eastern extension to the church previously built by St. Athanasius the Apostolic.

Then, in the days of the 82nd Pope Benjamin II (1327-1339 AD), the holy body of St. Mina was moved to the church of St. Mina in Fum el-Khalij on the outskirts of Cairo. In the days of the 116th Pope St. Kyrillos VI (1959- 1971), a part of his relics was moved back to its original location and was placed in the new monastery of St. Mina in Marriott.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Ascetic, p. 228
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE ASCETIC, ST.

This St. Mina lived for fifty-nine years in a monastery near Alexandria. He reached a high level of asceticism that he forgot all about himself. Also, in his honor to his monastery's Abbot, he used to bow low in front of him whenever he would enter his cell until the Abbot would give him his blessing. Such a practice of piety was used by the Abbot of the monastery to teach a lesson to the new monks entering the monastery. Some of those monks used to ridicule such practices of giving honor to the elderly monks. So, it happened once that Mina entered the cell of the Abbot and prostrated himself before him to the ground as he used to do while saying: “Bless me, father.” The Abbot chose to disregard his presence and left him bowing for hours until it was time for prayer. Then, he gave him the blessing, and only then, Mina stood upright. A young monk said to him: “By so doing, you have wasted your precious time while doing nothing.” The saint answered him: “No, I did not waste my time, because I did use that chance to recite the whole book of Psalms.”

God chose to honor this ascetic worshipper after his departure. So, while they were praying on him during his funeral, the church was filled with sweet fragrance as a testimony of the virtues by which he was adorned.

[The Faithful Synaxarion: 26 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, the Bishop, p. 229
passages.text:
Saint: MINA, THE BISHOP (The martyr) — Ordained as a Bishop

Ordained as a Bishop:

Then, St. Mina was called for the rank of a bishop by messengers sent by the pope. He cried for forsaking the wilderness, but after being told by the fathers that it was a call from God, he obeyed and went along with the pope's messengers, and the pope ordained him as a bishop on Tamai el-Amdid.

God granted him the grace of healing the sick and that of knowing the hidden matters in the minds of people. The other bishops all around used to visit him and seek his counsel. The multitudes from everywhere would come to him to hear his teachings. He was a contemporary to four of the popes of Alexandria, and he laid his hand upon some of them during their ordinations: Abba Alexandros II (704-729 AD), Abba Cosmas I (729-730 AD), Abba Theodore I (730-742 AD), and Abba Khael I (743-767 AD).

When the Lord Jesus Christ wished him to depart from this world, He informed him about it. So he called up the people of his diocese, urged them to abide in the upright faith, and to keep the Divine commandments. Then, he committed them to their True Shepherd Jesus Christ and departed to His Savior, who loved him. He was so mourned by his people, who buried him in a place he assigned to them ahead of time.

[The Synaxarion: 7 Hator]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina, pp. 236–237
passages.text:
Saint: MINA (The martyr)

This St. Mina was the familial brother of the 38th Pope of Alexandria St.

Benjamin I (623-662 AD). He endured so many tortures by those believing in the two natures for the Lord (the Chalcedonians). He was tortured by burning his sides with flames and breaking his teeth through continuous beating. During all his sufferings, he refused to submit to their request to accept the decree of the Chalcedonian Council. They finally cast him into the water to drown, where he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 80]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mina II, the 61st Pope of Alexandria, pp. 226–227
passages.text:
Saint: MINA II, The 61st POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Marriage and Virginity

His Marriage and Virginity:

After the repose of the 60th Pope of Alexandria Abba Theophilus (Theophanes: 952-956 AD), St. Mark's Seat became vacant. The entire Coptic congregation prayed to God to send them his replacement. The bishops and the priests set forth to the monasteries, where the Holy Spirit guided them in the monastery of Abba Macarius to a simple ascetic monk, called Mina. He was originally from the village of Sandala in Kafr el-Sheikh district, and he used to carry the same name before he became a monk. When his parents intended for him to get married, he kept silent until after the wedding ceremony. Then, when he joined his wife in seclusion, he preached to her the virtues of chastity and living a godly life, which she accepted. After they had lived together for three days, without any physical contact, she allowed him to withdraw to the wilderness silently. There, he became a disciple of one of the saintly old monks, to whom he revealed his situation and his chastity in the seclusion of his cell. His family, thinking that he has died, set over him great mourning. In the monastery, his virtues of asceticism, humility, gifts, broad knowledge, and simplicity became well known.

Then, when his spiritual father recommended him for the patriarchate, they took him by force to Alexandria, where he was ordained in December 956 AD. His papacy lasted for seventeen years and eleven months (956-974 AD).

records.question: Who was St. Shenouda the Archimandrite?
records.answer:
St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was a prominent figure in Egyptian monasticism, considered the most important representative of Coenobitic Monasticism in Egypt after St. Pachomius. He was given the title of Archimandrite, meaning "the head of the anchorites," because he practiced a life of seclusion periodically and encouraged monks to prepare for a more elevated monastic life of seclusion after practicing communal life for some years [1].

He served as the Abbot of the White Monastery in Attrib near Sohag in the desert of Thebes during the 4th and 5th centuries for more than 56 years, supervising about 2,200 monks and 1,800 nuns [1][3]. He accompanied Pope Cyril the Great to the third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus in 431 AD [1].

St. Shenouda was a spiritual and social reformer who linked worship with social life and emphasized practical love. For example, when Barbarians attacked Upper Egypt, he confronted them to release captives and opened his monastery to shelter thousands of prisoners, providing medical care and sustenance for months [2].

He was also an ecclesiastical political leader who opposed the Byzantine occupation and the Chalcedonian Council, encouraging Egyptians to stand firm in their Orthodox faith and patriotic spirit. He used his eloquence in the Coptic language to inspire his people against oppression and injustice [2][9].

His monastic system was stricter than that of St. Pachomius, involving a probation period outside the monastery, signed pledges, and structured worship and administration. He combined features from the monastic orders of Abba Anthony and Abba Pachomius, emphasizing study, work, and seclusion [6][5].

Despite his leadership over thousands of monks and nuns, he maintained a life of seclusion annually and lived to the age of 118, with 66 years as abbot [3].

He never allowed foreigners to join his monastic congregation; all his monks were of Coptic descent [1].

In summary, St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was a monastic leader, reformer, spiritual father, and patriotic figure who shaped Egyptian monasticism and defended the Orthodox faith during a turbulent historical period [1][2][3][5][6][9].
