passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 133
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA

St. Shenouda is considered the most prominent personality representing the Coenobitic Monasticism in Egypt after St. Pachomius. Therefore, he was given the title of Archimandrite, meaning (the head of the anchorites), on account that he used to practice the life of seclusion now and then. He also encouraged some of his monks to retreat to the wilderness after they practice the life of fellowship for a few years, yet without completely losing their relationship with the monastery. While St. Pachom saw in the Fellowship the climax of the monastic exaltation, St. Shenouda saw it as a transition stage that would prepare the soul for the more elevated monastic life of seclusion.

St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was the Abbot of The White Monastery in Attrib near Sohag in the desert of Thebes in the 4th and 5th centuries for more than 56 years. According to his disciple, who succeeded him, he supervised about 2,200 monks and 1,800 nuns during that time.

In the year 431 AD, he accompanied the 24th pope of Alexandria St. Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to attend the third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus.

St. Shenouda never allowed a foreigner to join his monastic congregation, but all his monks were of Coptic descent. That is why many European scholars avoided mentioning his name when they spoke about the Fathers of the wilderness. For many centuries, they did not try to translate any of his works.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 136–137
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation)

This was expressed in their firm stand against the hateful Chalcedonian Council when they refused to bow their heads before Emperor Mercian (450-457 AD), when he thought that he would be able to force them to adopt his Chalcedonian belief; contrary to the Orthodox doctrine which they inherited from their Fathers.

A Spiritual and Social Reformer;

Abba Shenouda felt that worship was bound to the social life, and religion was both an applied love as well as a spiritual love. Therefore, St. Shenouda and the thousands of his monks did not try to isolate themselves from Egyptian society. As an example, when the Barbarians attacked Upper Egypt and looted all the possessions and took thousands of citizens as prisoners, St. Shenouda dared to face the invaders and convince them to take the spoils, but to let the captives go free. He then opened his monastery before the thousands of captives to dwell there for three months, during which the monks dedicated their time to serve them, including seven physicians among the monks, to nurse their wounds. During that period, 94 persons died and were buried in the monastery, 52 babies were born, and 8,500 bushels of wheat and vast amounts of lentil and beans were consumed. From this example, we can imagine the number of guests who were served in the monasteries within that extended period; and how the monks got to believe in the practical love, as more critical virtue than any monastic law or system.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Care for the Nuns

His Care for the Nuns:

Abba Shenouda was a Father and Mentor, not only to thousands of monks but to 1,800 nuns as well. For them, he wrote multi-purpose letters to teach, guide, and hold them fast to the Upright Faith. But despite being a Father over such a vast number of monks and nuns, yet he kept on practicing his life of seclusion. So, he earned the title of Archimandrite. Every year, he used to spend some time in seclusion, during which no one dared to approach him.

He lived to reach 118 years of age, of which 66 years as the Abbot of several monasteries, some for monks and others for nuns. However, during those long years, until he reached that advanced age, God granted him health and strength to keep all his life working hard, from the time he received the leadership of the Red Monastery after the repose of his uncle Pistol. And through his persistent strife, he managed to establish the order of his monasteries; until he handed the flame shining to his disciple Wisa. He also managed to wake up in his fellow citizens their patriotic emotions toward their country.

[Fr. Tadros Yacob Malaty; The Coptic Church is a Church of Monasticism]

[The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute Saint, by K. H. Kuhn; pp. 2131-3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 133–134
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Youth

His Youth:

Shenouda is the Upper Egyptian Coptic (Sahidic) version of the saint's name. He used only the Upper Egyptian dialect in his writings, sermons, and daily talks. The Lower Egyptian (Bohairic) version of his name is Shenoute, meaning (The servant of God or the one dedicated to God).

Shenouda was born to pious Christian parents, who raised their son on the ideal Christian principles. His father had a field where he and his farmers worked; he also had herds of sheep, which he trained his ten years old son Shenouda to shepherd. The little boy used to be all day long with the other shepherds, to whom he gave his food and kept fasting the rest of the day, and instead of going directly back to his parents, he used to stand beside a well and pray until late at night.

With his Uncle Pigol:

When his father became aware of his son's behavior, he took him to his maternal uncle, the well-known Abbot Abba Pigol, and sought from him to bless his young son. Abba Pigol took the boy's hand and laid it on his head, saying: “You bless me, my child, for you will be a Father for so many peoples.” On hearing this, Shenouda's father was immensely rejoiced and left his little son in the monastery in the care of his uncle. So, he learned all the Christian virtues. He kept striving for spiritual perfection through fasting, praying, perseverance, and humility. Watching him with great interest, his uncle rejoiced in his rapid and persistent growth in knowledge and virtue. And, his joy was concluded by a night vision in which an angel of the Lord told him: “Put the Holy Eskeem on the young man Shenouda.” In the very early morning, Pigol woke up, prayed the prayer of the Eskeem, and girded the young Shenouda with it.

Through the following years, Shenouda lived in the “Red Monastery,” where his uncle Pigol was the Abbot of the monks. Since he got the honor of the Eskeem, he doubled his efforts in studying the Divine books, not only for his benefit but also of the monks and the visitors who came to the monastery, whom he gathered around him and taught them the Upright Faith.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 135–136
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Monastic System

The families of the monks and all the people around the monasteries were allowed to visit the monasteries on Saturdays to attend the service of Vespers and to listen to a sermon given by Abba Shenouda. Then, on Sundays, they would partake of the Holy Liturgy and the Sacraments, along with the monks. After the service, the monks used to offer a meal of Agapi to all the guests. Abba Shenouda established two schools inside the White Monastery compound; he encouraged the monks to learn since he believed that teaching was the most potent weapon against the pagan customs. He, as well, cared to establish schools for the natives in the surrounding villages. Abba Shenouda lived in an era enflamed with fiery events. During his time, three Councils were held: The third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus (431 AD), which he attended in the company of Pope Cyril I; the second Ephesian Council (449 AD) and the Chalcedonian Council (451 AD), which caused the split in the Holy Church. In that era, the paganism ultimately came to an end, after Emperor Julian the Apostate (360-363 AD) attempted earlier in vain to bring it back to life. During that time, also, the Egyptian Patriotism was recognized; when all the Egyptians stood up as one entity against the Chalcedonian intruders and rejected them, even when they took the religious form.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 134–135
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — The Archimandrite

The Archimandrite:

One day, the elderly monks heard a voice, saying: “Shenouda became an Archimandrite.” (Meaning head of the anchorites). The enflamed zealously of Shenouda, his exalted holiness, and the many Divine proclamations granted to him by the heavenly Father; drew multitudes of people to live under his guidance to learn the Christian virtues. And when Abba Pigol departed to the Church of the firstborn, they chose Shenouda to replace him.

His Monastic System:

Even though Abba Shenouda followed the monastic system that was prevailing in Egypt, yet he set up a plan for his monks to adopt. In that plan, there were certain differences concerning the way to apply for joining the Fellowship, the administration style, the worship practices, the emphasis on studying, and hand-work in addition to the seclusion option. In this manner, Abba Shenouda combined some features from the monastic orders of Abba Anthony and that of Abba Pachom. The Fellowship (Coenobitic) Monasticism set by Abba Shenouda was stricter than that of Abba Pachom. Its main highlights could be summarized as follows: • The person seeking the monastic life had to spend a probation period in houses outside the walls of the monastery, and not inside as it was in the Pachomian system. Also, the applicant before becoming a monk has to write down and sign a pledge and read it before his brethren inside the church; then, the signed promise would be kept in the archives of the monastery. • Each monastery was managed by a Father-superior, who was assigned by and reported to the Archimandrite, being the Father of all the monasteries. Annually, four general assemblies were held and attended by the whole congregation of monks, including the anchorites. These assemblies were to discuss the conditions of all the monasteries. Concerning the worship practices, each congregation of monks would recite short prayers before starting their work. And the private prayers consisted of Psalms and Church praises, which were to be recited in each monk’s cell according to the guidance of his spiritual father. For the collective prayers, the monks have to assemble four times a day: in the morning, noon, sunset, and evening. Yet they have to come and go in complete silence. Thinkingly in the prayers, they were reciting. Besides those prayers, the Holy Liturgy of the Eucharist was held once a week. The families of the monks and all the people around the monasteries were allowed to visit the monasteries on Saturdays to attend the service of Vespers and to listen to a sermon given by Abba Shenouda. Then, on Sundays, they would partake of the Holy Liturgy and the Sacraments, along with the monks.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, pp. 137–138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA (The martyr)

He lived during the 2nd half of the 7th century when the Arab invasion to Egypt has just begun. This saint was raised in a truly Christian way. He observed a lifestyle within God's commandments and guidelines. He did not stop at fasting, prayers and attending masses, but he was also a generous giver to the poor, and always visiting the sick and imprisoned. Some evil people were annoyed by his piety, so they went to the Arab governor, claiming that the saint was mocking their religion. So, they brought him over for questioning. St. Shenouda declared that he believed in Christ, who commanded his followers to love everybody. He explained to the governor that he was just doing that, and he never made fun of any religion. The governor did not accept his reasoning and ordered him to deny his Christ and join Islam. The saint refused to proclaim his pride in being a Christian. The governor put him through so many tortures, which he accepted gladly.

Finally, they beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] [Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, vol. 2, p. 85]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 127–128
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Ordained as a Bishop of Education

Ordained as a Bishop of Education:

On the 30th of September 1962, Pope Cyril VI appointed him to the bishopric of Christian Education and as Dean of the Coptic Orthodox Theological Seminary. He renamed him Bishop Shenouda in honor of the most renowned scholar and writer in Coptic, St. Shenouda the Archimandrite (348- 466). Under the leadership of Bishop Shenouda, the number of students at the Coptic Orthodox Theological Seminary tripled. Bishop Shenouda used to have weekly lectures in Cairo for the general public, which was attended by a vast number of believers.

Ordained as a Pope:

Bishop Shenouda was enthroned as Pope Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria and patriarch of the See of St. Mark on the 14th of November 1971 by an “Altar Lot,” nearly nine months after the death of Pope Cyril VI of Alexandria. He was the third Alexandrian patriarch to take the name Shenouda; his namesakes were Pope Shenouda I (859–880) and Pope Shenouda II (1047– 1077). Less than one year after becoming pope of the Church of Alexandria, in October 1972, Pope Shenouda visited the ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople and the Pope of Rome, becoming the first Alexandrian pope to do so since the Christological schism of the Council of Chalcedon in 451. In May 1973, he penned a Christological statement that was agreed upon with the Roman Catholic Church and the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox Churches about the Nature of Christ, in a step towards settling the dispute of 451 and moving towards Christian Unity. On the 10th of May 1973, he celebrated the return by the Roman Catholic Church of part of the relics of the 20th pope of Alexandria St. Athanasius the Apostolic. In September 1974, he went on a pastoral trip to visit the Ethiopian Church during the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie (1930-1974) of Ethiopia.

In April and May 1974, he became the first Archbishop of Alexandria to visit North America when he visited the US and Canada. It was the first of many visits to that part of the world during his long papacy. He also visited Australia 6 times. The first visit was in 1989. The second was in 1991, the third in 1993, the fourth in 1995 and the fifth in 1996. His sixth and final trip took place in November 2002. He conducted an extended “Silver Jubilee” tour for about seven months in 1996, which took him to Europe, Canada, the USA, and Australia.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 136
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation)

Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation):

Even though Abba Shenouda led a life of seclusion since his childhood, yet he was observing the world in which he lived. He attentively watched the events and the political disturbances taking place in the outside world. He perceived that the faithful disciple of Jesus Christ is the one who delivers His message to other men. On looking around, he noticed how his fellow citizens were burdened by the bitter servitude of worries and fears induced by paganism. He also realized that the Byzantine rulers were sucking the blood of the striving people and robbing the fruits of their labor. So, he dedicated himself to set them free; first from their fears, by confirming to them that the Divine care would protect them from any harm. He combined his teaching with action, by feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, treating the ill, and giving hospitality to the stranger. Above all that, he accompanied the oppressed to the court of justice to defend them; and when he failed to bring justice to them, he would bring their complaint up to the emperor. And, he would not have peace until the oppressed had judgment.

Once, in a public assembly, he stirred up the multitudes by saying: “The hearts of the rulers are filled with evil, deception, injustice, and greed. They have only one goal, to gather money at the expense of the poor. Who could count the troubles endured by our people from those rulers? I know some people who lack the necessary food for themselves and their cattle. I am sure they have the intention to turn the Egyptians to slaves and put the yoke on their shoulders.”

He used what God granted him of the gift of eloquence and writing to stir up the patriotic spirit in the people, addressing them only with the Coptic language in its Upper Egyptian dialect. By such pure Egyptian tongue, he managed to inflame their hearts with zeal, to wake up their spirit, and to make them perceive the honor of being Egyptians. That fire ignited in them by Abba Shenouda came to be the driving force, which enabled the Egyptians to stand firm before their occupation rulers. This was expressed in their firm stand against the hateful Chalcedonian Council when they refused to bow their heads before Emperor Mercian (450-457 AD), when he thought that he would be able to force them to adopt his Chalcedonian belief; contrary to the Orthodox doctrine which they inherited from their Fathers.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 125–126
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

On the 17th of March 2012, the long trip of pain which his holiness Pope Shenouda III has lived had ended and began the journey of the glories hidden from the human eyes. During those days when Egypt was living through his departure to Paradise, his funeral gathered all Egyptian categories; it included Muslims and Christians from all the denominations, leaders, and ordinary people. He had been a messenger of peace struggling in a difficult time and a man of peace, even in his departure from this world.

They all expressed their heart-felt deep grief, which shared by a lot of the presidents and institutions of the world uniquely and beautifully. His marvelous love for the leading figures in the Arab world; made some of them say: "He isn't the Pope for the Christians only, but he is the Pope for all the Arab countries." For his funeral, the people got crowded in such a compact fashion that three people died in the process, and six ambulances carried those who couldn't handle the unbelievable crowding. One of the broadcasters said: "I am not surprised to see some people here preferring to die in this crowded procession, just to have the blessings from his corpse!" The unique way that the people were expressing their grief of him after his departure was a natural fruit for the fertile seeds of love which he planted within them during his life.

Pope Shenouda III (1971-2012) was the 117th pope of Alexandria and the patriarch of the See of St. Mark. His episcopate lasted over 40 years from the 14th of November 1971 until his death on the 17th of March 2012. He was a conservative figure within the Church and was also highly respected within the Muslim community.

He became a monk in 1954 under the name Fr. Antonius el-Suriani. In 1958, he was ordained as a priest. In 1962, pope Cyril VI (1959-1971) summoned Fr. Antonius and consecrated him as a “General Bishop for Christian Education” under the name Abba Shenouda. In 1971, he was crowned as the 117th Pope of Alexandria under the title Shenouda III. In the end, pope Shenouda III died in March 2012 of lung and liver complications at his official residence.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, the Monk, p. 138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE MONK, ST.

This saint was a hearing-impaired elder monk who lived during the Fatimid era (909-1171 AD), in a cell near the town of Nousa, the province of Aga in the Daqahlyia governorate. The biography of this saint was written in the great work The History of the Patriarchs, which was started by Severus ibn al- Muqaffaå (died 987 AD) and was completed by others to cover the period ending in 1167 AD. One of the authors of this book sent the saint a message asking for his prayers on his behalf and the behalf of his brother Fahd, for both were put in prison through an order made by Badr el-Gamaly (~1070 AD) the commander of the army of the caliph Al-Mustansir bi-Allah (1035-1094 AD). The saint answered him, saying: “Today, the Lord Jesus Christ will set you both free.” On the same day, they were released.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 130]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda El-Bahnassawi, pp. 120–121
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA EL-BAHNASSAWI (The martyr)

St. Shenouda el-Bahnassawi was reported by some people to governor Maximus, who was appointed by Emperor Diocletian (284-305), that he was a Christian. The governor called him and inquired about his religion, and the saint confessed his faith in the Lord Christ. The governor ordered his men to cast him on the ground and to beat him with the rods to tear his flesh off and to scatter his blood around, then to throw him in a foul-smelling prison. God sent him the Archangel Michael, who healed his wounds, encouraged him, and gave him the good news that he would be receiving the crown of Glory.

In the morning, the soldiers found him standing in prayers. On reporting to the governor that they saw him sound with no wounds, he said that he was a sorcerer. Then, he ordered to hang him upside down and ignite fire underneath him. When it caused him no harm, he ordered pressing him in the Henbazin; and finally to cut his head off. His body was then cut to pieces and thrown away to the wild dogs. The dogs did not approach his remains all day. At night, the believers took his relics, covered them with precious spices, shrouded him, and buried him honorably.

[The Synaxarion: 14 Baramhat]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda I, the 55th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 123–124
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA I, The 55th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Shepherding

His Shepherding:

It happened once that during a papal pastoral visit to one of the monasteries of Upper Egypt, the Arabs attacked that monastery to rob and to kill. However, the pope bravely came out to them, carrying his cross. Once they saw him, they retreated before him and fled away. And with the repetition of attacks of those Arab barbers on so many monasteries, and because of the fear shown by the monks, the pope constructed a particular fortress building in every monastery.

After he returned to his throne, he sent a message of fellowship to his brother in the apostolic ministry: the Patriarch of Antioch, who not only replied by a similar note but, with it, he sent precious gifts.

His Care for the Upright Faith:

Being a pious scholar, this pope worked hard on confronting the heresies which spread among the believers.

In a village called Bukhnessa in the Marriott area, some people proclaimed that the Passions of Christ were not real, but they were imaginary. So, the pope went to them and guided them to the truth and brought them back to the true Faith. Also, during a visit to Upper Egypt, the pope found that the congregation of the town of Baliana has abandoned their two bishops and proclaimed the death of the Godhead. The pope debated with them and explained to them the upright faith, based on the Holy Bible and the Sayings of the Fathers, until they returned to the mother church and offered obedience towards their bishops.

That pope cared so much for the church's affairs and its various institutions. And, whatever remained in the patriarchates funds, he distributed among the poor. When he completed his unique struggle, he reposed in peace on the 14th of Baramhat 597 AM (869 AD), after he sat for about 21 years on St. Mark Seat.

[Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute I, by Subhi Y. Labib; pp. 2133-5]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda II, the 65th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 124–125
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA II, The 65th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Patriarchs Preoccupation with Wealth

The Patriarchs Preoccupation with Wealth:

During the ordination process, the clergy of Alexandria made it a condition on the papal candidate to promise that he would spend 500 dinars on their churches every year. Also, the archons made his pledge to refrain from receiving any bribes (simony) from those seeking clergy positions. Despite his promise to reject the Simonism in ordaining the clergy, yet he took a bribe to ordain a bishop for Assiut without even conferring with the people. That made the people of Assiut ban the new bishop from entering their city, and he had to go back in shame to his monastery. Not caring for the opposition of the archons, in particular Ibn Bakr, the pope issued a decree that all the possessions of the bishops should be inherited by the patriarchate after their death. The new system first applied to the bishop of Shenan, and then it continued to be applied until our present era; until pope Shenouda III (1971-2012), canceled it and decided to keep the diocese possessions of a reposed bishop for the one who would follow him. As a result of the erroneous behavior of that pope and his persistent seeking for wealth, the Church’s clergy wanted to deliver the affairs of the Church to a particular Council. However, the pope rejected their request. So, the whole congregation turned to prayers, asking God to protect His Church. The patriarch was inflicted by a problematic disease that caused him to shake violently, and all the physician’s attempt to cure it ended with failure; until he departed from this world in the year 1047 AD.

[Revealing the Secrets in the History of the Patriarchs, vol. 2, p. 11]

[Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: The History of the Coptic Church] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute II, by Subhi Y. Labib; p. 2135]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda II, the 65th Pope of Alexandria, p. 124
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA II, The 65th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Tolerance of the Caliph

After the repose of the 64th Pope Zecharias (1004-1032), the bishops and the archons recommended the monk Shenouda of the monastery of St. Macarius to sit on the papal seat. A night vision confirmed their choice to one of the bishops. He was ordained by the name of Pope Shenouda II (Sanutios: 1032-1046) in the year 1032; in the days of the Fatimid caliphate (909-1171).

The Tolerance of the Caliph:

At that time, it was the custom that the caliph would be paid by the Copts 6,000 dinars to get his approval on the appointment of their new patriarch. However, there was among the Copts a man of high status called Ibn Bakr. He managed to convince the caliph to issue an order to waive such a fee.

Out of the graces of God on the Copts during the time of this patriarch, the caliph Al-Zahir bi-Allah (1021-1036) followed the lead of his earlier ancestor the great caliph Al-Ăziz bi-Allah (975-996) in his tolerance with the non- Muslims, which resulted in a vast growth in the creative and artistic achievements in the country The caliph’s tolerance went so far to allow anybody converted to Islam to go back to his Christianity if that was his wish. He also allowed for building so many new churches.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Younan Nakhla El-Doweiry, the Archon, p. 362
passages.text:
Saint: YOUNAN NAKHLA EL-DOWEIRY, THE ARCHON

And adorned the building by an altar in the name of St. Anba Abram, which eventually turned into a church. • With his advanced age, his activity increased, and he set the foundation of a nursery and a house for the out-of-town female students, facing the building of the Society of el-MaĥAbbah on Jazerit Badran street. When the 116th Pope of Alexandria, St. Kyrillos VI (Cyril VI: 1959-1971) decided to establish a vast Cathedral in the name of St. Mark the Apostle on the land of Anba Roweis, the pope formed a committee to collect donations for such an enormous enterprise. He chose archon Younan Nakhla as one of its members. In the year 1972, the country president Anwar Sadat (1970-1981) bestowed on him the highest medal of Imtiaz (excellence) of the first grade. And, the governor of Cairo gave him a letter of appreciation on the day of Social Labor as an appreciation of his endless strife. After such shining conflict, he departed Paradise to enjoy the company of the Saints in the 1970s.

[The Faithful Synaxarion: 24 Toba]

records.question: Who was St. Macarius the Great?
records.answer:
St. Macarius the Great (~295-392 AD) was the founder of monasticism in the wilderness of the Scetis. He was greatly influenced by St. Anthony the Great, whom he visited twice. He was called "The Chosen Vessel" by the historian Socrates and "The Aged Youth" by Palladius due to his great discernment at a young age. He was granted the gifts of healing the sick and foreseeing the future. He was born in Shubshir in the district of Menouf to pious parents. His father, Ibrahim, was initially childless but was told by a divine messenger that he would have a son whose fame would spread worldwide and who would have spiritual children. This son was Macarius, who was obedient and graced by God from childhood [1].

Macarius was chosen as a reader in his village church. Although his father married him off against his will, Macarius pretended to be ill and went to the wilderness to recover. There, he had a vision of a Cherub who showed him the entire wilderness and told him that God had granted him and his spiritual children the whole mountain for worship. The Cherub accompanied him almost all his life [1][2].

Upon returning, he found his wife had died a virgin. He gave his inheritance to the poor after his parents died. He was ordained a priest but later considered himself unworthy and moved to another village. He endured false accusations and beatings silently. To avoid worldly glory, he fled to the inner wilderness of Scetis, where he lived in seclusion, building a church for the monks who gathered around him. He was known for his love of seclusion and would escape crowds by using an underground tunnel to a distant cave, praying along the way [2][3].

St. Macarius was known as a man of love and compassion, covering up the sins of others and showing love even to pagans, which led many to the faith. He performed many miracles, including healing the sick and raising the dead. He was also known for his teachings on fasting, perseverance, and the kingdom of heaven [9][13][15].

He died at the age of ninety-seven on the 27th of Baramhat, 392 AD. Before his death, he saw St. Anthony, St. Pachom, and a group of saints and angels. He instructed his disciples to hide his body, but it was later stolen and buried in a church for about 160 years before being returned to his monastery [4].

In summary, St. Macarius the Great was a pioneering monastic founder, a man of deep spirituality, love, and miracles, who lived a life of asceticism and seclusion in the Egyptian desert, greatly influencing Christian monasticism [1][2][3][4][9][13][15].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, pp. 17–18
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — His Upbringing and Marriage

St. Macarius (~ 295-392 AD) was the founder of monasticism in the wilderness of the Scetis. He was influenced considerably by St. Anthony the Great, whom he visited twice.

He was called by the historian Socrates (380-450 AD) ‘The Chosen Vessel,’ and Palladius (364-425 AD) said about him that he was worthy to possess such great discernment at the age of thirty, that he was called the ‘Aged Youth.’ He was granted the gift of healing the sick and the gift of foreseeing the future.Based on a decree issued by Emperor Valens (364-378 AD), the Arian bishop Lucius exiled the saint to an island in the Nile in Upper Egypt. As the saint was at a very advanced age, he reposed shortly after returning from exile.

His Upbringing and Marriage:

This saint was born in Shubshir in the district of Menouf to pious and righteous parents. His father, Ibrahim, had no children. Then one night, he saw someone sent by the Lord, who told him that the Lord will give him a son whose fame would spread around the whole world and whom God will give spiritual children. After a little time, he was given a boy he called Macara, (meaning the blessed), who was obedient to his parents, and on whom the grace of God dwelt since his childhood.

The young man Macarius was chosen by the priests and the people of the village to be a reader in their church. Once he reached maturity, his father got him married against his will. So, Macarius pretended to be ill for a few days, then asked his father's permission to go to the wilderness to recover. He prayed to the Lord Jesus Christ to help him proceed according to His will. In the wilderness, he saw a vision, as though a Cherub with six wings held his hand, brought him up to the top of the mountain, and showed him the entire wilderness, north, south, east, and west. Then, he told him: “God says to you that he has granted you and your spiritual children this whole mountain, to dedicate all your time for worship. Many leaders will come to this wilderness. Watch then, and remember what I am telling you: If you walked uprightly, I shall appear to you, and proclaim God's words to you.” It was said that this Cherub accompanied St. Macarius almost all his life.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, pp. 18–19
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — His Upbringing and Marriage

Watch then, and remember what I am telling you: If you walked uprightly, I shall appear to you, and proclaim God's words to you.” It was said that this Cherub accompanied St. Macarius almost all his life.

When Macarius returned from the wilderness, he found out that his wife has died while still a virgin. He gave thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, and when his parents died, he distributed all his inheritance to the poor and the needy. The people of Shebshir noticed his purity and chastity and took him to the bishop of Ashmon, who ordained him as a priest on the village church. They built for him a place outside the town, to which they came to get his blessings; and assigned someone to sell his handwork, and to get him his needs.

After a little while, he went to another village, for he counted himself unworthy of the priesthood or the honor his people were giving him.

In The Scetis:

On observing how virtuous the saint was, the devil brought on him a horrible trial; that he provoked a girl who committed evil with a young man to claim that it was St. Macarius who did it to her. Her folks insulted and beaten him violently, while he endured in silence. When it was time for that girl to deliver, she remained suffering in backbreaking labor for four days; until she confessed that she has falsely accused the innocent saint and proclaimed the name of the young man who seduced her. On hearing this, the relatives of the girl went to the saint, asking for his forgiveness for their aggression against him. St. Macarius escaped from them, to avoid the worldly glory. He was then in his thirties. Then, he decided not to return to his cell, so the angel of the Lord appeared to him, took him for a walk for two days until they reached the Natrun Valley. There, the saint said to the angel: “O master, designate a place for me to live.” The angel answered: “No! Lest you decide to leave it later on and would be considered disobedient to the Lord. The whole wilderness is yours; dwell wherever you want.” He dwelt in the inner wilderness, in the location where the monastery of St. Maximus and St. Domitius was built. It is known nowadays as the Baramus monastery.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, pp. 19–20
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — In The Scetis

He dwelt in the inner wilderness, in the location where the monastery of St. Maximus and St. Domitius was built. It is known nowadays as the Baramus monastery.

When he went to visit St. Anthony the Great, he said about St. Macarius when he saw him: “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit.” Then, St. Anthony set him with the holy Eskeem and he returned to the Scetis. Later on, when the number of the monks who gathered around St. Macarius became too many, he built for them a church. His fame spread that even the kings heard about him because of the many miracles which he was performing. The angel of the Lord then appeared to him, brought him to the top of the mountain, at the western salt-water lake, and asked him to move there for a while. The angel guided him in building a cell for him and a church for the multitudes, which would be coming to see him.

His Love for Seclusion:

St. Macarius asserted that the wilderness of the Scetis would lose its monastic meaning once civilization would infringe upon it. He said: “When you see the cells became too close to the cultivated land, then you should know that the end of the Scetis is approaching, and when you start seeing trees, then know that it is at the gates. Also, when you start seeing kids, then you should carry your leather clothing and run.”

Even in the wilderness of the Scetis, St. Macarius used to flee away from the crowds. According to St. Palladius, the saint dug for himself an underground tunnel that extended from his cell and ended in a small cave at a distance of almost half a mile. So, when too many people would come to visit his cell, he would secretly go through the tunnel to that cave, and nobody would find him. According to one of his devoted disciples, the saint used to recite twenty-four prayers on his way to the cave and twenty-four prayers on his way back.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, pp. 21–22
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

On the day of his departure, St. Macarius saw St. Anthony, St. Pachom, and a group of saints and angels. He delivered his soul when he was ninetyseven years old, on the 27th of Baramhat 392 AD. He commanded his disciples to hide his body, but some people of Shebshir came and stole it, built a church, and buried him in it for some 160 years; then, it was eventually brought back to his monastery.

Among his Sayings:

• While you are rebuking someone, if the anger moves within you, then you are fulfilling your evil desire. So, in your attempt to save your brother, do not lose yourself. • If we kept remembering the people's faults against us, then we are destroying our ability to remember God. • The long-suffering is perseverance, and perseverance is winning, and winning is life, and life is the kingdom of heaven, and the Kingdom of Heavenis God. • The well is deep, but its water is kind and sweet. The door is narrow, and the road is rough, but the city is full of joy and gladness. The tower is high and fortified, but inside there are precious treasures. Fasting is severe and burdensome, but it leads to the kingdom of heaven. Doing good deeds may be difficult and hard, but it saves from hell through the mercy of our glorious God.

[Hegomen Tadros Y. Malaty: The Coptic Orthodox Church; a Church of Asceticism; 1986]

Notes: [1] Some manuscripts mentioned that St. ‘Macarius’ did not get the grace of priesthood until he went to the Scetis.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius of Alexandria, pp. 12–13
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — Encouraging the Pachomian Monks to Work

During those days, St. Macarius did not eat any food. Then, he went to see St. Pachom, and told him: “Accept me father; and if you find that I do not fast, practice asceticism or do my hand-work; then you may kick me out of your monastery.”

St. Pachom sent him to live among the brethren monks, who were almost 1,400 in number. There, he spent with them the Holy Forty days. During those days, he was never seen eating nor sitting down; but always standing weaving the palm-leaves. Then, the brethren monks complained to Abba Pachom saying: “Where did you find such a person? Send this man away, for he has nobody. Did you bring him here to humiliate us? Send him away;

otherwise, we all shall escape from here.” St. Pachom answered them: “Just wait for a little while until God reveals to us his identity.” Then, St. Pachom requested from God to reveal to him the identity of that man, and God informed him that he was Macarius of Alexandria.

Then, after the Holy Liturgy, Abba Pachom brought St. Macarius to their gathering spot so that all the monks would see him. Then, he said to him: “Come over here, you honorable elder. How could that happen? You have hidden from us that you are Abba Macarius. For a long time, I have heard about you and longed to see you in person. In any case, I do thank you for teaching us, particularly, the young monks, how not to boast about their pious deeds even if they did their best; for they will never reach the measure of the Forty Days spent by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ the Son of the Living God; or the standard of your pious deeds. Now man, go back in peace to your place, for you have taught us and guided all of us enough. Pray on our behalf.” The monastery's monks, greatly rejoiced, sought the saint's blessing and prayers for them. Then, Abba Macarius left them to go back to his monastery.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Son of Basilides, pp. 22–23
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE SON OF BASILIDES (The martyr)

This St. Macarius was a member of a holy family which sent to heaven so many heroes of the faith like St. Basilides, the minister of Emperor Numerian (283-284 AD), St. Boctor the son of Romanos, St. Abadir, St. Irene, St. Yustus the son of Romanos, St. Theoklia, St. Abali, and St. Akladius, who was a relative of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) himself.

St. Macarius left the palace of Diocletian, so the angry emperor sent him accompanied by some soldiers to Alexandria to be tortured and killed there, but he first bid his mother farewell in Antioch. Then, when he reached Alexandria, he was left in jail for some time. Then, he was brought before Armenius, the governor of Alexandria. The saint confessed his Christ with Evangelic courage and rebuked the governor on worshipping the senseless idols. Armenius ordered his men to torture him. They chained him, cut his fingers and put vinegar on his wounds, rolled him over hot iron nails, and poured boiled tar over his head. The saint fell unconscious and saw the Lord Jesus Christ in a vision surrounded by a crowd of saints. He was comforted, and the Lord restored him to a sound and healthy condition. Although the governor was amazed, he resumed more tortures, by forcing two hot rods through the saint's throat.

Later on, the governor Armenius sent him to the city of Bshati. On their way, one of the soldiers fell dead after being knocked down by the governor's chariot. St. Macarius prayed on his behalf, and by the power of the Lord, the soldier was raised from the dead. After that miracle, the soldier and all the inhabitants of Bshati proclaimed their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

They took the saint to the city of Shatanof, then made him drink a cup of mixed poison, which did not harm him. Then, after he was subjected to so many other sufferings, he completed his great struggle by having his head cut off by the sword.

[Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 123]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius of Alexandria, pp. 16–17
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — His Exile and Repose

His Exile and Repose:

St. Macarius was exiled at the age of seventy-three by the Arian Emperor Valens (364-378 AD), to one of the Nile islands in Upper Egypt, along with St. Macarius the Great. In their exile, they suffered much torture for three years by orders from the evil emperor. The inhabitants of that island were idol-worshippers, and their highly respected pagan priest happened to have his daughter possessed by an unclean spirit. When the prayers of these two saints promptly healed her, many inhabitants on the island believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, and these two saints taught the inhabitants the Christian Faith until they returned to their monasteries.

St. Macarius continued his life in this spiritual path until he reached the right old age of ninety-five years. Then, he reposed in peace in the year 395.

St. Palladius, the historian, visited him with whom he had a close friendship. At the time of his repose, St. Palladius sat at the door of his cell to hear what he had to say. He heard him addressing himself, saying: “What do you want, O evil old man Macarius? You are already drinking wine and using oil. What else do you want?” Then, he was addressing a devil, saying: “Do you have anything against me? No! You will not find in me anything belonging to you. Get away from me.” Then, he addressed his body, saying: “Come on, O traitor horse. Do not be scared, as long as I am in you.”

His Writings:

He had so many laws, published in Paris in the year 1637. He also had letters about ‘The Souls of the Righteous after Death,’ published in Switzerland in the year 1696.

Of his Words:

• Since the day I became a monk, I never ate bread to satisfaction, nor slept to delight. None of the brave fathers fell ill; because they controlled their bodies, according to the reasonable limits.

[The Synaxarion: 6 Pashons] [Yousef Habib: St. Macarius of Alexandria; 1970]

Notes: [3] See: The Coptic Encyclopedia: Kellia, by Marguerite Rassart-Debergh; p. 1397…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Bishop, p. 17
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE BISHOP (The martyr)

He was the bishop of Edku, in the district of Rosetta in the province of Beĥeira, Egypt. He was one of the three saintly Maqars. He was exiled along with the 25th Pope St. Dioscorus (444-454 AD), after the Chalcedonian Council. He showed such a great zeal on the Orthodox Faith, and he held fast to the Orthodox doctrines, that Pope Dioscorus secretly smuggled him from his exile and sent him back to Alexandria to support the believers.

On his arrival there, he found a delegate of Emperor Marcian (450-457 AD), carrying the ‘Leo's Tome,’ trying to convince the fathers to accept it and sign it. When the delegate sought from St Macarius to do so, he refused and provoked the others not to accept it and to hold fast to the faith of their fathers. Provoked to anger, the emperor's delegate kicked him with his foot, so strongly, that the old saint fell instantly dead.

[The Martyrdom in Christianity; p. 80]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, p. 21
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — His Gifts

His Gifts:

The ‘Apophthegmata Patrum’ (Sayings of the Fathers) referred to the saint's wrestling against the demons. According to St. Palladius, the saint was granted the gift of performing miracles. He raised someone from the dead to save a heretic who did not believe in the resurrection of the bodies.

St. Macarius and the Two Saintly Women:

When he once sought from God to show him someone equal to him in his behavior, a voice came to him from heaven, saying: “So far, you have not reached the level of two women in Alexandria.” He inquired until he reached their house. They welcomed him and washed his feet. Inquiring from them about their story, one of them said to him: “We were not related to each other in the flesh before we were married to two brothers. We sought from them to let us be nuns; and when they refused, we vowed to spend our lives fasting until the evenings, and to practice continuous prayers. Each of us got a boy; when one of those boys would cry, one of us would hasten to embrace him and nourish him, even if he is not her own. We go through our lives in unity of views, unity in our ways, and the unity of our hearts is our goal. Our husbands work in shepherding; we are poor, but we are satisfied with our daily bread, and what remains, we give to the poor.” On hearing this, the saint cried out, saying: “Indeed, God looks at the hearts; and grants His Holy Spirit to whoever seeks Him.” He bid them farewell and returned to the wilderness. Also, in Osim, there was a monk who led some people astray by claiming that there was no resurrection from the dead. When the bishop of Osim came to the saint and told him about that monk, the saint went to see him and managed to bring him back from his vanity.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, p. 24
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS (The martyr)

On the 30th of Hator, the church celebrates the feast of St Macarius, the martyr.

[The Synaxarion: 30 Hator]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius II, the 69th Pope of Alexandria, p. 9
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS II, the 69th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

He wrote: “God protected us from his deeds. We asked Him, whose Name is great, to perpetuate His mercy and His grace; and to inspire us to give thanks to Him and to cause us not to forget the remembrance of Him through His goodness and glory.”

The papacy of Abba Macarius II was almost identical to that of the 10th Fatimid caliph Al-Aamer bi-Ahkam Allah (1101-1130 AD). The last significant event of the caliphate to be cited by the ‘History of the Patriarchs’ was an attempt at the end of the year 1121 AD by three youths from the east to assassinate the caliph's minister Al-Afdal ibn Shahinshah. That minister was a wise man who treated the Copts well. However, the jealousy of the caliph towards the vast influence of that minister, caused him to conspire on that crime. Two of those youths were cut down by the swords of his bodyguards, but the third managed to strike Al-Afdal with a sharp knife, and he was carried home to die of his wound. The caliph, who participated in his funeral, returned to seize the immense wealth he left behind, which included jewels, gold and silver objects, precious textiles and robes, the furniture that filled his palace and bags filled with four million gold dinars.

It is to be also mentioned that the caliph Al-Aamer, used to often visit the Nahya monastery northwest of the Giza district, to spend several days there, and every time he visited the monastery, he used to grant its monks 1,000 dirhams. He also gave on his first visit to the monastery about thirty acres of land for cultivation. The sum of what he donated to the monastery had reached 30,000 dirhams. Pope Macarius II reposed in the year 1128 AD.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 142] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Macarius II, by Subhi Y. Labib; pp. 1487-8]

Notes: [1] This big historical document began by ‘Severus Ibn al-Muqaffå.’It was continued by others including ‘Michael’, bishop of Tinnis (11th century, writing in Coptic, covering 880 to 1046), ‘Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrig’, deacon of Alexandria and pope ‘Mark III’ of Alexandria (for 1131 to 1167). [2] The Coptic Encyclopedia: Dayr Nahya, by Rene-Georges Coquin & M. Martin; p. 843-4.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius I, the 59th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 6–7
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS I, The 59th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Pastoral Visits

Pope Macarius I (932-952 AD) was born in a village called Shubra-Khit near Alexandria. However, he left his parent's house to enjoy the tranquility of the desert and became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius the Great by the name of Macary. His fame spread as being a monk of great asceticism and contemplation, characteristics that impressed the hearts of all who came to know him. When the 58th Pope Cosmas III (920-932 AD) reposed in the year 932 AD, the whole congregation unanimously chose to ordain him as a patriarch. A delegation of bishops and archons went to the monastery of St.

Macarius the Great, got hold of him, and took him to Alexandria, where he was ordained in the year 932 AD (648 AM).

His Pastoral Visits:

The first step he made was arranging a pastoral trip to visit his people and get to know their conditions on first-hand bases. During that trip, he passed through Shubra-Khit, his home town and went to the house where he spent his childhood. There, he found his mother sitting by the door weaving wool. He greeted her warmly, but she responded to his greeting even without raising her eyes toward him. He said to her: “Peace on you mother. Don't you know who I am? I am your son who left you to spend my life in the monastery as a worshipping monk, but the Divine grace granted me to sit on the seat of St. Mark our beloved preacher.” His mother then raised her eyes and looked at him, with a flood of tears flowing from her eyes. He became very disturbed and asked her what was wrong. Then, she answered him: “Yes. You have indeed got a great honor, yet its responsibility is so enormously serious. When you were a simple monk, you were only responsible for yourself, but now, sitting on the seat of St. Mark the Apostle, you became accountable for the whole people of the See of St. Mark. I could not help crying, supplicating to the Almighty God, who entrusted you with such an enormous task, to cover you with His grace and to help you carry your vast responsibilities.” Abba Macarius was shaken to the core for his mother's remarks, which he was sure of their truthfulness. So, he spent the rest of his life teaching the people and urging them to keep reading the Bible and the teachings of the fathers.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, pp. 20–21
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — The Man of Love

The Man of Love:

St. Macarius discovered that the real concept of seclusion, was not merely the isolation away from people, but rather the sincere desire to unite with God, the Lover of All humanity. So, the real recluse may physically flee away from people, yet he truly loves every person.

The spirit of love and compassion prevailed among his monks as a reflection of his love for them. St. Rufinus told us the story about the bunch of superb grapes which was presented to the saint, which he, in turn, gave to a sick monk, and how that bunch of grapes moved from one monk to another without being touched by any of them.

This saint was known for covering up the sins of others. About him, it was said: “He came to be as a god on earth. For, as the true God protects the world and covers up the sins of men, so St. Macarius covered the sins he saw or heard as if he did not see or hear.”

By his love, he gained many pagans to the faith. About him, it was said that he once was going from the Scetis to Nitria accompanied by his disciple who went ahead of him, and when the disciple encountered a pagan priest who was running, he told the pagan: “Where are you going, O devil?” The pagan priest stopped and beat the disciple so violently that he left him between life and death. Then, when the same priest encountered St Macarius, the saint praised him, saying: “May the Helper accompany you, O active man.” Amazed to hear those words from the saint, the pagan priest was pierced in the heart, and he did not let the saint go until he accepts him as one of his monks.

St. Macarius once went to cut palm leaves along with his disciples, but when they asked him the first day to stay and eat with them, he did. Then when they sought from him the same thing on the next day, he declined their invitation, and said to them: “You need to eat, my children, because you are still with bodies; but now I have no more desire to eat.”

When St. Macarius went to visit Fr. Pachom of Tabansin, the latter asked him: “When we have bad brethren, should we punish them?” St. Macarius answered him, saying: “Punish and judge fairly, those under your control, but never judge those who are from the outside; for it is written: "Do you not judge those who are inside? But those who are outside, God judges" (1 Corin. 5:12-13)”. St. Macarius used to visit daily one of the brethren for four months; in each time, the saint would find him having finished his prayers. The saint was amazed and told the brother: “You are an earthly angel.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius Magnes, p. 11
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS MAGNES

This saint was among the men who lived at the beginning of the 5th century. He was one of the apologists who advocated for Christianity. He probably was the bishop of Magnesia. He was the author of the work ‘Apocriticus,’ which was written in the form of a dialogue between a pagan and a Christian. His work included the lost material generated by Porphyry, who attacked the Christian Faith and the Scriptures in detail. The reproduction of Porphyry's material in the ‘Apocriticus’ preserved for us a form of anti-Christian literature in a fullness that had no parallel.

[E. Ferguson: Encyclopedia of the Early Church]

Notes: [1] [www.tertullian.org/fathers/macarius_apocriticus.htm] ‘The Apocriticus of Macarius Magnes’ By T. W. Crafer, D.D. Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, London, The Macmillan Co, NY,1919. [2] ‘Porphyry,’ was a famous Neoplatonist philosopher in the 3rd century…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius of Alexandria, pp. 14–15
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — The Bunch of Grapes

The Bunch of Grapes:

It happened once that someone brought to St. Macarius a splendid bunch of grapes, which he has not tasted for so long. Yet he overcame his desire and gave the bunch to a sick brother, who, in turn, gave it to another, counting him more in need for it. The bunch of grape kept on being carried from one cell to another until finally it was brought back intact to St. Macarius, who rejoiced in the lovely relationships between the monks. (Some believe that this incident happened to St. Macarius the Great).

His Miracles:

The saint managed to heal a countless number of sick people and those who were possessed by evil spirits. He was granted that power that by merely making the sign of the Holy Cross on those people, they would get healed.

Once, a hyena came to his cell and attempted to drag him by his robe. He followed it to its cave, where it brought its three handicapped cubs to the saint. Amazed at the wisdom of that beast, he prayed, put his hand on the three cubs, healed them, and went his way to his cell. After a while, the hyena came back holding by its mouth a piece of leather hide, which the saint kept using as a floor-mat until the day he reposed.

When it happened that there was no rain in Alexandria for an extended period, he was called over by the pope. Once he reached the papal residence, the rain started pouring and kept on until they sought from the saint to stop it. He then prayed, and it did.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius of Alexandria, p. 12
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — His Asceticism and Worship

His Asceticism and Worship:

He practiced several worship schemes, had great virtues, and trained into exalted asceticism, such as remaining for a whole five days with his mind entranced in heaven.

After spending some time managing schools for the seekers of baptism, he retreated to the desert of Nitra, where he became the Abbot of the monasteries over there. That area used to be called ‘The Place of Cells.’ It happened once that while walking in the wilderness along a strange road, he kept poking sticks in the ground to help him find his way back, and when he tried to go back, he found out that the devil removed those sticks hoping that he would get lost. He spent so much time until he found his way back, in the process, he got so thirsty, but God sent him a cow, to drink from its milk. Then, He helped him find his way back to his cell.

Encouraging the Pachomian Monks to Work:

Later on, St. Macarius heard about the Pachomian monastery in Tabansin near Luxor in Upper Egypt, and how its monks serve the people with the spirit of piety under the guidance of the great Abba Pachom, the father of the Cenobia (Monastic Fellowship). So, he changed his clothes to those of a farmer; then, he set forth to that monastery on foot. It took him about fifteen days to get there. When he arrived, he asked to meet with St. Pachom, whom God hid from him the identity of St. Macarius.

Then, he told St. Pachom: “Father, I beg you to accept me in your monastery, for I might probably become a monk.” Abba Pachom answered him: “I see you are an aged man and your body is frail, you might not be able to practice the harsh piety along with the ascetic brethren or to endure the continuous training they go through. You most probably would tumble and leave us, and then you end up talking against them. You rather go and stay in our hospitality house, remain there, and you will be fed until you decide to return.” So, St. Pachom refused to allow him to live among the monks on the first day, the second day, until the seventh day. During those days, St. Macarius did not eat any food. Then, he went to see St. Pachom, and told him: “Accept me father; and if you find that I do not fast, practice asceticism or do my hand-work; then you may kick me out of your monastery.”

records.question: من هو القديس مارجرجس الكبادوكي؟
records.answer:
القديس مارجرجس الكبادوكي هو شهيد مسيحي من منطقة الكبادوك في آسيا الصغرى، وُلد من أبوين تقيين غنيين ينتميان إلى عائلة شريفة. والده كان أناسطاسيوس واليًا على Melitene في الكبادوك، ووالدته ثاؤبستى من فلسطين ابنة والي اللد. استشهد والده عندما كان مارجرجس في الرابعة عشرة من عمره، فانتقلت والدته مع أولادها إلى ديوسبوليس بفلسطين. نشأ مارجرجس في حياة تقوى وشجاعة، وتميز في الفروسية والقيادة العسكرية، حتى أصبح أميرًا وقائدًا لفرقة كبيرة من الجنود، وكان محبوبًا لشجاعته وخصاله الحميدة. 

عندما أصدر الملك منشورًا بإبادة المسيحيين وهدم الكنائس، أعلن مارجرجس إيمانه بالمسيح وواجه الاضطهاد بشجاعة، حيث باع ممتلكاته ووزعها على الفقراء وحرر العبيد، ومزق منشور الاضطهاد علانية. تعرض لتعذيب شديد دام سبع سنوات، وكان الرب يقيمه بعد موته ثلاث مرات حتى استشهد في المرة الرابعة. صنع معجزات كثيرة، منها شرب السم دون أن يصيبه أذى، وإحياء الموتى، وهزيمة الأصنام بسقوطها وتحطمها عند رشم علامة الصليب. 

حاول الملك إغراؤه بزواجه من ابنته، لكنه رفض، وأرسل له فتاة لإغراءه في السجن، فبشرها بالإيمان فآمنت واستشهدت. كذلك آمنت الملكة ألكسندرة بإيمانه، فاستشهدت هي أيضًا. خشي الملك من ثورة بسبب أعمال الله على يد مارجرجس، فأمر بقطع رأسه في 23 من برمهات، فنال إكليل الشهادة. 

تحمل أيقونته رموزًا تعبر عن الكنيسة (العروس)، والشيطان (التنين)، وقوة الإيمان (الحربة)، وهزيمة الشر (هزيمة التنين). يُعتبر مارجرجس رمزًا للشجاعة والإيمان الراسخ في مواجهة الاضطهاد، وهو من الشهداء المحاربين في الكنيسة القبطية الأرثوذكسية. [2][3][4]
